papers.abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
authors: Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman, Antonio Torralba, Richard Zhang, Eli Shechtman
bullets: Introduces horizontal latent streams that persist across tokens while complementing the vertical depth-wise residual stream.
The latent states condition attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding—not merely sequence mixing.
A 406M-parameter Lattice model reduces validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 versus a parameter-matched Transformer.
Combining the Lattice with other residual enhancements further lowers perplexity to 13.61.
Improvements also hold across several recurrent and hybrid architectures, including variants outperforming baselines with 4× larger native states.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Recurrent backbones: FineWeb-Edu perplexity. Pure and Lattice GDN, Mamba2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba2 hybrid models (∼405M parameters, 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens) across multiple native-state sizes per mixer. Each Lattice model is iso-parameter with its pure counterpart and lowers perplexity at every state size. See Sec. 4.3.

Figure 3: Lattice of Latents vs. prior residual-stream enhancements. On its own, the Lattice lowers the base Transformer’s perplexity more than HC, mHC, or value residuals, and its gains compound with theirs: Lattice + HC + x0 reaches 13.76, the best overall. 400M models, 20B FineWebEdu tokens. See Sec. 4.2 and Appendix Sec. A.3.3.

Figure 6: Deconstructing the Lattice. Here we study a challenging regime where the vertical residual stream width is significantly reduced to 256-dim. LLLM ablations show how the proposed horizontal update enhancements (Sec. 3.2.1 and Sec. 3.2.2) recover most of the lost performance; trace the red bars from left to right. Eval post 10B-token pretraining. Note: 406M Lattice model beats transformer (with perplexity = 15.63, see Fig. 7). See Sec. 4.4 for more details.

Figure 1: Latent Lattice Language Model. Blue arrows denote the vertical latent hℓ t flowing through depth; orange arrows denote the horizontal latents rℓt , one per Lattice layer, flowing through time. The arrow from the top Lattice layer to the bottom layer of the next timestep illustrates the optional top-to-bottom feedback; the other two enhancements (input injection and the depth-wise readout stream) are omitted for clarity. See the project webpage for animations and a comparison with the base Transformer.

Figure 8: Allocating vertical and horizontal latents. Comparing Transformers with LLLMs at different allocations of vertical and horizontal latent widths (dmodel, dr) after 10B-token pretraining. See Sec. 4.4.

Figure 12: Zero-shot downstream accuracy of recurrent backbones. Nine-task average accuracy (%) of pure and Lattice Mamba2, GDN, and no-SWA GDN–Mamba2 hybrid models (∼405M parameters, 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens) across native-state sizes. Lattice boosts pure backbone performance on the nine-task average results. See Sec. 4.3.

Figure 13: Five-shot downstream accuracy of recurrent backbones. Nine-task average accuracy (%) of pure and Lattice Mamba2, GDN, and no-SWA GDN–Mamba2 hybrid models (∼405M parameters, 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens) across native-state sizes. Lattice boosts pure backbone performance on the nine-task average results. See Sec. 4.3.

Figure 14: Lattice of Latents vs. prior residual-stream enhancements: learned value residuals. Complementing Fig. 3, we add learned value residuals (“value”), alone and on top of HC + x0, for Transformers (gray) and LLLMs (red). The Lattice lowers perplexity in every configuration (3.0– 7.0%). FineWeb-Edu validation perplexity, ∼400M models, trained on 20B tokens. See Appendix Sec. A.4.2 for details on the learned value residual.

Figure 9: Ablating top-to-bottom residual-stream flow. Feeding each token’s top-layer state back into the bottom of the network at the next token adds a nonlinear path through the residual stream. Jacobi on vertical applies this feedback to the vertical residual stream, analogous to the concurrent Full-Bandwidth Transformer (Wang et al., 2026); Jacobi on Lattice applies it to the horizontal latents; the last bar applies both. We call it “Jacobi” because the feedback is trained and evaluated with three parallel, teacher-forced Jacobi sweeps (J3; App. A.2.3), at the cost of extra forward passes. Both forms of feedback help, and they compound: 16.94 (Transformer) and 15.52 (single-pass Lattice) fall to 14.92 with feedback on both. FineWeb-Edu val perplexity, trained on 10B tokens.

Figure 5: Horizontal latent update. On top of the Mamba-style affine update, we further introduce input injection, vstream (not shown) and an optional cross-timestep nonlinear flow. See webpage for animations.

Figure 10: Stateless vs. Lattice modulation: is recurrent history needed? We replace the horizontal latent in FiLM modulation with a stateless signal computed from either the token embedding (input-conditioned) or the incoming residual stream (residual-stream-conditioned), at matched ∼406M parameters. Lattice-conditioned modulation, which carries history across timesteps, clearly outperforms both stateless variants. FineWeb-Edu val perplexity, trained on 10B tokens.

Figure 11: Short-Conv vs. Lattice Static and dynamic width-4 short convolutions on q, k, v improve the Transformer; the Lattice matches dynamic convolution with fewer parameters, and the two compose: Lattice + dynamic convolution reaches 14.99. Parameter counts are shown below the bars. FineWeb-Edu val perplexity, trained on 10B tokens. See App. A.3.1.

Figure 7: LLLM vs. larger-depth and larger-width Transformers. Acting as a companion to the residual stream, the Lattice enables better performance than a deeper Transformer or naively increasing the residual-stream width; even 406 M LLLM(945, 256) outperforms both∼600 M alternatives on 10B-token pretraining. See Sec. 4.4.

Figure 4: How the horizontal latent acts. Transformer instantiation: the recurrent lattice latent r̂ℓt conditions the layer’s QKV and MLP computations; when the optional horizontal decoding head is enabled, the topmost horizontal latent also contributes to output decoding (not shown).

The performance trends are similar to the 20b token results in Tab. 1.
Table 6: Training hyperparameters shared across all runs unless otherwise noted.

Table 2: Native-memory geometry and query alignment in GDN. Each cell reports pure → Lattice, at matched native-state size and approximately matched parameters. Lower ranks mean the memory is concentrated in fewer directions; higher G1 means queries align more with the leading memory direction. The Lattice improves all three metrics at every state size. Values are averaged over all 22 layers and all heads, 1024 FineWeb-Edu sequences of 2048 tokens, and 15 positions per sequence just after a state update. See Sec. 4.4.
Table 5: Finetuned mathematical-reasoning Acc.

Table 7: Recurrent-backbone geometries and widths. Native state per mixer and residual width of the pure and input-injection+vstream Lattice models (all ∼405M parameters). Hybrid GDN and Mamba2 mixers use the GDN and Mamba2 geometries of the same column. Triadic GDN pairs use joint geometries (H,Edk, dv) = (16, 16, 64), (16, 32, 64), (16, 64, 64), (32, 64, 32), (16, 128, 64), and (8, 256, 128).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel LLM architecture axis (per-layer persistent latent streams) with broad architectural relevance.
papers.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
papers.tldr: Lattice of Latents improves language-model perplexity by adding persistent per-layer recurrent latent states that directly support computation alongside the standard residual stream.

papers.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
authors: Ruixi Yu, Dairu Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, Zekai Li, Zhuo Cao, Luyang Niu, Yingsheng Zhang, Sikai Liang, Ke Fan, He Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses whether frontier-scale VLM representations can strengthen vision-language-action policies.
Connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT and compares backbones from 2B to 552B under shared training.
With 10 demonstrations, the largest backbone reaches 87.8% versus 85.6% for a 2B model trained with 50 demonstrations.
LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, exceeding the maximum 31.3% reported for smaller backbones.
Real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains focused on contact-sensitive alignment.

Top right: the VLM encodes images and the instruction, and the action DiT uses these features and robot state to generate an action chunk. Middle: task success by backbone size. Base is the best dense backbone at or below each size. Bottom: inference latency on RoboCasa, sample efficiency on LIBERO Goal, and success on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO.

Figure 2 ScaleVLA architecture. The VLM encodes the images and the instruction, and the action head reads the output of its causal encoder. The action DiT alternates cross-attention and self-attention and generates an action chunk in four flow steps.

Figure 4 Backbone size and inference latency. Left: total parameters in each source model. Right: median time per action chunk on RoboCasa, with backbone and action head times shown separately. ScaleVLA uses four H200 GPUs; the other backbones use one each.

Figure 3 Simulation tasks. LIBERO tests tabletop manipulation, LIBERO-PRO perturbs the objects and scenes of LIBERO, RoboCasa tests kitchen tasks in out-of-distribution scenes, and DexJoCo tests five tasks that require coordinating two dexterous hands.

Figure 5 Plug In Charger on a real robot. Left: all three policies grasp and hand over the charger from in-domain layouts. ScaleVLA aligns and inserts the plug; the other two policies reach the socket but fail to insert the plug. Right: success rates in the in-domain and OOD settings.
Table 1 VLM backbones used in the experiments. Sizes refer to the total parameter count of each source model. MoE denotes a mixture of experts.

Table 2 LIBERO success rates (%). The first three rows report published results. Our policies train on each suite’s full demonstration set. The last column averages the four suites. Bold marks the highest success rate in each column.
Table 6 RoboCasa inference latency. Times are medians per action chunk on H200 GPUs. Bold marks the lowest latency in each timing column.
Table 3 LIBERO-PRO success rates (%). We test our LIBERO policies from table 2 under environment (Env.) and object (Obj.) perturbations without retraining [100].
Table 4 RoboCasa success rates (%). Gen-30 and Gen100 use 30 and 100 generated demonstrations per task, respectively. We test in out-of-distribution kitchens.
Table 5 DexJoCo success rates (%). We train one policy on all five bimanual tasks for each backbone and randomization setting (object or full). Bold marks the best of our backbones.

Table 8 Real-robot success rates and timing. Successes are counted over ten in-domain and fifteen out-of-distribution (OOD) trials. Insertion and completion times are medians over successful in-domain trials. Latency is the median round trip per action chunk at the robot client. Bold marks the most successes or the shortest time.

papers.selection_reason: Scaling VLA policies with frontier VLM backbones; directly targets vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
papers.tldr: ScaleVLA shows that connecting a 552B frontier VLM to an action diffusion transformer substantially improves robot policy sample efficiency, generalization, and precise manipulation while maintaining 216 ms median action latency.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/
authors: Rohit Gandikota, Arnab Sen Sharma, Adam Belfki, David Bau
bullets: Binding heads link text tokens and previous answers to their corresponding image regions.
A progress signal acts as a cursor marking how far through the image’s regions the model has written.
A selection step chooses the nearest unwritten region or stops generation.
Gaze heads execute the selected pointer, while language components convert the retrieved visual concept into an answer word.
Causal patching in Qwen3-VL models supports the mechanism across formats, photographs, languages, and model sizes from 2B to 32B parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Task setup: We provide an image strip with each panel containing a shape and a letter. We ask the model to retrieve the label of the panel that contains the queried shape. (b) The mechanism, with tokens across and layers down. The model solves the task early, at the shape token star, well before it answers: (1) binding heads match the request against the image and resolve a pointer to the matching panel. (2) Relay heads carry that pointer to the “:” token, where the answer has to be produced, and (3) gaze heads execute it to retrieve the letter from that panel. (4) Once T is written, binding heads bind it to its panel, and the model calculates its progress and (5) selects what answer to mention next (by repeating steps 3-5) or to stop if none is left.

Figure 3: (a) Relay heads transfer the pointer from the shape token to the colon. When each relay head may read only one token at a time, the pointer is transferred mostly when the relay heads at the colon token read the shape token. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on 500 heldout pairs. (b) A copied comma state skips a written panel at layers 20-21. When patching the source’s comma-token residual into the target’s colon-token residual, one layer at a time: at layer 20 the target skips to its next candidate, T, in 91.0± 2.4% of pairs, and in 70.0± 3.9% at layer 21. From layers 22-28 it takes the source’s next panel pointer, W, and from layer 30 the source’s letter, A. (c) A copied comma state says where the list goes on. With a more targeted setup, we find at layers 20 and 21 the model answers with the first candidate “after panel 4”, W, in 98.4± 1.1% and 97.6± 1.3% of pairs. The shaded band marks layers 20-21.

Figure 6: Only the shape token and the colon token change the answer. Each cell patches the source’s residual vector into the target at one text token and one layer, and counts the cases that answer with one outcome letter of Section 3. (a) T, the target’s own letter. (b) D, the source’s letter. (c) K, the target’s letter at the source’s panel. (d) P, the target’s letter inside the source’s shape. (e) R, the target’s letter where the source’s layout puts the asked shape. The shape token is shown in bold. The request, P, sits at the shape token up to layer 19. The pointer, K, sits at the shape token around layer 20 and at the colon token from layers 23-29. The source’s letter, D, comes through the colon token from layer 30. All panels use the 500 held-out pairs.

Figure 8: The selection rule fixes the number of heads. We patch the top K heads of each singlehead search together on the 100 validation pairs. These are the queries, image keys, and outputs at the shape token, and the values that the relay heads read at the colon token. (a) Cases whose next token is the letter the patch predicts. (b) Cases in which the published Gaze Heads look at the matching panel. The dotted line marks the 80% rule. The queries and the image keys first pass it on both readouts at 8 heads, with 83.5% and 80.5% for the queries and 85.0% and 84.5% for the image keys. The outputs and the relay values first pass it at 16 heads.

Figure 25: On comic images, the colon token holds the pointer at the same layers. We replace the target’s residual vector at the colon token with the source’s at one layer, as in Figure 2a, on cases with comic drawings under the markers and the longer prompt. (a) The target’s next letter. The pointer, K, peaks at 80.2% at layer 24, and the source’s letter, D, comes through from layer 30. (b) The panel the published Gaze Heads look at, with no head patched. At layer 23 they look at the source’s panel in 45.0% of cases.

Figure 23: Zeroing the language heads, against setting them. We patch the top K heads of the language search at every generated token, in runs asked in German, French, or Chinese on the heldout images. Solid purple: we zero the heads and the answer turns English. Dash-dot gray: zeroing breaks the output. Dotted light gray: we zero random heads. Dashed purple: we set the heads to their English average and the answer turns English, run up to 64 heads. (a) Colored shapes: 16 heads set to English give English in 100.0% of runs, and 16 heads zeroed give it in 62.7± 2.4%. (b) Objects: 100.0% and 23.7%.

Figure 10: Relay heads carry the pointer from the shape token to the colon token. (a) At the colon token, we let one attention head at a time read the source’s values from the shape token and the tokens after it, while its own query and keys stay unchanged. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on the 200 discovery pairs. The 16 relay heads that the search selects are outlined, in layers 19-35. (b) Each relay head alone reads the source’s value at one text token only, while its query, keys, and attention stay unchanged. Each cell is the mean gain of K over T on the held-out pairs. When all 16 relay heads read only the shape token, the target answers K in 47.3± 3.1% of cases, and when they read only the “?”, it does so in 9.9± 1.8%.

Figure 24: Choosing the language with no source. We set the top 16 language heads to their average output under the target language (columns), in runs asked in the question language (rows). Each cell is the percent of held-out images whose answer names its own concept in the target language. (a) Colored shapes. (b) Objects. Leaving English is the hardest direction.

Figure 19: Finding the gaze heads, and how they compare with the published ranking. (a) The number of heads shared in the top K of three rankings of all 1,152 heads: our query-patch search, the Gaze score measured on our task, and the published Gaze Heads ranking. From K = 16 to 128, our ranking shares more heads with the Gaze score on this task than with the published ranking, 20 against 10 in the top 32. (b) The top K heads of the two searches, patched together at the colon token on the 100 validation pairs. Patching their queries moves the answer to the source’s panel in 68.5% of cases at K = 8, and in 73.5% to 76.5% from 16 to 256 heads. This stays below the 80% rule, so the rule takes its best size, 32 heads. Blocking up to 256 heads from the image loses the target’s answer in at most 2.5%.

Figure 22: MLPs performing translation. (a) The language shift when we patch the output of one MLP at the colon token from the source, by target language, averaged over the three source languages. (b) The top k MLPs patched together, ranked over all languages and both questions, grouped by source language and averaged over its three targets. The top 4 MLPs are layers 32-35, and the top 8 are layers 28-35.

Figure 12: The state the comma token holds before the cursor forms. We copy the residual of a comma token, at one layer, into a colon token that has written nothing, and read the target’s next letter. (a) The same image, with r1 written (top) and with r2 written (bottom), on the held-out targets. With r1 written the target answers r2 in 65.8% of cases at layer 14 and 96.4% at layer 21. With r2 written it also answers r2, in 75.1% at layer 19, and answers r3 from layer 23 (82.4%). Up to layer 19 the copied state says only that one letter was written. From layer 20 the target starts after the written panel. (b) The skip experiment of Section 5.1, split by the shared first matching panel. Averaged over layers 0-17, the target skips it in 80.6± 4.5% of pairs when the shared panel is panel 1, 8.6± 3.3% for panel 2, and 4.7± 2.4% for panel 3. At layer 20 it skips in 99.5± 0.8%, 97.5± 2.2%, and 74.2± 7.1%, and at layer 21 in 53.2± 6.7%, 72.0± 7.4%, and 88.4± 5.1%. (c) The standard source, which has written the target’s first letter at r2 and has its own next matching panel at r4. The target answers with a count, r2, at layer 19 (86.5%), with the panel after the written one, r3, at layer 20 (68.4%), with the source’s own choice, r4, at layer 24 (87.6%), and with the source’s letter from layer 30. The shaded band marks layers 20-21.

Figure 27: The same heads work on images with no panels. Every bar uses the head sets selected on panel images, with no new search. (a) The single-answer tests, on the held-out pairs with panels (gray) and with no panels (blue). (b) The list tests, on the held-out list cases whose unedited runs are right. Random heads from the same layers move the answer in 0.0% of single-answer and list cases.

Figure 21: Language heads on the color question. (a) The language shift of each head, averaged over the 12 ordered pairs of English, French, Chinese, and German. We patch the output of one head at the colon token from the source, and measure how far the target’s color words move from its own language toward the source’s (log units). The top 16 heads are outlined. (b) The top k heads patched together, by target language. We add heads in the order of a ranking over all languages. (c) The Spearman correlation between the head rankings of each target language, over all 1,152 heads.

Figure 17: What the comma token’s residual holds, with no patch. (a) We train ridge probes on the residual of the last comma token on half of the held-out pairs of the list task, and read them on the other half. The written panel is named in 94.0± 2.8% of pairs at layer 12 and 100.0± 0.0% at 18. The probes read whether each panel is a matching panel with 95.9± 1.0% accuracy at layer 17 and 99.3± 0.5% at 21, from a chance level of two thirds. The next panel is named in 98.0± 1.8% at layer 18 and 100.0± 0.0% at 20. (b) Image attention of the binding heads at the comma token, by layer. At layer 21 they put 51.6± 1.9% of it on the next panel and 3.9± 0.2% on the written panel. (c) Image attention of the gaze heads at the comma token, by layer. At layer 20 they give 22.3± 0.6% to the next panel and 23.0± 0.7% to each other matching panel, and by layer 23 they give 61.9± 1.4% and 7.4± 0.4%.

Figure 4: (a) Gaze heads exist after layer 20. Pointer logit gain when one head’s query at the colon token is patched. The 32 gaze heads are outlined, all in layers 19-34. (b) Our gaze heads vs. the published Gaze Heads (Gandikota & Bau, 2026). Solid lines replace the queries and count the target’s letter at the source’s panel, K. Dashed lines let the heads read the source’s image values and count the source’s letter at the target’s panel, C. The vertical lines mark our 32 heads and the top 100 published heads. Our 32 heads beat the top 100 published heads, and random heads stay at or below 2.1± 1.0%. (c) Language heads set the language. Scoring the language change of a word when patching attention head outputs from a source in a different language. The 16 language heads are outlined, in layers 19-35. The color scale is capped at 1.6; L24H27 scores 5.03.

Figure 2: The pointer is resolved at the shape token by a few attention heads. (a) Patching the source’s residual at the colon token into the target, one layer at a time. Up to layer 20 the target keeps its own letter T; from layers 23-29 it answers K, the target’s letter at the source’s answer location, so the colon token holds a pointer to a panel; from layer 30 it copies the source’s letter D. (b) The same patch at every text token and every layer, tracking the logit of K: the pointer appears only at the shape token, around layer 20, and at the colon token, from layer 23. (c) The output of one attention head at the shape token replaced with the source’s, for every head; each cell is the mean gain of K over T, and the 16 heads selected by the search sit in layers 15-21 and are outlined.

Figure 5: At the shape token, the request comes before the pointer. We patch the shape token’s residual vector one layer at a time. The patch moves the request, P, up to layer 15, and the pointer, K, at layer 20, in 36.1± 3.2% of the held-out cases.

Figure 7: Queries carry the request, keys carry the layout, and outputs carry the pointer. Each cell patches one attention head at the shape token from the source on its own, averaged over the 200 discovery pairs. (a) We patch the head’s query and score the gain of P, the target’s letter inside the source’s shape, over T. (b) We let the head read the source’s image keys and score the gain of R, the target’s letter where the source’s layout puts the asked shape, over T. (c) We patch the head’s output and score the gain of K, the pointer, over T. The heads that each search selects are outlined: 8 query heads, 8 key heads, and 16 output heads, all in layers 15-21. The 16 output heads are the binding heads of the main text.

Figure 13: The heads that set the cursor at the answer token sit in the layers of the binding heads. We patch one head at a time at the answer token of the list task. In (a), the head reads the source’s image keys, and in (b), we replace the head’s output with the source’s. Each cell is the mean gain of the cursor’s letter on the discovery pairs. In (c), we set the head’s output to zero in the target’s own run. Each cell is the mean gain toward repeating the written letter on the discovery pairs. The 16 binding heads are outlined.
Figure 26: Images with no panels. Left: a single-answer image. Right: a list image in which the asked shape, a star, sits at four places.

Figure 20: Without the late MLPs, German and French answers fall back to English. We set the outputs of the top MLPs at the colon token to their mean over prompts in all languages, with no source. papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
authors: Blas Eugenio Vicco Zarate, Miguel Hern\'an Vicco
bullets: Targets continual RL under changing dynamics while preserving prior performance.
Evolves small neural-network policies without gradients and indexes them by detected dynamic regime.
Uses Bayesian policy reuse to retrieve archived specialists, with failure-driven search for new ones.
In 30-replicate CartPole ablations, the full architecture achieved 83.2% mean success across five test environments and showed the most consistent retention among variants learning harder tasks.
Adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and earned lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah; the evidence does not isolate gradient-free optimization or establish overall superiority.

papers.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
papers.tldr: ENA reduces forgetting in changing reinforcement-learning environments by archiving and reusing evolutionarily discovered specialist policies, though adaptation and returns remain below strong baselines in some settings.

papers.abstract: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colon\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $\Sigma$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
authors: Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser
bullets: Learns next-token generators from chain-of-thought demonstrations using bootstrap sampling and majority voting.
For binary tokens, achieves optimal sample complexity O((d_VC + log(1/δ))/ε), independent of demonstration length T.
For finite token sets, obtains a near-optimal bound using the Graph dimension, with only a log|Σ| factor gap.
Uses O(log(T/δ)) generators in the ensemble.
The ensemble can be distilled into a single generator using n log(nT) unlabeled prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of learning autoregressive next-token generators from CoT demonstrations; relevant to LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
papers.tldr: Bagging enables optimal, CoT-length-independent learning of autoregressive generators, with compact ensembles that can also be distilled into one generator.

papers.abstract: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.
authors: Steve Rhyner, Yubo Gao, Stefan de Lasa, Sankeerth Durvasula, Nandita Vijaykumar
bullets: Addresses MXFP4 nondeterminism, which complicates debugging, audits, and consistency between training and inference.
Collects quantization statistics to certify exact native matrix-multiplication results and applies exact kernels to uncertified or difficult cases.
Preserves quantization blocks and merges partial sums without rounding across matrix multiplication, attention, and weight-gradient computations.
In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, training states matched bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across multiple parallelism layouts.
Adds 11.8–60.5% training-step latency over non-exact MXFP4, while achieving up to 1.24× speedup over BF16 and 1.70× over deterministic BF16.

papers.abstract: Structure-level wildfire vulnerability assessment is critical for reducing losses in wildland-urban interface communities, yet existing methods often fail to combine parcel-scale ignition pathways with community-scale geographic coverage. This study introduces Wildfire-SSR (Satellite and Street-view for wildfire Risk), a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that integrates macro-scale satellite context with micro-scale street-view evidence. A Vision-Language Model extracts wildfire-relevant building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and converts them into structured semantic text. These features are spatially aligned with satellite imagery through a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder, while a frozen satellite-pretrained DINOv3 encoder captures overhead visual context. Alternative geolocation embedding strategies are evaluated to anchor text-derived features within each satellite patch. The framework is tested on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, using wildfire risk labels derived from relative post-event damage patterns to better represent inherent structural vulnerability. Rotary Positional Embedding provides the strongest spatial grounding, achieving a building localization F1 score of 0.6735 and a harmonic mean F1 score of 0.2476 for five-class pixel-level risk classification, outperforming unimodal baselines and an unanchored multimodal configuration. The model also shows a conservative bias in higher-risk classes, reducing severe-risk underestimation, and completes end-to-end assessment of the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU. Wildfire-SSR reframes cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment and provides a scalable tool for mitigation prioritization, resilience planning, and insurance-oriented wildfire risk assessment.
authors: Yu-Hsuan Ho, Yiming Xiao, Hao-En Lai, Ali Mostafavi, Samuel D. Brody
bullets: Addresses the gap between parcel-scale ignition pathways and community-scale geographic coverage in wildfire vulnerability assessment.
A Vision-Language Model extracts building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and aligns them with satellite context using cross-attention and geolocation embeddings.
Evaluated on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, with labels based on relative post-fire damage patterns.
Rotary Positional Embedding performed best, reaching a building-localization F1 of 0.6735 and a five-class pixel-level risk harmonic mean F1 of 0.2476.
The model reduced severe-risk underestimation and assessed the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU, supporting mitigation and resilience planning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed geolocation-aware multimodal framework for structure-level wildfire risk assessment. The pipeline addresses the limitations of isolated unimodal approaches by integrating macro-scale satellite imagery with micro-scale street-view data. A Vision-Language Model first extracts semantic building vulnerabilities from street-level images into structured text descriptions. To bridge the spatial disconnect between modalities, the geographical coordinates of the street-view captures are mapped to local relative coordinates and injected into CLIPencoded text embeddings. A decoupled cross-attention multimodal fusion decoder then aligns these geolocation-aware text features with overhead visual features extracted via DINOv3. The proposed model processes these fused representations into pixel-wise risk labels, which are then transformed into a detailed, actionable community-scale wildfire risk map.

Figure 2: Overview of the model architecture. Ground-level street-view images are first processed by a Vision-Language Model to extract structured semantic attributes, which are combined with their geographic coordinates to form spatially anchored text embeddings. A multimodal fusion decoder then integrates these location-aware micro-level features with macro-level visual features extracted from pre-event satellite imagery via a frozen satellite-pretrained vision encoder to generate precise, structure-level wildfire risk maps.

Figure 6: Pixel-level wildfire vulnerability predictions from the proposed RoPE-based multimodal framework (right) compared against the ground-truth building-level risk labels (left) for representative tiles in the Eaton and Palisades study areas. Colors denote the five ordinal risk classes from minimal to extreme; the comparison illustrates the model’s capacity to capture broad spatial patterns of structural vulnerability while highlighting residual confusion between adjacent low and moderate tiers.

Figure 5: Study area: final perimeters of the 2025 Eaton and Palisades wildfires in the Los Angeles region, showing the wildland-urban interface neighborhoods used for structure-level vulnerability evaluation. Perimeter data are sourced from the City of Los Angeles GeoHub (City of Los Angeles, 2025c).

Figure 4: Schematic representation of the geometric localization algorithm. To preserve view-angle perspective, orthogonal normal vectors (ns) are cast from the street-view camera’s heading direction. The intersection of these street vectors with the heading vectors (nb) originating from adjacent building centroids determines the precise spatial anchor point on the observed facade.

Figure 3: Structure of the two-way cross-attention block utilizing a decoupled attention mechanism. Geolocation embeddings (GEs) are injected specifically into the queries (Q) and keys (K) to facilitate spatial routing, while values (V ) remain purely semantic to preserve micro-level building attributes. The block consists of three sequential steps: sparse text self-attention to capture geometric dependencies between structural, sparse-to-dense cross-attention to update textual context with overhead visual data, and dense-to-sparse cross-attention to infuse the macro-level visual map with ground-sourced semantic details.
Table 3: Ablation study results on input modalities and geolocation embeddings. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 4: Results of the label reconstruction diagnostic experiment utilizing explicit risk levels as text input. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 1: Performance comparison of geolocation embedding strategies. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.
Table 2: Quantitative evaluation of building wildfire risk classification across pixel-level and building-level aggregated metrics. Best results are bolded, second-best are underlined.

papers.tldr: Wildfire-SSR combines satellite imagery, street-view semantics, and geolocation-aware fusion to assess structure-level wildfire risk across communities.

papers.abstract: Long video generation should keep the subject and background consistent while supporting rich, natural motion. However, autoregressive models are often distilled with distribution matching distillation (DMD) over short windows, which does not train them to keep this consistency over long ranges. As a result, the subject and background can drift over time. Methods that manage the key-value (KV) cache retain or retrieve history to reduce drift. Yet this history may itself have drifted. We propose Reference Forcing, which uses the initial frames as an appearance reference. We first build a teacher that uses attention masks to force each region of a new frame to attend to the same region in the initial frames. The teacher finds these regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models. We then distill this behavior into a separate attention path of the student, which needs no external models at inference. We further introduce value correction, which corrects drifted values in the KV cache toward the matching values of drift-free initial frames. Experiments show that Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency among long-video methods on different base models, and its advantage grows with video length. Ablations show both components are needed to gain consistency without losing motion. More visualizations and code are available at https://zhaosheng-thu.github.io/reference-force/
authors: Sheng Zhao, Haitian Zheng, Weikai Lin, Junjie Zhao, Yuhao Zhu
bullets: Addresses consistency loss caused by training autoregressive video models on short windows.
Uses segmentation-guided attention masks to make new-frame regions attend to matching regions in the initial frames.
Distills this reference-guided behavior into a separate student attention path that requires no external models at inference.
Applies value correction to move drifted KV-cache values toward corresponding values from the initial frames.
Reports state-of-the-art subject and background consistency across different base models, with larger gains for longer videos; both components preserve motion.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Reference Forcing. (a) Each chunk Xn is generated from the first chunk X0, the recent window, and noisy tokens, with the anchor path of (b) and the value correction of (c). papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.
authors: Kanchana Ranasinghe, Honglu Zhou, Dominick Reilly, Le Xue, Shusheng Yang, Juan Carlos Niebles, Silvio Savarese, Ran Xu
bullets: Introduces BLIP-Live-780K, a human-annotated dataset covering proactive response content and timing.
Proposes PAUC-F, which balances response timeliness with firing precision.
Studies model-agnostic inference and training pipelines for making offline VLMs proactive in streaming video.
Finds that sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured outputs consistently work best.
The BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieves state-of-the-art results on four proactive streaming benchmarks, with reported gains of up to 44% over baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.
authors: Zhaoning Zhang
bullets: The failure occurs at two stages: correspondence is present in visual tokens but is not reliably read out, and cross-image attention in a small set of heads is misrouted.
Across Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, and Gemma-3, answer-position probes outperform calibrated outputs by 15–25 points, while steering does not reliably change answers.
Redistributing attention in 16–32 identified heads causes 15–32-point accuracy drops, far larger than changes from random or attention-matched heads.
Training only the query and key projections of these heads improves SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points for Qwen3-VL-8B and 25.1 points for InternVL3.5-8B, with transfer to HPatches and BLINK.

papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
authors: Minjae Kwon, Amir Moeini, Shangtong Zhang, Lu Feng
bullets: Safe ICRL requires fixed-parameter policies to learn unseen constrained tasks from interaction histories while respecting a cost budget.
The revised Safe AD teacher explores according to remaining budget, then switches to an expert policy after observing reward or cost.
Training with dynamic budgets increases the diversity of return-and-budget histories and improves return while reducing cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah.
A-Lag reweights actions using predicted cost and an adaptive Lagrange multiplier updated from observed costs.
Across all five environments, A-Lag lowers mean episode cost but also lowers mean final return in four.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models trained on dynamic-budget histories (Dynamic) and on fixed-budget histories (Fixed), on the test tasks. papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
authors: Mart\'in Palos, Fernando Garc\'ia
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
authors: Shaohao Rui, Chaoyang Zhang, Xiaofeng Mao, Weijie Ma
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses under complex hand–object dynamics and real-time constraints.

On HandBench, achieves an FVD of 181.67 and MANO Dice scores of 93.02 for the full-sequence model and 92.49 for the three-step model.
At 540p on a single H200, reaches 18.03 FPS with 741 ms latency and 34.89 GB peak GPU memory; datasets, weights, and code will be released.

papers.abstract: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.

papers.abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.
authors: Zijian Zhao, Davide Di Monda, Domenico Ciuonzo, Yipeng Wang, Antonio Pescap\`e
bullets: Addresses the vulnerability of FSCIL-based NIDSs to mislabeled data during adaptation to emerging attacks.
Detects and removes mislabeled biflows, then samples calibrated synthetic features from clean data to restore class representation.
Uses an RFS teacher–student framework with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic-regression classifiers.
Evaluated on three intrusion-detection datasets, NAFN improves new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines by up to 52% and remains effective under 50% label noise.
Shows robustness in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings, with time-efficient adaptation.

papers.abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $\delta$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
authors: Jiarui Gan, Debmalya Mandal
bullets: Standard CMDP guarantees from the initial state may not ensure feasibility throughout execution.
S-CMDPs constrain the expected discounted cost of every continuation based on the current state.

A value-set iteration framework constructs an implicitly represented history-dependent policy.
The algorithm achieves ε-near-optimal reward with at most δ violation of each subprocess constraint, while computing actions in polynomial time per history.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

bullets: Addresses inefficient model initialization in model-based reinforcement learning.
Decomposes stacked Jacobian samples to recover neural-network weights and flexible nonlinearities.
Uses the recovered parameters to initialize a feedforward dynamics model.
On several benchmark environments, it outperforms random initialization and value training, and matches or exceeds Sobolev training.

papers.abstract: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.
authors: Bryan A. Plummer, Shan Lu, Keval Doshi, Noranart Vesdapunt, Wei Wang, Jim Thomas, Kah Kuen Fu
bullets: Addresses the gap between reduced FLOPs and real-world latency caused by replacing one large matrix with multiple smaller matrices.
Exploits twin layers with the same input to compute their shared forward pass only once.
Combines Factor Component Balancing and Block Contribution Balancing to represent layers more evenly and account for downstream effects.
Uses overparameterized factors during training to improve task performance without increasing test-time resources.
Across six models and nine benchmarks, achieves 2–6% gains without expensive finetuning and 1–3.5% gains with it at comparable computational cost.

papers.abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.
authors: Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Shuaishuai Cao, Di Wang, Haonan Guo
bullets: UHR scenes create a trade-off between global context, which hides small details, and high-resolution crops, which consume substantial context.
The study encodes high-resolution crops into 64 latent memory tokens for frozen multimodal backbones, isolating evidence retention from region selection.
Across two Qwen-VL generations, memory compresses crop tokens by 7.6–9.9× and improves accuracy by 2.5–4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image.
Replacing memory with another image or region lowers accuracy by 5.8–7.4 points, showing predictions depend on the encoded local evidence.
Results are consistent on XLRS-Bench and indicate that evidence availability governs the usefulness of compact visual latents.

papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of "cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.
authors: Hao Sun, Tao Hu, Shixiong Kai, Siyuan Xu, Wenqian Zhao, Mingxuan Yuan, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: Existing CLIP-based CIL methods rely mainly on global [CLS] and [EOS] features, overlooking local visual and textual information.
PACE selects the top-k important visual patches and textual tokens using global representations.
A cross-modal fusion module uses local text to refine visual features and local visual features to enhance text semantics.
A projection-based update strategy protects previously learned parameter directions during adaptation to new tasks.
Experiments on multiple CIL benchmarks show significant gains over state-of-the-art methods; specific datasets and numerical results are not reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

papers.abstract: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.
authors: Hao Wang, Ting Huang
bullets: The study compares five shipped harnesses across 18 tasks, four 0.75B–4.7B local models, and a 35.5B anchor using one deterministic checker.
Mingbird achieves the highest mean score at every tested model size, though only two of four pre-registered contrasts remain significant after Holm correction.
Harness effects mainly reflect whether runs leave artifacts on disk: 127 of 357 usable cells produced none, including 85 that exited normally.
Disabling executable completion checks has little consistent effect, while removing one repeat-blocking rule sharply reduces performance at 0.75B and causes artifact-free tasks.
Four model-size rungs are insufficient to determine whether harness effects systematically grow or shrink with scale.

papers.abstract: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged
authors: Zi Wang, Mahima Pushkarna
bullets: Creative AI can anchor users to generated artifacts, shifting them from active authors to reactive editors.
The proposed approach uses pre-generation belief controls so users can inspect, revise, and steer the AI’s interpretation first.
PaCC surfaces assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes during early ideation and prototyping.
A small exploratory study found directionally positive perceived agency and process control compared with familiar prompt-based tools.
Participants valued surfaced assumptions for revealing overlooked details, but reported divergent feelings about ownership and authorship.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC) interface for shaping AI’s beliefs before generation (§2). (A) Prompt entry with optional reference images. Creators control AI proactiveness (A1) across three tiers: literal extraction (low), reasonable scene inference (medium; e.g., adding a “party table” to the cat party), or creative liberty (high; e.g., a “disco ball”). Modality tabs switch between Image, Story, and Video (A2). (B) Belief Graph: An editable visualization of explicit entities (solid borders), AI-inferred entities (dashed borders), and relationship edges (e.g., “hosting”). (C1–C2) Clarification Questions: Offers 3–5 selectable options per question so creators can resolve ambiguity and guide the AI’s interpretation; clicking “You Decide” delegates a specific choice to the AI. (D1–D2) Entity Attribute Editing: Adjusts properties of individual nodes. (E1–E2) Media Attributes: Controls global scene aesthetics (e.g., lighting, style, pacing). By surfacing and aligning assumptions and possibilities prior to media generation, PaCC establishes the human intent as the anchor.
