papers.abstract: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.
authors: Yancheng Long, Xuanyu Zheng, Wei Chen, Luoyuan Zhang, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of finding and integrating fine-grained evidence in long, dense videos without overloading the planner’s context.
Uses a training-free agent framework where the planner adaptively controls inspection location, resolution, and sampling density.
Perception sub-agents independently analyze native audio-video and return compact evidence for iterative search and verification.
Achieves 88.6% on full LVBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash, outperforming same-backbone baselines while using 44% of the measured API cost of built-in agentic processing.
A Kimi K3 evaluation improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points; scope is limited to the reported benchmarks and backbones.

papers.abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuanchang Ye, Jiahao Yuan, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Weijun Xie, Ye Wei, Kaidi Xu
bullets: LEC can fail to control population selection-conditioned error because its threshold-dependent loss is non-monotonic and threshold selection is unstable.
SC-LEC compensates for this risk-transfer gap using the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference.
Two finite-sample certificates support threshold expansion: one based on rank crossings and another exploiting threshold-expansion structure.
Given a valid population anchor margin, the certificates ensure marginal SCER control; independent margin certification yields a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee.
Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show retention gains beyond the certified anchor, but conservative behavior when margins are small.

papers.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
authors: Shuyi Ouyang, Xiaojun Tang, Zijian Zou, Xintong Zhang, Mingli Song, Guannan Zhang, Hongwei Xue
bullets: Covers 211 creation and modification tasks across presentations, static graphics, animations/videos, and web interfaces.
Separately measures Task Fulfillment and Artifact Performance across content, organization, visuals, and delivery.

Evaluates nine model-harness configurations, whose overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52.
Artifact Performance explains 73.4% of the score gap between the highest- and lowest-performing configurations.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.
authors: Jinzhao Li, Yuan Xu, Jinxuan Wu, Yukun Wang, Yijia Lei, Hanyu Ji, Yinuo Chen, Zining Huang, Chi Zhang, Hang Ye, Yiwu Zhong, Honglei Yan, Panwang Pan, Yizhou Wang, Yin Li, Miao Liu
bullets: Targets the limitation of streaming video models that process user requests in isolation.
Supports proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction.
Uses contrastive supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA).
Introduces ALIVE-SFT-288K, ALIVE-RL-3K, and FSI-Bench for training and evaluating interactive behavior.
Reports the highest overall scores among compared models across four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench.

papers.abstract: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.
authors: Yucheng Xie, Fu Feng, Jing Wang, Xin Geng, Yong Rui
bullets: Addresses parameter overhead and fixed component assignments in existing decomposable pre-training methods.
Builds Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels while preserving the model’s native computational structure.
Uses calibrated condition-wise routing with shared priors, conditional adjustments, and complementary regularization.
Learns specialization and sharing rather than imposing predefined component assignments.
Reports better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines and stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv). (a) Paired FFN input columns and output rows form native Knowledge Units without matrix factorization. (b) Calibrated condition-specific routing combines a shared prior p with conditional logit adjustments qc to determine unit contributions. (c) Specificity-regularized optimization promotes polarized shared gates, diverse conditional deviations, and appropriate deviation magnitudes, enabling shared and specialized contributions to emerge during pre-training.

Figure 1. (a) Traditional knowledge diversion constructs SVDbased units with predefined shared–specific assignments, improving downstream adaptation (FDD) at the cost of degraded indistribution generation (FID) and substantial parameter overhead. (b) SGKDiv constructs units from paired native FFN channels and learns their contributions through calibrated routing, improving both generation and adaptation with modest parameter overhead.

Figure 5. Generation performance under varying classifier-free guidance (CFG). (a) FID and IS across CFG scales. (b) Precision–Recall trade-offs across the same CFG scales. SGKDiv improves quality over a broad guidance range while balancing fidelity and coverage.

papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets quality degradation beyond the training horizon, self-generated history, and increasing KV-cache costs.
WinTF builds a multi-step base using window-wise denoising with local bidirectional attention and causal access to prior history.
HieraKV reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality by adapting retained history across layers.
CuLT-DMD enables efficient long-rollout distillation by aggregating gradients across temporal positions while keeping one local computation graph.
On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30 seconds, while MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods through 60 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains a few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise a rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at a history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising.

Figure 3 WinTF learns rolling generation through parallel supervision of windows with progressive noise levels. Phase offsets expose the model to both short prefill windows and full decoding windows. Within each window, later chunks receive higher noise levels. The attention mask combines bidirectional interactions within a noisy window with access to clean preceding history, while isolating noisy windows from one another. This allows multiple windows to be trained in parallel, each conditioned on its own event prompt and preceding clean history.

Figure 5 CuLT-DMD combines supervision across a long rollout in each generator update. The top panel shows local distillation supervision from teacher and critic predictions. LongLive-style training updates the generator from individual windows while carrying detached history forward. CuLT-DMD instead keeps parameters fixed throughout the rollout and averages the local gradients before updating. This incorporates supervision from multiple temporal positions while retaining one local computation graph at a time.

Figure 6 AnnealCFG reduces the late-denoising extrapolation produced by constant guidance throughout 30s generation. Across prefill and early, middle, and late decoding, the left plots show the additional latent-update magnitude induced by guidance. The right plots show its share in the final 20% of denoising steps. Annealing lowers both the late-step peaks and their contribution to the total update. Results aggregate 32 paired prompts, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown by bands and whiskers.

Figure 7 KV recomputation refreshes historical context for generation beyond the training horizon. Fullhistory caching expands the context as video length grows, while sliding-window caching retains dependencies on evicted chunks. At the history threshold, recomputation selects sink, intermediate, and recent chunks and causally re-encodes them into a fresh cache. This bounds the retained context and removes cached dependencies on discarded chunks before generation continues.

Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within a per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer.

Figure 1 MovieRoll generates a minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with a new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt.

Figure 4 Layer-dependent attention patterns motivate hierarchical history retention. In the WinTF-trained model, shallow layers distribute attention broadly across historical chunks, while deeper layers place relatively more attention on the sink and most recent chunks. The heatmap and lower entropy and coverage plots show this shift with depth. HieraKV follows these patterns by retaining full historical context in shallow layers and restricting deeper layers to the sink and most recent chunks.

Figure 9 The Parallel Streaming Variational Autoencoder (PS-VAE) supports continuous video decoding through temporal caching and spatial parallelism. The upper panel shows how cached decoder states carry temporal context across arriving latent chunks, allowing each chunk to be decoded as it becomes available. The lower panel distributes high-resolution decoding across GPUs through row partitioning and boundary exchange. Together, these designs support streaming output and reduce per-GPU decoding cost.

Figure 10 Qualitative comparison of 10s single-event video generation. Under the same prompt of a mermaid combing her hair on a seaside rock, MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled retain recognizable subjects and consistent surroundings as poses and waves change. Rows compare methods evaluated under the same prompt, and columns show successive temporal intervals within each 241-frame video.

Figure 11 Qualitative comparison of 30s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled preserve the facial features, clothing, and surroundings of a man eating at a bar as the action continues. Rows compare methods under the same prompt, and columns follow the 721-frame sequence, showing how subject and background consistency evolve during generation.

Figure 17 Memory and latency comparison across full-history and sink--recent attention allocations. The left plot shows slower cache-memory growth when fewer layers retain full history. At 18 cached chunks, the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local layers reduces memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB and peak denoising-step latency from 33.8 to 15.8s relative to all-global attention. Measurements use MovieRoll-Base with CFG on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Each timed denoising step includes both conditional and unconditional DiT evaluations. Timing excludes KV recomputation and VAE encoding/decoding.

Figure 16 Ablation of long-horizon extrapolation strategies. All three strategies use the same Stage 1 MovieRollBase checkpoint to extend generation from 10s training clips to 30s videos. Full-history and sliding-window caching produce increasingly washed-out backgrounds, whereas KV recomputation preserves clearer subject and street details through the end of the sequence.

Figure 12 Qualitative comparison of 60s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves the diver and underwater environment with relatively stable colors as generation continues. Rows compare methods under the same diver-and-wreck prompt, and columns follow successive 10s intervals of the 1441-frame videos.

Figure 26 Examples of multi-event video generation with sequential prompts. The upper examples show threeevent, 30s videos from MovieRoll-Base, and the lower examples show six-event, 60s videos from MovieRoll-Distilled. Prompts change every 10s, with one frame representing each event. Both models retain recurring characters and settings as new interactions develop, such as a cat reacting to a robotic vacuum and a keeper responding to a seagull.

Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of 30s multi-event video generation. The sequence progresses from sketching a flower to observing a frog and raising a camera, with a prompt change every 10s. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts these action changes while retaining the botanist and rainforest setting. Each row shows one method, and each pair of columns corresponds to one event.

Figure 14 Qualitative comparison of 60s multi-event video generation. The sequence develops from paddling to successive interactions with an otter, including surfacing beside the kayak, handling a rock, and approaching the hull. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts this event progression while maintaining a consistent lake setting. Rows compare methods under the same six sequential prompts, and each column represents one 10s event.

Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise progression and temporal advances at a fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt.

Figure 24 Examples of 60s single-event videos generated by MovieRoll-Distilled. This first set of six examples includes miniature ships, an origami dragon, and underwater performances. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves subject appearance as waves, steam, and gestures evolve. Each two-row group follows one 1441-frame video from left to right and then top to bottom, with frame indices overlaid and its prompt below.

Figure 18 Ablation of HieraKV attention allocations. The comparison varies the allocation of 54 transformer blocks between full-history and sink–recent attention. With the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local blocks, the rider and horse remain recognizable throughout the sequence. All-global attention progressively crops the subje ts, while all-local attention shifts toward a close rear view.

Figure 22 User preference comparison for multi-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled wins a majority of judgments against every evaluated baseline, with win rates from 62.3% to 81.9%. Each bar reports win, tie, and loss rates from the MovieRoll-Distilled perspective under the same prompt sequences, pooling judgments across 30s three-event and 60s six-event videos with ties included in the denominator.

Table 8 Shared architecture and history-cache configuration of the MovieRoll models. Both variants use an 8.3-billion-parameter backbone with text conditioning, a causal video VAE, and a five-chunk active window. The first six transformer blocks retain full history, while the remaining 48 retain the sink and most recent chunks, preserving broad historical context through a small subset of layers.

Table 2 Comparison of video decoding speed, memory use, and reconstruction quality. Single-GPU PSVAE outperforms the tested tiling methods in runtime and reconstruction PSNR. Spatial parallelism further reduces decoding time and per-GPU memory. With eight GPUs, PS-VAE achieves a 3.97× decoding speedup over its singleGPU version while preserving high numerical agreement. Measurements decode 1441 frames at 480× 864 on NVIDIA H20 GPUs in FP16.

Table 9 Inference settings of MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled. Distillation reduces sampling from 50 steps to 5 while preserving the shared rolling-generation pipeline. MovieRoll-Base uses guidance annealed from 4 to 1, whereas MovieRoll-Distilled operates without CFG. Both use the same chunk and window sizes and rebuild their KV caches at the same history threshold. Denoising passes are counted per output chunk, with the conditional and unconditional CFG branches contributing separately to the reported count.

Table 1 Efficiency comparison of block-causal attention implementations. The comparison evaluates fullhistory attention with three or five windows on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. FBCA achieves the lowest forward and backward runtimes across fixed and varying input shapes, with preparation taking less than 0.1s when shapes vary. In multiple-shape tests, it also reduces peak memory relative to FlexAttention, supporting efficient training across inputs with different spatial resolutions.

Table 10 Training stages and hyperparameters of MovieRoll. The two base-model stages introduce single-event and multi-event streaming generation. ODE initialization then transfers the base model to a few-step student, and CuLT-DMD trains it on self-generated rollouts. The columns summarize the data and optimization settings supporting this progression. The two distillation phases are denoted by P1 and P2, while G and F identify the generator and fake-score critic in the optimization settings for each phase.

Table 6 Single-GPU inference efficiency for 60s video generation. The table compares denoising and endto-end costs across methods at the listed resolutions for 1441-frame videos on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Switching from FlashAttention-3 to SageAttention increases MovieRoll-Distilled end-to-end throughput from 1.52 to 2.04 FPS. Single-GPU throughput remains below the 24 FPS playback rate required for real-time generation.

Table 5 Quantitative ablations of training and inference designs. WinTF outperforms chunk-wise formulations, while the selected HieraKV allocation, KV recomputation, long-rollout CuLT-DMD, and AnnealCFG schedule achieve the highest total scores within their respective comparisons. Shaded rows identify these choices. Autoregressive formulations are evaluated at 241 and 721 frames, and the remaining comparisons use 721 frames. Higher ratings indicate better quality and less drift.

Table 14 Comparison ofGPT-5.2 andGemini-2.5-Proas video evaluators. Both evaluate the same 30s single-event videos and rank MovieRoll-Distilled first and MovieRoll-Base second. Method rankings agree closely, with Spearman correlation ρ = 0.930. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro because it provides greater score separation between methods, as shown by the statistical measures in the lower section.

Table 11 Rollout settings for the two CuLT-DMD training phases. Phase 1 uses single-event, 241-frame rollouts lasting 10s. Phase 2 extends training to two-event, 721-frame rollouts lasting 30s. Both phases average local gradients across each rollout, allowing one update to incorporate supervision from multiple temporal positions. Bounded score clips keep distillation supervision local as the generated sequence grows.

Table 15 Distribution of user-study judgments across baselines and video durations. The study collects 2616 preference judgments across single-event and multi-event comparisons. Each cell counts individual judgments for MovieRoll-Distilled versus the listed baseline at a given duration. Judgments are pooled across durations to calculate win, tie, and loss rates for each baseline, separately for single-event and multi-event generation. Each judgment contributes one vote, including ties.

Table 13 Conversion of HeliosBench quality and drift metrics to a common rating scale. The listed intervals map raw metric values to ratings from 1 to 10 for weighted aggregation. Higher quality scores and lower drift scores receive higher ratings, so higher converted ratings consistently indicate better performance.

Table 7 Inference scaling across GPU counts and attention backends. Increasing the GPU count improves MovieRoll-Distilled throughput with both backends, and SageAttention is faster at every tested count. On eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, the best setting generates a 60s video in 152.2s, reaching 9.47 FPS. Real-time generation at 24 FPS remains a limitation even with eight GPUs. Videos contain 1441 frames at 480× 864.

Table 12 HeliosBench metrics, evaluators, and aggregation weights. Five full-video metrics cover aesthetics, dynamics, motion smoothness, semantic alignment, and naturalness. Four drift metrics measure changes between the beginning and end of a video. The aggregation weights give greater emphasis to semantic alignment and naturalness while retaining contributions from all four metrics of temporal drift.

papers.title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
papers.tldr: MovieRoll is a framework for generating long-form videos by combining streaming fine-tuning, compressed context caching, long-rollout distillation, and stabilized long-horizon inference.

papers.abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and R\"auker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.
authors: Yiwei Qin, Muhang Xie, Xuefeng Li, Mohan Jiang, Dayuan Fu, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu
bullets: Benchleaking means benchmark test examples enter training data, causing scores to reflect recall rather than capability; it differs from benchmark-directed optimization without test-set access (“benchmaxxing”).

The proposed Anti-Hack score removes leaked examples from evaluation; average score penalties ranged from 1.3–1.5 points for some models to 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base.

papers.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.
authors: Sven Jacobs, Lukas Berning, Natalie Kiesler

Children’s voice prompts were brief, while 39.1% trusted the tutor’s answers to always be correct.
Human-like, clear speech did not guarantee accurate support or alignment with the learner’s program state.

papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of generating textual guidance with a large model before small-model generation.
Uses a trainable bridge to convert frozen sender hidden states into attention keys and values for the receiver.
Supports periodic review, where the sender updates guidance from the receiver’s partial output while preserving the receiver’s KV cache.
Improves reasoning and coding performance across independently trained model families, with gains comparable to a stronger sender pairing.
Transfers from math and coding training to general-knowledge tasks without domain-specific retraining.

At review boundaries, the sender prefills the newly generated segment and the resulting entries are appended to the latent memory, leaving the receiver’s KV cache untouched.

papers.abstract: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.
authors: Thodsaporn Chay-intr, Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn, Thanaruk Theeramunkong
bullets: Addresses Thai’s need for word- and morpheme-level boundaries beyond subword tokenization.

papers.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang, Hangfan Zhang, Shao Zhang, Shuai Li, Toru Takisaka, Chao Xu, Yi Zhou, Zhihao Tang, Xiao Wang, Bo Zhang, Shuyue Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ensuring correctness as AI-generated mathematical proofs become more abundant.
Uses separate theorem- and proof-formalization agents, accumulated proof experience, parallel verification, and selective semantic review.
Evaluated on demanding theoretical computer science tasks involving complex quantification and dependencies.
Reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset.
Completed formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks and produced simpler proofs, reduced dependencies, and reusable formal knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 6 | Pass@1 results (%) on Formal TCS Bench and RLMEval. Formal TCS Bench also reports compilation rates. RLMEval results are shown separately for PFR and TLB and combined as Total. PFR covers additive combinatorics and entropy methods from the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa project, with applications to linearity testing in TCS. TLB (Testing Lower Bounds) covers information-theoretic lower bounds for statistical hypothesis testing.

Figure 2 | Turing Agent coordinates theorem formalization (TF) and proof formalization (PF) agents. TF agents provide checked Lean statements and definitions, while PF agents construct proofs and request semantic review when needed. The resulting proof undergoes final verification. In its runtime, Turing Agent coordinates recursive DAG construction, parallel proof formalization, and selective semantic review. Figure 3 | Research-level TCS verification beyond standard benchmarks. Of the 121 TCS problems in OpenAI’s mathematical research collection, 22 had not been fully verified in Lean. Among these, we highlight three examples formally verified by Turing Agent using DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeekV4.1-Flash.

Figure 1 | Three challenges in automated formal verification. The formal statement must preserve the original claim (faithfulness), the code must pass Lean’s syntax and type checks (validity), and the proof must discharge all obligations without gaps (completeness). Our Turing Agent is designed to satisfy these requirements throughout the formalization process.
Figure 5 | Experience extraction and reuse during DAG evolution. PF agents use retained records to guide revisions and update the pool when later attempts yield useful findings.

Figure 4 | Selective semantic review in the proof DAG. PF agents request TF agents when a concept is unclear or a new definition is introduced. The TF agent checks whether the statement and its definitions preserve the intended meaning.

Green terminal nodes indicate those actually used in the proof, while gray nodes indicate those not used in the final proof. Leaf nodes with bold borders represent lemmas or theorems introduced by Turing Agent during the proving process and not present in the original paper. papers.abstract: Formation maneuver control enables a multiagent system to cooperatively navigate through constrained environments in collective motion. While various formation controllers exist, they rely heavily on high-quality and dynamically feasible reference trajectories provided a priori, making formation motion planning (FMP) essential. To address the computational challenges for high-dimensional joint trajectories faced by conventional constrained optimization-based solutions, this paper introduces a hybrid optimization-generative framework with a focus on affine formations, which provide the necessary spatial flexibility. By formulating the planning task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori estimation, we decouple multiagent objectives to leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors for dynamic feasibility, obstacle avoidance, and smoothness. We then interleave the generative process with projected gradient descent (PGD) to strictly enforce affine geometric constraints with safety guarantees. Simulations demonstrate that our framework generates highly smooth, collision-free plans that are readily trackable by common distributed controllers and outperforms state-of-the-art planners in various metrics.
authors: Zhonggang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Raj Thilak Rajan
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of planning high-dimensional joint trajectories for formation motion.
Formulates planning as constrained maximum-a-posteriori estimation using pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors.
Interleaves diffusion sampling with projected gradient descent to enforce affine formation constraints and safety.
Simulations show smooth, collision-free, controller-trackable plans with strong performance across multiple metrics.
Scope: focuses on affine formations and simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
authors: Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, Kun Wang, Ke Ma, Zhandong Mei, Huibin Li
bullets: Addresses the limitation of future predictions that ignore how proposed actions alter visual representations.
Uses a proposal–rethink–refine loop with latent multi-horizon predictions and residual corrections.
Adds affordance-guided observation–action memory plus near-fine, far-coarse prediction granularity.
Reports strong results across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and three real-world OOD conditions.
Diagnostics and ablations support complementary benefits from rethinking and affordance guidance, with two-pass latency reported across platforms.

papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.
authors: Mo Zhou
bullets: Cloud assistants face challenges involving data governance, continuous availability, and reliable physical actions in homes.
The home local server is used to organize nine recurring architectural responsibilities across whole-home systems.
Generative models handle perception, intent understanding, and planning, while deterministic checks, knowledge graphs, and authorization leases constrain actions.
Home control, companionship, and guarding share state and memory but differ in latency, error trade-offs, proactivity, and permissions.
Current benchmarks rely mainly on virtual environments; local deployment is not automatically safer, and social or medical effects remain insufficiently established.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.
authors: Ofir Gordon, Lior Dikstein, Paul Balanca, Idan Achituve, Douglas Orr, Hai Victor Habi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth growth from longer contexts and larger batches.
Combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats as a drop-in codebook-quantization replacement.
Uses beam search for large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks.
Introduces MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX format.
Reports lower WikiText perplexity, higher GSM8K accuracy, and the best NVFP4 LongBench average on Llama3 and Qwen3 among evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
authors: Lucas Schulze, Sucheth Shenoy, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Addresses uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics while limiting sensitivity to measurement disturbances.
Uses a gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network with stable linear filtering to encode context across frequencies.
Provides guarantees for exponential forgetting and finite-horizon, frequency-weighted context perturbation bounds.
In simulated and real manipulation tasks, it reduces high-frequency sensitivity and residual torque error, produces smoother motion, and degrades less under injected disturbances.
Evaluation includes model predictive control and real-robot frequency-sensitivity analysis; results are scoped to the tested low-pass realization.

papers.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Mevl\"ut Bagci, Maxim Konca

papers.abstract: Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors. We propose CALDS (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to adapt learned single-agent behaviors for coordinated execution. Building on individual dynamical systems (DSs) learned from demonstrations, CALDS enables cooperative adaptation through two key components: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of learned policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which ensures collision-free cooperation while preserving the spatial structure and convergence properties of the original behaviors. We evaluate CALDS across three diverse scenarios: assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening and object placement. Quantitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task success and enabling safe, coordinated simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrated behaviors.
authors: Saray Bakker, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses coordination, whole-body collision avoidance, and behavior preservation in cooperative mobile manipulation.
Uses learned dynamical systems from demonstrations as the basis for adaptation.
Combines Cooperative Policy Selection with Temporal Adaptation to select compatible behaviors and avoid collisions.
Evaluated in assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening with object placement.
Reports improved task success and safe simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CALDS for cooperative multi-agent adaptation in a restaurant scenario, where one robot cleans a table while the other places a cup on the cleaned area. Firstly, we generate a set of learned single-agent DSs for each task. In the multi-agent context, Cooperative Policy Selection ranks and selects the most promising combination, which Temporal Adaptation then adjusts to satisfy task constraints while ensuring whole-body collision-free trajectories, selecting the next-best combination if unsuccessful.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.
authors: Edoardo Cecchinato, Shun Inadumi, Angel Garc\'ia Contreras, Giuseppe Riccardi, Koichiro Yoshino
bullets: Existing visual grounding benchmarks often overlook ambiguity in real-world interactions.
JAG-D contains Japanese human–robot multimodal dialogues spanning visual and linguistic ambiguity.
The benchmark evaluates VLMs on ambiguity recognition and resolution using dialogue context.
Dialogue context substantially improves linguistic ambiguity resolution, particularly for Japanese zero anaphora.
The study examines whether gains come from dialogue semantics or conversational structure.

papers.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
authors: Yang Tian, Tianyu Zheng, Xiyuan Yang, Yaxin Du, Chengran Yang, Bo Zhao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, verifiable environments that provide timely signals for improving training value.
Converts real repositories into environments where agents implement complete projects from language specifications.
Uses an Environment Evolution Loop optimizing validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope.
Produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains.
Training on these environments improves results across NL2Repo-Bench and five long-horizon coding or agentic benchmarks, with further gains from environment evolution.

papers.abstract: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.
authors: Hongyu Ma, Hairong Qu, Shiqi Zhao, Yongsong Yang, Kai Shi, Jiahao Ai, Xin You, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting large-scale, geometrically grounded human manipulation data in unconstrained environments.
Combines geometric-temporal optimization and visual-inertial SLAM with WinDEX-Net, a fisheye-native stereo network using local detail and temporal context.
Provides distilled offline and causal-streaming models, plus a low-cost CyberCap capture system and the WinDEX-Hand dataset.
Achieves 43.61 FPS offline and 171 FPS streaming; reports 14.5-pixel reprojection error and 37.29 mm world-frame joint error on held-out evaluations.
Motion references improve reinforcement-learning task success by 7.6× over WiLoR and 3.6× over HaWoR, with demonstrated real-time arm-hand teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.
authors: Vincent Li Weixin, Chen Jingkun, Vicente Grau
bullets: Addresses the high cost of annotating every frame in long echocardiography sequences.
Uses a mean-teacher architecture with frozen, pretrained DINOv3 encoders and parameter-efficient adaptation.
Combines complementary losses, including temporal consistency, to generate segmentation priors for unlabeled frames.
Experiments on CAMUS and CardiacNet show improved performance over other scribble-supervised methods.
Reduces annotation requirements independently of sequence length while targeting temporally stable segmentation.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction enables efficient modeling of dynamic autonomous-driving scenes, but current methods suffer from two complementary failure modes: semantic leakage of traffic participants into the static representation and geometric drift of Gaussian locations across viewpoints. We propose \textbf{IGRecon4D}, a feed-forward dynamic scene reconstruction framework that addresses these failures with training-time instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning. Specifically, an instance-level semantic branch provides a potentially dynamic participant prior, which is distilled into dynamic-mask learning through the Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint to encourage high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions prone to dynamic-static leakage. In parallel, sparse LiDAR measurements guide dense depth estimation, and the resulting depths are back-projected to anchor Gaussian positions for improved multi-view geometric consistency. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes demonstrate improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant-region reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.
authors: Yifei Tong, Ziyang Huang, Yizhao Han, Xiaoxiao Long, Hao Zhu
bullets: Targets semantic leakage of traffic participants into static representations and viewpoint-dependent Gaussian drift.
Distills instance-level semantic priors into dynamic-mask learning using an Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint.
Uses sparse LiDAR to guide dense depth estimation and anchor Gaussian positions for better multi-view consistency.
Improves full-image reconstruction on Waymo Open Dataset and traffic-participant reconstruction in zero-shot nuScenes evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of IGRecon4D. The instance-level semantic branch supplies a potentially dynamic participant prior for dynamic-mask supervision, while the dynamic masks decompose the scene into static and dynamic Gaussians for rendering.

Figure 2: Dynamic-static Gaussian rendering. Dense depth maps are back-projected with camera parameters to obtain Gaussian positions. The predicted dynamic masks allocate traffic-participant regions with high potentially dynamic prior to per-frame Gaussians and the remaining regions to the global static Gaussian set, while sky Gaussians model low-opacity sky regions. All Gaussian components are jointly rendered with a differentiable rasterizer.

papers.abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.
authors: Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park
bullets: Addresses how robots can repurpose past observations for requests that were unknown when the observations were recorded.
Stores visual features independently of future goals and retrieves complementary evidence suited to each request and current scene.
Supervises retrieval using expert-action prediction, connecting memory selection to manipulation performance.
Uses a lightweight action interface and reuses repeated features and unchanged computations for efficiency.
Evaluated across four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios, demonstrating reuse across changing goals and scenes.

papers.abstract: Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.
authors: Thomas Woehrle, Linus Ericsson, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley
bullets: Existing expressive NAS spaces rarely support autoregressive sequence modeling and typically impose strong structural biases.
The proposed einspaceAR search space represents and constructs autoregressive models from fundamental operations.
Experiments show that einspaceAR can discover capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch.
The approach is presented as a reusable blueprint for adding autoregressive modeling to other expressive search spaces.

papers.abstract: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.
authors: Yunchan Jeon, SooGon Kim, Seungwook Kim, CheolWon Lee, Jongmin Lee
bullets: Addresses poor cross-species generalization caused by limited 3D-labeled bird data and long-tail diversity.
Replaces AniMer+’s binary same-family contrastive signal with a continuous, generative prior based on Linnaean rank distances.
Applies the prior to the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model, with learnable selection strength and noise scale.
Outperforms AniMer+ on both metrics for unseen-species CowBird and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB.
Ablations attribute the unseen-species gain mainly to taxonomic structure, especially distinctions across orders beyond family-level labels.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method at a glance. (a) The AniMer+ [1] encoder produces AVES [12] shape codes β from a single image. (b) Across species, β is regularized by an OU [10] prior parameterized by learnable (α, σ,µ) over a fixed Linnaean [2] rank distance matrix; the NLL of this Gaussian is LOU. (c) LOU replaces the family-level contrastive term of AniMer+ (wcon=0), so that on birds Ltotal = LAVES + λOULOU. Blue: the existing network and fixed taxonomy. Orange: what we add.

Figure 4: The prior tightens the shape codes without distorting phylogenetic signal. (a, b) What tightens: k-NN family purity rises and the spread of the per-species mean β falls with λOU on CtrlAVES3D [29] training codes; the 10−4 bars are a single constant-LR run. (c) What is preserved: the β distance between the mean shape codes of two species measures how different the model predicts their shapes to be. All 136 species pairs, sorted along the x-axis by this distance without the prior (gray), move closer at λOU=10−5 (orange, seed 0) but stay in nearly the same order.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on two CUB [32] test images (top) and two CowBird [6] test instances (bottom). For each species, the first panel shows the input with the ground-truth keypoints (green dots) and a red circle on the baseline’s worst keypoint; the retrained AniMer+ baseline (red crosses) and the OU fine-tune (blue crosses) follow, and gray lines join each prediction to its ground-truth keypoint. The badge is the per-image PCK@0.1.

Figure 1: Beyond family labels. The 17 training species of CtrlAVES3D on the Linnaean tree [2], colored by order. The height at which two lineages join marks their lowest shared rank, from same family up to outgroup; each rank sets the distance dtax that our prior reads (Figure 2b). The familysupervised contrastive loss of AniMer+ [1] keeps a single bit of this tree: whether a pair joins below the dashed red line. Our Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) prior uses every rank, pulling the shape codes of two species together more strongly the more closely they are related, so the shape space carries graded structure rather than a same-family indicator.

Figure 3: Real vs. permuted taxonomy ablation. CowBird [6] AUC and PCK@0.1 under three configurations: (a) the AniMer+ [1] baseline, (b) the OU prior with a label-permuted distance matrix, and (c) the OU prior with the real Linnaean [2] distance matrix (both OU runs at λOU = 10−4, constant learning rate; Section 4.1).

Table 1: Comparison against AniMer+ [1] on the avian benchmarks. CUB [32] and the CtrlAVES3D [29] test split evaluate seen-species; CowBird [6] is the unseen-species out-ofdistribution (OOD) benchmark. For ours we report the mean ± sample standard deviation over five random seeds. AniMer-A [20] is the avian-only variant; AniMer+ and ours are unified bird+mammal models; AVES and HMR2.0 are the baselines reported by AniMer+.

Table 3: Procrustes-aligned 3D errors on the CtrlAVES3D test split (309 images, 17 species). pa-MPJPE denotes the mean per-joint position error; pa-MPVPE denotes mean per-vertex position error. Lower is better. Ours is a single run (seed 0). Values follow our canonical-frame scaling; see Appendix S6 for details.

Table 2: Rank-granularity ablation: progressively richer distance matrices on the same operating point as Figure 3. The family-only kernel uses values in {0, 1, 5} (same family vs. not), the order-only refinement uses {0, 1, 2, 5} (adds the same-order distinction), and the full Linnaean kernel uses {0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6} (cross-order ordinals as the default). All three kernels use 0 for the same species and 1 for the same family, and differ only above the family level; genus-level structure cannot be varied on this training set, because the 17 species contain no congeneric pair. We use 5 rather than 6 as the cross-order placeholder for the family-only and order-only kernels so that they share a single cross-order bin, isolating the rank-granularity axis from changes in cross-order distance scale.
