papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
authors: Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fast-evolving contact forces and slow API-only model decisions.
Uses calibrated force sensing or joint torques with self-terminating force primitives that return on contact events.
Converts force traces into physical quantities with uncertainty for model reasoning instead of exposing raw force streams.
Introduces HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables.
Reports large gains in real and simulated zero-shot success, with performance matching expert controllers on HiddenPhys.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ForceHarness, illustrated with one logged call. Blue marks the command path and teal the force path. papers.abstract: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.
authors: Jing Yi, Cehao Yang, Hualei Zhang, Haitao Li
bullets: Addresses token-to-action misalignment and conflicting teacher policies in autoregressive VLM distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CAMOPD. (3) Conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates specialists without target data (C̄g ↓ ⇒ γg ↑) to reweight asymmetric recovery gradients under L = Laction + λLanchor. (4) Zero-shot deployment runs the consolidated pixel-only student on unseen games.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large audio-language models (LALMs) have broadened audio understanding across speech, sound, and music, with tool-based agents further supporting these tasks by invoking predefined audio tools. However, a persistent gap remains between perceiving acoustic content and using it as evidence for reasoning: recognizing what is audible does not ensure that a model can identify which cues resolve an uncertain decision. To bridge this gap, we propose Think2Listen, an evidence-centric learning framework for agentic audio understanding. Guided by evidence before commitment, Think2Listen couples iterative reasoning with a targeted LALM interaction to actively seek acoustic cues that distinguish competing hypotheses and revise candidate judgments based on the observations returned. It learns what to ask, how to use evidence, and when to stop, using observation-induced changes in candidate-state to inform training credit. Extensive evaluations on two benchmarks spanning seven audio categories demonstrate that Think2Listen achieves (I) enhanced multi-step audio reasoning, with gains in overall accuracy of 5.08%--17.67% over competing audio agents; and (II) improved audio understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, boosting overall accuracy by 2.29%--13.10% over the corresponding baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JinWang79/Think2Listen.

papers.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill

Across merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios, it improves success and reduces delay versus the potential-game baseline, with no observed collisions.

papers.abstract: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

papers.abstract: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.
authors: Yibo Bai, Likui Zhang, Jinglei Zhang, Zhengbin Pang, Xingshen Song, Xiaoqing Yin, Jinsheng Deng

Fuses geometric and visual features for coarse metric estimation and conditions each step of temporal generation.
Jointly predicts world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and hand shape.
Reports substantial reductions in camera-space and world-space MPJPE, wrist error, and acceleration error relative to HaWoR.

papers.abstract: Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.
authors: Gabriele Giuseppe Di Marzo, Mariano Ram\'irez Montero, Maximilian St\"olzle, Rodrigo P\'erez-Dattari, Cosimo Della Santina
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing alternative valid outcomes within continuous, autonomous dynamical systems.

papers.abstract: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts.Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

papers.abstract: Even in multi-camera setups, occlusions can leave individual body joints with only a single usable 2D observation. Such an observation defines a viewing ray but leaves the joint's depth undetermined. We introduce Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D joint locations. To reduce monocular depth ambiguity, we propose geometry-conditioned depth prediction, which combines image features with previously reconstructed 3D body geometry as contextual depth cues. We further introduce learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT), which augments differentiable algebraic triangulation with predicted depth constraints, enabling reconstruction even from a single contributing camera while preserving the benefits of geometric triangulation when multiple views are available. The reconstructed 3D poses subsequently guide depth prediction in the next iteration, allowing depth estimates and 3D geometry to progressively refine each other. Experiments on CMU Panoptic demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average performance across evaluated camera subsets and unseen camera arrangements. BoE is particularly effective under sparse camera coverage, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the challenging three-camera setting.
authors: Erik Brorsson, Kilian Freitag, Josef Bengtson, Kristofer Bengtsson, Lars Hammarstrand, Knut {\AA}kesson, Fredrik Kahl
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of joints observed by only one camera, where 2D observations provide a viewing ray but not depth.
Predicts per-camera joint depths using image features and previously reconstructed 3D body geometry.
Uses learnable depth-aware triangulation to combine predicted depth constraints with geometric triangulation, including single-view reconstruction.
Iteratively refines depth estimates and 3D pose geometry using each to guide the other.
On CMU Panoptic, achieves state-of-the-art in-domain results and improves prior state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points with three cameras.

figures.caption: Figure 2. BoE decoder architecture and geometry-conditioned depth estimation. (a) Each decoder layer extracts image evidence through projective attention and predicts per-view 2D joint locations, confidences, depths, and depth gates. Learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT) fuses these measurements to update the 3D poses, while separate branches update appearance features and predict pose scores. (b) Target-depth masking (TDM) constructs a separate joint sequence for each target joint, excluding only its own reference-depth embedding while retaining its image feature. (c) Pose-context modeling (PCM) processes the masked sequences using a shared encoder and selects the contextualized feature of each target joint for depth prediction.

Figure 1. Overview of BoE. Starting from initial 3D pose queries, the decoder projects joints into calibrated camera views to extract image evidence. Each view provides 2D joint and geometryconditioned depth predictions, which are combined through LDAT to update the 3D poses. The updated poses serve as references for subsequent decoder layers, enabling iterative refinement.

Ground truth is shown in red, while predictions are shown in other colors. BoE more accurately reconstructs heavily occluded joints, including the right hand and foot of the orange pose, the feet of the turquoise pose, and the left leg of the blue pose (colors refer to the top-row predictions).

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
authors: Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu
bullets: Targets the remaining inference bottlenecks in long-video generation: repeated denoising and KV-cache operations across video chunks.
Uses Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations.
Applies Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical KV-reading budgets across layers and attention heads.
Uses Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to select informative spatial tokens while preserving coverage.
Achieves up to 2.28× speedup on Self-Forcing and 1.86× on LongLive, with consistently improved quality and no pretrained-parameter changes.

papers.abstract: Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot's perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.
authors: Utkarsh Bajpai, C\'{e}dric Pradalier, St\'{e}phanie Aravecchia
bullets: Targets in-row driving, row turning/skipping, and inter-row traversal in semi-structured farms.
Models diverse navigation behaviors as SE(2) local paths conditioned on the robot’s goal and depth observations.
Introduces RowNavBench, an Isaac Sim benchmark spanning vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varied layouts and vegetation.
Achieves 87% success, versus 44% for a retrained generative behavior-cloning baseline.
Benchmark, data, and code are planned for release upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $\pi_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.
authors: Jaehyuk Lee, Yeajin Lee, Suhyun Bae, Donghun Lee
bullets: Attention scores poorly reflect how visual tokens affect predicted actions, while online action-sensitivity scoring is computationally expensive and biased by prior pruning.
POKE computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with fewer than 0.3M parameters.
At inference, the student scores observations without backpropagation or previous masks, and diversity selection retains informative tokens.
Keeping 32 of 512 tokens achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on π0.5, with 1.85× and 1.26× speedups on LIBERO.
The method reports larger gains on LIBERO-Plus than competing attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
authors: Majun Zhang, Yuan Guo, Decheng Wu, Jiayang Xu, Changhao Pan, Fan Zhuo, Xiaoda Yang, Chenyuhao Wen, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Dense self-attention becomes a major bottleneck as image and video token sequences grow.
The proposed 4+1+3 framework analyzes static and dynamic sparsity, selection granularity, reuse, and correction for omitted interactions.
It links algorithmic choices to three system dimensions: data organization, execution, and dataflow.
The survey reviews evaluation metrics, implementation considerations, open challenges, and future research directions.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. The 4+1+3 framework for sparse attention. The source, evidence construction, granularity, and support specification determine which query–key pairs are retained. Reuse avoids repeating work across denoising steps, and correction compensates for contributions from omitted pairs. Data organization, execution, and dataflow determine how the sparse attention workload runs on hardware. The tile example shows how the shape of the support affects computation. Both patterns retain 16 query–key pairs, but with 2× 2 tiles, the scattered pattern requires computing 56 entries and the tile-aligned pattern requires only 16.

Fig. 1. Development timeline of representative sparse-attention methods and systems, showing a shift from algorithmic sparsity design toward tighter algorithm– system co-design for more structured and efficient sparse execution.

Dark gray cells mark mandatory or structural connections, such as global anchor rows and columns, self-blocks, and the second axis of a factorized pattern. Orange cells mark auxiliary connections, such as random additions, secondary routes, and long-range or multiscale links.

TABLE II The 4+1+3 design space for sparse attention in visual generation. The four support construction dimensions describe information sources, how evidence is derived, the unit of selection, and the rules specifying which connections are retained. The auxiliary dimension covers reuse and correction. The three system dimensions describe how sparse data is organized, how workloads are executed, and how data moves through the system. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
authors: Ruiyang Jiang, Xinyang Liao, Weikai Huang, Yuqi Niu, Junjie Zhou, Yubin Zheng
bullets: Frames multimodal memory failures as nine error types across four stages: Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer.
Finds that most failures originate before the final answer, with early errors propagating as misleading evidence.
Shows that evidence-based diagnosis alone can misattribute an error to the stage where it becomes visible.
Uses backward fact tracing and memory-grounded diagnosis to repair the responsible stage before re-answering.
Improves accuracy on Mem-Gallery and MemLens, and also benefits MuRAG and A-Mem, using a 4B backbone.

papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
authors: K2 Team, Zhengzhong Liu, Haonan Li, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Rupesh Kumar Srivastava, Mikhail Yurochkin, Hadi Abdine, Yash Akhauri, Adharsh Babu, David Bellamy, Jalaj Bhandari, Dani Bouch, Wail Bouhedja, Weili Cao, Ahmad Chamma, Po-Chun Chang, Junlin Chen, Lingjie Chen, Zhoujun Cheng, Kyle Chickering, Ryandito Diandaru, Evan Dufraisse, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Bilal El Bouardi, Desai Fan, Richard Fan, Chengqian Gao, Rifo Ahmad Genadi, Jonathan Geuter, Charles Guille-Escuret, Willis Guo, Dhawal Gupta, Seungwook Han, Tingxu Han, Shibo Hao, Besher Hassan, Guowei He, Ming Shan Hee, Joel Hestness, Yu Huang, Yuan Huang, Haolong Jia, Linghao Jin, Junu Kim, Lingjing Kong, Nurkhan Laiyk, Andrej Leban, Liqun Ma, John Maggs, Amr Mohamed, Mukhesh Narra, Omkar Pangarkar, Aldo Pareja, Khiem Pham, Varad Pimpalkhute, Nikhil Ranjan, Elizaveta Rebrova, Hector Ren, Shaurya Rohatgi, Guokan Shang, Jianshu She, Chufan Shi, Aaryamonvikram Singh, Daria Soboleva, Kartik Sreenivasan, Suqi Sun, Yuekai Sun, Bowen Tan, Liping Tang, Shengkun Tang, Muzi Tao, Mallikarjuna Tupakula, Micah Villmow, Hongyi Wang, Huijuan Wang, Renxi Wang, Yongxin Wang, Yuqi Wang, Zhenting Wang, Shicheng Wen, Yingquan Wu, Anze Xie, Andrew Xing, Matthew Yang, Shuanghai Yu, Kerem Zaman, Zenan Zhai, Hongli Zhan, Xuezhou Zhang, Anshun Asher Zheng, Zhe Zhou, Richard Zhuang, Eric P. Xing
bullets: The fleet targets math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and other general-purpose workloads.
Mixture-of-Value Attention and softplus attention gating improve reasoning efficiency; a 36B-A4B model nearly matches a same-data 32B dense model with one-seventh the active parameters.
Uno provides lossless diffusion adapters that accelerate decoding by up to 2.2× without requiring a separate draft model.
The models are reported to lead or remain competitive with strong open models of similar size on agentic and coding benchmarks.
The release includes checkpoints, data, logs, training/evaluation/infrastructure code, development pipelines, and a 22T-token shared corpus for reproducibility and scaling studies.

Figure 50: Agent evaluation harness: the trusted control box holds all secrets and routes each task by capability: browser, tool, and lighter filesystem tasks run in a fresh-per-task Docker sandbox, while computer-use tasks run in a disposable golden-image VM. Each task combines an input package, a task family and a sampled plan, from which an LLM writes the request. Figure 2: Mixture-of-Value Attention in the 36B model. A router selects 4 of 64 nonlinear value experts and combines their weighted outputs into the values used by attention. Each expert produces values for all eight KV heads jointly. Since only the combined values are cached, the KV-cache size is unchanged. Solid arrows carry representations, and dashed arrows carry routing decisions or weights. Query/key positional embeddings, attention-output gating, the output projection, and the residual connection are omitted for clarity.

Figure 1: Training time of all six K2-Horizon models, measured from W&B run logs and drawn on a shared axis of training days. The 32B and 36B-A4B rows show pre-training, mid-training and SFT only; each includes four mid-training stages plus an SFT with final decay. Gaps between stages (data preparation, ablations, queueing) are excluded. Pre-training, mid-training and SFT durations are wall-clock run times, with mid-training stages separated by white lines; RL durations sum the logged rollout-step times. Thin bars below a row are RL experts trained in parallel, so each RL block spans its longest serial path. The 375B post-training takes 13.3 days (RL 4.7, SFT 8.6 in two phases: a constant-learning-rate phase, run in two segments, then a linear decay); the 7B and 3.7B take 14.1 and 13.2 days, and the 0.9B 3.6 days. Ticks mark events of negligible duration (checkpoint averaging, weight merging) or without a logged duration (FTPO; the first 0.9B math RL stage, delivered as a checkpoint).

Figure 38: RL360 architecture. The rollout, sandbox, inference, and training layers communicate through explicit service boundaries and can be scaled independently. Miles collects trajectories and rewards, Harbor executes agents in task environments, SMG routes inference requests to SGLang, and Megatron-LM updates the policy.

Figure 17: Overview of PRism data processing. Curation combines archived events with repository code, and annotation adds semantic labels. The resulting corpus provides inputs for five synthesis branches. The prism is schematic; band widths are not to scale.

Each O*NET task is matched to servers by embedding similarity, and an occupation with several matched (task, server) pairs is expanded by an LLM into a self-contained workplace request, a cross-tool workflow and an answer key; information-withheld variants (dashed) omit key parameters so the agent must ask for them. Rollouts run against LLM-simulated tools and, for multi-turn data, a role-inverted simulated user that sees only the agent’s final replies.
Figure 32: Factoid & Source-Specific Question Generation Pipeline. Well-posed factoid questions drive factual recall capability, while ambiguous source-specific questions drive abstention capability.

(1) A subtree around a central result is selected from the paper’s proof graph; boundary results become assumptions and internal results become subtasks. (2) Proposer–reviewer pairs write the subtasks and harden the central question. (3) An executed reference solution and a checker per subtask decide the answers; three quality checks (cold solve, shortcut probe, consistency check) send the task back for revision or reject it. (4) In Harbor, a solver is rewarded only if every checker passes. Violet: agent roles; teal: executed code.

Figure 19: Building RL coding environments from GitHub pull requests. Filtering reduces the annotated PR corpus with deterministic rules, then scores survivors with an LLM judge and draws a domain-balanced sample stratified by difficulty. Rewriting derives the reference patches from the diff without a model and uses the model only for the task specification, the predicted environment, and the test commands. Environment synthesis is an agent loop that produces a container image. The two checks below it are distinct: acceptance is mechanical, whereas the trajectory judge runs a solver against an already-accepted environment and decides whether it is worth training on. Solid arrows carry artifacts and dashed arrows carry feedback: acceptance failures return to the responsible sub-agent, and judged misalignment returns to the rewrite stage. Filter thresholds, the eight scoring dimensions of the filtering judge, the checklist items, and the selection rule are given in the text.

Figure 33: How one PR chain becomes a single long episode. Each PR is attempted in its own fresh agent session against the same working tree, so state reaches the next turn two ways: through the filesystem, which accumulates, and through a compacted handoff, which does not. Per-turn context therefore stays roughly constant however long the episode runs, while cumulative token usage climbs until it crosses the budget, at which point the run stops and the partial episode is kept. The whole episode runs inside a sandbox in which the network tools are gated: dependency installs resolve against a local package mirror and git operations against a local repository mirror, so a build can still fetch what it needs while the obvious routes to the upstream change are closed. The gating is at the tool layer rather than the network layer, so the public internet remains reachable by an agent that writes its own client; we did not observe this in the trajectories we inspected. The number of turns an episode reaches is set by the budget rather than by the number of PRs the chain offers.

The run then resumes from step 82,001, and the final trajectory over the same steps (blue) shows no excursion. (c, d) Distributions of episode duration and of peak z-score (Equation 12) on the accepted trajectory, for the two phases; triangles mark the examples in (a) and (b), and the wide excursion lies on an erased branch and is not counted.

Figure 24: Condensed mining prompt. Queue construction is deterministic for a fixed dataset and exclusion set; scientific and runtime feasibility are assessed from the paper and executable repository.

Figure 48: Mean score by safety domain (further out is better; both panels share the same radial scale). Left: K2-Horizon (solid, filled) against K2-V2 (solid, unfilled) and Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (dashed) under the same harness and judge (K2-V2 runs 87 of the 88 tasks). Frontier-level on direct-harm refusal and multi-turn safety; behind Kimi K3 on over-refusal, bias, and cyber/privacy but ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash overall. Compared to K2-V2, the profiles cross: K2-V2 is wider on adversarial surfaces, whereas K2-Horizon is wider on over-refusal and truthfulness. Right: the K2-Horizon family. Figure 13: Socratic teacher–student dialogue generation. Hard, prime-free problems are posed to a student agent that sees only the problem. A teacher agent that also sees the reference answer checks each attempt and either probes the student’s reasoning or, once the attempt is correct, ends the dialogue. Completed dialogues are rendered as pre-training documents from the student’s perspective.
Figure 35: Fraction of tasks solved without and with the advisor, by category. Advised reruns are applied only to tasks the solver failed on its own.

Figure 23: Task factory. A coding agent runs this loop without supervision: it finds a problem with a checkable answer, grounds it as a Harbor task, passes it through three gates that are never skipped, measures its difficulty against a real agent, and logs every attempt, pass or fail, to a ledger that it reads before building the next task.

Figure 36: How a new dataset is processed: load the source, test it with the general converter and process_entry, decide whether a fix is needed, find the cause, write and test a dataset-specific fix, and save the output for each dataset.

Figure 30: From technical documents to interactive simulator tasks. A design agent defines the task, and an implementation agent writes the simulator. Candidates are checked for correct execution, repeatability, and direct leaks of hidden values. A policy using only information available to the solver must then beat both inaction and random actions by a preset margin in average score across the same test seeds. Eligible failures receive bounded repair and are checked again. Accepted tasks support trajectory generation and automatic scoring.

Figure 42: Knowledge Work expert pass@k during RL, in non-overlapping bins of 250 prompt groups. pass@k is the unbiased estimator 1− ( n−c k ) / ( n k ) over the n = 32 samples each prompt receives, counting a sample as correct when its base reward exceeds 0.5.

Figure 28: The research lab. Ten researcher agents with distinct personas and skills act on one shared, real-time world through a command-line tool, and a Concordia game master enforces the rules and checks four win conditions. Competition comes from non-exclusive pulls on open problems, where the first accepted paper scoops the rest, and from the leaderboards and the race for public engagement. Collaboration comes from the larger credit pot for co-authored papers, payments and escrowed deals, shared git repositories, and the collaborative variant in which the whole team pursues one goal. Figure 37: Token cost of the three tool presentation formats. (a) Average size of the rendered tool block per sample. On our data (771K samples with tools, 249K unique toolsets), Markdown uses 18.5% fewer tokens than JSON and XML 15.2% fewer. The savings are similar or larger on BFCL and τ2-bench toolsets. (b) Per-tool savings over the 747K unique tools in our data, grouped by the tool’s size in JSON. Markdown is shorter than JSON for 99.5% of tool uses. Small tools save the most (up to ∼48%), because JSON syntax makes up a larger share of them. Tools over 1K tokens save only about 7%. All averages are weighted by how often each tool or toolset occurs.

Figure 15: Predicting benchmark scores of large models from small-scale runs. Stage 1 fits a scaling law to each validation set’s loss over a grid of small models and evaluates it at the target model size P and token budget N . Stage 2 maps losses to each benchmark’s score with a sparse regression fitted on separate ablation runs, and is applied to the extrapolated losses. Shaded boxes are data; unshaded boxes are fitted models or inputs to them.

Figure 16: Production pre-training mixes by category (% of training tokens), using the categories of Table 16. Slices run clockwise from the top in legend order. Left: the mix used for the dense 3.7B, 7B, and 32B models and the 36B-A4B model. Right: the second-phase mix of the 375B-A23B model. Shares sum to 100 up to rounding.

Table 1: Architecture configurations of the K2-Horizon family. All models use SwiGLU feed-forward networks. Backbone counts exclude the input embedding and output projection matrices; total counts include both. For sparse models, the dense FFN dimension applies to the initial dense layers; subsequent layers use the listed expert configuration. FFN denotes a feed-forward network. Figure 18: Abbreviated annotated PR record. Selected fields are shown in a compact notation; ellipses mark omitted paths and diff context. Full records also contain base files, commit patches, events, annotation scores, and rationales.

Figure 12: A document is a dataset of tokens: each token is a label for the context before it. An error such as 2 + 2 = 5 is one mislabeled token, and the tokens around it remain correct labels. This is why we do not discard synthetic trajectories that contain mistakes.

Table 3: Mid-training recipe. All models use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. For each stage, the table lists the context length, the global batch size in tokens, the number of optimizer steps, the resulting token count in trillions, the peak learning rate, the number of warmup steps, and the weight decay. Weight decay is set once per model and shared across its stages, except the 0.9B model. Mid-training starts from the average of the final pre-training checkpoints: four spaced 1,500 steps apart for the 375B model (phase-2 steps 235,500 to 240,000), four spaced 4,000 steps apart for the 3.7B and 7B models (steps 1,088,000 to 1,100,000), and six spaced 5,000 steps apart for the 32B and 36B models (steps 1,075,000 to 1,100,000); the 0.9B model uses no averaging. Sequence lengths use k = 1,024 tokens. †Before stage 1, the 0.9B model runs a brief context-extension phase of about 2,000 steps on separate data, which is not listed in the table.

Table 40: Accuracy and TPF of Uno, Mercury 2, Diffusion-Gemma, and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion on agentic and non-agentic benchmarks. Subscripts report TPF. papers.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.
authors: Yong Liu, Zhanpeng Shi, Peicong Lin, Zhenyi Zhong, Yizhou Dang, Wendi Wu, Haoling Li, Shuangjia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the separation between biomolecular structure models and language models.

The structure head receives protein information only through the LLM’s residue states and achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808, 0.635, and 0.900 on three evaluated sets.
Compared with an ESM2-3B/SimpleFold-3B baseline, differences were inconclusive for 100–299-residue chains and lower for 300–600-residue chains.
Protein training reduced accuracy on the evaluated 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%.

papers.abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.
authors: Ruizhe Wang, Rui Liu, Hongliang Chen, Junyi Guo, Fangyu Wu, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets assembly hierarchy inference from individual parts and target illustrations.
Fuses a dedicated SVG encoder with representations from a pretrained vision-language model.
Uses RHPO to reward hierarchy-preserving equivalent solutions rather than only matching one reference tree.
Adds repair-cost feedback to prefer decisions requiring fewer downstream corrections.
Achieves the best Equivalent-Hard F1 among evaluated methods, including a 17.69-point gain over GPT6-Astra on an IKEA-derived test set, with strong independent-dataset performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Assembly architecture and RHPO training (a–c) The indexed parts and target drawing illustrate four assembly steps. Each resulting subassembly maps to an internal node of the reference tree, also shown in nested JSON. (d) For a fixed goal or action, unassisted rollouts estimate full success (Q) and tree quality (V). Separate repair rollouts estimate the mean number of subsequent repairs (C). At the first certified downstream error, the verifier rolls back, replaces the erroneous merge using the annotated graph and reference tree, and resumes the frozen policy. GRPO uses Q and V at both decision levels and favors lower repair cost among eligible candidates with near-best quality and a certified paired cost gap. Action-only distillation transfers probability mass from verified invalid actions to verified valid actions while preserving the mass on unknown actions.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices ("clients") while preserving data privacy. However, real-world deployments involve clients that observe continuous data streams from evolving environments while operating under strict resource limitations. Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.
authors: Manuel R\"oder, Frank-Michael Schleif
bullets: Targets local concept drift and global client drift caused by asynchronous, imbalanced participation.
Uses bounded-memory, lightweight sampling to select informative and diverse stream instances under limited labeling and compute budgets.
Embeds server guidance into local optimization as an update-level correction without discarding scarce labeled data.
Evaluated under gradual, sudden, and recurring drift; sampling and correction provide compounding benefits.
Improves the speed and robustness of global convergence in heterogeneous, resource-constrained settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of STORMGUIDE-FL from two perspectives, Data View and Intuition View, in an exemplary wildlife monitoring scenario. Both follow data point xt i, sensed from stream Ui on FL client Ci at timestep t. Accepted and annotated pairs (xt i, y t i) form the local training set Di for the Remote-Guided Local Model Update (Section 3.4), where the server remote guidance variate cS corrects every gradient step toward the global optimization trajectory. The resulting guided refinement θ⋆i is folded into the updated client variate c+i , and the deltas (∆θi,∆ci) are sent back to the FL server S for aggregation (Section 3.5).

papers.abstract: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further shows that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
authors: Qixuan Wu (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Xiaole Yang (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Yuguang Yang (School of Electronic and Information Engineering, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Canyu Chen (National College for Excellent Engineers, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Linlin Yang (Communication University of China, Beijing, China), Haixia Pan (School of Software, Beihang University, Beijing, China), Guodong Guo (Lane Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, West Virginia University, Morgantown, USA), Baochang Zhang (School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing, China)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating pretrained temporal video representations into existing VLA policies.
Uses linear test-time training to maintain a compact temporal visual state and retrieves action-conditioned features during flow-based generation.
Formulates flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem, solved with FISTA and approximated efficiently through diagonalization and rescaling.
Uses only 1.74–2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps.
Improves LingBot-VLA on RoboTwin 2.0 from 87.12% to 90.04% in clean settings and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomization; flow-step gating raises ablation success from 72.0% to 82.0%.

papers.abstract: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of . The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.
authors: Subham Kundu (TCG Crest)
bullets: Claude identified 3/4 Atari policies, detected copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, and recognized a sycophantic Gemma finetune in all 6 runs.
One-shot edits repaired MountainCar from 0% to 100% success and LunarLander from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps in 4/5 environments.
Without training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9×9 Go network winning 85–94% against three PPO opponents.
Editing Qwen3.5-0.8B with 10–50 practice-problem forward passes raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 58.1%, GSM8K to 68.2%, and IFEval to 54.2%.
Unlike the original study, edits targeted output behavior—mainly final-norm scaling and changing the “Wait” logit—and did not help Gemma, which rarely loops.

papers.abstract: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
authors: Yongji Fu, Yijiong Lin, Yi Zhou, Yi Qi, Guanqun Cao
bullets: Addresses sensor-dependent differences that hinder transferring representations and combining multi-sensor tactile data.
Uses multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training to learn shared spatiotemporal features.
Jointly trains on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction using paired videos from matched contact events.
Experiments show cross-sensor translation and transferability to downstream perception tasks.
Scope: applies to optical tactile videos and relies on paired cross-sensor observations of corresponding contacts.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of TacBridge. Multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training and event-paired cross-sensor learning yield a shared spatiotemporal tactile representation. The learned representation supports controllable tactile video generation conditioned on source-video features and target-sensor information. We further evaluate the learned representation on downstream tactile perception tasks and new real-world tactile data.

Fig. 3: Tactile attribute classification on a real robot. A robot arm presses a GelSight sensor on two fabrics and records one tactile reading per fabric. The frozen TacBridge encoder turns each reading into multi-layer patch tokens, and a linear probe trained on our real-robot fabric recordings maps them to 24 sigmoid attribute scores. Attributes reported as present are shown in blue and attributes reported as absent are struck through. The chips illustrate the output format with the annotated attributes of these two fabrics; the measured accuracy is reported in Table III. The encoder is not updated at any point.

Fig. 2: Target-conditioned tactile translation. Each row fixes one sourcecontact video, recorded by the sensor named in the row label: GelSight Mini, GelSlim, DIGIT, and a second GelSight Mini contact. Each column requests one target sensor: GelSight Mini, GelSlim, DIGIT, and GelSight. The cell outlined in orange is the recorded source frame and always lies in the column of that row’s own sensor, so it falls on the diagonal for the first three rows and returns to the GelSight Mini column for the fourth. Every other cell in a row is a decoding of the same latent under the target-sensor condition of its column. Switching that condition changes imaging colour, marker layout, and texture, while the contact location and deformation of the source are largely retained.

papers.abstract: In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.
authors: Wei Tang, Tong Wei, Jiahao Zhang, Min-Ling Zhang, Lijie Hu, Fakhri Karray
bullets: Unlabeled tasks provide only class names and images, making incorrect hard pseudo-labels prone to self-reinforcement.
The method corrects CLIP’s class-prior bias and refines predictions with a fixed-prior von Mises–Fisher mixture over whitened features.
Soft posterior targets train the classifier and select its fusion weight with CLIP via closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation.
Theoretical results show posterior targets best approximate true-label predictions in mean-square error; argmax mainly loses information on ambiguous images.
PACIL achieves the best average incremental accuracy across all 18 evaluated settings without labeled training data.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PACIL on task t. (1) Class-prior correction: the prior selection rule chooses P sel t between the raw and the debiased zero-shot distribution. (2) Posterior label-distribution estimation: EM of a vMF mixture on whitened features keeps P sel t as a fixed perimage prior and combines it with a tempered likelihood into the soft labels qi. (3) Soft-label analytic learning and fusion: the analytic classifier Wt is fitted to qi, and closed-form LOO selects the weight ωt that fuses it with zero-shot CLIP.

Figure 1. Discarded true labels and average accuracy. (a) Training images (%) whose true label is discarded when each keeps only its top-scored labels, on the first task of Aircraft (half-base), for zeroshot CLIP, N2L after three self-training refinements and PACIL. (b) Average accuracy Ā (%) of the methods of Table 1 on its zerobase (Z) and half-base (H) settings, each axis spanning the lowest (inner ring) to the highest value (outer ring). Numbers are the Ā of ZS-CLIP (gray), N2L (blue), and PACIL (red).

(c) ωt selected on each task (dots, mean over three runs) and its mean per setting (ticks). Bottom rows give the means over all settings, and in (c) the line spans the range of ωt.

Change in (a) Ā and (b) AT (%) relative to PACIL when hard pseudo-labels replace the label posteriors (Hard labels), the final EM is skipped (w/o EM) or run with L = I (w/o whitening), on the zero-base (Zero) and half-base (Half) settings of four datasets.

papers.tldr: PACIL improves unlabeled class-incremental learning by replacing brittle hard pseudo-labels with analytically refined soft label posteriors and using them to calibrate CLIP fusion.

papers.abstract: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.
authors: Zhichao Huang, Changheng Cai, Song Ren, Zhichen Zhao, Hongsen Liu, Chaoyang Zheng, Wenxi Wu, Yichen Long, Yuan Fang, Luya Wang, Gufeng Liu, Yuchen Wang
bullets: Addresses the need to prepare for handovers before an explicit response cue, while deciding whether to respond or cancel.
Maps frozen V-JEPA 2 features into a language decoder alongside native visual inputs, using only evidence available at each decision time.
EviBridge-E separates recent and historical evidence with timing and spatial information; EviBridge-I preserves temporal order and adds interaction tokens.
On FuGIBench, the best EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I variants score 0.6448 and 0.5892, versus 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective native baselines.
Benefits extend across target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests.

papers.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.
authors: Yuanyan Song, Kezhi Wang, Xinmian Xu, Yongmin Li
bullets: A supervisor agent decomposes user requests and dispatches subtasks to worker agents through parallel or serial workflows.
A two-level retry mechanism is used to improve execution reliability.
Energy minimization jointly optimizes agent selection and resource allocation while satisfying latency and QoS requirements.
An alternating-optimization scheme uses SCA, Lagrangian relaxation, Gale-Shapley or LLM-based selection, and KKT-based service-time allocation.
Simulations report lower energy consumption than benchmarks, while Qwen/Llama experiments show higher task execution success rates.

papers.abstract: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.
authors: Jhen-Ke Lin, Chung-Chun Wang
bullets: Tests whether models understand a scene as a whole rather than relying on local adjacency.
Evaluates piece count, interlocking geometry, and reconstruction of the reference scene separately.
All evaluated models produced plausible scenes globally but failed to maintain coherence across scattered pieces.
Models often miscounted pieces; without provided outlines, pieces rarely interlocked or reconstructed the reference.
Target layouts improved piece fitting, while reference images did not improve counting or fitting.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Every system draws the picture, but none scatters it as a jigsaw. Five generators receive the same brief (a forested island in a crater lake). Top: each system’s picture drawn whole, which a program then cuts into nine interlocking pieces. Bottom: the same system asked for the nine pieces scattered on a plain background, from text alone. Labels give the pieces found and the interlock score (Sec. 4). Each exact cut above has 9 pieces and scores .94. The scene is chosen by a fixed rule.

Figure 3. Each system falls short in its own way. (a) Share of outputs with too many pieces (up) or too few (down). The rest have exactly N . (b, c) Scores of single outputs. Boxes span the middle half of the outputs, whiskers the 5th to 95th percentile, and black bars mark the median. In (c), dashed and dotted segments are reference marks from Tab. 2, drawn at each N . Gray boxes are the whole-scene controls. Each system has 128 outputs per N in (a, b) and 64 in (c).
