papers.abstract: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.
authors: Patricia Pauli, Matthieu Barreau
bullets: Addresses the computational difficulty of training and verifying neural control Lyapunov functions (CLFs).
Uses Polyak–Lojasiewicz networks to represent nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates.
Constructs a surrogate closed-loop system that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by design.
Combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction inspired by Sontag’s universal formula.
Provides local and global stability guarantees and demonstrates effectiveness through numerical examples.

papers.abstract: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.
authors: Xue Yang, Haonan Cai, Xinyu Hang, Zhimeng Huang, Xuanyi Liu, Chuanmin Jia, Siwei Ma
bullets: Introduces paired scientific experiments with mutually exclusive expected outcomes and a single changed condition.
Evaluates ten text-and-image-to-video models using an independent vision-language model blinded to prompts and labels.
Scores a pair as correct only when both videos show the scientifically correct outcomes.
Finds that models often generate the same outcome for both conditions, indicating unreliable scientific reasoning.
The benchmark dataset and evaluation code will be publicly released.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.
authors: Zheng Wang, Yuang Liu, Sachith Abeywickrama, Yangkai Ding, Tao Yu, Xinyu Zhang, Hongbo Wang, Qi Ye, Xuefeng Jin, Zhangchun Zhao
bullets: Addresses error propagation, high computation, and limited parallelism in sequential multi-agent refinement.
Uses latent-space intra-agent convolution to jointly refine related features.
Uses inter-agent graph convolution to exchange information according to collaboration topology.
Reports 5.04% higher performance, 17.27% lower inference cost, and 45.11% lower latency than RecursiveMAS on MATH-500.
Supports diverse collaboration patterns through adjacency-matrix representations.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions. Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data. We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities. Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98\% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2\% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56\%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8\% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.
authors: Murad Dawood, Oezge Drama Berkenkamp, Antonio Gonzales Marin, Nutan Chen
bullets: Addresses the need for reference trajectories at runtime and poor transferability in conventional whole-body imitation.
Trains with whole-body tracking rewards and a privileged critic, while withholding reference joint trajectories from the actor and avoiding teacher distillation.
Encodes demonstrated style directly into a velocity-conditioned policy from a single random-walk motion.
Achieves at least 98% simulated success and completes every Unitree G1 trial under held-out velocity profiles.
Scope: performance degrades substantially on held-out slow walking, where competing tracking and distillation methods also fail on hardware.

papers.title: Driving the Style: Velocity-Conditioned Whole-Body Control from Motion Demonstrations

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.
authors: Jiameng Li, Minye Wu, Matthew B. Blaschko
bullets: Targets computational redundancy among activated experts in MoE multimodal large language models.
Uses query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and modality-specific thresholds for each layer.
Calibrates skipping by minimizing masked reconstruction error relative to default expert activation.
Improves over existing expert-skipping methods across 9 benchmarks, especially under aggressive skipping.
On KimiVL-A3B-Inst, retains over 96% performance with 83% expert skipping and achieves 1.7× faster prefilling.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.
authors: Jingkai Shang, Edgar Torres, Duy Nguyen
bullets: Addresses varying local reconstruction difficulty under a shared solver budget.
Optimizes a continuous per-patch step budget using differentiable soft rollouts and geometric fidelity.
Projects optimized budgets to discrete values for the final flow-matching rollout.
Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN report strong reconstruction quality and support patch-specific allocation as the source of benefit.
The method is accuracy-oriented and incurs additional test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.
authors: Jeremy Baffou, Pascal Frossard, Dorina Thanou
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of multiple dynamical patterns in latent representations and the lack of graph-based generation in regime-inference methods.
Factorizes latent states into discrete system-level regimes and continuous entity-level dynamics.
Uses inferred regimes to condition system dynamics, supporting regime tracking and simulations under alternative modes.
Learns forecasts and regimes self-supervised, without regime annotations.
Recovers meaningful modes on controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Model architecture. A) Framework: At each time step, the model first updates the deterministic recurrent state ht. Conditioned on this state, the encoder infers the regime rt and the entity latents zit . Together with ht, they are then used by the decoder to predict the next-step features Xt+1. B) Encoder: The encoder proceeds hierarchically. A GNN first extracts node- and graph-level embeddings (embit, embGt ), which are used to infer the regime rt via a transition module. This regime then conditions a mixture-of-experts (MoE) to produce the entity-level latent states zit.

Figure 1: Example of regime-conditioned graph rollouts. A) The system can evolve according to distinct dynamics referred to as regimes. B) Given an observed graph sequence acting as context, we forecast future node features while inferring the latent regime trajectory that conditions the rollout. The regime exposes which dynamical mode drives the predictions and allows alternative regime-aware futures beyond forecasting alone.

Figure 3: Hierarchical state representation. Entity-level embeddings are aggregated and combined with the global state hGt to infer a latent regime rt that governs system-wide dynamics. This regime then conditions a MoE module to produce entity-level latent states zit, linking global behavior and individual evolution.

Figure 4: Regime-conditioned rollout probes. From a shared context, we clamp regimes during rollout. Dashed lines show regimespecific trajectories; the solid line is the observed future. Regime names are assigned post hoc from dominant motion patterns.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
authors: Tom A. Lamb, Philip H. S. Torr, Tim G. J. Rudner
bullets: Targets the lack of formal reliability guarantees for LLM judges used in safety-critical oversight.
Defines judge risk on safety classifications of prompt–response pairs from a deployed generator.
Combines tighter PAC-Bayes bounds with efficient parameter coding and standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning, without a validation holdout.
Introduces LoRA-GT, a shared-scale quantisation method that achieves the tightest certificates with minimal predictive degradation.
Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, certificate tightness depends more on adaptation complexity than base-model scale; excessive quantisation eventually harms risk.

papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.
authors: Xudong Ling, Wenjie Luo, Chaorong Li, Tianxi Huang, Tao He, Guiduo Duan
bullets: Addresses the cost and blurring caused by independently sampled generative ensemble forecasts.
Uses a vision-language model to generate a textual storm-evolution scenario that conditions a Rectified Flow generator.
Shares early sampling steps across ensemble members, then branches with fresh noise for local convective details.
Uses support-consensus decoding instead of pixel averaging to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores.
Across six datasets, achieves the best high-threshold CSI, with reported relative gains of over 10%–84%; an 8-member ensemble costs 5.2× rather than 8× a single forecast.

papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.
authors: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee, Dylan Campbell, Rahul Shome
bullets: Addresses the blind PnP problem for calibrated cameras with unknown correspondences.
Fourteen image moments up to order four identify the pose for almost every noiseless 3D point set with at least 20 points.
Uses a learning-free moment-matching initialization, followed by joint pose and correspondence-weight refinement.
Across three benchmarks, reduces median rotation error by 5–170× versus the best learned baseline, with and without outliers.
Remains accurate with as many outliers as inliers; on dense ETH3D scans, accuracy improves with larger point sets.

papers.abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.
authors: Biwen Yang, Zhe Cao, Jin Zhang, Haoyang Sun, Zonglu Hu, Jintao Zhao, Zhehao Zhang, Kaizheng Chen, Chengyi Liu, Chengyu Wei, Siyuan Wu, Ruiheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the problem that retained, transported, or subsurface heat can affect later contact outcomes.
Tracks spatial and depth-resolved thermal state for both contact partners through contact, transport, and separation.
Produces synchronized RGB-thermal observations, states, actions, and event-level task checks on one execution clock.
Provides a paired six-task benchmark with 4,448 trajectories and integrations for MuJoCo and Isaac Sim.
Reported studies show improved contact-site selection with visible thermal history and higher transfer completion when training uses dynamic histories.

papers.abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.
authors: Markus Peschl, Dana Kianfar, Daniel Dijkman
bullets: High-fidelity generalization to unseen motions is compute-intensive due to interference across diverse motion tasks.
Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP) introduces a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state–reference pairs.
It outperforms on-policy and off-policy RL baselines in simulation and real-world tracking across multiple datasets, by up to 10%.
The work establishes a QTOP scaling law and reports limited dataset-size impact in moderately sized GPU-hour regimes.

papers.abstract: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.
authors: Yeon-Jae Kim, Sangwon Kang, Byung-Kwon Min
bullets: Addresses assembly when parts lack shared coordinate frames, consistent scales, and predefined inter-part relationships.
Optimizes each part’s translation, rotation, and scale using a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model.
Uses same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic representation to provide structurally aligned transformation gradients.
Requires no part-layout annotations, category-specific priors, assembly training, or bounding-box initialization.
Outperforms supported geometric-registration and compositional-layout baselines in part-wise transformation estimation; ablations identify view-aligned conditioning as critical.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.
authors: Haozhe Zhu, Dan Yuan, Chenghao Gu, Feike Xu, Yue Wen, Shin'ichi Konomi
bullets: Benchmarks 11 open- and closed-source VLMs using 620 questions across 13 subtasks and three EEG capabilities.

The strongest evaluated model scores only 41.63% overall, with cross-modal EEG alignment as a major bottleneck.
Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can improve recognition of EEG patterns and connect them to neurological knowledge.

papers.abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.
authors: Tao Tao, Anke Tang, Enneng Yang, Zhi Hou, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Targets storage growth from separately deploying specialists and interference from dense weight merging.
Retains each specialist’s feed-forward block as a routable expert and compresses experts with a shared floating-point anchor plus binary, row-scaled deviations.
Uses closed-form alternating factorization from source weights alone, then adapts token-level routing by updating fewer than 0.6M parameters.
Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, it uses 20.3 GB—1.16× one dense specialist and 59.6% less than the uncompressed MoE.
Across 22 benchmarks and R2R, factorization is nearly lossless on 21/22 benchmarks; VSI-Bench is the main exception, likely due to weaker cross-frame evidence use.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.
authors: Shenghao Xiong, Xiaolin Chang
bullets: Temporal inconsistency between modalities can corrupt fused representations and cause driving-policy failures.
STA jointly optimizes when to delay observations and which modality to attack, using historical states instead of modality-specific noise.
The method uses clean policy actions to identify sensitive decision patterns and includes theoretical analysis of distribution shift and modality selection.
In CARLA, STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest PPO baseline with 17.8% fewer attack attempts and also generalizes to a VLM-based policy.
The results emphasize temporal consistency and robustness as important for safe autonomous driving.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed Split Temporal Adversary (STA). At each time step, the adversary observes the current state and driving policy information, then decides whether to attack based on the attack budget and policy awareness. If activated, it selects which modality to manipulate (visual or numerical) and replaces the selected modality with a delayed observation from the history buffer. This creates cross-modal temporal misalignment that leads to erroneous control decisions by the driving policy.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.
authors: Manan Suri, Dinesh Manocha
bullets: Addresses growing costs, extraction errors, and missed cross-session patterns in text-based memory systems.
Uses a recurrent hypernetwork and gated latent state to consolidate session knowledge into a fixed-size adapter.
Combines consolidated parametric memory with verbatim episodic retrieval for complementary recall and detail.
Outperforms reported agentic and gradient-based baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three 2–7B open models.
Builds memory 3–151× faster than extraction systems and improves accuracy by 12–15 points when episodic retrieval misses evidence, and 4–5 points with an oracle buffer.

papers.abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Shangchen Zhou, Wenzheng Zeng, Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Organizes 114 robotic reward-model methods into five families: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid.
Identifies a gap in common evaluations: demonstration-order agreement and policy gains may not measure task fulfillment.
Introduces RRM-Bench-1K, containing 1,117 real-robot videos with task-state and camera-evidence labels plus four contrast suites.
Across 27 evaluators, final scores rank whole executions effectively, while dense credit more often tracks temporal progression than task state.
Releases RRM-Hub, supporting 14 existing reward models and standardized capability testing; needed fidelity depends on the downstream decision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor's estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.
authors: Margaux Edwards, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
bullets: Targets unnecessary processing and sensing when the primary sensor is already sufficient, improving efficiency and supporting application constraints such as passive stealth.
Uses the primary sensor’s match score to estimate when performance is poor and selectively acquire the second sensor.
An online threshold adapts to a user-specified second-sensor usage rate without modality-, PR-method-, or environment-specific calibration.
Works with both single-frame and sequence-based place recognition across multiple datasets, descriptors, and sensor combinations.
Recovers 55% of the available gain at 25% second-sensor usage and 81% at 50%.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.
authors: Haixiang Wu, Zhihao Guan, Yang Yang
bullets: Equal fusion can overwhelm proprioception despite its rich dynamic information; inter-joint coupling is identified as the key action-determining structure.
Inverted State Encoding forms a proprioceptive prior with per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention.
State-Visual Grounding allows joint tokens to query visual evidence for goal and calibration information.
Inverted Action Chunking independently decodes per-joint trajectories.
ACiT improves success on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, especially those requiring dynamics and coordination; the design also improves pi_0 execution efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ACiT architecture, organized by its three modules. (a) Inverted State Encoding: per-joint depthwise 1D convolutions turn each joint’s history into one token, and self-attention among the tokens gives the proprioceptive prior Pt . (b) State-Visual Grounding: the joint tokens query the visual tokens of the multi-view observations and produce grounded tokens Gt . (c) Inverted Action Chunking: Gt is the memory of a transformer decoder whose learnable joint queries output one T -step trajectory per joint.

Figure 11: The six RoboTwin 2.0 tasks used in Sec. 4.2, viewed from the head camera. Both arms are visible in each panel; the randomized split varies object poses, colors and the background of the same scenes.
Figure 12: Out-of-distribution dark background. ACT, DP, FM and ACiT on the four tasks under the background shift.

Figure 1: Motivation. (a) Embodiment: a dual-arm robot has 14 joints, each with its own state history, while the action space has a much lower effective dimensionality (PR 1.44–4.42) and strong inter-joint coupling, the state therefore should not be compressed into one shared vector. (b) Biological inspiration: proprioception forms a body-centered prior in S1, vision reaches PPC via V1 only to remap and calibrate the goal, and M1 issues the command. The two modalities are not symmetric, and their order is fixed. (c) Conditioning interface: ACT concatenates a single-frame state with vision into one condition shared by all joints; ACiT keeps the per-joint prior as the primary condition, retrieves visual evidence per joint, and decodes one trajectory per joint.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.
authors: Jiaming Jiang, Yuzhe Huang, Baokun Yang, Hao Liang, Li Gao, Haoran Guo, Pei Lin, Shengcheng Luo, Chenxi Xiao, Wanlin Li, Ziyuan Jiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring tactile models across sensors with different mechanisms and observation formats.
Pairs observations from 24 sensors across four sensing families with wrench measurements, avoiding direct tactile-to-tactile pairing.
Uses sensor-specific input adaptation and a shared encoder trained to reconstruct wrenches, producing a common physical feature space.
Improves single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baselines.
TaF-Policy combines tactile features with vision and robot states, achieving higher average success on the reported simulated and real-world task sets.

(b) Six-dimensional wrench reconstruction and alignment with EMA wrench embeddings provide shared physical supervision. The learned representations are evaluated on single-frame wrench estimation, temporal wrench estimation with historical wrench inputs, cross-sensor retrieval, and robotic manipulation using TaF-Policy in simulation and the real world.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.
authors: Hengrui Liu, Wenbo Xu, Ziqi Sheng, Wei lu
bullets: Addresses high inference latency caused by long conditioning and video token sequences.
Training-free routing adapts computation across sources such as videos, images, audio, text, and generated content.
Balances attention mass and approximation risk to select source-specific thresholds per query.
Achieves up to 1.46× end-to-end speedup in video editing while preserving editing quality and unedited regions.
Also applies to Reference-to-Video generation, achieving up to 1.36× speedup without degrading quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of QASK-Edit. The process begins with the generation of summaries for blocks, sub-blocks, and second-level sub-blocks. For each query tile, we independently select a routing threshold for each key source within the risk budget, based on the residual risk introduced by approximate calculations. This routing threshold then determines whether to perform exact or approximate calculations. Finally, we aggregate the contributions of all key sources into a single softmax and output the final result.

Figure 1. Qualitative video editing results of QASK-Edit on MiniMax-H3. Three sampled frames are shown for each source–edited video pair, covering diverse editing tasks such as clothing modification, object replacement, and scene recoloring. papers.tldr: QASK-Edit accelerates diffusion-transformer video editing by adaptively sparsifying attention for each query and key source while preserving quality and fidelity.

papers.abstract: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.
authors: Wei Tan, Kunming Luo, Hongyu Yan, Yu Zhang, Zihao Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Lei Xie
bullets: Targets the computational cost of cross-view attention, which grows with the number of views and spatial resolution.
Maintains full-resolution attention within each view and uses compact proxies for communication across views.
Iteratively rebuilds and refines proxies, reusing attention parameters during each denoising step.
Across FLUX and Stable Diffusion backbones, GLPA improves efficiency and multi-view reconstruction quality.
On FLUX, it provides a 2.65× attention-computation speedup, higher reconstruction IoU, and lower NVS LPIPS; Stable Diffusion shows a 1.80× speedup and improvements on all five reported metrics.

papers.tldr: GLPA accelerates consistent multi-view image and normal-map generation by replacing costly dense cross-view attention with refined global proxies while preserving detailed within-view processing.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
authors: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang
bullets: The study traces every token commit from four off-the-shelf DLMs across math, code, translation, and summarization tasks.
Most tokens become confident near the leftmost masked position, so frontier-only committing retains similar speed while reducing premature commitments.
Committing one token per step does not fix errors caused by committing ahead of the frontier.
Fallback commits make up 11–35% of commits and initiate 61–72% of failures avoided by left-to-right decoding.
Early end-of-sequence commits can truncate answers; changing the failure-starting step repairs errors more often than changing an earlier step.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes threshold decoding behavior in diffusion language models, relevant to LLM decoding and efficiency.
papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Threshold decoding in diffusion language models is fast but loses accuracy mainly when it commits tokens ahead of the left-to-right frontier, especially through fallback decisions.

papers.abstract: Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG (Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects, with 1.7~million joint configurations across 793 objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object's point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4\% lift success on training and 69.9\% on held-out objects, and it lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.
authors: Xinyi Yu, Yunshuang Li, Daniel Seita, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the lack of whole-arm grasp data and the difficulty of teleoperating wrapping motions for large-object pickup.

Uses a diffusion model to generate whole-arm grasps from object point clouds, combined with collision-free motion planning and squeeze-and-lift execution.
Achieves 85.4% lift success on training objects and 69.9% on held-out objects in simulation.
On a physical Franka arm, successfully lifts objects in 70 of 100 trials across 10 IKEA objects.

(b) Motion planning. The arm follows an RRT-Connect path to the selected arm grasp configuration, and the same squeeze-and-lift execution completes the pickup.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, yet the learning benefits of longer trajectories may not scale proportionally with their computational cost. We investigate how supervision utility evolves with trajectory length. Controlled experiments reveal diminishing returns from additional supervised tokens, while showing that later positions remain learnable and exhibit substantial cross-position supervision transfer. Gradient analysis further identifies shared update components across response positions and diverse position-specific residuals whose cross-rollout consistency decreases at greater depths. Motivated by these findings, we propose Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD), which reduces redundant supervision by randomly varying rollout horizons while preserving access to deeper response states. SH-OPD samples a shared horizon for each training batch, enabling efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling overhead. We characterize the resulting reweighting bias and derive a compute-reweighting trade-off under standard optimization assumptions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that SH-OPD achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of the per-update cost of standard OPD, while maintaining competitive code generation performance at around 60% of the baseline cost. These results highlight the benefits of efficient supervision allocation across response depths.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.
authors: Kangjie Zhou, Sukai Wang, Yuhan Xiao, Qinghang Liu, Zhejia Wen, ChunXuan Jiao, Wei Shan, Guanghui Ren, Maoqing Yao, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses executor drift and unreliable stopping decisions that can cause errors to propagate across subtasks.
Uses plan–execute–verify–recover cycles with a progress verifier that confirms subtask completion and triggers dual-phase recovery after route deviations.
Co-trains the executor on action prediction and progress reasoning to improve progress awareness and corrective control.
Adapts training through a two-stage curriculum using expert demonstrations, corrections, progress supervision, and policy-generated trajectories.
Achieves state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods without additional navigation datasets on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with further validation in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed closed-loop agentic framework with test-time verification and recovery. Two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum learning, which clones expert actions and then co-trains intra- and inter-subtask on-policy action corrections with progress-reasoning supervision, produces the low-level VLN executor, while the high-level multimodal agent maintains landmark memory and accepted anchors and orchestrates subtask planning, progress verification, and dual-phase failure recovery.

Fig. 1. Comparison of long-horizon VLN execution paradigms. End-toend policies map the complete route instruction and visual observations directly to actions, with route progress implicitly inferred within the action policy. Hierarchical planner–executor pipelines without outcome verification dispatch local subtasks and advance based on executor termination. Our LeaP-VLN couples progress-aware execution with progress verification and dual-phase recovery to ground subtask transitions in observed outcomes and limit error propagation.

For every subtask, the egocentric observation is paired with the corresponding top-down map, where the colored trajectory indicates the agent’s stage-wise navigation progress. In the top example, the agent sequentially executes all subtasks and successfully reaches the target location. papers.abstract: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.
authors: Jiaxing Zhao, Hanwen Wang, Di Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Jing-Ran Su, Yanheng Li, Qian Zha, Jiaxi Li, Hongbin Xie, Haoran Zhang, Xuan Song, Haoxuan Che
bullets: Addresses the limits of textual self-evolution, which cannot reliably enforce action admissibility for discrete or irreversible actions.
Synthesizes Grounded Executable Action Rules (GEAR) from execution feedback.
Represents rules as typed specifications, compiles them into deterministic guards, and validates them offline via trajectory replay.
Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; violations fall from 70% to 0% on ScienceWorld and 40% to 1% on WebShop.
Reported score gains are +10.1 on ScienceWorld and +8.0 on WebShop.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are often evaluated by converting model outputs into discrete answers. The conversion protocol determines which scores become predictions and can strongly influence the reported results. We introduce RAMP (Readout Aware Multimodal Protocol), a systematic framework that compares direct yes/no token logits, surface-form scores, and typed or reversed A/B interfaces under fixed model checkpoints and paired visual questions. On 500 POPE adversarial questions, typed versus bare readout changes accuracy by $-20.2$ percentage points for SmolVLM-256M, $-16.4$ for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and $+1.8$ for Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Paired transitions reveal extensive prediction changes even when the net accuracy difference is small: 79 of 104 binary ChartQA items change correctness for SmolVLM-500M, despite a $+1.0$-point net difference. We further analyze prompt wording, candidate forms, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration. An independent offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions from saved raw scores with exact agreement. Our findings establish answer readout as a measurable component of multimodal evaluation and provide a reproducible protocol for analyzing model comparisons.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.
authors: Barkin Dagda, Vinal Asodia, Iman Sharifi, Peng Wei, Saber Fallah
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate action prediction and explicit traffic-law compliance in VLA driving policies.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.

papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.
authors: Angel Martinez-Sanchez, Ross Greer
bullets: Distinguishes prospective instructions given before actions from retrospective labels written after observing them.
Introduces ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road video, and vehicle trajectories.

papers.abstract: While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Younghwan Kil, Joonhyeong Park, Giung Nam, Juho Lee
bullets: Addresses quality and semantic drift caused by indiscriminate global safety interventions in text-to-image diffusion models.
Uses probabilistic monitoring to activate suppression only when harmful content is detected.
Applies Grad-CAM for spatially localized removal of harmful concepts.
Introduces a VLM-based evaluation framework to assess both safety and context preservation beyond NudeNet.
Reports improved safety–fidelity balance and plug-and-play compatibility with existing safety frameworks.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models often synthesize policy-violating content, necessitating robust safeguards and rigorous evaluation frameworks. However, current approaches remain largely monolithic in both execution and evaluation, limited to coarse-grained categorization within broad unsafe concepts. Such approaches fail to account for the specific constituent factors of a violation, resulting in weak learning signals and allowing model collapse to bypass safety checks. To overcome these limitations, we propose Example-Based Spatial Guidance (EBSG), a training-free method that utilizes user-editable exemplar packs to provide granular spatial guidance for precise concept steering. Unlike existing methods that coarsely steer the entire image away from a broad concept, EBSG decomposes these categories into specific sub-concepts via exemplar text-image pairs, providing explicit, localized steering signals for more robust safety control. Furthermore, we introduce a vision language model (VLM)-based evaluation protocol that provides a fine-grained assessment, avoiding the pitfall of conventional binary evaluators that permit model collapse to bypass safety checks. Empirically, EBSG achieves state-of-the-art erasure performance across diverse safety datasets and concept categories, spanning four nudity benchmarks, seven I2P harmful-concept slices, and four MJA metaphor categories, while supporting multi-concept removal and transferring to a modern backbone, SD3.
authors: Younghwan Kil, Giung Nam, Joonhyeong Park, Jinwoo Shin, Juho Lee
bullets: Targets weaknesses in coarse, monolithic safety methods that overlook the constituent factors of unsafe concepts.
Decomposes broad concepts into specific sub-concepts using exemplar text-image pairs, producing localized steering signals.
Introduces a fine-grained VLM-based evaluation protocol designed to reduce loopholes from binary safety evaluators and model collapse.
Reports state-of-the-art erasure performance across multiple nudity, harmful-concept, and metaphor benchmarks.
Supports multi-concept removal and transfer to the SD3 diffusion backbone.
