papers.abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning seeks to minimize joint risk over all seen tasks, yet historical data are unavailable for direct optimization. We observe that, for classification, preserving the model's decisions on previously learned classes helps retain old knowledge. This motivates Decision-Preserving Regularization (DPR). Penalizing changes in all pairwise old-class logit margins reduces algebraically to a centered relative-logit penalty. We further apply spectral whitening to remove the classifier's spectral scale bias. Because the global classifier supplies the decision constraints for the next stage, it must remain calibrated across all seen classes despite the drift of stored old-class statistics during representation updates. We therefore fit a closed-form affine map from paired current-task features to transport old-class Gaussian means and covariances into the updated feature space, then calibrate the global classifier using these distributions and current-task features. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1K under cold-start protocols, comparisons with state-of-the-art methods show that DPR achieves higher accuracy in most settings while remaining highly efficient. Code is available at https://github.com/bnufw/dpr.
authors: Qi Zhu, Ziang Gan, Wanting Zhang, Libao Zhang
bullets: Targets the loss of old-class knowledge when historical exemplars are unavailable.
Regularizes pairwise old-class logit margins, yielding a centered relative-logit penalty, and applies spectral whitening to reduce scale bias.
Uses a closed-form affine transport to update stored old-class Gaussian statistics after feature drift.
Calibrates the global classifier with transported old-class distributions and current-task features.
Across four benchmarks and cold-start protocols, DPR reports higher accuracy in most settings with low computational cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DPR. (a) Decision-preserving regularization preserves pairwise old-class margins while allowing a shared logit shift. Spectral whitening of the centered old classifier yields a basis V for uniformly penalizing feature drift along old-class discriminative directions during new-class learning. (b) A closed-form affine map fitted to paired current-task features compensates stored old-class means and covariances for representation drift. Gaussian old-class features sampled from the compensated statistics are combined with real current-task features to calibrate the global head WT for unified inference and next-stage decision regularization.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).
authors: Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu, Ji Liu
bullets: Expert pruning reduces GPU memory but can lose the functions of removed experts.
GEAR gates and reuses scaled outputs from reliable activated experts to reconstruct pruned-expert behavior.
GEAR² adds an ultra-lightweight missing-mass residual for functionality that reuse cannot capture.
Across five 16B–106B MoE LLMs and 25%–50% pruning, it improves over baselines on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with gains up to 2.75 percentage points.
The approach is evaluated specifically in training-free, aggressively pruned MoE settings.

papers.abstract: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.
authors: Runzhe Wang, Huilin Lu, Shengjie Liu, Li Dong, Zhihuai Zhu
bullets: Naively accumulating cross-task memory can hurt performance, sometimes performing worse than a memoryless ReAct agent.
Before each action, the agent predicts an expected outcome; a concurrent critic compares the result with that expectation and records a binary reward plus reflection.
Each procedural memory entry receives an online-updated utility score under a noisy-OR model, guiding retrieval, eviction, and merging.
Across 707 AgentBoard tasks in eight domains, AdMem solved 441 tasks versus 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline.
The human-readable memory is auditable and diagnosable, but also presents an attackable surface; gains concentrate where cross-task structure transfers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Information flow between the environment, the actor, the critic, and the long-term memory store. The three modules run in separate threads: the actor never blocks on the critic, so memory writing and evaluation overlap with acting. The actor’s short-term memory (STM) holds the task instructions, the task and memory tool specifications, and the current task’s short-term trace, with environment facts surfaced through a priority-ranked semantic heap and event summaries through a scope-ordered episodic stack (Section 2.3); retrieved long-term memory (LTM) enters the same context. Every action the actor sends to the critic carries the expectation the actor committed to before acting, which is what the critic scores the realized outcome against; the resulting per-action reward travels to the store alongside the new procedural entry and updates the utilities of the entries that were retrieved for that action (Section 2.4).

Table 1: Task completeness (C, the fraction of tasks solved) and average progress (P, the mean of the per-task progress score pi ∈ [0, 1]) on the eight AgentBoard domains, using Claude Haiku 4.5 as the backbone for every method. Bold marks the best value in each column. Each domain is a fixed task set of the size given in the second row, so completion counts are recoverable exactly from C (e.g. 63.4% of 134 is 85 tasks); we use those counts for the Fisher exact tests reported in the text. Each configuration is streamed once over the task set in a single lifelong episode. On the three 20-task domains a single task is worth 5.0 points of C, which is why we base per-domain conclusions on the tests rather than on the point differences alone.

Table 2: Aggregate view of Table 1 over all 707 tasks. Intervals are Wilson 95% binomial intervals on the pooled completion rate. Macro-avg. C weights the eight domains equally rather than by task count; we report both because WebShop and ScienceWorld together hold 48% of the tasks. Against ReAct, the pooled difference is significant for AdMem (+53 tasks, two-sided Fisher exact p = 5× 10−3) and significant in the negative direction for AWM (−76 tasks, p = 7 × 10−5). Because all three methods are run over the same 707 tasks, both comparisons are paired; both remain significant under the least favorable exact McNemar test consistent with these margins (p = 0.03 and p = 5× 10−3 respectively, Appendix C).

LTP: the long-term procedural store only — per-step retrieval with critic-generated reflections and the reward-based utility retained — with short-term planning and context management removed. AdMem: all components. STP and ReAct are single-epoch by construction, since neither carries anything across tasks. For LTP and AdMem the task set is streamed again each epoch without resetting the long-term store, so the epoch axis measures accumulation rather than repetition of a fixed store; entry utilities carry over with the store, so an entry that proved unhelpful in an earlier epoch enters the next one already down-weighted.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.

papers.abstract: Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited. To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving. The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants. We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance. Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios. ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
authors: Saksham Gupta, Michael Li
bullets: Speculative decoding normally stores target and draft KV caches, creating substantial extra memory use.
The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, preserving the target model’s correction rule.
The proposed K4V4 scheme uses per-channel keys and per-token values, co-designing precision with quantizer layout.
Across six model pairs, draft-cache memory falls 66.20% and total cache memory 23.95%.

papers.abstract: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

papers.abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.

papers.abstract: Semantic visual classification commonly aligns visual embeddings with semantic spaces induced by pretrained text encoders. However, such spaces are typically high-dimensional, weakly aligned with visual feature geometry, and insufficiently discriminative for downstream classification tasks. We propose TaSS, a framework for learning a task-adaptive low-dimensional semantic space that preserves semantic structure while explicitly optimizing class separability. TaSS is constructed through a parameterized geometry transformation of pretrained text embeddings that enlarges inter-class margins via distance reshaping and improves intra-class compactness through prototype-preserving semantic constraints. The resulting semantic space maintains meaningful semantic relationships while producing a discriminative geometry tailored for classification. Frozen visual encoder features are subsequently aligned to TaSS using a lightweight MLP, enabling improved discriminative learning without fine-tuning pretrained backbones. We further provide theoretical analysis showing that TaSS preserves semantic consistency while enforcing enhanced inter-class separation and controlled intra-class variance. Extensive experiments on skeleton-based human action recognition, video classification, and image classification benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing semantic alignment approaches, with gains exceeding 3 percentage points on average and up to 8.5 points on challenging datasets.
authors: Nikalal Kaldera, Wanqing Li, Chris Bunn, Philip O. Ogunbona

papers.abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift
authors: Geunsoo Song, Jiwon Seo, Hoeseok Yang, Youngmin Yi

papers.abstract: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.
authors: Haolun Ma, Ziyi Liu, Zizhuo Xu, Chuhan Hu, Lei Li
bullets: Frames trajectory rendering as spatial data management: anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared data.
Uses anchor and occluder indexes to query holed frustums, avoiding decoding anchors that are out of view or provably occluded.
Shares decoded Gaussians across consecutive views, decoding each requested anchor once per view group while preserving per-view selection.
Employs a hybrid CPU–GPU pipeline to balance selection and grouped decoding under bounded memory.
Experiments on large-scale public scenes report substantially lower trajectory-rendering latency with preserved image quality.

papers.abstract: Visual adversarial perturbations can substantially impair large vision-language models (LVLMs) despite introducing only subtle input changes. To understand how these small changes cause substantial errors, we investigate their optimization and propagation through the model, revealing two key findings. First, stronger attacks rely on finer iterative optimization, while subtle input perturbations induce representation discrepancies that are amplified layer by layer through the vision encoder and persist in the language model. Second, disrupting the alignment between within-patch input patterns and the model's computation reduces clean-adversarial representation discrepancies and substantially weakens attacks. Together, these findings suggest that adversarial effectiveness depends on both fine-grained perturbation patterns and their coupling with the model's computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SmoothShift, a lightweight, training-free defense that combines local smoothing and spatial transformations. Smoothing weakens fine-grained perturbation patterns, while spatial transformations disrupt their alignment with the encoder's patch grid. SmoothShift requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or additional model inference. Experiments cover three LVLM families on four datasets and robustly fine-tuned Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models on eight classification datasets. Evaluations across eight attack methods and multiple perturbation budgets demonstrate improved robustness while largely preserving clean performance. SmoothShift also provides robustness gains under defense-aware attacks using mixed-gradient BPDA with EOT.
authors: Xiaoqing Chen, Jiayi Ouyang, Dongrui Wu
bullets: Adversarial attacks exploit subtle perturbations whose representation discrepancies are amplified through the vision encoder and persist into the language model.
Attack strength depends on fine-grained iterative optimization and the coupling between perturbation patterns and model computation.
SmoothShift combines local smoothing with spatial transformations to weaken perturbation patterns and disrupt patch-grid alignment.
It requires no model updates, auxiliary networks, or extra model inference.
Across multiple LVLM and CLIP settings, attack methods, and perturbation budgets, it improves robustness while largely preserving clean performance, including against defense-aware attacks.

papers.abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.
authors: Yuanhang Gao, Xiangrui Yang, Lingyuan Meng, Yuanfeng Chen, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Generic latent KV compression requires costly reconstruction before RoPE and attention during decoding.
Exact execution requires the latent map to preserve RoPE rotations, allowing mixing only among coordinates with shared frequencies.
GaugeRoPE combines a RoPE-compatible carrier with an approximate position-independent residual key–value correction.
The training-free method achieves 5.85× KV compression on Mistral-7B with quality close to the full-cache baseline.
Direct latent execution provides up to 2.48× the decode throughput of the uncompressed baseline; results also extend to MHA.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $\delta_1$ < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.
authors: Hualie Jiang, Yujie Luo, Ziyang Song, Ximeng Li, Zhiqiang Lou, Rui Xu
bullets: Average scores hide severe, directional, and shared failures across images and models.
The proposed evaluation separates failure rate, structural accuracy, and scale bias, dispersion, and error, while identifying shared versus model-specific failures.
Across 18 evaluations on 4,406 images, the best failure rate remains 7.7%; 78.8% of failures retain intact structure and 98.3% disappear after scale correction.
Failures shared by many architectures are concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; objects, ground-truth intrinsics, and larger models often reduce—but do not eliminate—them.
The authors recommend reporting per-image failure rates, separate structure/scale metrics, and results stratified by the number of failing models.

papers.abstract: Proposal-conditioned scene predictions can lack a common object-level reference across candidate trajectories. Aggregate planning scores also leave the objects and times associated with violations implicit. We present WTR-Drive (World-Task-Risk Driving), a Drive-JEPA-based planner that separates shared scene estimation from proposal-conditioned reasoning. A proposal-independent World Memory estimates object states, map structure, and future motion by re-reading the original visual features at each refinement round. Proposal feedback updates a residual Task branch without writing back to World Memory. This branch guides refinement through candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback. A final Task readout supplies candidate-conditioned features for scoring. We derive structured risk targets from existing candidate-scoring rollouts without additional simulator calls. For at-fault collision and time-to-collision violations, the targets encode event existence, association with shared object slots, and the first violation time bin. On the NAVSIM navtest split, WTR-Drive achieves 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2 (expert-frame sequential evaluation). These scores are 0.96 and 0.44 points above the published Drive-JEPA values, respectively. Candidate-level analysis shows that higher best-candidate scores can coexist with lower selected-trajectory scores, revealing a gap between candidate quality and selection effectiveness.
authors: Haoyu Xing, Shaobing Ding, Guanglei Zhao, Guanhua Zhao, Nawu Peng, Mingyang Hou
bullets: Addresses missing shared object references and implicit violation details in proposal-conditioned planning.
Uses a proposal-independent World Memory for object states, map structure, and future motion.
Adds a residual Task branch with candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback for trajectory scoring.
Supervises collision and time-to-collision risks using event existence, object association, and first-violation timing.
On NAVSIM navtest, reports 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2, above published Drive-JEPA scores; analysis exposes a candidate-selection gap.

papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR.
authors: Mengfei Duan, Yuheng Zhang, Guoqiang Zhao, Yuanfan Zheng, Kailun Yang, Zhiyong Li
bullets: Targets errors from occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection that make voxel features spatially unreliable.
Uses Local Semantic Consistency and cross-view semantic consensus to estimate structural stability and filter unreliable correspondences.
Models stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions with class-conditional diagonal Gaussian proxies.
Trains independently parameterized heads with reliability-scaled perturbations, then averages their predictions at inference without sampling.
Experiments across multiple datasets and backbones report gains in semantic occupancy, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration.

papers.tldr: VoxSAOR improves semantic 3D occupancy prediction by modeling voxel-wise aleatoric uncertainty and training robust ensemble heads against reliability-aware feature perturbations.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.
authors: Chaehee Song, Seokil Ham, KiHyun Seol, Jihyun Lee, Yubin Choi, Changick Kim
bullets: Attention importance can change unevenly under semantics-preserving perturbations, exposing local instability.
Different pruning criteria often select substantially different token subsets despite similar performance, revealing global inconsistency.
CoRePruner is a training-free method using instruction-aware diversity and reliability-aware attention.
It improves performance across image benchmarks, MLLM architectures, and token budgets, particularly under aggressive pruning, while remaining competitive for video.
The study argues that reliability should be a central criterion for visual token selection.

papers.abstract: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.
authors: Yiyuan Ge, Changxing Ding, Ziyu Hao, Zijie Zheng, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action-relevant supervision in unlabeled human videos for robot policy pretraining.

Act uses these representations for robotic manipulation across diverse simulated and real-world tasks.
The abstract reports significant gains over current state-of-the-art methods, without specifying quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.

papers.abstract: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, $\pi_{0.5}$, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.
authors: Xu Su, Shunlong Xiao, Qintao Yi, Mingkuan Zhao, Xinmiao Yu, Yizhe Li, Zihan Wang, Bokui Chen

Improves success on the 11 hardest tasks by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points for LingBot-VLA, π₀.₅, and Fast-WAM, respectively.

Gains depend on trajectory-consistent internal representations: external visual encoders add no further benefit, while mismatched caches increase error; scope includes RoboTwin 2.0 and one Flexiv task.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.

papers.abstract: Real-time camera-controlled video re-filming aims to synthesize target views from a streaming source video under online user-specified camera trajectories. This task poses two key challenges: maintaining synchronization and content consistency across views, and achieving low-latency rendering with long-horizon stability. Existing approaches are predominantly designed for offline full-sequence processing and rely on bidirectional attention or costly depth-based geometric preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming scenarios. To address these limitations, we develop a teacher-to-student framework that distills a high-fidelity bidirectional re-filming teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student. We introduce Cross-Frame Injection to interleave each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent, thereby establishing direct cross-view correspondence and improving content consistency. To ensure stable long-horizon generation, we further propose Shared Relative RoPE, which bounds temporal indices within the pretrained range, and Cycle Streaming Tuning, which exposes the student to extended cyclic trajectories during streaming training. These designs enable low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.
authors: Youcan Xu, Xinjie Huang, Jiaxin Shi, Hengye Lyu, Zhen Wang, Jun Xiao, Long Chen

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $\pi_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.
authors: Jingru Guo, Alessandra Russo, Joey Bose, Christos Ziakas
bullets: Flow-based VLAs are difficult to fine-tune with on-policy RL because multi-step ODE sampling is slow and rollout groups have low variance.
VLA-SSD conditions a single-jump generator on a Brownian path to create a stochastic one-step action policy.
The method provides a conditional action density for likelihood-ratio RL algorithms.
On LIBERO, distillation reduces action-head forward-pass time by 7.7× with a 5.5% relative success-rate decrease.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

Uses V-JEPA with an attentive pooler at roadside units to produce compact future-scene embeddings.
Sends embeddings to vehicles, where a TinyLlama model and visual adapter answer natural-language traffic queries and assess scene dynamics.
In a digital-twin urban traffic environment, it reports 97.77% collision-prediction accuracy and 89% F1 while reducing communication payload by several orders of magnitude.

papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.
authors: Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters
bullets: They build on SuperMimic, using a learned robot world model and analytic policy gradients through imagined short rollouts.
The training loop, including MuJoCo Warp simulation, is compiled with JAX and parallelized across up to four GPUs.
XMimic tracks all 40 LAFAN1 clips with a Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes on four H100 GPUs.
XSoma learns rough-terrain locomotion with a one-second horizon, no critic, and exact computation of non-dynamics quantities such as foot terrain height.
The reported speedups are 3.7× over BlinkMimic and 12.3× over FastSAC, with XSoma using one-eighth as many environment steps as FastSAC.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.
authors: Xuannan Liu, Tian Lan, Zekun Li, Xing Cui, Zhengfeng Yu, Feihu Jiang, Qianghuai Jia, Longyue Wang, Zhao Xu, Weihua Luo, Peipei Li, Ran He
bullets: Addresses strategy lock-in and coupled execution in automated post-training.

Scores 39.02 on PostTrainBench, outperforming Claude Code by 7.32 and GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex at 36.23.
Scope: evaluated on PostTrainBench; code is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.
authors: Peng Qin, Tao Zhao
bullets: Addresses the conflict between stable knowledge retention and adaptive, explainable exploration in continual robot navigation.
Uses two-stage behavior cloning to transition from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning.
Introduces a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy critic to reduce value extrapolation errors during this transition.
Experiments on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks show stable retention and meaningful behavioral explanations.

papers.abstract: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.
authors: Anik Jha
bullets: Pruning 75% of experts from a 122B reasoning MoE causes verbatim reasoning loops on 44/120 development problems, versus none for the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization.
A sampling penalty and stop-and-redraw policy recover some loss without weight changes.
Method B adds rank-8 adapter corrections to kept experts and restores two experts per layer, trained layer-by-layer against the unpruned model’s expert outputs on pruned-model activations.
On 130 untouched easy/medium LiveCodeBench problems, B solves 116 versus 104 with matched decoding controls, a +9.2 percentage-point difference.
B costs 1.7× wall time; it shows no meaningful gain on HumanEval+ or MBPP+, and evidence is limited to one model, quantization, and benchmark family.

papers.abstract: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.
authors: Minxuan Hu, Qishi Zhan, Ziheng Chen, Zhengtao Yao, Zihan Dong, Jiayu Yi, Wenxi Sun

papers.abstract: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.
authors: Shaohua Hu, Xusheng Gu, Haofei Yang, Minghao Shao, Nanhui Zhao, Caoyun Fan, Fangming Li
bullets: Jointly training n-gram embeddings with a backbone limits when they can be applied.
The authors study incremental-training choices for learning rate, vocabulary size, and injection position.
The best incremental-training configuration differs from the best configuration used during pretraining.
Newly learned knowledge is stored mainly in the n-gram embedding, while the backbone’s general ability is retained.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The side-branch structure of Engram and the three key configurations during augmentation and incremental training (yellow boxes). The n-gram embedding branch leaves the backbone’s computation graph untouched: et is retrieved with the n tokens ending at position t as the key and, weighted by the gate αl,t, additively merged into the residual stream at the insertion layers. The insertion layers are chosen from [0, . . . , L] and multiple layers may be used; the vocabulary size determines the number of slots in the n-gram embedding table; both are fixed once the model is augmented. The learning rate is set separately for the backbone and the n-gram embedding, forming the dual-learning-rate scheme.

papers.abstract: Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. However, its multi-input multi-output (MIMO) computation, exponential-trapezoidal discretization, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) introduce dense, element-wise, and sequential operations. Despite kernel fusion, conventional GPUs execute these operations inefficiently. Our characterization of Mamba-3 hybrid models reveals numerous kernel launches, substantial data movement, and increased register pressure that reduces warp occupancy and memory-latency hiding. We propose RescuCore, a specialized GPU execution unit for Mamba-3 inference that retains other hybrid model layers on existing GPU resources. Integrated alongside CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) sub-partition, RescuCore shares the register file, shared memory, and warp schedulers. Dense projections remain on conventional GPU resources, while RescuCore pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO computation, recurrent state updates, and output gating to reduce kernel fragmentation and intermediate data movement. We select BF16 after evaluating multiple numerical formats, preserving model accuracy with an estimated area overhead of 5.9% of an A100 die for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4. We evaluate RescuCore using cycle-accurate Accel-Sim simulation, RTL synthesis, and synthesis-informed AccelWattch power modeling. Compared with conventional GPU execution, RescuCore achieves 1.4-9.4x speedup and 1.4-5.0x energy reduction during prefill, and 1.3-2.8x speedup and 1.2-2.6x energy reduction during autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the potential of GPU-integrated specialized execution for SSM-based hybrid models.
authors: Shiva Raja, William Desueza, Ajay Joshi
bullets: Mamba-3’s MIMO computation, discretization, RoPE, and recurrent updates cause kernel fragmentation, data movement, and register pressure on conventional GPUs.
RescuCore integrates alongside CUDA and Tensor Cores, while leaving dense projections on existing GPU resources.
It pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO, state updates, and output gating to reduce intermediate data movement.
Using BF16, the design estimates 5.9% A100 die-area overhead for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4.
Simulation and synthesis-based evaluation reports 1.4–9.4× prefill speedup and 1.3–2.8× decoding speedup, with corresponding energy reductions.

papers.abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.
authors: Benhao Huang, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Hector Liu
bullets: Feeds each token’s top-layer state into the next token’s input and is compared with a vanilla Transformer at matched compute.
Across model sizes and data regimes, it generally improves the value of both FLOPs and unique tokens, except when data is very scarce relative to model size.
With fixed unique data, it reaches a target loss using less compute; with fixed epochs, it reaches the target using less unique data.
A shared scaling law models latent feedback as equivalent to using a larger Transformer and generalizes accurately to a held-out model size.
Reported maximum savings are 48% compute and 47% unique data; downstream tasks show the same trend.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that latent feedback (feeding top-layer states to the next token) acts as a compute and data amplifier, effectively reducing the need for multiple training epochs.
papers.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
papers.tldr: Latent feedback makes language-model training more compute- and data-efficient than spending equivalent compute on repeated epochs, especially when unique data is plentiful.

papers.abstract: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.
authors: Abulikemu Abuduweili, Changliu Liu
bullets: Standard Koopman controllers can stabilize the learned latent model while leaving the deployed nonlinear plant locally unstable.
Stability transfers when learned and true closed-loop dynamics match to first order on the embedding’s tangent space; approximate matching yields a robustness margin.
TIK estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces this tangent-space matching, while using a bilinear predictor for state-dependent actuation.
Across four unstable benchmarks, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilized the nonlinear plants, unlike all 40 Standard Koopman controllers.
TIK achieved 88% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with 0.25 ms planning and controlled simulated seven-joint arms in 1–5 ms per step; stability testing was inconclusive under high noise.

papers.abstract: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.
authors: Kazuo Aoyama, Hiroshi Sawada, Shota Kita, Akihiko Shinya, Masaya Notomi
bullets: Parameter limits from fabrication, footprint, and control overhead constrain optical neural-network expressivity.
The design targets statistically uniform transformations and strong information mixing per parameter.
Compared with Mach–Zehnder-based rectangular meshes, the butterfly topology uses simpler building blocks and logarithmic depth.
Computational evaluations report lower matrix-reconstruction error and higher classification accuracy, especially at restricted parameter counts.
Graph-theoretic and matrix-based measures provide a physically interpretable framework for evaluating parameter-efficient designs.

papers.tldr: A logarithmic-depth butterfly architecture using phase-shifter–beam-splitter pairs improves expressive, parameter-efficient unitary transformations in coherent optical neural networks.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.
authors: Emilio Ferrara
bullets: Introduces 854 benchmark items in 427 minimal pairs of 2D rigid-body chain-reaction scenes, with simulator-computed outcomes.
Tests 30 models across 10 families, using hint ladders from identifying the deciding step to providing the exact calculation.
Without assistance, frontier models achieve at most 72% on the deciding person and 34% on both paired cases.
Providing the deciding calculation raises frontier-model accuracy to 82–92%, while small open-weight models remain near chance.
Fluent scene descriptions or pointing to the relevant step are insufficient; models must independently derive and compute hidden quantities such as speeds.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks physical reasoning from still images for models that plan/act in the physical world, directly relevant to embodied AI and spatial reasoning in multimodal models.
papers.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
papers.tldr: DominoBench shows that leading vision-language models struggle to predict multi-step chain reactions from still images because they fail to compute the decisive physical quantity.

papers.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
authors: Keiji Kimura, Yuma Ichikawa
bullets: Targets GPTQ’s greedy separation of discrete integer selection from continuous scale optimization.
Uses Hessian-aware local search: each integer update recomputes its group’s closed-form optimal scale, followed by periodic joint scale refinement.
Starts from scale-refitted GPTQ candidates, so unregularized JointQ does not increase layer-wise calibration error relative to GPTQ.
Across four models and four settings, it improves average zero-shot accuracy in 14/16 comparisons and perplexity in 12/16.
Diagonal Tikhonov regularization helps prevent severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation; JointQ remains a drop-in GPTQ replacement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces JointQ, a method for joint scale-and-integer quantization in LLMs that improves accuracy in low-bit regimes by optimizing scales and integers jointly.
papers.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: JointQ improves GPTQ post-training quantization by jointly refining integer assignments and group scales, especially in challenging low-bit and large-group settings.

papers.abstract: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}. We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.
authors: Yuanbo Tong, Haoyuan Li, Jibiao Jiang, Zirui Wang, Yuchen Li, Jiamou Liu
bullets: Conventional CLIP and DINO similarity metrics miss personality inconsistency across story scenes.
ViStoryBench-Personality combines an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon with six metrics for alignment, stability, and behavioral coherence.
Across seven T2I systems, abstract traits and scene emotions rarely improve personality consistency over neutral prompts.
TBV translates personality traits into concrete, renderable visual constraints without training.
TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to 22.1%, especially in models with stronger language conditioning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV) framework. Phase T anchors the character’s OCEAN personality profile; Phase B derives context-sensitive behavioral tendencies via a self-correcting loop; Phase V maps behaviors into concrete visual constraints through the expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon.

Figure 1: Trait collapse vs. trait expression. Given the same narrative scene, baseline prompts (C1, left) produce generic or emotionally dominated behavior, while TBV prompts (C4, right) translate the OCEAN profile into concrete visual constraints, maintaining personality-consistent expression. Bottom: the TBV framework decomposes abstract personality traits into behavioral tendencies and then into renderable visual cues via an expert-validated lexicon.

Figure 4: Qualitative case study across five open-source systems on the same representative story shot. C1 uses only the base narrative prompt; C2 adds abstract OCEAN trait labels; C3 adds a deduced scene-level emotion label; C4 injects explicit TBV-derived visual constraints. Across models, C1–C3 often preserve the broad scene layout but tend to produce generic, weakly visible, or emotion-dominated behavior. C4 more consistently introduces personalityrelevant visual evidence, such as exploratory gaze, forward-leaning posture, and open gestures, illustrating the qualitative mechanism behind the PAS and RS gains in Table 2.

Figure 5: Qualitative case study for the two closed-source APIs. Because GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana perform internal prompt rewriting, we evaluate them only under C1 and C4 conditions. Compared with C1, C4 produces more explicit personality-relevant behavior, including more active body orientation, exploratory engagement with the environment, and less purely scene-driven affect. This qualitative shift is consistent with the quantitative PAS and RS gains reported in Table 2.
