papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and mitigates personality inconsistency in text-to-image foundation models; fits multimodal foundation model behavior and prompting.
papers.title: Trait Collapse in Text-to-Image Generation: Evaluating and Mitigating Personality Inconsistency in Visual Storytelling
papers.tldr: Text-to-image models can preserve a character’s appearance while losing personality-consistent behavior, so the authors introduce a benchmark and prompting framework to diagnose and reduce this “trait collapse.”

papers.abstract: Recurrent sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state space models (SSMs), are often trained to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token when their output sequence is complete. During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.
authors: Simon Dr\"ager
bullets: Studies EOS halting using a controlled task: repeat an input sequence a specified number of times, then emit EOS.
Tanh RNN hidden states encode the remaining copy count in a low-dimensional linear subspace, with shared states across different repeat counts.
An affine state shift corresponding to one fewer remaining copy causes EOS one copy earlier while preserving the shortened sequence in 94.4% of new sequences.
Linear SSMs separate repeat-count information across two-dimensional rotation planes whose relative phases align near stopping.
Intervening on these representations disrupts halting while largely preserving copied content, supporting their causal role.

RNN entries are means over the five models, and SSM entries are ranges across the five models. The fixed-direction rows pool the targets r = 1, 2, 4, 5, starting from a rollout of three copies. Since the SSM rotations preserve almost all of the copied content, their complete-sequence accuracy rounds to the same range as their stopping accuracy.

Each replacement propagates ∆JK t over the final copy of the shorter target. We add the result to the trajectory of the longer count and decode it through Wy, without rerunning the network. Continuation accuracy is the fraction of these reconstructions whose output matches the output of the unmodified network. The exact row is a numerical check.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the mechanistic basis of End-of-Sequence (EOS) token generation in recurrent sequence models (RNNs and SSMs), contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures.
papers.title: Halting in Recurrent Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Recurrent models halt by encoding how much sequence remains: tanh RNNs use a shared countdown representation, while linear SSMs rely on phase alignment across rotation planes.

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.
authors: Yumin Zheng, Qingtian Zhu, Ziyan Zhu, Kailu Song, Yinqiang Zheng, Jun Ding
bullets: Addresses the challenge that serial ST data are dense within sections but sparse along the axial direction.
Uses a conditional implicit neural representation with graph-autoencoder latent compression, pseudo-label signature conditioning, and depth-dependent FiLM modulation.
Applies correlation alignment to encourage consistent cross-slice covariance in latent features.
Evaluations on held-out measured sections show improved reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation versus general-purpose INRs and adapted ST baselines.
Scope: designed for pre-registered ST sections and estimates, rather than directly measuring, continuous 3D expression.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HoloGene. We first compress high-dimensional gene expression into latent embeddings via a graph autoencoder, then use PSN to distill training-expression partitions into coarse signature guidance, and synthesize a continuous 3D latent field using a decoupled, FiLMconditioned INR with CORAL regularization to handle inter-slice anisotropy and regularize slicespecific representation variation.

Figure 6: Qualitative results of virtual slice synthesis on representative 3D samples. We visualize measured reference slices and the corresponding predictions from different methods; marker-level outcomes vary across genes and sections, while aggregate comparisons are reported in the main text.

Domain maps show ground-truth annotations in the first row and predicted-expression clusters mapped to annotation colors in the remaining rows. See full results in Section A. B) Querying HoloGene between measured sections provides model-based interpolation estimates with smooth STMN2 variation. See full results in Section C.

Figure 10: Annotation-referenced cell–cell communication (CCC) preservation on the two primary datasets. Rows and columns denote anatomical annotations used for post hoc sender–receiver grouping. For each dataset, we compare ground-truth CCC interaction scores, HoloGene-predicted CCC interaction scores, prediction-minus-ground-truth residuals, and top ligand–receptor interaction overlap rates. (A) MOSTA E16.5. (B) Whole mouse brain. HoloGene recovers similar label-pair communication structures to the ground truth, with small residual differences and high overlap of top ligand–receptor interactions across most annotation pairs.

Figure 8: Annotation-referenced CCC network preservation on (A) MOSTA E16.5 and (B) whole mouse brain. Nodes denote anatomical annotations, and directed edges show top-scoring senderto-receiver ligand–receptor communication connections. Ground-truth and HoloGene-predicted networks show similar high-confidence communication topology, indicating that virtual-slice synthesis preserves higher-order interaction structure.
Figure 9: Visualization of virtual-slice evolution for two gene markers. The leftmost and rightmost panels show measured slices, and the intermediate panels show synthesized virtual slices.

Figure 3: Ablation on LCORAL: UMAP visualizations colored by section ID and anatomical regions on the whole mouse brain data (Zhang et al., 2023). Enabling LCORAL leads to better cross-slice mixing and less visual separation by section ID.

Figure 5: HoloGene preserves CCC patterns in MOSTA E16.5. (A) Ground-truth and HoloGenepredicted communication scores with their differences in the testing set. (B) Overlap rate of top significant ligand-receptor interactions recovered by HoloGene across annotation pairs. Darker blue indicates higher recovery.

Figure 1: HoloGene reconstructs holistic 3D gene fields from discontinuous ST sections. By lifting sparsely sampled 2D slices into a continuous 3D field, HoloGene enables volumetric downstream analysis, including spatial-domain recovery, cell–cell communication inference, and pathway enrichment.

papers.abstract: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.
authors: Yiyun Chen, Zewen Liu, Shengpu Tang, Max S. Y. Lau, Wei Jin
bullets: Targets reliable multi-horizon epidemic forecasts with both accurate means and calibrated uncertainty.
Uses neural evidence to update a bounded internal multiplier and advance a finite-memory renewal state for future means.
Adds a heteroscedastic Gaussian head with validation-selected log-variance regularization to model predictive uncertainty.
Across four surveillance benchmarks, it achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, with reductions up to 14.2% versus the strongest baseline.
It also leads on CRPS at horizons 4–6, including improved performance during the abnormal 2019–2020 influenza season; ablations support complementary roles for its components.

papers.abstract: Directly aligning trajectory-distilled video generators slashes rollout costs and optimizes the deployed few-step model without teacher fine-tuning or re-distillation. However, conventional flow-matching preference objectives assume single-head local velocity supervision, mismatching the finite-interval, block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators such as Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) and Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD). Naively supervising only the primary initial-subinterval velocity sub-head rather than the fused block-average velocity at block starts (DirectAlign) induces a severe training--inference mismatch that degrades quality below the unaligned baseline. We introduce BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework that constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals-seamlessly supporting DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler. We further build a unified post-training pipeline integrating offline pairs, reward-free semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection and objective-aware block scheduling. Experiments on multi-reference video generation across MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and an in-house model RefVid-V4 show that BlockAlign consistently outperforms unaligned distilled models and DirectAlign in structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality. Notably, our approach unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving statistically significant human preference gains over PDD baselines (54.0% vs. 33.3% wins/losses, or 61.8% non-tie win rate on RefVid-V4; 51.3% vs. 34.7%, or 59.7% non-tie win rate on MiniMax-H3) and up to an 82.7% win rate against DirectAlign.
authors: Jingyuan Zhu, Biaolong Chen, Yangyang Qin, Shengyang Shen, Yaohua Wang, Weiming Bai, Miao Lu, Aixi Zhang
bullets: Trajectory-distilled generators use finite-interval, block-average transitions, which conventional single-head preference objectives mismatch.
BlockAlign constructs valid block-boundary states, queries fused block-level velocities, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals.
The framework supports DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler.
A unified pipeline combines offline pairs, semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection.

Across two multi-reference video-generation models, BlockAlign improves structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality, with reported human preference gains over PDD and DirectAlign.

papers.abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.
authors: Wenhao Li, Chong Xiao, Xiaokun Bai, Rundong He, Zhuang Qi, Xusheng Liang, Zhibin Wu, Qiangchang Wang
bullets: LLM fusion can override readable visual or audio evidence when transcript information is available.
MR-Bench evaluates language shortcuts using four typed sentiment benchmarks and 900 human-validated clips from seven sources.
Language-shortcut clips expose a measurement issue: text-only answer inversion can reach 94.4%, so accuracy alone does not prove non-verbal reasoning.
CoVeR trains unimodal views as judges and withholds fused supervision when their predictions disagree.
CoVeR achieves 61.7% language-shortcut and 93.6% non-verbal-shortcut accuracy in standard mode; robust mode improves the former to 63.0% but reduces the latter to 84.8%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Constructing MR-Bench. Candidates are clips whose unimodal judgments disagree with the words (here a CH-SIMS clip with human unimodal labels on [−1, 1]); a panel of four text-only LLMs keeps a language-shortcut (LS) candidate only if the majority misreads its transcript, and three annotators keep a clip only if the majority recovers the label from the full clip and the misleading polarity from the shortcut channel. Models are then asked the same binary question from every input they support.

Figure 5. Three ways to fuse. LLM-Fusion supervises the fused prediction on every sample (left); the test-time override lets confidently disagreeing views of the frozen model replace the fused decision (middle, Eqs. (3) and (4)); CoVeR trains the views as unimodal judges and withholds the fused task loss wherever a judge disagrees with the text judge (right), running the full view alone at test time.

Fusion models are trained on the training split of each source and averaged over three seeds; they inherit its label prior (dotted: the constant answer “negative”, 61.9%), so they are compared within their family. Every zero-shot MLLM is far below chance; inverting a text-only model’s answers alone reaches 94.4%, so LS accuracy is read together with the 280 NS clips.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and mitigates language shortcuts in LLM-driven multimodal fusion; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reliability.
papers.title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning

papers.abstract: Tractor-trailer systems are difficult to control, especially unstable during reverse motion, and their dynamics depend on difficult-to-measure factors, including road friction and suspension coefficients. We introduce a learned dynamics model for tractor-trailer control and compare it with a reduced-order dynamics model with Fiala tire forces as an analytic baseline. Specifically, we compare a model predictive path integral (MPPI) controller that uses the learned dynamics model to an MPPI controller that uses the analytic model, as well as to three additional baseline controllers. In the main closed-loop tracking experiments across four simulated environments, MPPI with learned dynamics achieves mean speeds closer to the target magnitudes and lower root-mean-square (RMS) hitch angles than MPPI with the analytic model at every tested setpoint, with higher completion rates in seven of eight reverse configurations.
authors: Aaron Chen, David Shen, Taekyung Kim, Kaleb Ben Naveed, Dimitra Panagou
bullets: Tractor-trailer control is challenging because reverse motion is unstable and key dynamics factors are difficult to measure.
The study compares MPPI using learned dynamics with MPPI using a reduced-order Fiala-tire model and three other controllers.
Across four simulated environments, learned-dynamics MPPI tracked target speeds more closely and reduced RMS hitch angles at every tested setpoint.
It achieved higher completion rates in seven of eight reverse configurations.
Results are limited to simulated closed-loop tracking experiments.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision--language--action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep--shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision--language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision--language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35\% success across the four standard suites and 72.6\% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.
authors: Ruichen Deng, Qinyu Zhao, Yong-Hyun Park, Mutian Tong, Liang Zheng, Jiatao Gu
bullets: Targets vision-language-action control with tractable action densities and a single maximum-likelihood training objective.
Combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks.
Uses a deep–shallow design: deep blocks process multimodal conditioning, while shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation.
Reports 98.35% success across LIBERO’s four standard suites and 72.6% on LIBERO-Plus without further fine-tuning.
Ablations indicate that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement improve closed-loop success.

figures.caption: Figure 1: NF-VLA architecture for training and sampling. Vision–language features and proprioception are projected into a shared prefix Ct that conditions only the deep flow block. (a) Training maps normalized, Gaussian-perturbed action chunks through the shallow blocks and the deep block to latents Z, evaluating affine coefficients in parallel and optimizing the exact negative log-likelihood. (b) Sampling reverses the blocks, recovering tokens autoregressively from Gaussian noise before Tweedie denoising and action unnormalization.

Figure 2: Effect of NF-VLA design choices on LIBERO success. Bars show success rates for the baseline and three ablation variants across the four suites; diamonds show suite averages rounded to one decimal place. Prefix and AdaLN variants condition both the deep and shallow blocks.

papers.tldr: NF-VLA uses a jointly trained normalizing-flow policy to generate and refine robot actions from vision, language, and proprioception, achieving strong manipulation performance with one learned density.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.
authors: Jianwen Wu, Meiling Wang, Junkang Zhou, Yipeng Shen, Haoran You
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of 3D full attention over large spatiotemporal token sequences.
Separates mostly input-stable positional attention from a smaller input-dependent content residual.

papers.abstract: Safety filters for heterogeneous robot teams fail because of missing constraints, overestimated braking capabilities and conflicts between individually satisfiable constraints. We present OntoCBF, which compiles a domain ontology with a class taxonomy, typed relations, safety axioms and a dynamics profile per robot class into a control barrier function filter with one quadratic program per agent. Description-logic entailment supplies the constraints of any team online, including those that follow from chains of relations and from classes defined by what a robot carries, so the existing safety axioms cover new robot classes, payload classes and combinations. We prove that a subclass may reuse the braking capability of its parent whenever it can produce every velocity of the parent, a property separate from subsumption. For box-bounded double integrators this property is also necessary, and every loss of safety then begins with a conflict. Once three robots interact, the safe set of pairwise barriers contains states from which a collision is unavoidable, and such states persist in larger teams under any fixed capability reduction. In a simulated warehouse where humans ignore the robots, a filter written for the design classes violates safety in 89-100 % of the episodes with unseen classes. In all scenarios, including one with 32 robots, OntoCBF violates safety in 20-70 % of the episodes, each time after a conflict, with a median deepest intrusion of 10-17 % of the keep-out distance. A multi-agent PPO policy trained with the filter in the loop lowers the rate of infeasible quadratic programs, nearly all of them conflicts, by 18-41 %.
authors: Peng Wu, Seyede Fatemeh Ghoreishi, Nathan Bastian, Mohsen Imani, Tian Lan, Mahdi Imani
bullets: Motivation: Existing safety filters miss derived constraints, overestimate braking capabilities, and fail when individually valid constraints conflict.
Method: Compile class taxonomies, typed relations, safety axioms, and robot-specific dynamics into one control-barrier-function quadratic program per agent.
Contribution: Description-logic entailment supports unseen robot, payload, and combined classes; the work also characterizes when subclasses can reuse parent braking capabilities.
Results: In warehouse simulations, design-class filters violated safety in 89–100% of episodes with unseen classes, while OntoCBF violations occurred in 20–70% of episodes and followed conflicts.
Scope/limitation: With three or more robots, pairwise-safe states can still lead unavoidably to collisions; policy training reduced infeasible programs by 18–41% but did not eliminate conflicts.

papers.abstract: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.
authors: Liu Zhenyuan, Bharath Seshadri, Bailey Miller, George Kopanas, Ionnais Gkioulekas, Bernd Bickel
bullets: Addresses inference of interior temperatures when thermal images cover only part of an object’s surface.
Models steady-state conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solves it with a direct boundary integral equation.

Samples depth-rendered collocation points while handling depth discontinuities and near-surface evaluation with density subtraction.
Experiments on synthetic and real data, including Dirichlet and mixed Dirichlet–Robin boundaries, match analytical solutions and outperform FEM solvers in accuracy.

papers.abstract: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.
authors: Jiazhen Liu, Yanghao Wang, Chaolei Tan, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of representing intermediate spatial states in text or latent tokens without explicit image correspondence.
Uses a locate-mark-read procedure over the visual token grid as a task-dependent reasoning canvas.
Trains one model jointly for spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing.
Outperforms specialized MLLM-based methods across six benchmarks, with gains also holding for a stronger backbone.
Provides a unified framework for integrating explicit visual marks directly into MLLM visual features.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SelfMark. (1) Locate: after reading the image and the question, the MLLM emits a type token, here <PTS>, and fills in mask placeholders, one per patch, in a single forward pass; a lightweight head turns them into the locate conditions. (2) Mark: a lightweight editor, which never sees the image, translates the conditions into mark features on the same grid as the visual tokens. (3) Read: the same MLLM reads the original visual tokens and the question, followed by the mark tokens, and answers. Dashed orange parts are used only in training: Lloc fits the conditions to position labels, Lmark aligns the mark features with the target Z∗, the frozen-ViT features of the marks drawn on a blank canvas, and the answer is trained with CE and RL; no marks are drawn as pixels at inference.

Figure 1. Four ways of thinking with an image. A simple counting task reveals how different approaches handle visual evidence. (a) Think in text translates visual structure into words, risking plausible but ungrounded descriptions such as “rows of five.” (b) Draw in pixels relies on an external vision module to annotate the image, inheriting its missed detections. (c) Latent imagination encodes intermediate visual states in a handful of latent tokens, leaving their spatial grounding implicit. (d) SelfMark takes a different route: the MLLM first locates the targets, a lightweight editor marks them in its visual feature space, and the MLLM reads the resulting marks alongside the original visual tokens. Each dot corresponds to a located object, turning counting into explicit, inspectable visual reasoning. The same locate–mark–read procedure handles the other tasks with other marks (bottom).

papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single policy can control many arm-hand combinations and transfer to pairings and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks, encodes each joint's morphology with attention biased by the kinematic tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm-hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair. Project website: https://davidlxu.github.io/dexformer2-web/.
authors: Lixin Xu, Ke Zhang, Xinyu Liu, Jie Tan, Senming Tan, Jiaju Yin, Yating Feng, Xiaoyi Lin, Xiyue Dong, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses the need to train a separate grasping policy for each arm–hand pairing with incompatible joint interfaces.
Canonicalizes robot joints using validity masks, morphology-aware attention over kinematic trees, and Transformer-XL memory for embodiment-dependent dynamics.
Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands; achieves 89% stable success on seen pairings and 51% on six held-out pairs.
Transfers without fine-tuning to four new hand types and, via retargeting, to parallel grippers; ablations identify memory, kinematic bias, and pairing coverage as important.
A distilled policy transfers zero-shot from simulation to a physical Flexiv arm with two hands, including a held-out pairing.

The critic, used only in training, has the same structure with its own weights and memory. Bottom: MorphNode. A body encoder (arm, hand, and mount MLPs) gives bt; MorphAttention attends over joint and context tokens with topology biases and pools them to rt; gated fusion gives the spatial code st = LN(bt + αrt).

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.
authors: Olatunji Oni, Sanhita Sengupta, Marc De Benedetti, Nathanial Eddy
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of manually inferring study-specific line boundaries from complex longitudinal oncology treatment histories.
Uses clinician adjudications to calibrate confidence, identify cases needing review, and continuously estimate residual error.
Feeds completed clinician reviews back to the model as evidence for subsequent assignments.
In simulations of 136 clinician-adjudicated multiple myeloma patients, 44.6% review yielded 5% residual error, versus 62.2% with LLM self-confidence and 81.9% with random review.
Scope: performance was evaluated in simulations for multiple myeloma and may depend on the study-specific adjudication rules and available clinician evidence.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of evidence-calibrated selection. LLM assigns a LoT across the treatment histories of a real world cohort. ECS estimates confidence of each assignment based on adjudications already collected by clinicians on similar decisions and prioritizes the patients with the least supported assignments for manual adjudication. Each completed review is added to the evidence base used to score the next assignments, and is fed back to the model as a precedent. The right schematic shows the resulting reduction in residual error relative to random review.

Figure 3. ECS requires fewer review rounds. (A) Accuracy among unreviewed patients and (B) residual error by review round, with five patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range across 100 sub-cohorts. (C) Mean number of rounds required to reach 5% residual error for batch sizes of 2 to 20 patients per round. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. (D) Relative reduction in review rounds achieved by ECS against LLM confidence and random review.

Figure 2. ECS reduces residual error with less clinician review. (A) Residual error across the cohort as a function of the share of patients reviewed, where reviewed patients are given the clinician’s assignment. (B) Error among patients not yet reviewed. Random (gray) selects patients in random order. LLM confidence (blue) selects patients with the lowest LLM self-reported confidence first. ECS (green) selects patients with the lowest evidence-calibrated confidence first. Oracle (dotted navy) selects only patients whose current assignments are wrong, serving as an idealized benchmark for the best achievable selection. Results are shown for 100 sub-cohorts of 100 patients with seven patients reviewed per round. Lines indicate the mean, and shaded bands indicate the interquartile range. Red dotted line indicates 5% residual error.

Figure 4. ECS provides a calibrated estimate of residual error. (A) Calibration of patient-level confidence for ECS and LLM self-reported confidence, evaluated on the same unreviewed patients at every round after the first (66,500 patient-rounds; bins with fewer than 200 patient-rounds are not shown). Dotted line indicates perfect calibration. (B, C) Observed residual error (median and interquartile range) and the residual error estimated from (B) ECS confidence in the ECS arm and (C) LLM self-reported confidence in the LLM-confidence arm. Vertical lines indicate where the estimated residual error first reaches 5% (solid) and where the observed residual error first reaches 5% (dotted).

Table 1. Clinician advance rates and LLM errors by transition type and drug class. Transitions in the full cohort grouped by the change in line-defining agents between consecutive regimens, with supportive agents excluded, and within each type by the drug classes involved. Clinician advance rate indicates the share of transitions adjudicated as a new LoT. LLM errors indicate calls made without adjudicated examples that disagreed with the clinician, shown as counts and as a share of all 56 errors.

Table 2. Review burden, review rounds, and accuracy by review strategy. Values are means over 100 sub-cohorts of 100 patients. Review burden is the share of the cohort reviewed before residual error fell to 5% and remained there, with seven patients reviewed per round. papers.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
papers.tldr: Evidence-calibrated selection enables LLM-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication by directing clinicians to the least-supported cases and using reviewed cases as precedents.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.
authors: Nick Ryan, Peter A. Devine, Ben Sirb, Hannah Sansford, Alex Chiocchi
bullets: Addresses continual-learning degradation, especially catastrophic forgetting when new updates overwrite prior knowledge.
Trains each document-specific adapter once offline using synthetic questions targeting base-model weaknesses, then reuses it at query time.
Uses parameter isolation: the base model and previously cached adapters remain unchanged as the private corpus evolves.
The adapter-data generation process improves from prior outcomes and new workload examples.
Reports a 38.2% relative accuracy improvement over the base model on the EDO enterprise document Q&A benchmark; designed for overnight adaptation on local hardware.

papers.selection_reason: Cached per-document adapters trained at test time for continual specialization; directly matches test-time learning and continual learning.
papers.title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Microfitting enables continual specialization by caching a separately trained adapter for each document, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while improving enterprise document Q&A accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.
authors: Yuyang Tian, Desen Sun, Shuncheng Jie, Lishan Yang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Problem: Uncompressed activation caches impose high memory and bandwidth costs, while post-edit compression may require buffering over 100 GB per request.
Method: Compresses reusable activations during serving and supports selective reuse for masked edits.
Method: Uses a scheduler designed to balance faster cached edits with initial generation requests.
Result: Sustains over 2× the baseline request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment.
Result: Speeds up edits by 2.4–4.5× and initial generations by 1.3–2.2× while preserving image quality.

papers.selection_reason: Compressed activation cache serving for multi-round diffusion editing reduces memory and bandwidth, fitting efficient-AI memory-efficiency goals.
papers.title: TileCache: Serving Multi-Round Diffusion Image Editing with Compressed Activation Caches
papers.tldr: TileCache makes multi-round diffusion image editing more memory-efficient and responsive by compressing reusable activations and scheduling edits alongside new generations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising $\pi_{0.5}$'s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: https://umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround/.
authors: Umer Siddique, Peilang Li, Yongcan Cao
bullets: Actuation shifts from remounting, wear, or latency can cause VLA policies to fail or behave unsafely.
The method learns deployed-robot dynamics through task-agnostic motor babbling and re-grounds the VLA’s intended motion.
It activates only when a shift is detected, while staying close to the policy’s original plan.
Across two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings, ReGround restored near-oracle success and was safer than linear calibration.
For example, it improved π₀.₅ success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency.

(b) ReGround reads the intended path with the training-body model fnom (blue), re-grounds it with a trustregion MPC in the deployed-body model fdep (orange), and a CUSUM monitor enables it only after a shift.
Figure 2: Demonstration of actuation-shift for frozen π0.5 across 8 Libero tasks. Success is shown in filled and solid while unsafe rate is shown in hollow and dashed.
Table 2: Per-task test success rate of frozen π0.5 (base) and ReGround (RG).

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time re-grounding of frozen VLA policies under actuation shift; directly targets vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Right Goal, Wrong Body: Re-grounding Frozen VLAs under Actuation Shift
papers.tldr: ReGround adapts frozen vision-language-action models to changed robot actuation at inference time, restoring performance without retraining, rewards, or demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.
authors: Moshe Kimhi, Idan Kligvasser, Yotam Intrator, Regev Cohen, Ehud Rivlin
bullets: Caches a full-depth appearance representation as a read-only temporal anchor and combines it with selected partial features from the current frame.
A lightweight controller selects encoder exits before processing, using shallow computation for stable scenes and deeper computation when visual conditions change.
Separates temporal appearance reuse from geometric alignment: current calibration defines geometry, while a motion-conditioned adapter handles ego motion.
On nuScenes, achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP with 2.16× lower latency than dense DETR3D; StreamPETR sees a 1.92× speedup with similar accuracy.
Scope: the method targets temporally redundant driving sequences and relies on policy-based recognition of semantic driving regimes.

Blue markers are drift-quintile means with scene-bootstrap 95% intervals; black lines are isotonic fits. Reported 𝜌 intervals all include zero. Absolute error is not reuse-induced degradation.

Figure 1 | Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory. While standard multi-camera 3D detectors execute a full-depth vision transformer for every frame, EvoMem3D treats the dense detector-interface representation as a recurrent memory. A lightweight policy dynamically allocates transformer depth based on ego motion and scene change, updating the persistent high-level memory with shallow current-frame evidence.

We project the pre-encoding controller’s output logits across 700 training clips into two dimensions using tSNE and partition them into four clusters (colorcoded). A manual audit of 10% of the data reveals that the policy organizes driving dynamics into four interpretable regimes without explicit behavioral labels: low-speed cruising, sharp turns, dense scenes, and fast motion (qualitative examples shown in Fig. 4).

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive-depth temporal caching and motion-conditioned memory reuse for efficient multi-camera 3D detection; directly targets inference memory/latency and embodied spatiotemporal memory.
papers.title: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection
papers.tldr: EvoMem3D accelerates multi-camera 3D detection by adaptively reducing image-encoder depth and reusing temporally stable appearance features while preserving current-frame geometry.

papers.abstract: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.
authors: J\"urgen Paulhart ([core] Informationstechnologie / Eldric), Peter Sch\"uller (NeuraMix AI GmbH,Technische Universit\"at Wien)
bullets: Addresses repeated failures and unreliable self-reported success in agent and robot task execution.
Uses a delta-rule associative matrix to find relevant procedures, plus ordered step records to retrieve subsequent goals, outcomes, and deletions.
Stores episodes only when success is confirmed by tests, tool results, external checks, or people—not by the agent’s own claim.
In simulation, external verification increased solved tasks from 35% to 79%, compared with 96% self-reported completion.
On 100,000 synthetic episodes, retrieval preserved episode ordering and memory isolation; median lookup took 16 ms on a laptop and 40 ms on a server node.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a specific episodic and procedural memory architecture for tool-using agents and robots, fitting the subtopic of robot learning and manipulation by providing a method for skill acquisition and interaction history retention.
papers.title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
papers.tldr: A two-part episodic and procedural memory lets tool-using agents and robots learn only from externally verified outcomes while retrieving applicable procedures and ordered next steps.

papers.abstract: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformable and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DAPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain represen-tation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DAPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8x in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.
authors: Beining Han, Jia Deng
bullets: Targets non-rigid manipulation tasks that are too slow or difficult to model accurately in simulation.
Learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain variables.
Distills the learned policy into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor controller.
Uses explicit domain representations to select parameters that improve downstream task performance.
Evaluated on six tasks, achieving 1.5–3.8× task-metric gains with optimized parameters and zero-shot real-world transfer.

papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real RL for dexterous tool use, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: DAPPT: Domain-Aware Policies from Procedural Trajectories for Sim-to-Real Dexterous Tool Use
papers.tldr: DAPPT enables zero-shot sim-to-real dexterous tool use with deformable materials by learning from procedural trajectories without simulating those materials.

papers.abstract: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.
authors: Jiahang Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Junsong Wang, Zhenzhi Ying, Siqi Hou, Naohiko Sugita, Liming Shu
bullets: Addresses unreliable hand-kinematics estimation from any single modality under changing conditions.
Uses Vision and EMG Transformers with one learnable query per joint degree of freedom for context-adaptive multimodal fusion.
Evaluated on synchronized data from 10 participants, achieving mean R²=0.88 and MAE=2.80°.
Outperformed vision-only, EMG-only, and alternative fusion baselines; gains were strongest for visually ambiguous joints and conditions.
Synthetic occlusion tests indicated greater robustness than vision-only estimation, supporting demonstration capture and dexterous robot learning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed multimodal fusion framework. The framework takes synchronized egocentric RGB images and forearm HD-sEMG signals as inputs. The vision branch extracts spatial hand-region tokens from cropped RGB patches using a ViT backbone, while the EMG branch converts windowed hand-crafted sEMG features into temporal EMG tokens using a Transformer encoder. After adding modality embeddings, tokens from both modalities are concatenated and fused by a query-based Transformer decoder, in which each hand DoF is represented by an independent learnable query and mapped to its corresponding joint angle through a shared multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression head for continuous estimation of 20 hand joint angles.

Fig. 2. Experimental setup for multimodal data acquisition. (A) An RGB camera was set on the forehead of the participant. 10 motion-capture cameras were arranged around the experimental area to record the hand movements of the participant. The red, blue, and yellow boxes indicate the egocentric RGB camera, motion-capture cameras, and the hand–forearm sensing setup, respectively. (B) Functional schematic of the wireless HD-sEMG acquisition unit. The unit comprises three main functional parts. The power-management unit (PMU) supplies power to the acquisition and processing circuits. The EMG signal-processing path receives the differential signals generated between the electrode-array channels and the wrist-mounted common reference electrode, and performs amplification, band-pass filtering, analog-to-digital conversion, and onboard signal processing. The microprocessor controls signal modulation and demodulation and communicates with the host computer through the radio-frequency wireless interface. (C) Placement of motion-capture markers and the HD-sEMG acquisition system. Reflective markers were attached to anatomical landmarks on the dorsal hand to record hand kinematics, with three palm markers defining the palm reference frame. Two 64-channel HD-sEMG electrode arrays were placed over the forearm flexor and extensor regions, respectively. Each array was connected to a wireless acquisition unit, and a wrist-mounted reference electrode provided the common reference for differential recording.

Fig. 4. Temporal trajectories of predicted angles for 20 hand joint DoFs under different input modalities with the palm facing down. The fusion model follows the ground truth more closely and stably than the EMG-only and vision-only models.
Fig. 3. Overall comparison of fusion, vision-only, and EMG-only models using R² and MAE (°) metrics.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of reconstructed hand meshes under different input modalities. From left to right, the columns show the egocentric image, ground-truth hand pose, fusion result, vision-only result, and EMG-only result. The fusion model produces hand poses that are closer to the ground truth.

Fig. 6. DoF-specific modality attention patterns and representative temporal analyses of the proposed fusion model. (A, B) EMG and visual attention mass for individual hand DoFs, together with the relative MAE changes of the proposed DoF-query Transformer and the global-query variant with respect to the vision-only and EMG-only baselines, under the palm-facing-down and palm-facing-side conditions, respectively. Vision attention mass is displayed downward for visual comparison. (C)–(G) Ground-truth joint angles, EMG-only, vision-only, and fusion model predictions, and EMG attention mass for the thumb, index, middle, ring, and pinky finger, respectively, under representative motions. These examples illustrate that modality-attention patterns vary across DoFs and adapt dynamically to the temporal context.

The lower section compares fusion decoder methods under the multimodal setting. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation across 10 participants for R² and MAE (°). Bold values indicate the best performance within each comparison.

papers.abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.
authors: Luciano Bozzi, Christian Celidonio, Umberto Nuzzi, Massimo Biagini, Stefano Cherubin, Asbj{\o}rn Djupdal, Tor Andre Haugdahl, Andrea Aliverti, Alessandra Angelucci, Giovanni Agosta, Gerardo Pelosi, Paolo Belluco, Samuele Polistina, Gaia Strada, Luigi Sossi Ortega, Alexandra-Ioana Albu, Riccardo Volpi, Luigi Malag\`o, Michael Schneider, Xabier Eguiluz, Haritz Saiz, Mar\'ia Viqueria
bullets: Targets fatigue, stress, and harsh-environment monitoring for pilots and warfighters, with HUD and haptic feedback interfaces.
Integrates body/squad-area mesh networking, secure RISC-V edge devices, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning.
On a public wearable dataset, XGBoost achieved 0.901 accuracy and 0.920 F1, while a feature-based Transformer achieved the highest AUC at 0.963.
Plans HW/SW co-design, pruning, quantization, distillation, precision tuning, and possible Processing-in-Memory acceleration for constrained deployment.
Key gaps include physiological-signal and textile validation, reliable low-latency communications under mobility and interference, and lightweight post-quantum security with robust device identity.

papers.abstract: We present RoboKit, a high-performance, general-purpose toolkit for parallel differentiable optimization in robotics, built on three principles: (i) Performance and flexibility: GPU-parallel multi-seed solvers pair sampling with versatile optimizers, running 2-60$\times$ faster than task-specific baselines across seven tasks; (ii) Geometry, rendering and physics: hybrid and coarse-to-fine representations accelerate collision, differentiable rendering and simulation, optimizing 4096 grasps in 2.97 s; (iii) Integration with learning: costs are differentiable and simulation is parallel, so RoboKit both distills optimization into policies and trains RL; distilled policies run 9-240$\times$ faster at comparable accuracy, and RL reaches a GPU baseline's scores up to 2.1$\times$ sooner on the same simulator.
authors: Jianglong Ye, Xuanbin Peng, Conor Mc Gartoll, Changwei Jing, Lai Wei, Jiali Chen, Xueyan Zou, Xiaolong Wang
bullets: Uses multi-seed, GPU-parallel solvers combining sampling with flexible optimizers.
Employs hybrid and coarse-to-fine geometry, rendering, and physics representations for faster computation.
Reports 2–60× speedups over task-specific baselines across seven tasks.
Optimizes 4,096 grasps in 2.97 seconds and enables distilled policies to run 9–240× faster at comparable accuracy.
Accelerates reinforcement-learning progress to baseline scores by up to 2.1× on the same simulator.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.
authors: Shi Bin Hoo, Magnus Buehler, Omar Swelam, Frank Hutter, Lennart Purucker
bullets: GPT-6 Astra programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving mean ROC AUC 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline.
It diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic data while largely preserving benchmark performance.
It writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, including reversing linear trends and approximating square waves from sine waves.
The results suggest LLM-driven programming can complement optimization and provide tools for probing and intervening in TFM computations.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that LLMs can program tabular foundation models via weight-space reasoning and KV-cache editing, offering a novel method for model intervention and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: LLMs can directly program, repair, and steer tabular foundation models by manipulating weights or KV caches without gradient-based optimization.

papers.abstract: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.
authors: Bart M. N. Smets, Gijs Bellaard, Pieter Wils
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between overly restrictive built-in equivariance and costly data augmentation.
Introduces an architecture that can become equivariant to selected symmetry groups based on the training data.
Provides a post-training fingerprint indicating which symmetries are relevant and to what degree.
Demonstrates the architecture and fingerprinting process on image classification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: An input image is first converted to a set of geometric tokens through splatting. GLInT processes these tokens to, in this case, classify the image. After training, the model can be inspected to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that tells us which of our candidate symmetry groups are relevant (shown are the subgroups of Aff+(2) that we used, see also Fig. 3).

Fig. 4: MNIST test errors over 20 independent training runs. We train ViT on both the original MNIST and a rasterized version of our splatted MNIST to show the fidelity of our tokenization method. We also train GLInT with and without noise to show that fingerprinting noise does not degrade performance.

Fig. 3: The set of symmetry subgroups of Aff+(2) we are interested in. Green arrows add translations. Red arrows add rotations. Blue arrows add isotropic scaling. Purple arrows add area-preserving maps.

Fig. 2: Top row: a sample from the MNIST dataset [10] (28 × 28 pixel images). Bottom row: splats made with a higher order Gaussian splatter using 16 Aff+(2) × R3 tokens (3 coefficients per splat since we use 3 orders of Gaussians). Every column shows the fingerprint IH of the corresponding symmetry group H. Note that all fingerprints are unique.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a soft-equivariant architecture that learns geometric invariance and symmetry groups, providing a mechanism for geometric reasoning and spatial understanding in neural networks.
papers.title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
papers.tldr: A soft-equivariant transformer learns which geometric symmetries matter for a task and exposes them through an interpretable symmetry fingerprint.

papers.abstract: Learning manipulation tasks from few demonstrations requires abstractions that capture the changes relevant to task completion, such as object poses in rigid-body manipulation. However, tasks such as cleaning are defined by changes in visual state rather than object pose, making the choice of task representation less clear. In this work, we propose Cleanly-DINO to learn visual task spaces from few demonstrations. Given a mask of a task-relevant region and frozen ViT features, Cleanly-DINO fits a projection to isolate a task space and fit a progression metric to it. We train the model on diverse cleaning examples and evaluate its ability to localize incomplete task regions and transfer across visual domains. We also study its utility for robot learning by using it as an observation encoder and reward signal in a reinforcement learning setting. Finally, we deploy our fitted model within a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to evaluate its use in guiding task execution.
authors: Adrian R\"ofer, Melika Shekarriz, Jos\'e Arce y de la Borbolla, Iman Nematollahi, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses cleaning tasks where success depends on visual-state changes rather than object poses.
Uses task-relevant region masks and frozen ViT features to learn a projected task space and progression metric.
Trained on diverse cleaning examples to localize incomplete regions and transfer across visual domains.
Evaluated as an observation encoder and reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Deployed in a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to guide task execution.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Cleanly-DINO approach for learning visual task spaces. We train our model from video sequences with masks for the task-relevant region. We embed the images and train a projection layer under a self-supervised contrastive objective to separate the initial from the final task state. In the projected task space, we select anchor points to measure task progress as movement between these. In deployment, we use our model trained on cleaning tasks to identify dirty regions in an unseen setting in order to drive a robotic wiping pipeline and to serve as the observation space and reward for a reinforcement learning agent.

Figure 4: Impression of our real robotic setup and the robot’s observation, and before and after examples. The robot is tasked with wiping the table in front of it in places it identifies as dirty. It does so competently on the regularly patterned tablecloths, as well as the plain wooden table. The method fails to generalize to the irregularly patterned tablecloth in the bottom right.
Figure 2: Impression of the six tasks in our dataset. We use a combination of self-recorded and internet videos. Each second row shows the hand-crafted labels we use for evaluation.

Figure 3: Cross-domain study: Left: Providing training data from the target domain (k) always works best, but training on up to three foreign domains also boosts performance. Importantly, adding out-of-domain data has almost no negative impact. Right: Training on one source task and then adding demonstrations for another target task benefits the target without costing the source. The gain is greater for the Linear head, but this is due to its lower starting point. These gains are limited without the abstention filter.
