papers.abstract: Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives. We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput. Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.
authors: Dvir David Biton, Shay Hahiashvili, Nadav Keren, Gil Einziger, Roy Friedman
bullets: Targets Semantic Approximate Membership Queries: safely rejects queries when no indexed vector can meet a similarity threshold, with no false negatives.
Summarizes embeddings using spherical caps; one representation supports arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction.
Uses about 2% of raw FP32 embedding memory and eliminates approximately 20–100% of index accesses at cosine similarity 0.95 across five real-world datasets.
Placed before a FAISS flat index, improves throughput by up to 382% and about 116% on average while preserving range-search results.
Benefits are strongest for tight thresholds, expensive retrieval, and highly clustered embeddings; lower thresholds are also evaluated.

Fig. 4. FPR (top) and modeled throughput improvement (%, bottom) versus Mfilter/Mraw at τ = 0.05, one column per corpus. Auto (thick black line, stars) and seven fixed encodings are shown: SPQ 16× 12, 12× 12, 6× 8, and TQ1–TQ4, selected by mean rank of accesses saved across corpus–budget cells. The model combines batched filter-query cost and acceptance rates with a mean flat-index lookup cost of 5.29 ms from end-to-end measurements. The horizontal axis is logarithmic; the bottom vertical axis is symmetric-log, with negative values indicating slowdowns. Curves show means over five folds. Fig. 1. Embeddings on the unit sphere are covered by k caps, each defined by a direction ui and an angle θi. A query vector is accepted for verification if it falls within at least one widened cap.

Each point averages FPR and log10 V over five folds for one encoding–budget pair, using the seven fixed encodings in Figure 4 with the same markers. papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability. Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances. On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/CECAR.
authors: Byeongju Kim, Hoonki Lee, Byungjun Kim, Inyul Ra, Yongjin Kim, Yongseong Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: On-device MoE inference is constrained because all expert weights cannot fit in memory, requiring SSD transfers for non-resident experts.
Cache hit rates are fundamentally limited, and binary cache-aware routing can cause unstable expert selection.
CECAR predicts each expert’s expected reuse distance with an ML-based cache policy and favors experts likely to be reused soon.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it reaches 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer GPU with 16 GB VRAM and outperforms fully DRAM-resident baselines in decode speed.

papers.abstract: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Zilin Huang, Zihao Sheng, Sikai Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the exploration–exploitation dilemma caused by limited world-model training coverage and scarce failure examples in driving logs.
Stages recoverable failures in simulation and uses an expert to label visited states with actions and values before deployment.
Uses a chunked latent world model with a risk-aware sampling-based planner that penalizes collisions.
Continuously refines the world model online when driving encounters situations outside offline coverage.
Achieves the best reported route completion and reward per step on CARLA routes, plus the highest episode reward in MetaDrive among compared methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Technical overview of SAFER, illustrated with its CARLA instance. The numbered badges link each part to its scene of the analogy in Fig. 2. (a) Stage and Annotate: the expert, weaker Roach checkpoints and scripted hold and late-brake events drive until the first violation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value (Section 3.2). (b) Foresee: from the context Mt of the past BEVs, the dynamics imagines the 16 latents of a candidate chunk in one pass, and heads read them as the behavior-cloned prior, the reward and its five factors, survival, value and collision risk (Section 3.3). (c) Evaluate: every 0.1 s, the planner scores 135 candidate chunks on their imagined futures (Eq. (28)), refits its sampling distribution to the 16 best in each of two iterations and executes the first action (Section 3.5). (d) Refine: the planner’s own driving fine-tunes the dynamics, the reward and the risk head online, while the encoder, the prior and the value stay frozen and the planner scores with slowly moving EMA copies (Section 3.6). The crash frame in (a), the context frames in (b) and the candidates and risk curves in (c) are from a recorded collision of the corpus (Fig. 5a); the other two BEV frames are illustrative.

Figure 2: An everyday analogy for SAFER (top) and the corresponding stages of the method (bottom, detailed in Fig. 3); the numbered badges link each stage to its scene. (1) Parents praise what works and point to negative examples, so that the child need not fail first. (a) Likewise, weaker drivers and scripted perturbations stage failures in simulation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value. (2) The child learns what each choice leads to. Hard work (action) brings good grades (reward), a far goal is worth pursuing (value), and staying out all night is risky (risk). (b) Likewise, the world model foresees these quantities for each candidate action chunk, and (c) the planner scores the candidates by their return minus a price on risk. (3) Away from home, school and work keep reshaping the beliefs while the core ones stay. (d) Likewise, the planner’s own driving refines the dynamics and the reward and risk heads, while the prior and the value, whose targets only the expert provides, stay fixed.

Figure 1: Learning paradigms for autonomous driving, compared by where the experience beyond competent driving comes from. The glyph under each paradigm shows the coverage of its data (gray) and how the paradigm treats it. Exploiting (blue) spreads the candidates over the coverage and takes the best one up to its edge, but no further. Exploring (orange) grows the coverage at the price of failures (red crosses), the paradigm’s own or, for SAFER, failures that others make, labeled by the expert (teal). A step out of the coverage that does not grow it is misjudged (?). (b) A world model learned online (Hafner et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024) still explores by failing. papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.
authors: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
bullets: Long-output reasoning requests can suffer KV thrashing, repeatedly losing and recovering state while producing little output.
Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in CPU memory and transfers them efficiently using fused gather/scatter kernels with double buffering.
Age-based readmission and protected decoding turns prevent repeatedly stalled requests; hidden-state length estimates guide preemption victims.
On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request waited over 50 seconds, while p99 time per output token decreased 50.7% versus recomputation.
The full replay finished 10.7% sooner, with 12.0% higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Advancing from individual embodied intelligence to swarm embodied intelligence is a key step toward scalable, general-purpose embodied intelligence. Complex tasks often require multiple agents to divide responsibilities, coordinate handovers, and manipulate shared objects collaboratively. However, existing robot learning methods rely primarily on individual demonstrations, which provide limited supervision for modeling dependencies among agent actions, while collecting multi-robot demonstrations at scale remains difficult. Human egocentric demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, yet distributed observations from multiple participants cannot directly supervise decentralized policies. We introduce EgoSwarm, the first robot learning framework for learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. EgoSwarm collects more than 50 hours of collaborative experience using a robot-free multi-person egocentric system. We introduce the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP) and Swarm Interaction Token (SIT) to recover cross-agent interaction relations from distributed observations and transform this experience into local supervision consistent with deployment-time information constraints. We further propose SwarmVLA, which transfers knowledge of swarm behavior to decentralized policies conditioned on local observations, local history, and limited neighbor messages. SwarmVLA achieves a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks. Project page:https://xitong-c.github.io/EgoSwarm_Page/.
authors: Ziqiang Liu, Xitong Chen, Min Li, Yiqun Li, Zhuoping Yin
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable multi-robot demonstrations and the difficulty of learning dependencies among agents’ actions.
Collects over 50 hours of collaborative experience with a robot-free, multi-person egocentric system.
Introduces Swarm Interaction Packets and Tokens to recover cross-agent relations and create deployment-consistent local supervision.
Proposes SwarmVLA, a decentralized policy conditioned on local observations, history, and limited neighbor messages.
Reports a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EgoSwarm. EgoSwarm is the first robot learning framework for decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. It reconstructs cross-agent interaction in the form of the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP), encodes deployment-available interaction information into the Swarm Interaction Token (SIT), and learns locally executable collaboration policies through SwarmVLA.

Figure 3: EgoSwarm pipeline for decentralized multi-robot collaboration. (a) Multimodal egocentric recordings are temporally aligned and reconstructed into quality-annotated Swarm Interaction Packets (SIPs). (b) A causal CTDE teacher learns coordination representations and action flow fields from collective interaction supervision, which are distilled into the decentralized student policy. (c) During deployment, each robot constructs local Swarm Interaction Tokens (SITs), aggregates quality-aware neighbor information, and generates future actions from the resulting Action Context.

Figure 5: Real-world multi-robot collaborative task execution. The figure illustrates representative execution sequences of the three evaluation tasks: Multi-Robot Flexible Handover (MRFH, top), Dynamic Collaborative Transport (DCT, middle), and Large-Scale Deformable Object Manipulation (LSDOM, bottom). Frames progress from left to right; red arrows indicate robot motion directions, and dashed circles highlight key interaction regions.

Figure 2: EgoSwarm Capture and shared human–robot sensing interface. Human participants wear SwarmEgo sensing heads to record synchronized multi-person egocentric demonstrations. Each sensing head integrates task and scene cameras, infrared cameras, an IMU, and UWB sensing. The robot platform reuses the same sensing interface and UWB infrastructure, reducing the perception gap between human demonstrations and decentralized robot deployment.

Figure 6: Evaluation of SIP relative-geometry reconstruction. (a) Optical motion capture provides reference poses for ground-truth evaluation. (b) Translation and rotation error distributions over 30 independent multi-person interaction segments. SIP achieves a translation RMSE of 4.8 mm and a rotation RMSE of 2.6◦.

Figure 4: Composition of the SwarmVLA training data. The dataset consists of three complementary sources for decentralized multi-robot learning: human swarm data for cross-agent interaction experience, robot adaptation data for embodiment alignment, and joint robot teleoperation data for task-specific collaborative action supervision.

papers.abstract: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it. We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured. Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests. Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.

bullets: Addresses changing workloads under continuous batching, where the best kernel-fusion granularity varies by iteration.
Chooses between persistent megakernels and fused-kernel chains using offline-measured performance crossovers.
Peaks at 4,345× real time on H100 SXM and 6,367× on B200, outperforming tuned vLLM at measured peak concurrency.
Maintains comparable WER to vLLM and serves 8× more concurrent requests within a 400 ms p95 completion-time budget.
Optional accuracy–throughput trade-offs, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13–16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs.

papers.abstract: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.
authors: Alexandre Audibert, Fran\c{c}ois Portet, Benoit Favre, Maja Jonck Hjuler
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized pictogram grammar and parallel text–pictogram data for training MLLMs.
RAPS combines rule-based transcription with LLM concept extraction and pictogram-vocabulary retrieval, covering entities, numbers, and polysemous words without adding new rules.
Produces 1.4 million French parallel pairs, with 300,000 released publicly.
Human evaluators rank RAPS transcriptions above the rule-based state of the art.

Reference-based metrics distinguish clearly different systems but struggle to rank strong systems reliably; an instruction-tuned model supports text or pictogram input and pictogram, speech, or text output.

papers.abstract: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.
authors: Zhuoyue Zhang, Jian Liu, Jihua Zhu, Ajmal Saeed Mian
bullets: Masked point-cloud video modeling can leak target motion through target positions and bidirectional temporal context.
PointWM converts completion into forecasting using only earlier frames, last-seen target positions, and timestamps.
An unsupervised latent action models future information not determined by the past.
On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer, it improves F1@50 by 24.9 offline and 29.1 with strictly causal inference versus training from scratch.
The method is evaluated for point-cloud video pretraining and its broader effectiveness beyond this setting is not established in the abstract.

The student encodes the same full clip into zf ; the latent-action modules read these features, which are regularized by LVIC. Context branch. With causal temporal masking retaining only the frames before a one-frame gap, the weight-shared student encodes these frames into zc. papers.abstract: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and SAM 3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4% with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.
authors: Ho Tim Tsui, Jongyun Kim
bullets: Binary target masks preserve target location while reducing sensitivity to pad appearance, with prompts specifying the target.
A novel banana-themed pad reduced success from 75.6% to 12.0% because the original SAM 3 prompt rarely detected it.
Selecting a revised prompt restored success to 68.4% without updating the policy weights.
For missing masks, mask filling improved landing more than the tested centroid or area corrections.
Temporal tracking produced masks more often but also hallucinated masks after the pad disappeared, without reliably improving landing success.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
authors: Ali \c{S}enol
bullets: Study 1 found that retaining prior replies reduced success on sharded math tasks for GPT-4o-mini and Mistral-7B; Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction without significance.
Study 2 introduced CDR-Stream, a 100-turn state-tracking benchmark with matched per-turn difficulty and exact answers.
Full-history accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within 20 turns, whereas solver-verified state summaries preserved substantially higher accuracy.
Consistency, logical coherence, stability, and tested drift monitors provided no robust, model-general early warning; single streams detected only very large drops.
The findings support storing task state outside the transcript and monitoring performance across sessions.

papers.abstract: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.
authors: Zhoubin Kou, Cong Shen
bullets: Targets efficient neural reception for MIMO-OFDM across varying bandwidth allocations and channel conditions.
Combines shared resource-element and pilot representations with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention.
Uses shared parameters and relative positional information for soft detection without inference-time updates.
Bounded frequency neighborhoods make forward-pass computation grow linearly with bandwidth under fixed configuration and symbol count.

In 5G NR-compatible evaluations, it outperformed the implemented NRX and DeepRx-MIMO baselines at training bandwidth and retained lower pre-decoding error across bandwidth extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests.

papers.abstract: Background: Before laryngoscopy, clinicians assess the likely cause of hoarseness and whether to suspect a precancerous or malignant lesion. Whether voice-based artificial intelligence (AI) supports pre-laryngoscopic categorization is unknown. Methods: We developed an auditory large language model that generates a patient-level assessment card (provisional category, voice-quality ratings, and rationale) and a prespecified malignancy alert from voice recordings, patient information, and acoustic measures obtained before laryngoscopy at one center. We evaluated both in a held-out test set and a later cohort. In a sequential reader study, 32 otolaryngology clinicians categorized held-out cases without AI and, 1 to 2 weeks later, reviewed their initial categories with the card (without the alert). Results: Across 800 paired assessments, reader accuracy was 49.8% before and 56.8% after review (difference, 7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.7 to 13.5; P < 0.001); 99 categories changed from incorrect to correct and 43 from correct to incorrect (ratio, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.22 to 5.31). Accuracy rose 14.7 points when the model was correct and fell 8.7 when incorrect. Provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation. The malignancy alert flagged 85.7% and 86.8% of precancerous or malignant lesions. Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions increased from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review (difference, 21.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.3 to 42.0). Conclusions: In this single-center study, clinicians' pre-laryngoscopic categorization accuracy was higher after reviewing the AI assessment card, although the sequential design cannot fully separate AI assistance from reassessment; gains depended on model correctness without clearly selective adoption. Randomized and external evaluations, including of the malignancy alert, are needed.
authors: Siyuan Hou, Shuting Yang, Zengrui Jin, Liyu Cheng, Siyin Wang, Yunhan Shi, Xueyan Li, Rong Hu, Yuhong Lin, Qiyu Chen, Yanru Li, Ji Wu, Bowen Zhou, Mangsuo Zhao, Wen Xu, Chao Zhang
bullets: 32 otolaryngology clinicians assessed 800 cases before and after reviewing AI-generated assessment cards.
Reader accuracy increased from 49.8% to 56.8%, with more incorrect-to-correct than correct-to-incorrect category changes.
Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions rose from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review.
The model’s provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation; its malignancy alert flagged about 86% of relevant lesions.
The sequential, single-center design limits causal interpretation, and the malignancy alert was not evaluated in the reader study.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.
authors: Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan, Nur Ahmad Khatim, Mansur Arief
bullets: Replays one fixed training log from the same Q-table under three conditions: all updates, skipped bad-experience updates, or neutralized penalties.
Demonstrated on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluated in closed-loop CARLA driving.
In CARLA, the full agent reached the goal from 33/40 starts, while skipping or neutralizing bad experiences succeeded from none.
For 46 of 47 decisions preceding failures, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences—median size one—reproduced the failing action.
The conclusion is scoped to the evaluated tabular agent and environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness: https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/GEM-MM
authors: Yuanshan Chua, Xuejiao Zhao
bullets: Standard preference objectives perform similarly under small multimodal preference budgets, suggesting they are largely entropy-blind.
GEM-MM samples on-policy candidates, targets high-entropy reasoning decisions, penalizes uncertain answers, and uses group-normalized policy gradients.
With a 3,000-prompt budget, it improves entropy-depth preference and implicit-reward accuracy over baselines.
Hallucination rates decrease on AMBER and CHAIR, while performance also leads across HallusionBench granularities.
The method can collapse when exceeding the fair preference budget, defining an important scope limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the GEM pipeline instantiated by GEM-MM for vision-language models (adapted from Zhao et al. [2026a]). Given a multimodal query x = (xI , xQ) (text-only q in the original figure) drawn from a preference pool {a−, a+}, the Reflective Inference Engine πθ elaborates k chain-of-thought candidates; Cognitive Filtering computes per-token entropy and an entropy-guided score that rewards fork tokens while penalizing uncertain final answers; SEGA forms a contextual group advantage and applies a full-parameter gradient update. The cognitive feedback loop returns only to the inference engine (updated policy), which then re-samples candidates on the next cycle and does not re-enter the entropy-scoring block directly.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Nikos Theodoridis, Reenu Mohandas, Sushil Sharma, Ciar\'an Hogan, Ganesh Sistu, Anthony Scanlan, Tim Brophy, Ciar\'an Eising
bullets: Addresses the lack of safety-critical, long-tail scenarios in existing autonomous-driving benchmarks.
Introduces counterfactual scenes with crossing or standing pedestrians and stationary cars inserted into the ego vehicle’s path.
Uses pixel-level matched original and edited scenes to isolate the causal effect of hazards on predicted trajectories.
Evaluations of four VLAs and two WAMs find weak, often negligible reactions to inserted hazards.
Fine-tuning ReCogDrive on edited scenes improves braking, generalizes to unseen objects and real scenes, and preserves nominal driving performance.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.
authors: Hanbo Zhang, Lianlei Shan, Liuhaichen Yang, Zezhi Tang
bullets: Standard candidate resampling quickly saturates because candidates differ mainly by noise, not by distinct plans.
A lightweight planner proposes latent plan hypotheses, while a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan in a single backbone pass.
Plans are learned from demonstrations without plan labels or rewards; the policy selects the highest-likelihood action chunk.
On CALVIN ABC→D, eight plan-conditioned candidates achieve 69.9% success versus at most 64.9% for matched plan-free or same-plan baselines.
Benefits are strongest when tasks have multiple solutions: PlanDiv removes more failures on LIBERO-Long and reaches 51/54 real-arm trials on two multi-solution tasks.

The latent planner turns Kmax learned seeds ξk into plan hypotheses zk with a prior αk; only the top-K by prior are decoded, so one checkpoint serves any budget K ≤ Kmax. One shared masked-diffusion executor decodes a candidate chunk Âk under each plan in S=4 unmasking steps, so the candidates come from K different plans instead of K samples under one condition. The policy executes the candidate with the highest score, by default the mean log-probability of its tokens. (b) Training. The masked reconstruction loss of a demonstration chunk under each plan gives soft responsibilities wk that weight the execution loss; no plan labels or rewards are used. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Yuxuan Tian, Yahui Han, Xinyu Tan, Feiyu Wang, Zongwei Lv, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of processing thousands of image tokens and the risk of missing small, answer-relevant regions.
Uses a two-stage, question-conditioned process: low-resolution region glancing followed by native-resolution re-encoding of relevant areas.
Selects final tokens with Evidence-Tempered Diversity, balancing scene coverage with predicted answer evidence.
At 5% of visual tokens, retains 91.6% of Qwen3.5-4B’s full-token performance across 14 benchmarks and improves over prior baselines.
Provides 3.1× faster time to first token on 4K images, with especially strong gains on text-rich tasks and transfer to other MLLMs.

papers.abstract: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.
authors: Bahaeddin T\"urko\u{g}lu
bullets: 39 of 48 architectures added to Hugging Face Transformers in 2025 reuse at least two of three core blocks from earlier models, often Llama-derived.
Only 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims included controlled ablation comparisons.
Just 4 of 40 reports disclosed more than one training run, and 1 reported data mixture, token count, and compute together.
The study identifies seven reporting rules and demonstrates them on two technical reports.
It assesses reporting practices—not model quality—and notes that untested claims may still be valid.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.
authors: Yipeng Sun, Jiajun Wang, Siyuan Mei, Yan Xia, Siming Bayer, Vincent Christlein, Andreas Maier
bullets: Zero-pair alignment succeeds on natural images (COCO) but fails on environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D CT.
Successful alignment must identify the shared cross-modal subspace and orient the mapping within it; medical imaging is hardest because this subspace explains little variance.
LightAlign uses a few image-text pairs and ridge regression to jointly locate and orient a mapping between frozen encoders.
A text-only classifier can then predict findings from mapped medical images without finding-level labels.
On CT and chest X-ray benchmarks, LightAlign achieves strong results with substantially fewer pairs and generalizes to an out-of-distribution hospital dataset.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body imitation from monocular video requires both a robust universal tracker and high-quality real-time reconstruction. We present MoViC, a framework that uses live RGB video as a control signal for humanoid robots without wearable tracking devices. The framework combines monocular human motion reconstruction, robot retargeting, and a transformer-based behavior foundation model. The policy receives proprioceptive history, a single explicit next-step reference, and a compact frequency-domain motion representation that supplies temporal context without explicitly stacking future reference frames, which reduces the input dimension and network size. During deployment, our extrapolation method bridges the 10-Hz visual estimation with 50-Hz controller, enabling asynchronous visual processing and policy execution. Hardware experiments further demonstrate highly dynamic motion tracking and device-free teleoperation of bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks from live monocular RGB input. Project page: https://movicproject.github.io/ .
authors: Yimin Han, Jiahui Zhang, Wanyue Li, Zeren Luo, Yeke Chen, Liu Zhao, Peizhuo Li, Xiaoyu Ji, Shihao Dong, Xuechao Chen, Zhangguo Yu, Annan Tang, Peng Lu
bullets: Combines monocular human-motion reconstruction, robot retargeting, and a transformer-based behavior foundation model.
Uses proprioceptive history, one explicit next-step reference, and a compact frequency-domain motion representation for temporal context.
Extrapolates visual estimates from 10 Hz to support a 50 Hz controller with asynchronous perception and policy execution.
Hardware experiments demonstrate dynamic motion tracking and bimanual and single-arm manipulation from live RGB input.

papers.abstract: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.
authors: Vedant Telrandhe, Sushil Sharma
bullets: Robot attempts incur measurable wall-clock time, joint travel, actuator wear, and human intervention costs.
The testbed uses a self-built SO-101 arm, two demonstration-trained ACT policies, vision-based success detection, and per-attempt cost logging.
Across 51 minutes of hardware operation, a fixed retry limit lost 36% of execution time to failures versus 27% for a feasibility rule; the difference was not significant and saved no robot time.
Failures did not cluster, so immediately retrying after failure was no more likely to succeed than other attempts.
Log replay suggests cost-aware scheduling can recover sensible choices without a hand-set retry limit; concentrated demonstrations also improved local success from 8/20 to 10/10.

(4) The detector scores the result; here the cube has settled in the tray. (5) The ledger writes one row for the attempt; the values shown are a real row from our logs. (6) The arm returns to the pose every demonstration started from, and the loop repeats. The dashed arrow is what this paper adds: today’s scheduler records the cost but never reads it, and the proposed scheduler decides with it.

papers.abstract: Video creative plagiarism refers to the unauthorized reproduction of creative ideas across videos despite substantial differences in visual appearance, posing a new challenge to video copyright protection. However, existing video copy detection methods primarily focus on visual content similarity, struggling to capture abstract creative that are entangled with specific visual realizations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel task, named Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD), and propose an iterative creative evidence tracing framework, termed CreaTrace, to verify creative similarity and accurately localize the corresponding evidence segments. Specifically, we design a Multimodal Semantic Event Segmentation strategy to divide similar long videos into coherent narrative events, facilitating event-level dataset construction and retrieving similar segments. Based on these events, CreaTrace employs Coarse Creative Matching to identify candidate event pairs through narrative semantics and camera language. Then CreaTrace presents Creative Decoupling to disentangle abstract creative patterns from specific visual realizations. Meanwhile, Creative Swap Contrastive Learning is devised to enhance creative consistency through cross-realization feature swapping. Benefiting from the above designs, our CreaTrace enables accurate creative similarity detection and temporal localization, while providing interpretable evidence report. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CreaTrace across diverse creative plagiarism scenarios.
authors: Chang Liu, Sheng Li, Zhenxing Qian, Xinpeng Zhang
bullets: Introduces Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD), targeting unauthorized reuse of creative ideas beyond visual copy detection.
Segments videos into coherent narrative events using multimodal semantic event segmentation.
Uses coarse creative matching to retrieve candidate event pairs based on narrative semantics and camera language.
Separates abstract creative patterns from their visual realizations and applies creative-swap contrastive learning for consistency.
Experiments show effective and robust creative similarity detection and temporal evidence localization across diverse plagiarism scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of our CreaTrace inference pipeline.

Figure 4. Overview of our CreaTrace. We propose two key designs to learn creative representations: Creative Decoupling and Creative Swap Contrastive Learning. The former disentangles creativity from specific video features through learnable queries, while the latter exchanges realization features and leverages contrastive learning to enhance creative consistency. Benefiting from above designs, our CreaTrace can effectively capture shared creative patterns for evidence localization.

Figure 3. Overview of MSES. MSES consists of four stages: adaptive clip generation, semantic abstraction, boundary detection and event understanding. By integrating multimodal cues and semantic similarity, MSES segments long videos into coherent events and extracts structured information, including event summaries, actors, actions and temporal boundaries, to support event-level dataset construction.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Simulation experiments at an unsignalized intersection achieve a 100% success and reductions in following-HDV acceleration variation of 65.5% and 44.0% relative to PIWM and DreamerV3, respectively. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.
authors: Sen Shen, Ning Liu, Xiangrui Kong, Yingwei Li, Dongkun Han
bullets: Targets socially compatible AV behavior at unsignalized intersections by balancing passage efficiency with HDV interaction burden.
Uses an interaction-aware latent world model for imagined policy improvement, plus off-policy replay to calibrate both value and policy from finalized interactions.
Simulation achieved 100% intersection success and reduced following-HDV acceleration variation by 65.5% versus PIWM and 44.0% versus DreamerV3.
Ablations associate value calibration with lower HDV burden and policy calibration with improved passage efficiency.
Under out-of-distribution traffic shifts, the method produced lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.

papers.abstract: The emergence of foundation models has marked a transformative shift in AI, enabling robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks through putative zero-shot learning. Large Language Models and Vision Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in tasks such as image interpretation, report generation, and question answering by effectively learning from multimodal data-images paired with associated text often with minimal supervision. In the healthcare domain, this ability to align visual and textual information reduces the reliance on extensive manual annotations, as models can leverage existing clinical reports and imaging data to learn meaningful representations. This integration holds promise for improving diagnostic support, treatment planning, and overall patient care, even in data constrained settings. In this review, we provide a definitive taxonomy of the medical VLM landscape, tracing the evolution from early Contrastive Alignment and Generative MLLMs to the cutting edge frontiers of Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures. We critically examine the "medical bottleneck" identifying the persistent challenges of data scarcity, the "hallucination" risks in generative diagnostics, the computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.
authors: Taha Razzaq, Murtaza Taj, Asim Iqbal
bullets: Medical VLMs align clinical images with associated text to support image interpretation, report generation, and medical question answering.
The review presents a taxonomy spanning contrastive alignment, generative multimodal LLMs, dense pixel grounding, sparse mixture-of-experts, and reasoning-incentivized architectures.
Potential applications include diagnostic support, treatment planning, and improved patient care in data-constrained settings.
Key challenges include limited medical data, hallucinations in generative diagnosis, computational demands of 3D imaging, and insufficient standardized clinical evaluation.
The scope is a review of the field rather than a report of new experimental results.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to move an object yet still need to learn where it belongs. When a person rejects a placement, the robot must decide whether the correction applies only to that situation or expresses a broader rule. We study this problem in CRAFT (Contextual Requirement Adaptation with Frozen Tools), a framework for learning local requirements without retraining robot skills. It records physical success separately from whether an action meets the requirement. Our scope ladder uses memory when an action has already been judged in a nearly identical situation. Elsewhere, it combines memory, explicit rules and a learner for requirements beyond those rules, weighting their predictions by how well they predicted earlier feedback. Controlled studies show gains over correction memory alone in utility, which rewards acceptable actions and charges for mistakes and questions. In camera-grounded robot simulations, the ladder asks fewer questions than language-model agents with persistent memory, but some of those agents take fewer wrong actions and succeed more often after requirements change. All execution failures and timeouts remain in the evaluation. These results support combining specific memories with broader rules, while leaving reliable adaptation to changing requirements unresolved. All evidence comes from simulation with generated requirements and simulated feedback.
authors: Peng Zhang, Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Jochen Renz
bullets: Separates physical execution success from whether an action satisfies the requirement.
Uses a scope ladder: reuses feedback for near-identical situations, otherwise combines memories, explicit rules, and a learner.
Controlled studies find higher utility than correction-memory-only approaches.
In simulated camera-grounded tasks, it asks fewer questions than language-model agents with persistent memory, though some alternatives make fewer mistakes and succeed more after requirement changes.
Results are limited to simulations with generated requirements and simulated feedback; reliable adaptation to changing requirements remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.
authors: Achintya Yadav
bullets: Five models were evaluated on a six-class scene dataset with and without synthetic pre-training, then deployed on an ESP32-S3 and RP2040.
With full real data, synthetic pre-training produced no detectable accuracy gain; with 10% of real data, the CNN improved by 2.715 pp across three seeds.
On the ESP32-S3, the main model required 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ per inference, with no detectable deployment-cost change from pre-training.
The same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ on the RP2040; its largest 96 px variant exceeded the board’s flash capacity.
INT8 outputs matched reference kernels only after patching a vendor-kernel memory overrun, so host scores alone were insufficient for validation.

papers.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.
authors: Chaoqun He, Wannian Yi, Changyi Sun, Chaojun Xiao, Lijie Wen
bullets: OPSD suffers from a termination mismatch: students may stop before enough progress or continue after reasoning stalls.
TA-OPSD adds Stop/Continue Distillation to align continuation decisions with the teacher.
Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training discourages repetitive continuations in failed student trajectories.
On mathematical reasoning with Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, and 8B models, TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines.
Ablations and behavioral analyses associate the two objectives with reductions in their respective termination failures.

The two objectives augment the original OPSD objective and jointly teach the student when to continue reasoning and when to stop.

papers.abstract: We present Lao Siji, an end-to-end driving policy that ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models. Instead of training from scratch on a general-purpose vision backbone, we adapt openpilot, an open-source L2 production model. We freeze its vision encoder and fine-tune the policy layers with an ego-state adapter and a route memory. On closed-loop rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes, we supervise the policy with a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction and a body-extent loss for road and obstacle clearance, while distilling the base model's remaining outputs to retain car following. Ablations show that self-correction samples carry the gain, while the clearance loss substitutes for them where no teacher exists. Longitudinal safety instead rests on the base model's lead-vehicle estimate behind a rule-based speed layer. Longer training, imitating human logs, and human-log speed targets yield either no measurable gain or adverse effects. Without further training, Lao Siji also places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey. The final training takes only one GPU-hour and shifts the weights by 3.9% from the shipped model. Code will be released after review.
authors: Chengzhi Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Jinchang Xu, Weichao Zhuang, Guodong Yin
bullets: Ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge and performs competitively on HUGSIM and Odyssey without additional training.
Freezes openpilot’s vision encoder while fine-tuning policy layers with an ego-state adapter and route memory.
Uses privileged-map supervision for lateral self-correction, a body-extent clearance loss, and output distillation to preserve car-following behavior.
Ablations identify self-correction samples as the main source of gains; clearance loss helps when teacher supervision is unavailable.
Training takes one GPU-hour and changes only 3.9% of the shipped model’s weights; several longer-training and human-log strategies provide no benefit or hurt performance.

papers.abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.

Naive text-based trimming breaks BPE tokenization by removing intermediate merge tokens; merge closure repairs this with only 5.9% more rows.
A Good-Turing trim certificate estimates tokenizer shift and required text from trimming data alone, closely matching observed behavior across languages and settings.
Across six models and 11 languages, certified trims removed a median 89.7% of rows, with bits-per-character increasing by at most 2.0% while predictions were preserved.

papers.abstract: Agentic navigation must maintain goals and adapt actions from incomplete evidence despite execution failures and delayed inference. We present AgenticJevNav, which links goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution. The Agent plans from RGB, odometry, memory, and feedback, retaining goal ownership while authorizing a bounded action set. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked/failed execution or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern decision application. A single executor and independent RGB reflex constrain motion. Goal revisions revoke obsolete requests and actions before replanning. Across six simulated task families, AgenticJevNav achieves 73.33% SR over 60 trials, 21.67 percentage points above the next-best Agent-only aggregate control under differing historical protocols. A real-world GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment achieves 70.0% success over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting. Together, the simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, while remaining failures highlight opportunities to improve grounding, approach planning, and runtime.
authors: Shuning Zhang, Shuli Zhang, Yunheng Wang, Wei Lu, Jiaxi Zhang, Yihang Kang, Tao Wang, Xiangyu Chen, Yixiao Feng, Kai Sheng, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses navigation under incomplete evidence, execution failures, and delayed inference.
Integrates evidence memory, event-triggered Jev reviews, version/freshness checks, and bounded action authorization.
Uses a single executor, an independent RGB reflex, and goal-revision mechanisms to prevent obsolete actions.
Achieves 73.33% success across six simulated task families and 70.0% success on a real GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment.
Remaining failures point to grounding, approach planning, and runtime limitations.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Xinheng Zhang, Haoyu Xiong, Chao Jing, Xiaohan Zhang, Linshan Li, Hongbang Fan, Xingyu Chen
bullets: WAMs can be distracted by task-irrelevant future-state content, such as static backgrounds.
DiffWAM jointly predicts future frames, robot actions, and latent differences between consecutive observations.
Its Mixture-of-Experts design uses World, Action, and Diff Experts with attention masking to isolate their roles.
The World and Diff Experts are removed at inference, so the method adds no inference overhead.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks.

The World and Diff Experts receive the same noised future-frame latents, share their first N −M layers, and use independent final M layers for state generation through denoising and latent-difference prediction through regression, respectively. Structured unidirectional attention separates the expert pathways. At inference, both visual prediction experts are removed, retaining only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert without additional inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
authors: Chenhao Ding, Jizhou Han, Lixin Xiu, Muyao Wang, Songlin Dong, Hideki Nakayama
bullets: Addresses the underuse of feedback from previous navigation episodes in online VLN.
Success-Failure Memory retrieves task-relevant successful and failed experiences using incoming instructions.
Prior-Anchored Adaptation reinforces successful trajectories, suppresses failed ones, and limits drift from a frozen pretrained policy.
Evaluated on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE with five navigation backbones, showing consistent gains.
On REVERIE unseen validation, DUET’s SR rises from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
