(b) Success–Failure Memory: Before navigation, the incoming instruction triggers the retrieval of the most similar experience from the entire memory based on instruction similarity, together with a randomly sampled experience. (c) Prior-Anchored Adaptation: The preceding episode and recalled experiences jointly update the policy through reference-relative outcome learning and pretrained-policy regularization.

(b) Success memory: recalling a successful experience guides the agent toward the target phone. In both cases, Task-Cued Recall reaches the intended destination, while uniform replay fails.

papers.tldr: R2A improves online vision-and-language navigation by retrieving past successful and failed episodes and adapting the policy without source data or expert supervision.

papers.abstract: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360{\deg} field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.
authors: Hai Nguyen, Tarik Taleb, Qize Guo
bullets: Targets identity ambiguity caused by low-resolution transmission and fragmented tracks in 360° panoramic video.
Uses ECIA to decide when extra high-resolution evidence is needed, HIVE to select a useful historical timestamp, and gated fusion with identity safeguards to integrate the retrieved crop.
Works with four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining or changes to detection boxes or the underlying tracker.
On held-out QuadTrack and zero-shot DualPano-MOT sequences, it reduces identity switches by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, with IDF1 gains up to 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points.
Reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% versus continuous Full-HR acquisition under the stated offline JPEG-based acquisition model.

papers.abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.
authors: Muhan Xiao, Shijian Li
bullets: Targets looped LMs whose shared block runs multiple times per token, making autoregressive decoding expensive.
Pipelines prompt-lookup draft tokens into later loops, allowing each depth to check and potentially replace them.
Only full-depth readouts commit tokens, preserving exact-arithmetic sampling behavior with fixed random draws.
Without training, it averages 1.73× the speedup of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling; an optional draft head raises this to 1.99×.
The method is lossless under exact arithmetic and applies across any number of checks and draft chains.

papers.abstract: Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios, where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and evolve at different rates. This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping, localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.
authors: Francisco Mart\'in Rico, Francisco Miguel Moreno, Juan Sebasti\'an Cely Guti\'errez, Esther Aguado, Miguel \'Angel De Miguel Para\'iso, Jos\'e Miguel Guerrero
bullets: Existing navigation stacks tightly couple mapping, localization, planning, and control, making them difficult to extend, compare, and analyze for timing.
EasyNav uses an explicit shared navigation state as the sole interface between components, with compatibility and timing contracts.
The architecture supports interchangeable pipelines across spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames.
Real-robot experiments cover indoor laser navigation and large-scale indoor-outdoor GPS/3D LiDAR navigation across multi-level routes.
Under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency versus Nav2 from 377 to 33 ms indoors and 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while using less CPU and memory.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.
authors: Ji Guo, Xiaolong Qin, Jin Jiang, Yijing Liu, Pei Ke, Aiguo Chen, Wenbo Jiang
bullets: Backdoor poisoning creates strong language priors for target tokens, which also drive hallucinations.
Backdoored VLMs hallucinate target tokens frequently across varied inputs, unlike clean models’ largely random hallucinations.
HalluProbe enhances hallucinations during decoding and analyzes the consistency of hallucinated-token distributions.
Evaluated across six attacks and three models, it achieves over 90% detection accuracy and outperforms existing methods.

papers.abstract: Driving world models usually generate videos from six pinhole cameras with separate optical centres and small overlaps, and must learn to keep these views consistent. We present PanDWM, which stitches them into one $360^\circ$ panoramic band. Camera boundaries then fall inside one image, so keeping the views consistent means keeping the image continuous, and each pixel still records its camera ray. Conditioned on layouts, a causal student generates the band window by window in four steps; it is distilled from a causal teacher and trained on its own rollouts. A feed-forward decoder lifts each frame along these rays into 3D Gaussians, and static Gaussians from neighbouring frames complete them into 4D scenes. On nuScenes, scored in one stitched $360^\circ$ view, PanDWM has lower FID and FVD than the multi-camera baselines at $8$-$46\times$ their speed, and keeps its 50-step teacher's FID while lowering FVD by 22-25%.
authors: Jiajun Sun, Zeyu Zhang, Zeyu Ren, Guangfeng Jiang, Yang Zhao, Hao Tang
bullets: Stitches six camera views into one panoramic band, making cross-view consistency an image-continuity problem while preserving camera-ray information.
Generates the panorama window by window with a four-step causal student distilled from a teacher and trained on its own rollouts.
Lifts frames into 3D Gaussians and combines neighboring-frame static Gaussians to form 4D scenes.
On nuScenes, it achieves lower FID and FVD than multi-camera baselines while running 8–46× faster.
Compared with its 50-step teacher, it maintains FID and reduces FVD by 22–25%.

papers.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.
authors: Zhuo-Yang Song, Zeyu Li, Qing-Hong Cao, Ming-xing Luo, Hua Xing Zhu
bullets: Characterizes document representations using document distinguishability and document dimension.
Models inference as a flow through this two-coordinate phase diagram across Transformer depth.
Most of 156 untrained-model flows reach collapse or noise regions, while 8 trained models across 5 architecture families enter and remain in the central region.
A discrete Langevin description attributes this difference to saddle-like versus stable-node effective forces.
On Pythia-1.4B, training is interpreted as a phase transition linking representation geometry to model behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representation geometry and phase-transition-like behavior in trained language models, relevant to LLM understanding.
papers.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
papers.tldr: The study proposes a phase-diagram view in which trained language models maintain useful representation geometry during inference, unlike untrained models that tend toward collapse or noise.

papers.abstract: Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.
authors: Wesley Maia, Angel Martinez-Sanchez, Maitrayee Keskar, Ross Greer
bullets: Sidewalk accessibility is person-dependent, so one label per scene or mobility aid can misrepresent individual users.
PassCal separates shared scene description from personal interpretation using frozen VLM features, detected barrier properties, and user-specific calibration.
With eight answers, Brier score improves from 0.550 to 0.479 on held-out users and scenes; direct VLM prompting reaches 0.562.
Conformal risk control produces passable, blocked, or “depends on you” statements with bounded expected error; decisive-scene coverage rises from 27% to 42% at 5% risk.
Audit-supervised barrier properties improve all tested vision and VLM encoders and outperform attributes from a sidewalk-navigation VLM.

papers.abstract: Training autonomous driving models requires large and diverse datasets, collected primarily by vehicles. Scaling them entails investment in fleet operation, data processing and annotation. Road infrastructure records traffic and multi-vehicle interactions, yet the viewpoint gap between roadside and onboard sensors limits its direct use for training. Here we introduce AnyR2V, a framework that transforms multimodal roadside observations into seven-camera surround-view videos for different vehicle perspectives. It aggregates sequential observations into a shared scene representation of geometry and road-user motion, then renders appearance, depth and layout conditions along target-vehicle trajectories. Supervised by spatiotemporally aligned roadside-vehicle pairs, AnyR2V generates surround-view videos guided by scene structure and road-user motion. Existing roadside 3D bounding boxes are transformed into target-vehicle coordinates and paired with generated images, allowing one traffic recording and its annotations to yield training data from multiple vehicle perspectives. We construct R2V360, a dataset of 89 real traffic sequences at an urban intersection, with aligned multimodal roadside data and onboard surround-view videos. AnyR2V outperforms six scene reconstruction methods in image fidelity and in depth and semantic agreement between generated and real onboard images. We further evaluate generated videos along other vehicles' trajectories by adding them to real training data. Adding generated frames equal to 50% of the original real training frame count improves mean average precision (mAP) by 3.3-3.4 AP-points across three 3D object detectors on the real onboard test set, relative to real-data-only baselines. These results demonstrate that roadside traffic records can provide training data from multiple vehicle perspectives, offering a new data source for autonomous driving.
authors: Yichen Zhang, Zihan Wang, Hao Chen, Runyi Huang, Ruixue Zong, Jing Wang, Yunong Mao, Lei He, Keqiang Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability limits of collecting vehicle-mounted autonomous-driving data.
Aggregates roadside observations into a shared representation of scene geometry and road-user motion.
Renders appearance, depth, and layout from target-vehicle trajectories, using aligned roadside–vehicle pairs for supervision.
R2V360 contains 89 real urban-intersection traffic sequences with aligned roadside and onboard data.

Generated data improved 3D detector mAP by 3.3–3.4 AP points when adding frames equal to 50% of the real training set; evaluation is based on this urban-intersection dataset and real onboard test data.

figures.caption: Figure 8: AnyR2V framework for roadside-to-vehicle surround-view video generation. a, Construction of the shared roadside scene. Sequential roadside point clouds and images are aggregated using 3D tracking annotations to construct a static background and instance geometry for dynamic objects. Together with object trajectories, these form a shared scene that can be queried at specified times. Instance geometry remains fixed, while position and orientation vary along each trajectory. b, Rendering of target-view conditions. Camera poses and capture times are determined along the trajectory of the recording vehicle or another target vehicle. The shared scene is rendered into appearance, depth and layout conditions, which respectively provide observed colours, relative depth distributions, and object categories and spatial extents. c, Video generation with tri-modal conditioning. The three conditions are encoded by a frozen video encoder and concatenated. A trainable condition embedding and four control blocks inject conditioning residuals into the frozen video backbone, guiding the progressive generation of video latents from Gaussian noise. The seven videos for a given vehicle are generated jointly and decoded separately for each camera by a frozen decoder. Videos for different vehicles are generated independently using the shared scene and model parameters. Flames and snowflakes indicate trainable and frozen modules, respectively. P denotes a linear residual projection; CFG denotes classifier-free guidance, applied here to text conditions; and UniPC is the sampling solver. Text and flow-time inputs and training supervision paths are omitted.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of generated images and their semantic segmentation maps. Rows show, from top to bottom, the six Gaussian-splatting baselines, AnyR2V (OURS) and real onboard images (GT). All segmentation maps are predicted by the same Mask2Former model.

papers.selection_reason: Roadside-to-vehicle surround-view video generation for scaling autonomous driving training data.
papers.title: Beyond Vehicle-Centric Data: Scaling Autonomous Driving through Roadside-to-Vehicle Generation
papers.tldr: AnyR2V converts roadside traffic recordings into multi-perspective, seven-camera vehicle-view videos that improve autonomous-driving detector training.

papers.abstract: Compositional Zero-Shot Learning (CZSL) recognizes unseen attribute--object pairs by recombining primitives from seen compositions. Existing methods stop sharing evidence at deployment: fixed prototypes cannot exploit unlabeled test streams, while composition-wise refinement cannot propagate corrections across pairs sharing a primitive. We introduce PRISM, an online CZSL framework that extends primitive sharing to test-time adaptation. Its Hierarchical Knowledge Accumulation Module (HiKAM) factorizes prototype migration into composition-, attribute-, and object-level residual banks. A Priority Visual Memory Queue (PVMQ), initialized by Prototype Queue Initialization (PQI), grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence. The same adaptive core supports exhaustive Full PRISM and recall-calibrated Adaptive PRISM-Lite, which selects candidate budgets from held-out ranks. Comprehensive closed- and open-world experiments on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA demonstrate the state of the art, with Full PRISM achieving the best open-world AUC and harmonic mean on all three benchmarks and the best closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA. Fine-grained long-tail and non-stationary primitive-block evaluations reveal gains on under-supported concepts and stable adaptation under prolonged skew. Adaptive PRISM-Lite further delivers substantial efficiency gains in the full open-world space with only a small accuracy cost. PRISM thus combines primitive-shared online adaptation, multimodal grounding, and candidate-aware inference.
authors: Jianhua Wang, Zhihang Zheng, Yang Liu, Jiale Du
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed prototypes and pair-specific updates that cannot use unlabeled test streams or share corrections across related attributes and objects.
Uses HiKAM to update composition-, attribute-, and object-level prototype residuals, extending primitive sharing to test-time adaptation.
Grounds text updates with bounded visual evidence through a Priority Visual Memory Queue initialized by PQI.
Full PRISM achieves the best reported open-world AUC and harmonic mean on UT-Zappos, MIT-States, and C-GQA, with strongest closed-world results on UT-Zappos and C-GQA.
PRISM-Lite reduces open-world inference cost with only a small accuracy decrease; evaluations also show gains for long-tail concepts and stability under prolonged distribution skew.

papers.title: PRISM: Primitive-Integrated Separable Modulation with Priority Visual Memory Queue for Compositional Zero-Shot Learning
papers.tldr: PRISM enables compositional zero-shot models to adapt online by sharing visual and textual evidence across related primitives, improving open- and closed-world recognition while supporting efficient candidate-aware inference.

papers.abstract: We ask whether a compact universal multimodal embedding models can produce better search embeddings by running the same layers again. Looped transformers add computation with nearly unchanged model size, making them an appealing alternative to a larger encoder. Their success in language-model reasoning and recent use for retrieval motivate the idea, but higher retrieval scores alone do not reveal what an extra pass contributes. We study eleven loop designs and training variants on three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture. Our protocol distinguishes whether a model uses its extra pass, whether its image states respond to the query, and whether those updates improve retrieval. We prove that an image placed before the query remains query-independent through repeated layers when information only travels forward. We then open a query-to-image path in three ways, including order-alternating recurrence, which places the query first on the next pass. Each path produces query-sensitive image states. For bidirectional attention and order alternation, freezing later visual updates does not lower accuracy. On all 78 datasets of the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark version 2 (MMEB-V2), a standard added loop loses 0.46 points against its trained control; an intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36. A model pretrained with recurrence gains +4.23 points over its own loop-removed control and benefits from query-conditioned image updates when answering visual questions or locating objects from text.
authors: Zhizhang Hu, Yue Zhang
bullets: The study evaluates 11 loop designs and training variants across three checkpoints of one vision-language architecture.
A standard added loop slightly hurts performance: −0.46 points versus its trained control on all 78 MMEB-V2 datasets.
An intermediate generative stage changes the effect to +0.36 points, while recurrence pretraining yields a +4.23-point gain over its loop-removed control.
Order-alternating recurrence and bidirectional attention create query-sensitive image states; freezing later visual updates does not reduce accuracy in these designs.
Query-conditioned updates are especially useful for visual question answering and text-based object localization.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Which task groups benefit from recurrence? Axes partition all 78 MMEB-v2 datasets; points average dataset-score differences from each model’s own trained control. Scores use top-1 hit rate for images and videos and nDCG@5 for documents, on a 0–100 scale. The retrofit uses order-alternating recurrence. The native control uses the same pretrained weights without repetition and trains longer. The zero ring separates gains from losses.

Figure 3. Query dependence and useful visual updates are separate properties. Left: dataset-averaged relative visual-state differences after pass or cycle 1 and 2 when only the query changes (one checkpoint). This measures hidden states, not retrieval accuracy. Right: changes in the eight-image-task score under visual freeze; circles show seed-matched changes and bars their means. Opening a query path produces sensitivity without an accuracy cost under freeze for the measured added loops. The native loop is strongly affected; Figure 4 tests whether its dependence is query-specific.

Figure 4. Which tasks need the image to be updated under the right query? In the native LoopVL embedder, second-cycle visual states are replaced by states computed from the same image under another instance text; actual text states are retained. Dots show two seeds and short bars their means. Scores use MMEB’s diagnostic candidate pools. Question answering and grounding are more affected than composed retrieval. Generic text-to-image inputs provide a zero-change control.

Figure 1. Using an extra pass is different from improving the model. On the 16-dataset diagnostic, the same trained Qwen3.5-2B loop improves by 1.27 points when its second pass is enabled. A separately trained single-pass control still scores higher. The middle and right points use exactly the same loop checkpoint. Boxes count layer applications, with the repeated eight-layer block sharing its base weights. The plotted score axis is restricted to show the differences.

Figure 2. More depth does not automatically change who can read whom. Arrows show possible information flow, with the arrowhead at the reader. Both passes in the fixed image-first order let the query read the image. Order-alternating recurrence places the already image-informed query before the image on pass 2, opening a reverse path through the same causal block. States and positional indices are permuted together, and the output is restored before the gated residual. The prelude and coda run once; only the middle block is reused. Opening a path permits dependence but does not guarantee that training will exploit it.

Figure 5. The same image, two questions. Maps show per-patch relative changes in visual hidden states after pass or cycle 2, using a prespecified Visual7W example [31]. Models use native grids on a shared, unclipped scale. These are state-difference maps, not attention or saliency maps.

Table 1. Complete 78-dataset evaluation. Each difference uses the control in its own training group. The overall score averages all datasets, rather than averaging the three family means. The native loop-removed control trains longer to approximately match observed conversion time. These two model groups are not an architecture-matched comparison. Bidirectional and query-sandwich variants are not assigned an unmeasured full-benchmark score.

Table 2. Repeated diagnostic comparisons. Loop minus its trained control on the 16-dataset mean, in points. The bidirectional control has the same attention change; the generative control has the same extra training stage. The native control has approximately matched observed training time.

papers.selection_reason: Studies layer reuse and query-conditioned updates in multimodal embedding models; relevant to multimodal foundation model design.
papers.title: When Does Reusing Layers Help Multimodal Embeddings?
papers.tldr: Reusing transformer layers helps multimodal retrieval only when recurrence enables useful query-conditioned image updates and is supported by training.

papers.abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.
authors: Chansu Han, Seok-Hwan Choi, Takeshi Takahashi
bullets: Text-site ($T$) DiM interventions increase attack success on mixed image-text and audio-text inputs.
Equivalent interventions at perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E/P/F$) show no comparable lift.
Probes suggest the method is informative at $T$ but weak or near chance at $E/P$ for the studied DiM family.
Attacks track harmful text more than image or audio content, with the reported VLGuard result showing modest absolute ASR growth from 0.030 to 0.150 at $T$.
The conclusion is recipe-scoped: it concerns intervention accessibility, not the absence or complete representation of refusal outside the text decoder.

papers.selection_reason: Studies intervention localization and safety behavior in multimodal LLM derivatives, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model understanding.
papers.title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?

papers.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.
authors: Zhanjiang Yang, Lijun Sun, Yueming Li, Meng Li, Yijun Yang
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization of existing MORL methods beyond task- or objective-specific policies.
Uses a multimodal diffusion transformer with likelihood-free flow matching to model diverse trade-off trajectories.
Trains in three stages: large-scale pre-training, curated-data mid-training, and few-shot post-training on new tasks and trade-offs.
Outperforms prior methods on most D4MORL tasks, including zero-shot interpolation/extrapolation and few-shot adaptation in continuous control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Network architecture of Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for MORL. FP2 is a rectified flow-based model with a multi-modal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) backbone that denoises state-action chunks and is guided by multimodal conditions including numerical and textual preferences and multi-objective returns. FP2 is trained offline and deployed as an online policy.

Figure 2: Three-stage training pipeline of Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2). In Stage 1, FP2 is pre-trained to learn diverse long-horizon trade-off behaviors based on large-scale trajectories Dpre. In Stage 2, FP2 is continuously mid-trained to align policy behavior with the target preference using curated high-quality Pareto non-dominated trajectories Dmid. In Stage 3, FP2 can be further post-trained to efficiently adapt to unseen preference configurations or new tasks with the remaining trajectories Ddrop or a very small amount of new task data Dtask. (See Sec. 4.3 for more details.)

Figure 1: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for MORL. FP2 is a rectified flow-based policy conditioned on numerical and textual user preferences. Through principled pre- and mid-training on diverse datasets (yellow region), FP2 learns a reusable multi-objective trade-off prior that generalizes to out-of-distribution preferences and can be efficiently adapted to new locomotion tasks (blue region) via few-shot post-training.
Figure 6: Cross-task performance comparison.
Figure 10: Preference generalization on the Amateur datasets. In each panel, FP2 (left) and MODULI (right) are shown with OOD points in color and dataset points in gray.19
Figure 11: Preference generalization on the Expert datasets. In each panel, FP2 (left) and MODULI (right) are shown with OOD points in color and dataset points in gray.20

papers.abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.
authors: Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, Nehal Kathrotia, Priyanka Tiwari
bullets: Targets prompt bloat, excessive token consumption, and error-prone loops in reflective multi-turn agents.
Uses a two-stage process: penalty-free skill discovery followed by accuracy-guarded pruning and code offloading to workspace utilities.
Evaluated across four models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench.
Reduced output tokens in 11 of 12 configurations, by up to 80% versus unconstrained EvoSkill, while improving mean accuracy on every benchmark.
Lowered total token usage and serving cost across all configurations, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

papers.abstract: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.
authors: Mi Luo, Lijun Yu, Adams Wei Yu, Ang Cao, Baochen Sun, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Nan Hua, Yuan Hao, Alex Dimakis, Ya Xu, Ed H. Chi, Xuezhi Wang, Yinxiao Liu
bullets: Tests counterfactual boundary cases where nearly identical frames have different true futures.
FlipTest evaluates 11 models across 1,680 frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks using minimal pairs, matched controls, and dense sweeps.
All models fall short; the best achieves 18.3% pair accuracy, below random guessing, and responds similarly to consequential and inconsequential changes.
A vision-language model and coding agent more accurately detect the relevant boundaries, suggesting the information is visible but missed by video models.
The results challenge pure next-frame prediction and call for models that identify causal world states controlling future dynamics.

papers.abstract: In 2025, there was a total of 358 weather-related disasters worldwide affecting millions of people. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Previous approaches treat the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories without considering obstacle avoidance. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. 1 where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust.
authors: Pranav Nedunghat, Jeffrey Mao, Praveen Merumugumala
bullets: Targets autonomous drone navigation through complex obstacles to deliver supplies and locate survivors.

papers.abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.
authors: Mohammad Al-Jarrah, Yuhang Mei, Karen Leung, Bamdad Hosseini, Amirhossein Taghvaei
bullets: Frames imitation learning as conditional sampling of action chunks given observation histories.
Introduces three variants: optimal transport policy (OTP), flow matching policy (FMP), and stochastic interpolant policy (SIP).
Unlike Diffusion Policy, uses the empirical demonstration distribution rather than a fixed Gaussian reference.
On Push-T and robomimic Square, the methods are competitive with Diffusion and Consistency Policies while requiring smaller networks and shorter training.
OTP minimizes inference cost with one evaluation; SIP achieves the strongest scores among the proposed methods at higher cost.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning from monocular video enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how 3D environments evolve over time, supporting physical world understanding and embodied intelligence. Existing efforts primarily address observed-dynamics understanding, whereas agents in dynamic environments also require future-dynamics prediction beyond the observation boundary. Moreover, external geometric processing and textual descriptions can increase inference complexity or lose information when representing continuous dynamics. These limitations motivate a shared internal state that preserves observed dynamics and remains predictive beyond the input video. Accordingly, we present Pros4D, a framework for modeling evolving 4D worlds in latent space that unifies retrospective understanding of observed-dynamics with prospective reasoning for future-dynamics prediction. Specifically, Pros4D-Engine derives geometry-grounded supervision and constructs paired examples for both tasks, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates them across eight spatial task categories spanning dynamic cameras, objects, and scenes. At the model level, Pros4D compresses observed dynamics into latent observed states and autoregressively rolls them forward into latent future states. 4D Latent Alignment (4DLA) grounds these states through complementary visual-semantic and geometric supervision, while joint language supervision connects them to task reasoning. Experiments across benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines in both capabilities.
authors: Rongxin Gao, Dongxuan Liu, Chu Li, Chengyang Ji, Jialing Huang, Runyu Chen, Kairun Wen, Chenxin Li, Jingrui Ye, Haosong Zhen, Xinghao Ding, Yue Huang, Yuzhi Huang, Xiaodong Tu, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between recognizing observed dynamics and forecasting dynamics beyond a video’s observation window.

Pros4D-Engine creates geometry-grounded training examples, while Pros4D-Bench evaluates eight dynamic spatial reasoning categories.
Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines on both observed-dynamics understanding and future-dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.
authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Uses shared initial and final layers around independently parameterized parallel branches, with Wide-Shallow, Narrow-Deep, and Balanced variants.

Across controlled pretraining scales, branching provides gains beyond width and depth changes and works across fusion functions.
The approach is most effective in middle layers and is evaluated within the reported pretraining and single-GPU inference settings.

papers.abstract: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.
authors: Haidong Hu
bullets: Existing latent world models prevent representation collapse but do not give embedding distances clear meaning.
Sense replaces anti-collapse mechanisms with one cross-entropy loss based on directed distance.
The encoder is trained without a predictor; the predictor is later fitted by plain regression to fixed embeddings.
Across four pixel environments, Sense detects irreversible transitions with AUC 0.95–1.00, versus 0.39–0.59 for LeWorldModel.
Sense achieves 100% goal-reaching on TwoRoom and maintains near-zero or lowest failure as goals move farther away, depending on the environment.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal safety alignment heavily relies on a text-centric paradigm, assuming risks are explicit in language or globally prominent in images. However, real-world hazards are often visually subtle or peripheral, causing existing models to fail due to their reliance on coarse, global visual representations. In this work, we study fine-grained visual safety alignment and introduce a challenging 1,200-sample benchmark across four domains, where hazards necessitate localized inspection. To address this, we propose Fine-Grained RLAIF (FGR), a reinforcement learning framework that casts image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy. FGR employs a decomposed reward design to jointly align three core safety behaviors: (i) where to look via a visual evidence reward, (ii) when to act via a tool-formatting constraint, and (iii) how to reason via visually grounded safety explanations. FGR achieves accuracy ranging from 86.71% to 93.00%, consistently outperforming strong multimodal and agent-based baselines.
authors: Chunxue Xu, Yiwei Wang, Yujun Cai, Songze Li
bullets: Introduces a 1,200-sample benchmark spanning four domains, focused on hazards requiring localized visual inspection.
Frames image zoom-in as a learnable perception policy through reinforcement learning.
Uses decomposed rewards to guide where to look, when to use the tool, and how to produce visually grounded safety explanations.
Reports accuracy of 86.71%–93.00%, outperforming the evaluated multimodal and agent-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Experiments near vehicle handling limits must keep three questions apart: what a maneuver requests, what the closed-loop system executes, and whether the task is completed. We present DynLimit, a simulation platform that organizes this process end to end. Scenarios are composed from road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects; planners and controllers attach through a shared observation and control interface; a vehicle adapter runs either a license-free four-wheel model or an external dynamics solver; and synchronized records feed task evaluation, replay, and response inspection. The platform carries a task-oriented evaluation method that pairs a prescribed reference demand with a sampled passing set and event-aligned diagnosis. Across eight task families, three friction environments, and three reference-assisted baseline chains we executed 450 runs: 360 nominal, 18 locally refined, and 72 with prescribed initial offsets. Method differences depend on the task family, equal aggregate pass counts arise from different passing cells, and local refinement narrows two sampled transitions without locating a continuous boundary. Two case comparisons show why sideslip or tire-utilization peaks cannot replace task constraints. The three views therefore stay distinct in every reported run: an outcome can be traced from the prescribed demand, through the executed response, to the task rule that decided it. Code is available at https://github.com/Yang2581/dynlimit
authors: Yang Xiao, Yongzhi Liu, Sunan Zhang, Kang Wang, Guodong Yin, Weichao Zhuang
bullets: Supports composable scenarios with road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects.

Across eight task families and three friction environments, it found that methods with equal aggregate pass counts can differ in which task conditions they pass.
Shows that sideslip and tire-utilization peaks alone cannot substitute for task-specific success criteria.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical high-speed legged locomotion requires motion planners to balance safety foresight with online computational efficiency. Although short prediction horizons reduce rollout costs, they provide limited safety foresight, and strict safety constraints severely restrict the feasible trajectory space. We propose a recovery-guided model-based diffusion (MBD) framework for safety-critical legged locomotion. It incorporates a learned terminal recovery critic into short-horizon trajectory optimization. Specifically, the critic approximates the worst-case future clearance margin along rollouts of a designated recovery policy. We introduce a feasibility-guided refinement strategy that combines within-horizon constraints and terminal recoverability at each sampling stage, while retaining feasible elites to mitigate sampling-support loss. Across 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, our approach achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, while requiring substantially less computation than long-horizon MBD baselines. A project page is available at https://zack4417.github.io/rg-mbd/.
authors: Lei Zheng, Shivam Sood, Mithun Vanniasinghe, Guillaume Sartoretti, Armin Lederer
bullets: Short prediction horizons reduce computation but offer limited foresight, while strict safety constraints shrink feasible trajectories.
The method adds a learned terminal recovery critic that estimates worst-case future clearance under a recovery policy.
Feasibility-guided refinement enforces current-horizon constraints, terminal recoverability, and preserves feasible elite samples.
In 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, it achieved zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success.
The approach required substantially less computation than long-horizon model-based diffusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.
authors: Nur Afsa Syeda, Mohamed Elmahallawy
bullets: Targets security gaps in vision-language-action models, especially conditional suppression of backdoor behavior.
Proposes three designs: Cross-Modal Trigger, Self-Suppressing Trigger, and Multi-Trigger.
Evaluations on SmolVLA and OpenVLA show reduced detectability, 63–71% attack success, and preserved clean-task performance.
The attacks also evade STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection, highlighting suppression as a key threat dimension.

papers.abstract: Lightweight 3D building models support urban spatial analysis, but their production often requires dense scene reconstruction, building extraction, and mesh simplification. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is more efficient than conventional multi-view stereo, existing large-scale methods lack semantic selection and parallel instance-level training. We present SemLite-GS, a building-centric framework that reconstructs lightweight building meshes from large-scale UAV oblique imagery. First, an orthographic reference map establishes globally consistent building identities, which are propagated to oblique views to form camera-instance pairs and regions of interest. Second, semantic-selective parallel PGSR training jointly processes multiple pairs within relevant image regions while updating only target Gaussians; contextual Gaussians remain fixed to preserve visibility. Third, architectural planes extracted from rendered depth, opacity, and normal maps guide signed distance field optimization, producing meshes with adaptive polygon allocation and well-defined structural boundaries. Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that our SemLite-GS substantially reduces building reconstruction time compared with representative full-scene 3DGS methods. With comparable polygon budgets, SemLite-GS achieves superior preservation of dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions compared with conventional dense reconstruction followed by mesh decimation. The source code is available at https://github.com/IRIS-LAB-whu/SemLite-GS.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

papers.abstract: Water--land cross-domain robots require continuous localization across land, transition and underwater phases, where sensor characteristics and availability change abruptly. Existing datasets and conventional metrics are not designed to capture transition-induced degradation and failures. We present \textbf{M-CROSS}, to the best of our knowledge, the first multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for SLAM across continuous water--land transitions. It provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth measurements; 6DoF pose ground truth; sensor-wise medium-state annotations; and medium-dependent sensor degradation models. We establish a transition-aware protocol comprising the Trajectory Completion Rate (TCR), Piecewise Absolute Pose Error (PW-APE), Transition End Error (TEE), and Transition Survival Period (TSP), which measure trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and localization survival under prolonged partial immersion, respectively. Experiments with 6 representative SLAM systems show that existing methods fail to maintain both localization accuracy and trajectory continuity across the full set of water--land transitions, exhibiting transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures. M-CROSS is publicly available https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCross-Dataset
authors: Yan Dong, Tianyi Wu, Junyu Yang, Shaoqiang Qiu, Zefeng Yan, Tao Zhang, Bin Han

Evaluation of six representative SLAM systems reveals transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures.
Dataset and benchmark are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Conventional experience replay typically applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, overlooking variations in how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures change during sequential training. To address this limitation, we propose Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), an exemplar-adaptive supervision mechanism that regulates anatomical preservation according to source-referenced knowledge drift. DCSRL operates within a reliability-guided replay framework that selects informative historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics while adaptively regulating replay during training. For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and subsequently measures changes in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted anatomical structures. These complementary drift measurements are aggregated and normalized to generate bounded, exemplar-specific coefficients that dynamically adjust boundary and structural replay losses without modifying the underlying memory-selection policy. We evaluate DCSRL under sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, comparing its performance with regularization-, distillation-, and replay-based continual-learning approaches. Experimental findings indicate that DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, particularly under heterogeneous imaging conditions, although trade-offs remain in knowledge transfer across tasks. These findings suggest that source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning offers a promising direction for adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.
authors: Zahid Ullah, Jaeyoon Seo, Jihie Kim

papers.abstract: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.
authors: S M Mahbub Murshed
bullets: Evaluates stale retrieval on 892 real-world updating facts with source-derived validity labels.
Shows retrieval rankings can look identical even when reader accuracy differs by up to 65.6 points without dates.
Introduces Contamination@5, which identifies stale-memory failures that current@1/current@5 miss.
Finds removing lexical anchors severely harms freshness, while entity resolution on writing and querying recovers most of the loss.
Compares supersession handling in Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem, and ERASE, and releases data, evaluation tools, and baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.
authors: Yikang Qiao, Jianye Zeng, Duan Huang, Ziying Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free framework separating permutation, retention, precision, and statistical replacement effects.

Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements reduced accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points, respectively.
Additional experiments show that transformation effects depend on original feature values and evaluation setting.
Provides empirical guidance for evaluating visual-token transformations and designing multimodal interfaces.

papers.abstract: A distributed multi-robot object transportation strategy is proposed for objects of unknown shape, size, geometry, mass and mass distribution without any prior knowledge about the object or number of robots involved in the transportation process. Robots follow the boundary of the object and dynamically determine viable pushing points. A novel object-model-free heading-error-driven pushing effort regulation method is proposed to promote goal-directed object motion; robots regulate their pushing effort using individual and collective heading errors. Robots dynamically relocate around the object boundary if a pushing point is lost or the required pushing effort exceeds its capability to correct its heading. The proposed method is validated using simple and complex shapes with convex and non-convex boundary regions and dynamically changing weight distribution of objects. Detailed analysis on the effects of robot distribution and initial object pose on the transportation performance in terms of required time and path efficiency is also presented. Scalability analysis revealed that object transportation time is dependent on the number of pushing surfaces available which in turn depends on the object size, shape, and set inter-robot safety distance. The proposed system yielded highly efficient object paths with consistent elapsed transport times over several trials robust to external disturbances such as non-uniform friction between contacting surfaces and robot wheel slip.

Validation covers convex and non-convex shapes, complex geometries, changing weight distributions, friction variation, and wheel slip.
Transport paths were highly efficient with consistent elapsed times across trials; scalability depends on available pushing surfaces, object properties, and inter-robot safety distance.

papers.abstract: Progress in autonomous navigation in off-road environments requires not only advances in algorithms, but also robust and capable physical platforms suited to both development and deployment. Today, off-road autonomy is typically developed and tested at one of two extremes of vehicle scale, each with different drawbacks. Full-size vehicles are capable but expensive, require large logistic infrastructure for deployment and maintenance, and expensive when pushed beyond their limits. RC-scale vehicles are small and inexpensive, but limited in the terrain they can traverse and the payload that they can carry, which includes their sensors and compute. We present the AlphaTruck platform, which leverages recent advances in compact sensing and compute to integrate multimodal sensing, embedded CPU-GPU compute, and an onboard autonomy stack for high-speed, off-road navigation, all integrated into a large-scale, 1/5th RC vehicle chassis. AlphaTruck is designed as both a research testbed and a field-deployable platform for commercial and defense missions such as survey, search and rescue, and agriculture, with the capacity to carry task-specific payloads. At 1/5 scale, the autonomy stack, sensors, and batteries all compete for the same mass, power, and cooling budget, so the platform must balance five needs: mobility over rough terrain, rich sensing, onboard computation, payload capacity to carry the autonomy stack while leaving room for task-specific equipment, and practical operation and repair. Thus, AlphaTruck navigates off-road environments autonomously at 6-10 m/s using only onboard sensing and compute.

papers.abstract: Although object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) approaches are usually evaluated in simulation, which offers scale and repeatable environments, real-world deployments are rarely examined beyond feasibility demonstrations. This paper presents the deployment of Room-Mediated Co-occurrence, an ObjectNav policy that reasons over Room Probability Vectors (RPVs), on two robotic platforms (Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4) through a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge. We study how these semantic priors generalise to physical environments and describe the adaptations required to transfer RPV from simulation to hardware, covering sensing, localisation, and the action interface. Across 66 trials on Spot, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university postgraduate research facility, RPV achieves a raw Success Rate (SR) of 0.455. Our analysis identifies undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatch between the room lexicon and physical layout as plausible contributors to the 8.4 percentage-point gap between the real-world SR and the reported simulated SR of 0.539. Code is available at https://github.com/Matthew-K-Chua/rpv-ros2-bridge.
authors: Matthew Chua, Adam Scicluna, Gavin Paul

On Spot, evaluates 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university research facility.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.
authors: Abhinav Gupta, Nissan Pow
bullets: The study compares computation reuse across replanning calls with simply reducing denoising steps on LIBERO-Goal.

Caching offers limited speedups when fresh steps and image/video processing remain necessary; estimated savings were at most 11–14% in one setup.
Cache performance degraded when cached steps covered more of the flow path or noise was resampled, motivating evaluation under deployed sampler settings.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D$^2$C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D$^2$C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D$^2$C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D$^2$C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.
authors: Julian Martinez, Ruchika Singh, Mohammad Afrazi, Kooktae Lee
bullets: Addresses real-time monitoring of dynamically evolving air-pollution distributions, including plumes leaving a fixed monitoring area.

Simulations under mild and strong winds show better Sinkhorn-distance performance than tested baselines; baselines lose tracking under rapidly shifting plumes, while D²C adapts.

papers.abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.
authors: Parsa Mirtaheri, Mohammadreza Armandpour, Keivan Alizadeh, Iman Mirzadeh, Parshin Shojaee, Aryo Lotfi, David Harrison, Mehrdad Farajtabar
bullets: The study compares in-context learning (ICL), GRPO reinforcement learning, SDPO self-distillation, and their combinations under a shared online adaptation protocol.
ICL delivers the largest standalone improvement, increasing mean success from 28.8% to 49.4% across four environments.
Combining ICL with GRPO achieves the best reported mean success at 51.6%; GRPO improves every tested ICL policy, while SDPO has mixed effects.
ICL reduces environment lookups and attempt length, but can cause agents to skip task inspection and verification.
GRPO helps restore inspection and verification while retaining ICL’s reduced lookup behavior.
