papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation missions must satisfy timed and conditional requirements that can be expressed in signal temporal logic (STL). While a practical means of monitoring these requirements is from camera images, this is challenging because STL robustness depends on physical margins, such as distances and clearances, that are not directly observed. Rather than learning a separate visual monitor for each formula, we learn a shared latent representation from multi-view images and decode physically meaningful margins for individual predicates. Co-training the encoder with predicate decoders increases the certification rate from 58.7% to 96.3% compared with a frozen encoder, despite nearly unchanged predicate sign accuracy. STL semantics then compose these margins into robustness estimates for any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. We further calibrate the decoding errors of selected STL clauses using conformal prediction, yielding two-sided intervals that certify both satisfaction and violation and propagate through interval STL to any formula composed from the clauses. In simulated kitchen missions (LIBERO), our monitor correctly predicts satisfaction or violation in 98.9% of 4662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas. For missions lasting up to 17 min, calibrated bounds establish satisfaction or violation for 96.9% of missions without incorrect conclusions. A single calibration also provides simultaneous 91.0% coverage across all 255 conjunctions of eight clauses, allowing new formulas without recalibration.
authors: Xinpei Ni, Glen Chou, Samuel Coogan
bullets: Targets timed and conditional robotic manipulation requirements that are difficult to monitor from images because STL robustness depends on unobserved physical margins.
Learns a shared multi-view latent representation with predicate-specific decoders, then composes decoded margins using STL semantics without retraining per formula.
Conformal calibration produces two-sided robustness intervals and propagates guarantees through interval STL to certify both satisfaction and violation.
In simulated LIBERO kitchen missions, it achieved 98.9% correct decisions over 4,662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas.
Scope: results are demonstrated in simulation and for trained predicates; calibration is needed for selected STL clauses, though one calibration supports new formula conjunctions.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the challenge of monitoring physical constraints (STL) in robotic manipulation using a shared latent visual representation to decode physical margins, bridging perception and physical safety.
papers.title: Physics-Grounded STL Monitoring from Image Observations
papers.tldr: A shared vision model decodes physics-grounded margins from images to monitor arbitrary STL formulas, with calibrated intervals that reliably certify satisfaction or violation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based driving planners can generate multiple trajectories for the same scene, but these candidates vary in quality. Can their internal states reveal which candidate will be better before denoising is complete? We systematically study this question in three pretrained planners: Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, using linear probes to predict final trajectory quality from intermediate states and evaluating candidate ranking and selection on held-out scenes. Across all three planners, we observe that states from the first denoiser evaluation already support informative selection, while further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality. Further analyses show that readout depends on the representation and reader, and that selection can coexist with limited overall ranking accuracy. These findings motivate an early-selection method that selects after the first denoiser evaluation and completes only the chosen candidate. This reduces computation relative to fully denoising every candidate and improves open-loop trajectory quality over random selection across all three planners. In particular, it reduces Alpamayo's average displacement error by 17.8% and 13.4% in one- and four-camera configurations, respectively. Closed-loop evaluations also show higher mean driving scores and progress.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Ziyang Leng, Yuxin Bao, Zhihao Zhao, Bolei Zhou, Xugui Zhou
bullets: Across Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, first-step states already support informative candidate selection.
Further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality.
Linear-probe readout varies by representation and reader, and selection can work despite limited overall ranking accuracy.
Selecting one candidate early and fully denoising only it reduces computation versus denoising every candidate.

The method improves open-loop quality over random selection across all planners; Alpamayo’s average displacement error drops 17.8% and 13.4% for one- and four-camera setups, with higher closed-loop driving scores and progress.

papers.abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $\epsilon$-stationary control in $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $\epsilon$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/\epsilon$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.
authors: Zherong Pan
bullets: Recasts unconstrained K-step control as a single min–max problem with strongly convex lower levels.
Uses only gradients and projection, updating all levels in parallel without Hessian or KKT solves.
Achieves an $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iteration bound, with an exponent independent of the number of levels $K$.
Smooths contact constraints using fixed-width bands to avoid requiring constraint qualifications; shrinking bands can worsen complexity.
In navigation experiments, PSK reached all goals with 16 levels and had lower equal-time loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation was better in 10.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.
authors: Siqi Zhu, Suozhi Huang, Yi Zhao, Jiaxuan You
bullets: Targets the latency caused by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers for each generated token.
Uses a training-free pipeline where suffix lookups can extend shallow predictions and admit multiple future tokens together.
Batches high-scoring draft candidates from different loop depths, then verifies them at full depth while preserving the model’s autoregressive distribution.
Across seven benchmarks, achieves average speedups of 5.85× on Ouro-2.6B and 5.13× on Huginn-3.5B over greedy decoding.
Outperforms LoopAhead in speedup by 40% on Ouro-2.6B and 25% on Huginn-3.5B.

papers.abstract: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $\alpha$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $\alpha$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$\alpha$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.
authors: Peize Ding
bullets: Tests viewing direction while keeping object centers fixed, isolating changes in perspective, shading, and shadows.
Across eight pretrained models, feature differences trace $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ in a scene-shared 2D plane.
The plane remains stable across lighting, colors, floors, and object shapes.
Readouts generalize to camera positions outside their training paths in seven of eight models, unlike geometry-based decoders.
In PixArt-$\alpha$, the representation appears abruptly in one block and persists later, but editing it changes objects rather than viewpoint; transfer to scanned objects is also examined.

papers.abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.
authors: Aarav Srivastava, Vishwas Sathish, Rajesh P. N. Rao
bullets: Evaluates visual generalization by changing one or more factors while keeping ProcTHOR layouts, objects, goals, and starts fixed.
Surface material changes cause most of the average success degradation; clutter and lighting have comparatively little effect.
Global image-statistics shifts do not reliably predict navigation performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially hurt end-to-end agents.
A model-based agent planning over frozen DINOv2 features achieves the highest reported full-shift success (0.83), but remains sensitive to surface appearance.
Results span model-free RL, model-based RL, and frozen-visual-representation agents, highlighting the need for appearance-invariant planning representations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators. We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.
authors: Pol Mestres, Varun Gabbita, Jason H. K. Siu, Sergio A. Esteban, Hampus Serneke, Joel W. Burdick, Aaron D. Ames

Permits biased value and gradient estimators, enabling integration with PPO-style methods.

Proves convergence toward approximate KKT points and decay of violations from unsafe initial policies.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real whole-body control on a Unitree G1 and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.

papers.abstract: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.
authors: Mengyu Yang, You Zhang, Vishnu Raj, Olha Townsend, James Hays, Andrea Fanelli, Gautam Bhattacharya
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization caused by limited real-world audio-visual data.
Automatically localizes sound sources, estimates relative 3D trajectories, and renders binaural audio.
Spatializes VGGSound to provide larger-scale training data.
The resulting model improves spatial reasoning and generalization while remaining competitive on semantic tasks.
Scope: performance depends on automatically estimated source locations and trajectories.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. Project page: https://camma-public.github.io/endocomparer
authors: Shi Li, Lalith Sharan, Jo\"el L. Lavanchy, Kun Yuan, Lorenzo Arboit, Nabani Banik, Elif Yazici, Maria Vannucci, Vinkle Srivastav, Pietro Mascagni, Nicolas Padoy
bullets: Addresses the limitation that most surgical VLMs process one video at a time and struggle to compare cases.
Uses Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA: separate low-rank adapters for each video over a shared frozen vision encoder.
Uses Perceive-then-Compare chain-of-thought reasoning to describe each video before deriving a comparison answer.
Introduces EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice video-pair questions spanning cholecystectomy and gastric bypass.
Outperforms generalist and surgical VLMs on identifying and specifying video differences, with improved robustness to video swapping.

papers.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.
authors: Angelo Moroncelli, Alessandro Leanza, Loris Roveda
bullets: Studies when guidance changes desired properties while preserving others, emphasizing request-dependent local geometry.
Uses a cosine-gain predictor, damped inverse correction, and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits.
Across 8,923 local-regime instances, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79; condition number correlates at -0.11.
Across images, audio, robotics, and control/planning, including character motion generation, the method links geometry to downstream gains.
In 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR by 3.25 dB over Adam with equal derivative traversals.

papers.abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.
authors: Hamidreza Hasani Balyani, Mahtab Movahhedrad, Seyed Pouyan Mousavi Davoudi
bullets: Pointwise uncertainty bounds are insufficient because unsampled geometry can change the first surface encountered in a new view.
Using Lipschitz envelopes and an epipolar reduction, the authors characterize the complete attainable set of first-hit depths and construct a valid scene for every attainable value.
They provide a necessary-and-sufficient test for whether multiple proposed first hits can arise from one shared scene, even when the attainable set is disconnected.

In a rectified setting, the sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter is max{Lh+2ε, 2ε/(1−bL)} for bL<1; ambiguity can persist above the critical threshold, and measurement noise can destroy stability at it.
A rational validation oracle and ten-scene evaluation distinguish solver correctness under the model from failures of the assumed scene class, including narrow but incorrect learned-depth bands.

These are analytic constructions, not measured prevalence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.
authors: Hamidreza Hasani Balyani
bullets: Across 15,170 held-out trials, stated payoffs shifted reports in both image and text conditions.
Exact compliance with a three-unit reporting incentive was lower from images than text for three of four small open VLMs; one model showed no reliable gap.
Adding the true value as text to image prompts eliminated the image–text gap across models.
Writing the visual reading before the final report sometimes removed the gap, but effects varied by model and prompt wording.
Visual input did not reliably increase truthfulness: several models still shaded reports even when told the client wanted the truth.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.
authors: Qi Chen, Zifeng Cheng, Zhiwei Jiang, Qing Gu
bullets: Addresses pseudo-autoregressive behavior and function-word-first bias in diffusion language models.
Uses token-level gradients to identify semantic tokens and prioritizes preserving them during progressive masking.
Reweights semantic-token losses to reinforce their early prediction.
Matches strong autoregressive baselines in text writing and code generation while improving semantic coherence.
Achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $\pi_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.
authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu
bullets: Existing world-action models waste capacity reconstructing mostly static backgrounds instead of modeling robot and object motion.
The method learns residual feature changes between current and future frames in frozen DINOv3 space, emphasizing manipulated regions.
A lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT jointly models actions and visual residuals using conditional flow matching.
Without robot pretraining, ResWAM reports strong results across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot tasks, with 92.7 ms latency.
Scope: results target action-conditioned visual prediction and manipulation; the abstract does not establish broader settings beyond these evaluations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a depth-aware path planning and collision avoidance framework for the safe navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered environments with low-height obstacles. Conventional LiDAR-based navigation systems, while accurate for mapping and localization, fail to detect transparent or low-height obstacles, whereas vision-based systems are prone to noise and occlusion. The proposed framework integrates RGB-D depth sensing, rule-based obstacle avoidance, and the NavfnROS global path planner to drive the robot from an initial point to a goal point. The proposed approach is implemented on the Husky A200 robot, equipped with a Kinova Gen3 arm, to form a complete setup for a robotic nursing assistant. This system features a multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control in the ROS-Gazebo environment. Experimental evaluations in a simulated cluttered environment demonstrate up to 40\% higher success rate and 35\% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines. Furthermore, real-world experimental results validate the proposed approach as a computationally efficient and safety-aware navigation solution for autonomous healthcare robots.

papers.abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

bullets: Across three instruction-tuned model families, the best probing direction was not the best steering direction for truthfulness or sentiment.

Probe directions transferred across models more reliably than steering directions.
Steering toward “unknown” increased abstention mainly on uncertain errors, with little correction of otherwise answerable errors.

papers.abstract: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

Applies hierarchical relation-guided rewards to align modality evidence, relation-state prediction, and final outputs.
Improves RGB-T grounding and robustness to sensor degradation over Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving general RGB-T reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: 3D object detection is critical for intelligent transportation systems. LiDAR has been widely adopted for accurate geometric measurements; however, purely geometric representations remain ambiguous under sparse observations and occlusions, while cross-sensor multimodal fusion suffers from calibration and synchronization errors. To overcome these challenges, we leverage an Ouster LiDAR to construct PALIN (Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR), a large-scale intrinsically pixel-aligned multimodal dataset jointly capturing geometry and NIR intensity, comprising approximately 8,000 annotated frames from static urban intersections and diverse mobile suburban scenes. Building upon this dataset, we propose CMambaFusion, a novel fusion framework consisting of a four-directional Cross-Mamba module for bidirectional cross-modal interaction and a Gated Concat-Mamba module for joint feature refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PALIN enables effective multimodal learning, and CMambaFusion achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over both LiDAR-only and representative fusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.

papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.
authors: Antal van den Bosch
bullets: Session-local drafters require no training and make drafting nearly free while a verifier reuses its KV cache.
Most-recent prompt lookup improves speedup by up to 0.09 over earliest-match lookup; session-memory weighting and backoff add no measurable benefit.
On medical and legal text, selective abstention saves 3–4 J per 100 tokens, whereas unselective drafting is faster but uses similar energy to plain decoding.
Drafted outputs match greedy decoding in 94% of generations; divergences occur only at numerical near-ties.
Repetition penalties reduce long-generation speedups to 1.1–1.2×, though recency remains beneficial and a minimum match-length floor consistently saves energy.

papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.
authors: Lucia Licakova, Niklas Schmidinger, Lukas Hauzenberger, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Depth recurrence increases effective depth but normally grows autoregressive KV memory with each iteration.
The authors evaluate looped Transformer hybrids using recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks plus periodic attention anchors.
A Parcae-style recurrent workspace and stabilising adapter are tested to constrain recurrence and improve stability.
Recurrent KV replay trains later iterations to reuse KV states written by selected earlier iterations.
Hybrid quality depends on sufficiently frequent attention anchors and the choice of recurrent mixer; KV replay retains near-baseline performance while reducing cache sharing overhead.

papers.abstract: Image steering aims to provide fine-grained control over concepts in generated images, enabling targeted and continuous manipulation without broadly altering the generation process. Recent steering methods for diffusion models primarily focus on the text-conditioning space or rely on costly auxiliary training. Deviating from that, we here propose a novel steering approach that extracts visual concept directions directly from the image-side activations of Diffusion Transformers. Specifically, we showcase few-shot concept extraction in the activation space using a simple difference-of-means estimator over intermediate residuals. We observe (a) scene-level concepts such as lighting, weather, and style are distributed across image tokens, as well as (b) local concepts such as object colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes are concentrated in specific regions. Towards controlling both concepts, we introduce a new unified training-free framework that uses global difference-of-means for (a) distributed concepts and masked difference-of-means for (b) local concepts, preventing local signals from being diluted by global averaging. Notably, using only a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs, our method identifies and extracts reusable concept directions that can be injected at inference for continuous steering. Quantitatively, our method outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, as well as is competitive with specialized editing models. Our results suggest that as concept directions can be applied at patch level, our method enables precise targeted and compositional steering, manipulating multiple concepts in the same image.
authors: Nabyl Quignon, Antitza Dantcheva
bullets: Uses difference-of-means over intermediate image-side residual activations to extract reusable concept directions from a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs.
Applies global averaging for distributed scene concepts such as lighting, weather, and style.
Uses masked, region-specific averaging for local concepts including colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes.
Injects extracted directions at inference for continuous, targeted, and multi-concept steering without auxiliary training.
Outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, while remaining competitive with specialized editing models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our few-shot concept extraction and steering pipeline. (1) We start from a small set of negative and positive prompt pairs, optionally with masks for localized concepts extraction. (2) We extract residual activations from a selected Diffusion Transformer block and estimate a concept direction using difference-of-means between positive and negative residuals. For global concepts, this is computed over all image tokens and for local concepts, it is restricted to the masked region patches. (3) At inference time, the resulting concept vector is injected into transformer blocks to steer generation, either globally or within a selected region.

Figure 2: Qualitative examples of concept steering. We show representative examples of our method across different concept families. Each row corresponds to a held-out prompt and visualizes the effect of increasing the steering strength α. The examples illustrate that extracted concept directions can produce smooth steering while preserving the main content of the image.

Figure 3: Compositional and targeted steering. Examples of different concept directions being applied to different regions in the same image. By selecting the spatial area to steer, our method enables targeted steering such as changing two different objects with two different colors or textures, as well as modifying different attributes of two persons. Notably, global concepts can be combined, as shown with snowy + anime in a single inference steering pass.

Figure 4: Edit success versus content preservation. We compare methods using ∆VQA to measure whether the requested edit is achieved and LPIPS to measure visual drift from the original image. Better methods appear toward the upper-left, indicating stronger edit success with less content drift. We note that ∆VQA slightly decreases at steering level 5, as some concepts appear at lower strengths and stronger interventions can lead to oversteering.

Figure 5: Extraction layer ablation. We sweep the layer used to extract the concept direction while keeping the injection range fixed. Layer 18 provides the strongest trade-off between edit success and content preservation.

Figure 7: Qualitative ablation samples – face concept: beard. Top row of each panel: extractiontimestep ablation. Bottom row: extraction-layer ablation.
Figure 8: Qualitative ablation samples – object concept: blue. Top row of each panel: extractiontimestep ablation. Bottom row: extraction-layer ablation.

Figure 11: Real-image steering with FLUX.2. Concept directions extracted exclusively from synthetic prompt pairs transfer to real reference images across multiple concepts. For each example, increasing the steering strength α progressively increases the presence of the target concept while preserving the reference image. Figure 9: Qualitative ablation samples – global concept: snowy. Top row of each panel: extractiontimestep ablation. Bottom row: extraction-layer ablation.
Figure 12: Qualitative examples of concept steering. We present more qualitative samples across concepts.

Figure 10: Representative failure cases. We show examples of semantic mismatch, spatial drift, and concept entanglement. Table 2: Injection range ablation. We compare several injection ranges while keeping the extraction configuration fixed. Blocks 18–56 gives the best overall trade-off.

papers.title: Few-Shot Visual Concept Extraction for Steering Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: A training-free, few-shot method extracts global and local visual concept directions from Diffusion Transformer activations for precise, compositional image steering.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.
authors: Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham, Khoi Nguyen, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Uses dense pixel-level CLIP features instead of mask-wise embeddings for fine-grained, proposal-free localization.
Selects a target region in a pivot view and propagates it across views with a video segmentor.
Lifts 2D tracks into 3D Gaussians using visibility voting to produce consistent segmentation masks.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups.
Supports efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our approach. We present a novel query-based framework for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation. Given multi-view images and a text query, we extract pixel-level CLIP features to produce similarity maps and identify a 2D pivot instance region. The pivot is refined and propagated across views within a fixed frame budget using a Tracking Segmentor with our Mask Refinement module to ensure geometric consistency and coverage. The resulting masks are lifted to 3D Gaussians via visibility voting, forming an occlusion-aware 3D instance mask, which is rendered at novel views to obtain high-quality 2D instance segmentation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can memorize and reproduce training samples during inference, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Existing inference-time mitigation methods often suppress conditional information globally, which may reduce memorization but can also harm semantic alignment and image quality. In this paper, we revisit memorization from the perspective of cross-attention heads. Through systematic analysis and targeted ablation, we find that memorization is mainly driven by a small subset of shallow-layer attention heads with abnormally strong semantic control, rather than by the entire cross-attention mechanism. Motivated by this finding, we propose Projection-based Top-k Attention Head Suppression, a targeted inference-time mitigation method. Our method first identifies the top-k attention heads most related to memorization using a semantic-control score, and then removes their condition-specific components through directional projection between conditional and unconditional representations. This design selectively weakens memorization-related features while preserving useful semantic information. Extensive experiments on different diffusion models and datasets show that our method effectively reduces memorization and achieves a better trade-off between memorization mitigation and image quality than existing approaches.
authors: Puwei Lian, Yujun Cai, Songze Li, Yuezu Lv, Guanghui Wen
bullets: Memorization is concentrated in a few shallow-layer attention heads with unusually strong semantic control.
The method identifies the top-k memorization-related heads using a semantic-control score.
It removes condition-specific components via projection between conditional and unconditional representations.
Experiments across diffusion models and datasets show reduced memorization with a better quality–mitigation trade-off than existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our framework. The left panel illustrates the computation of multi-head attention. Based on this process, we introduce two modifications on the right panel: (1) Identifying attention heads with strong semantic control through attention map analysis. (2) Applying projection-based suppression to mitigate memorization-related components in the selected heads.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison with baselines. The first column shows the memorized training images, while the remaining seven columns present the results of baselines and our method. Our method achieves a superior balance between memorization mitigation, semantic consistency, and image quality compared with existing baselines.

Figure 5. SSCD-CLIP trade-off curve comparison with baselines. Our method consistently lies in the lower-right region compared with all baselines. This demonstrates that, under the same SSCD level, our approach achieves higher CLIP scores. In other words, given comparable semantic alignment, our method provides the most effective suppression of memorization.
Figure 7. SSCD-CLIP trade-off on MS-COCO fine-tuned SD v1.4. Our method achieves a better balance between memorization mitigation and semantic alignment than baselines.

Figure 8. Temporal distribution of outlier semantic-control attention heads across denoising timesteps. Each row corresponds to a layer, and each column corresponds to one generated sample. In each subplot, the x-axis denotes the denoising timestep, and the y-axis denotes the attention head index. Each cyan point indicates that the corresponding attention head is identified as an outlier semantic-control head at that timestep. The horizontal and temporally continuous patterns show that memorization-related semantic control is not random or transient, but is mainly carried by a stable subset of attention heads that persist across most denoising timesteps.

Figure 1. Examples of semantic-control scores across attention heads. Memorized images tend to activate a few distinctly prominent attention heads, whose semantic response strengths are substantially higher than those of other attention heads. In contrast, non-memorized images exhibit a much smoother and more uniform distribution of semantic strength across attention heads.

Figure 3. Layer-wise analysis of attention heads with strong semantic control. Memorized images exhibit a larger number of high semantic-control attention heads in the shallow layers, especially layers 0∼3. In deeper layers, the statistics of memorized and nonmemorized samples become similar.

Figure 4. Ablation study on attention head groups. We evaluate different suppression factors ϵ ∈ {0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6}. Suppressing the Top-3 heads produces the largest reduction in SSCD Score, while suppressing the Bottom-3 heads has little effect.

Figure 9. SSCD–FID trade-off on SD v1.4. Lower FID indicates better generation quality.

Table 9. Mitigation results on different memorization types. AM denotes all memorized samples, VM denotes verbatim memorization, and TM denotes template memorization. We report SSCD and CLIP scores under SD v1.4 and SD v2.0, with four hyperparameter settings for each method. Lower SSCD indicates better memorization mitigation, while higher CLIP indicates better prompt-image alignment.
Table 8. Memorization mitigation results on Stable Diffusion 3. Our method achieves the best balance between memorization mitigation and semantic alignment.

Table 1. Progressive Layers ablation study for mitigation. Suppressing layers 0–3 provides the most substantial mitigation, while extending suppression to deeper layers yields diminishing benefits at the cost of semantic fidelity.
Table 2. Segmented layers ablation study for mitigation. Early layers (0 ∼ 3) contribute most significantly to mitigation, while suppression in deeper layers yields limited benefits.
Table 7. Generation quality on non-memorized prompts. Our method preserves semantic alignment and distributional quality on non-memorized inputs.

Table 5. Memorization detection results on SD v1.4 and SD v2.0. The competitive performance further supports our finding that memorization is associated with shallow-layer attention heads exhibiting large conditional–unconditional attention discrepancies.

papers.title: Memorization Lives in a Few Attention Heads: Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models via Projection-Based Suppression
papers.tldr: A small number of shallow cross-attention heads drive diffusion-model memorization, and selectively suppressing them can reduce memorization while better preserving image quality and semantic alignment.

papers.abstract: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.
authors: Lavinia Ghita, Dhruv Desai
bullets: Compares AdamW, diagonal AdaGrad, two Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon under a common forward-KL objective and fixed budget.
Evaluates four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs across scales.
AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale.
SOAP often matches AdamW’s KL but has substantial trainer-time overhead; Shampoo variants vary by model pair.
Optimizer conclusions depend on the distillation objective and feasible systems recipe.

papers.abstract: Considering the motion continuity and stability of 3D objects over short inter-frame intervals, introducing multi-frame settings in scene flow estimation can potentially address occlusion. In this paper, we propose a two-frame backbone, SimpleFlow3D, which integrates dense information from the image plane and sparse information from the depth dimension in a decoupling-followed-by-coupling manner by hierarchically constructing the 3D motion feature. SimpleFlow3D achieves SOTA results with minimal parameters. We also propose a weight-sharing multi-frame framework to splat the previous 3D motion feature to the current estimation process. The framework unifies the first and non-first frame inference by constructing pseudo inputs. After combining the proposed framework and backbone, the newly born multi-frame method SplatFlow3D further advances the state of the art. It achieves lower errors than the two-frame backbone, with fewer parameters than current methods. On both KITTI and Spring, SplatFlow3D ranked 1st over all published and submitted methods. Experiments show that SplatFlow3D improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and generalization to real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/SplatFlow3D.
authors: Bo Wang, Dekang Zhu, Jian Li, Zhipeng Meng, Bo Wang, Dewen Hu
bullets: SimpleFlow3D decouples image-plane and depth information before coupling them to construct hierarchical 3D motion features.
A weight-sharing multi-frame framework splats prior 3D motion features into the current estimation process using pseudo inputs.
The multi-frame design improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and real-world generalization.
SplatFlow3D reports the best performance on KITTI and Spring among published and submitted methods, while using fewer parameters than current methods.

papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of space activities, near-Earth space is becoming increasingly congested, leading to a higher risk of spacecraft collisions and space debris generation. Recent close-proximity encounters and collision incidents necessitate efficient and cost-effective onboard systems for space object detection (SOD) and collision avoidance. While deep learning (DL) enabled Edge AI using low-cost vision sensors on single or multiple satellites has shown promises for SOD, significant challenges remain, including limited datasets, small SOD, and the lack of comprehensive performance assessments. This paper presents a collaborative Edge AI framework for multiview SOD and systematically benchmarks DL models and fusion strategies. Results show that higher image resolution significantly improves small SOD. For multiple views, image-level fusion reduces the combined communication and inference latency by 30.13% and 32.80% on average compared with feature-level and attention-based fusion across the evaluated inter-satellite link (ISL) bandwidth. For larger view sets, feature-level and attention-based fusion achieve better detection accuracy at the cost of analysis in the sensing-communication pipeline, revealing that multiview collaboration introduces minimal latency overhead under ISL constraints when reception capacity is not exceeded. Our work provides valuable design insights for future collaborative satellite network design, supporting the emerging space situational awareness and space traffic management requirements.
authors: Xingyu Qu, Peng Hu
bullets: Motivated by increasing orbital congestion and the need for efficient onboard space-object detection and collision avoidance.

Feature-level and attention-based fusion can improve accuracy with larger view sets but add sensing–communication pipeline cost; conclusions are scoped to evaluated ISL bandwidths and reception capacity.

papers.abstract: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.
authors: Ruihong Zeng, Puning Yang, Jinghui Zhang, Shen Gao, Xiangliang Zhang, Preslav Nakov, Xiuying Chen
bullets: Introduces Role-playing Unlearning: removing target-role style and knowledge, not just factual information.
Maps roles to more independent Mixture-of-Experts subspaces for finer control and interpretability.
Uses specialization and disentanglement losses to separate role-specific expert distributions and capabilities.
RoleBench-Unlearn evaluates the task across multiple backbone LLMs.
Experiments report precise target-role forgetting with better preservation of non-target roles’ language quality, knowledge, and persona consistency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.
authors: Jinyu Li, Zhiming Zhang, Hao Fang, Hongyao Yu, Bin Chen, Albert Ma, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Addresses response-level reinforcement learning, which can penalize correct content alongside hallucinated claims.
Uses on-policy self-guidance with direct and reciprocal token weighting based on grounding support.
Applies guidance only when overall and hallucination-specific advantages agree.
Employs a reference-calibrated reward to improve factuality without encouraging information omission.
Outperforms evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR while retaining multimodal capabilities.

papers.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.
authors: Nong Minh Hieu, Antoine Ledent
bullets: Addresses limited theoretical understanding of how sparse connectivity affects generalization.
Analyzes deep networks whose layer-wise weight matrices satisfy ℓp quasi-norm constraints for 0<p≤1.
Provides bounds interpolating between classical norm-based guarantees and parameter-counting bounds.
As p approaches zero, the bounds depend on the square root of the number of nonzero parameters and are tighter than existing parameter-counting results.
Experiments show milder dependence on initial architecture in over-parameterized settings, reflecting sparsity learned from natural data.

papers.abstract: Modern autonomous driving and driver assistance systems rely predominantly on cameras, radars and LiDARs for environmental perception. However, these modalities face different environmental limitations, including poor illumination for cameras and adverse weather for LiDAR. Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.
authors: Ziang Liu, Shiming Wang, Joseph Adeola, Julian F. P. Kooij
bullets: Addresses limitations of camera, LiDAR, and other conventional sensors under poor illumination or adverse weather.
Introduces a horizontally arranged microphone array and the AcousticScenes real-world driving dataset with synchronized acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds, and 3D annotations.
Proposes AcousticBEV, which predicts moving traffic participants’ BEV center locations conditioned on the ego vehicle’s speed.
Reports F1 scores of 47.7 ± 1.2% on Easy scenarios and 45.1 ± 1.4% on Difficult scenarios, outperforming classical and learning-based baselines.
Demonstrates low-cost acoustic sensing for nearby moving-vehicle localization in azimuth and distance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.
authors: Braghadeesh Lakshminarayanan, Ojas Phadake, Qi Chen, Dominik Baumann
bullets: Pretrained diffusion controllers may generate unsafe trajectories when deployment constraints change, such as added or repositioned obstacles.

papers.abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.
authors: La Jiang, Lingfeng Chen, Jiaqi Zhu, Fengrong Guo, Jiehua Zhang, Panhe Hu, Li Liu, Zhen Liu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 405 large SAR images averaging 7153×7153 pixels.
Covers 10 tasks, including visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning.
Uses manually annotated evaluation samples with assistance from a semi-automatic captioner.
Tests both general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs.
Finds persistent difficulties in interpreting large scenes and accurately perceiving small targets; the benchmark is open-sourced.
