papers.abstract: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.
authors: Patrick Passos
bullets: The study tested a fixed reminder mechanism that reinserts the agent’s last finding after context loss.
Across 98 tasks, 47 were solved with reminders versus 48 without; the estimated effect was compatible with ordinary run-to-run noise.
An initial 48-task result favored reminders, but a later 50-task extension reversed direction and did not replicate the finding.
The agent rarely wrote notes, and reminder injection occurred in only 47%–65% of compactions; repeated actions per compaction were also null.
The results do not evaluate agent-written memory and suggest that task sets of this size cannot reliably support single-run memory claims.

papers.abstract: Robust 3D lane detection requires accurate metric road geometry recovery from visual inputs, yet conventional RGB-based approaches suffer from fragile lane evidence under adverse illumination, motion blur, and long-range perspective compression. Event cameras offer complementary high-temporal-resolution, high dynamic-range structural cues that are robust to these challenges, but their sparse, motion-dependent responses cannot be directly fused into consistent 3D geometry. In this paper, we present the first attempt to introduce event cameras into 3D lane detection. To enable systematic research, we first build two multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations: DSEC-3DLD (real-world sequences) and Ev-OpenLane (large-scale simulated sequences). We further propose RETR, a structure preserving transformer that converts complementary RGB and event observations into coherent 3D lane geometry. RETR first aligns modality consistent evidence through Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion, then preserves thin and uncertain lane structures with Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation, and finally decodes ordered lane hypotheses using a Geometry State Decoder with proposal conditioned initialization, reference conditioned query evolution, and diversified geometric inquiry. Extensive experiments show that RETR achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, especially showing strong improvements in challenging lighting and complex road geometry scenarios. Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/duskswell/RETR.
authors: Jingtao Dong, Hao Zhuang, Hao Yang, Liyuan Pan, Wei Liang
bullets: Introduces DSEC-3DLD and Ev-OpenLane, multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations.
Fuses RGB and event evidence using Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion to align complementary cues.
Preserves thin and uncertain lane structures through Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation.
Decodes ordered 3D lane hypotheses with a geometry-focused state decoder.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, with notable gains under challenging lighting and complex road geometry.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of RETR. RETR converts synchronized RGB and event observations into metric 3D lane geometry through a structure-preserving RGB-event pipeline. Modality-specific encoders first extract multi-scale RGB and event features {Fl r}Ll=1 and {Fl e}Ll=1. RCF aligns both modalities at each scale by using a co-activation response Ml to emphasize jointly supported lane evidence and bidirectional Cross Attention Blocks (CAB) to exchange complementary context, producing fused features {Zl}Ll=1. UASC aggregates the fused hierarchy into Fc while preserving thin and uncertain lane structures. It combines context and structural branches and gates detail refinement using high-frequency response A, learned detail cue D, and entropy-based uncertainty E. The query generator and geometry decoder finally predict ordered 3D lane hypotheses, including lane existence, 3D coordinates, and visibility.

Figure 1: Overview of our DSEC-3DLD dataset. Each column presents one synchronized driving sample, including the RGB image, event frame, 2D lane annotation, and metric 3D lane annotation. The selected examples cover challenging real-world conditions such as tunnels, low illumination and strong exposure changes.

Figure 4: Annotation pipeline of DSEC-3DLD. We first prepare synchronized RGB images, event frames, and LiDAR points through cross-sensor alignment and calibration-based projection. Then, we construct a multi-source annotation pipeline with an image-based annotation branch and a geometrycue branch. The image-based branch provides refined 2D lane annotations, while the geometry branch provides sparse geometric supervision and depth cues. These complementary sources are jointly refined to generate metric 3D lane ground-truth.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on DSEC-3DLD and Ev-OpenLane. We compare RETR with the RGB-only LATR baseline under challenging illumination and road-geometry conditions. Each example shows image-plane lane predictions on the left and corresponding 3D geometry and top-view projections on the right. Red, green, and yellow denote ground truth, RETR, and LATR, respectively. Zoom in for details.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.
authors: Yin Xu, Yongbo Yang, He Sun, Miao Sun, Mingjun Xiao
bullets: Addresses excessive activation memory, client-specific token-importance patterns, and communication overhead in federated long-context fine-tuning.
Combines Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation, Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination, and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery.
Reduces peak memory by up to 88.35% versus conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% versus forward-only LoRA at 16K context length.
Evaluated on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B, with improved performance under certain non-IID settings and compact progressive update transmission.
Scope: results focus on the reported models, 16K context length, and selected non-IID federated settings.

papers.abstract: Generative models increasingly write a chain of thought before drawing, and report large gains from doing so. We ask what that text contributes, by substitution rather than ablation: holding the generator, sampler and seeds fixed, we replace the think block with controlled alternatives and measure the image. Across a unified model with a think mode, a reinforcement-learned reasoning generator, and a planner driving a frozen diffusion model, the same picture emerges. Content-free prose of matched length is worth nothing or less ($-0.05$ to $-0.15$). One sentence from an unrelated 8B model, naming the subject and a few identifying details, matches the generator's own plan in three to six times fewer conditioning tokens. The value sits where the referent is in doubt: writing down a name is worth $+0.33$ when it is right and $+0.05$ when it is wrong, and where the generator already succeeds the whole effect is $-0.07 \pm 0.07$. Cutting a plan at the text encoder's window leaves 272 of 286 images byte-identical, and a plan rewritten to fit that window ties a bare identification ($+0.003 \pm 0.044$), so a plan contains nothing the identification does not already supply. Field-level interventions find only colour executed reliably, and a control writing the same sentences into the user prompt shows that limit belongs to the generator rather than to the planning channel. Two judges and two annotators replicate the central contrasts. A think block earns its keep as a specification of what to draw, not as a plan that is carried out.
authors: Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, Qibin Zhao
bullets: Controlled substitutions show that matched-length, content-free prose provides no benefit and may hurt performance.
A short external sentence naming the subject and key details matches the model’s longer plan using 3–6× fewer conditioning tokens.
The benefit is concentrated in ambiguous cases where correctly identifying the referent matters; otherwise the effect is negligible or slightly negative.
Truncation and rewriting experiments show that the plan’s useful information is already captured by a compact identification.
Only colour is reliably executed among tested field-level interventions, and the same limitation appears when text is placed directly in the user prompt.

papers.title: A Think Block Is Conditioning, Not a Plan
papers.tldr: Think blocks improve image generation mainly by specifying what to draw, not by providing an executable plan.

papers.abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.
authors: Yinghao Li, WeiHsien Lee, Zeyu Zhang, Canyang Zhao, Ke Fang, Xing Li, Bing Liu
bullets: Addresses whether brain activity can provide task-level intent without symbolic commands or hand-designed skills.
Uses a hierarchical framework: neural activity is read once as intent, then a learned visuomotor policy closes the control loop.
In counterfactual grasping, changing the neural intent changed which object the robot grasped, even when vision alone could not determine the target.
Representing the full neural population latent improved grasp completion from 69% to 81% across 132 held-out scenes; direction-only decoding did not help.
Intent effectiveness depended on neural location and timing: preparatory PMd signals supported grasping, with PMd outperforming M1 in one dual-array session.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The NI-ACT framework. (A) Control division. Conventional BCIs decode continuous velocity commands at every time step and keep the user inside the fast control loop. In NI-ACT, cortical activity supplies a task-level intent token once per task, sent at task start, and an embodied policy closes the fast perception–action loop with the robot and its environment. (B) Network architecture. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) maps binned PMd and M1 spikes to a 128-D population latent, a 2-D goal direction, and 7-class direction logits; an intent interface (Hard-7, Soft-2D, or Full-Latent) passes one of these to an action-chunking transformer (ACT) that also observes two cameras and the joint state, and the policy predicts 32 future joint targets. Fig. 3a gives how each interface enters the policy.

Figure 3: Architecture and data protocol of NI-ACT. (a) The frozen temporal convolutional encoder maps a window of binned spikes to a 128-D population latent z, from which a direction head reads a unit goal direction v̂ and a class head reads 7-way logits ℓ. The interface G selects one output: Hard-7 (one-hot of arg max ℓ) and Soft-2D (v̂) are appended to the 9-D joint state, giving 16-D and 11-D state inputs; Full-Latent (z) is kept separate from the joint state, projected from 128 to 512 dimensions, and enters the transformer encoder as its own intent token. The interfaces therefore differ in content, dimensionality, and injection pathway. Both camera images pass through one shared ImageNet-initialized ResNet-18, giving 7 × 7 feature maps (49 tokens per camera). With the VAE disabled, the latent token is constant. The encoder (4 layers) attends over all tokens; the decoder (1 layer, 32 learned queries) and a linear head predict 32 future 9-D joint targets. (b) Neural trials are split into training and held-out sets before any pairing. Each of the 207 counterfactual demonstrations is paired with a training trial of the same target direction, and the resulting intent is held constant over every frame; ACT is trained by behavior cloning, one policy per interface and neural source. At deployment, each of the 132 held-out scenes receives a held-out trial of its target direction; the intent is read once and held fixed while the policy replans every 32 steps. No neural trial is shared between training and evaluation. Trial counts refer to the monkey-J recording.

Figure 2: What the three interfaces pass to the policy, read from one frozen encoder (monkey J, PMd, movement-onset window) on all 426 held-out trials. (a) Hard-7: the one-hot vector of arg max ℓ, shown for one example trial per direction; each row has a single nonzero element. (b) Soft-2D: the unit direction v̂ of every held-out trial on the unit circle; dotted lines mark the true directions. (c) Full-Latent: the 128-D latent z of the same example trials as in (a); each direction is a distinct pattern across all dimensions.

papers.title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: NI-ACT shows that a brief intracortical neural signal can specify a persistent manipulation goal while a vision-and-proprioception policy autonomously executes the task.

papers.abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.
authors: Akhil S. Anand, Xun Shen, Marc Peter Deisenroth, Sebastien Gros
bullets: Co-design couples system design with the policy operating it, since each affects the other.
The design gradient separates direct design effects from indirect effects through the design-dependent optimal policy.
Policy sensitivity is computed with the implicit function theorem applied to the policy-gradient stationarity condition.
A proof-of-concept algorithm combines this sensitivity with stochastic value gradient policy optimization.

On a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional designs, it consistently outperforms Bayesian optimization and evolution strategies; convergence to an approximately stationary design is proved.

Curves show the best co-design performance found so far relative to the shared initial design, JD − JD(θ0), with mean ± SE over 25 trials; the percentage gaps quoted in the text are of the absolute final JD (Appendix E.2).

papers.selection_reason: Gradient-based co-design of systems and RL policies is transferable to robot morphology and control co-optimization.
papers.title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
papers.tldr: A differentiable-simulator method jointly optimizes system designs and RL policies by computing how the converged policy changes with the design, avoiding costly black-box design search.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Junqin Yang, Kai Wang
bullets: Targets critical stages such as grasping, alignment, and insertion, where generalist VLA control may be imprecise or unstable.
Trains specialized atomic-skill policies with a shared RL Token state representation and the VLA policy’s reference action.

Achieves 90.47% average Macro-F1 across four LIBERO task suites, 7.08 percentage points above an MLP router.
Raises Tube Transport full-task success from 20.04% to 85.67% in simulation.

papers.abstract: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Mahdi Nobar, Alisa Rupenyan, John Lygeros, J\"urg Keller
bullets: Targets conveyor-borne object tracking despite model mismatch, camera delays, measurement errors, and noise.
Combines an inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a Soft Actor-Critic residual policy trained in a digital twin.
Uses a delay-compensated Kalman filter to fuse out-of-sequence camera measurements and estimate target position.
Simulation and hardware tests show mean tracking error decreasing from 1.1–1.4 mm to 0.3–0.7 mm across the tested conveyor speeds.
The approach achieves errors below a frequency-domain performance bound for the evaluated controller class.

papers.abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.
authors: Zhiyang Niu, Huayuan Shen, Chuanjie Li, Mengmeng Zhao, Jiajia Zhang
bullets: A frozen encoder converts teacher outputs into semantic vectors, while a stage-aware student uses scheduled self-history and joint supervision.
The 13.2M-parameter student trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and makes decisions in 0.14 ms with no teacher, decoder, or text-generation calls.
Semantic behavior remains closely aligned with the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs changes 64.7% of decisions versus 12.8% for a matched donor.
The surrogate achieves 0.7783 deployment-decoder balanced accuracy and enables large sweeps 15× faster than the teacher, with zero LLM calls.
The gain is attributed primarily to the deployment schedule; content contributes at the teacher-forced operating point.

papers.title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
papers.tldr: Staged semantic distillation produces a fast, non-LLM surrogate that preserves free-form semantic signals from a staged LLM agent using one recorded trace.

papers.abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.
authors: Ruizhe Xie, Honghua Chen, Binglin Wang, Tong Guo, Xu Tang, Puti Yan, Shaoxiong Cai
bullets: Addresses the latency of autoregressive action-by-action decoding in robot navigation.
Training-free decoder evaluates the complete short-horizon action-prefix tree in one forward pass while preserving conditional action distributions.
Uses score margins to adaptively choose how many actions to execute before observing again.
Achieves nearly 3× faster action decoding and improves success/SPL, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points on reported benchmarks.
On a Unitree GO2, improves navigation success and reduces mean inter-action wait by about 160 ms, excluding network transmission time.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of parallel action decoding. The instruction and observation history are formatted as the model query x, followed by candidate action tokens. An attention mask restricts each candidate action token to attending only to the query, its branch ancestors, and itself. The VLN backbone processes the resulting sequence in a single forward pass. The hidden state of the last query token and those of all candidate tokens are then decoded into action distributions through the shared LM head. The last query token predicts the first action, so K = 3 uses two candidate levels. Scoring K = 4 adds a third level with 27 candidate tokens.

Figure 5. Real-world deployment trajectories on a Unitree GO2. The left and right scenes show a corridor and a classroom, respectively. In each scene, both methods start from the same position and receive the same instruction shown above. Baseline and Ours correspond to the autoregressive and parallel decoding variants of StreamVLN, respectively. Across the decision steps shown in these two scenes, our method reduces the average wait by 172 ms.

Figure 2. Comparison between autoregressive and parallel decoding. Autoregressive decoding (left) requires three sequential forward passes to predict a1, a2, and a3, whereas parallel decoding (right) computes all candidate action distributions in a single forward pass. For each action prediction, the visible tokens (highlighted) are identical along the corresponding branch in both methods, yielding equivalent conditional action distributions in exact arithmetic.

Figure 3. Adaptive execution via joint path scoring. Nodes are labeled with conditional action probabilities, while L(path) denotes cumulative joint log-probabilities. The greedy path can be outscored by the selected path in joint probability. The scan compares the fixed greedy prefix with its strongest alternative at each depth. When their score margin falls below δ, the highestscoring branch at that depth is executed and deeper actions are skipped. Here, m1 = 0.58 > δ continues the scan, whereas m2 = −0.18 < δ at δ = 0.2 selects a left turn followed by a forward step (L → F ).
Figure 4. Success rates on the GO2 over 20 trials per environment, using the same StreamVLN policy, instructions, and start poses. Bar labels show success rates and successful-trial counts.

Figure 6. Additional Unitree GO2 deployments. (a) Office. “Turn left ahead, walk to the door, and stop in front of it.” (b) Outdoors. “Go straight along this road, climb the stairs, and stop before the glass railing.” (c) Classroom. “Go straight down this road to the end, and stop beside the table at the podium on your left.”
Table 1. Complete-reply latency across decoders. Speedup is relative to native autoregression on the same backbone.

Table 5. Joint selection and adaptive execution. Joint only selects the plan with the highest joint score at a fixed depth (two actions for Uni-NaVid and four for StreamVLN); Ours selects the depth adaptively. Metrics and rank markers follow Table 2.

Table 6. Adaptive versus fixed execution (SR/SPL, %). All variants select plans by joint score. Fixed variants execute up to k actions and end early on stop. Avg. k refers to adaptive execution and excludes the final decision ending in stop. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best SR/SPL scores.

Table 4. StreamVLN action-decoding latency with a preloaded cache. Timing starts with the cached history and current query ready, excluding visual preprocessing and cache construction. For each trajectory, the median of ten timed repetitions is used; values average the three trajectories.
Table 3. Mean latency (ms) to generate a complete reply at each prediction horizon K.

SR, SPL, and OS are percentages; NE is in meters. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best results within each backbone and dataset.

papers.title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation

papers.abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.
authors: Kejia Fan, Yajiang Huang, Jianheng Tang, Jinfeng Xu, Huiping Zhuang, Anfeng Liu, Houbing Herbert Song, Yunhuai Liu
bullets: Addresses continual service construction where evolving, heterogeneous data can cause catastrophic forgetting.
Uses gradient-free residual blocks with closed-form solutions to overcome the underfitting of single-layer analytic methods.
Employs a cross-recursive least-squares strategy for distributed continual training.
Theoretical and experimental analyses support improved heterogeneity invariance and deep representation.
With 20 residual layers, accuracy improves by 8.85%–9.83% over a single-layer analytic baseline, while computational costs fall by over 94% versus gradient-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
authors: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das
bullets: Benchmarks 10 hospital chores in Isaac Sim, each with five scored sub-tasks linked by persistent state.
Tracks chain-break locations, post-failure behavior, and drift between estimated and true position.
Uses a scripted robot as a solvability check and evaluates agents through image-based, skill-level tools.
In 15 preliminary runs, 2 completed all five sub-tasks; only three chores had scripted-robot proofs.
Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by another call and 111 by a non-failing call; results are not yet a full benchmark.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD
authors: Zhi Xu, Yinqi Wu, Feng Zhang, Xiaotong Zhang, Hong Yu, Han Liu
bullets: Addresses training settings where ground-truth solutions are unavailable.
Generates briefs from questions alone, covering relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls without giving a final solution.
A frozen teacher uses each brief to guide the student’s on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching.
Evaluated on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 across three Qwen3 model sizes.
Both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD in these evaluations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.
authors: Jiayu Chen, Jinye Hu, Maoliang Li, Anqian Cen, Hailong Zou, Zihao Zheng, Xinming Wei, Guojie Luo, Jie Zhang, Xuanzhe Liu, Xiang Chen

papers.abstract: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.
authors: Bing He, Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Zhongyuan Wu, Ke Xu, Tao Zhuang, Yuxuan Xie, Zhongyuan Liu
bullets: Motivation: Existing video world models mainly render engine-authored motion, underusing their generative capacity and limiting gameplay diversity.
Core design: A GameWM-engine maintains rules, state, camera, and world layout; a GameWM-VM generates appearance and interaction details.
System components include an interaction-centered data engine, interfaces for character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions, and models ranging from 5B to 33B parameters.
A real-time causal variant supports gameplay while preserving the engine-computed timing and outcomes.
The design aims to give players personalized characters, worlds, and skills without changing the underlying game mechanics.

papers.abstract: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints. We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.
authors: Zhekai Ren, Jiaming Wu
bullets: Studies correction and preservation of semantic scene memory under finite update budgets.

Repeated training on unchanged content improves early correction but underperforms changing-history training at 32 updates.
Short-budget errors mainly retain obsolete values; longer updates progressively replace them, with most cases remaining jointly correct after step 16.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce systematically unfair demographic outcomes when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified. For example, prompts describing nurses without specifying gender may disproportionately generate videos depicting female nurses. Mitigating unfairness in T2V generation is particularly challenging: training-based methods that modify model internals require architecture-specific access and risk disrupting temporal consistency, while sampling-based methods often incur costly pre-deployment video generation. We present the first conditional online approachability formulation of attribute-level fairness for T2V generation. Building on this formulation, we introduce Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play framework that maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory. Using generated videos at inference time as feedback, Mem2Fair selects prompt-level attribute interventions based on the deviation from each concept's prescribed fairness target, without training or separate pre-deployment sampling. Experiments demonstrate that Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over the unmodified generator and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions, while maintaining comparable prompt-video alignment and video quality. We further demonstrate its effectiveness on commercial black-box T2V models.
authors: Pengyu Chen, Jiaming Zhang, Xiaohua Feng, Yuyuan Li, Chaochao Chen
bullets: Addresses demographic bias when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified.
Formulates attribute-level fairness as a conditional online approachability problem.
Maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory to track deviations from prescribed fairness targets.
Uses inference-time video feedback without model training or costly pre-deployment sampling.
Improves fairness across attributes, prompts, and target distributions while preserving alignment and video quality, including on black-box commercial models.

papers.abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.
authors: Hao Fu, Qian Feng, Hanbin Zhao, Jiahua Dong, Xu Tan, Lina Wei, Chao Zhang, Hui Qian
bullets: Addresses forgetting of old-task knowledge, reduced zero-shot transfer, and underfitting of new tasks under privacy and memory constraints.
Uses Task Subspace Projection to identify seen and unseen tasks through task-specific subspaces and feature projection.
Uses Dynamic LoRA to allocate low-rank adapters across transformer layers according to task distributions.
Evaluated on 11 datasets with three metrics, showing the method’s effectiveness.
The abstract does not report specific numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The training process of the DLoRA module in our method. The DLoRA module integrates LoRA into the first Lt transformer layers of both the image and text encoders. The gating mechanism before the LoRA modules in the image encoder determines whether to activate the LoRA based on the feature F ′ v(x) derived from the original CLIP. Only the LoRA and the gating mechanisms are trained, while the remaining parts are kept frozen.

Figure 1: (a) Comparison with existing methods. Unlike ZSCL, our method eliminates the need for additional storage and improves parameter efficiency. Compared to MoE-Adapter, our approach incurs significantly lower computational overhead with fewer trainable parameters. In contrast to DIKI, ours not only achieves higher accuracy but also precisely distinguishes whether samples belong to previously seen tasks (Precise Task ID). (b) Mechanism comparison. Existing training-free CTI applies the same NTA operation to both seen and unseen tasks, restricted by a weight “W ”. Conversely, our TSP module explicitly identifies the boundary between tasks, directing unseen samples to the original CLIP while processing seen samples with DLoRA. (c) Performance trade-off. Our method achieves a superior trade-off between average accuracy (both seen and unseen tasks) and parameter efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 3: The workflow of the TSP module of our method in training and inference processes. During training phase, for image dataset of every task, the TSP module decomposes the image features via SVD and selects top r singular vectors from the right singular vector matrix to be the corresponding task subspace. During inference phase, for every test sample, the TSP module computes the cosine similarity between the raw feature extracted from original CLIP and the subspaces associated with each seen task. The result is compared against a threshold, denoted as “thres.”. The sample is classified using the corresponding DLoRA module if the cosine similarity exceeds the “thres.”. Otherwise, the original CLIP model is utilized to classify the sample.

Figure 6: Visualization of six task-specific distributions generated by the TSP module. We randomly selected 1,000 samples from each dataset. The majority of samples are correctly classified, as shown by their corresponding colors. A small number of samples are misclassified as unseen tasks, while an even smaller number are incorrectly assigned to other seen tasks. Overall, the TSP module achieves an accuracy exceeding 90% for each task.

Figure 4: The distribution of similarity scores for the TSP module across different tasks. The red line denotes a threshold set at 0.96. The majority of samples exhibit similarity scores above this threshold. The dense distribution of similarity scores also indicates the TSP module’s capability to effectively capture and extract critical information from each task.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
authors: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang

Proposes OmniFocus, combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Yanjun Fu, Quanzeng You, Jiadong Guo, Yujie Lu, Sai Charitha Akula, Haiping Wu, Miao Liu, Sanghamitra Dutta, Lu Yuan
bullets: Identifies SFT data quality—not increasingly complex RL—as a key bottleneck for combining logical reasoning with visual tool use.
Introduces a fully automated data engine that creates challenging, visually grounded questions and human-like, structured Zoom-in tool traces.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B on LogT data was evaluated across seven benchmark test sets.
Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieved stronger results than prior SFT+RL methods using 3.1× less data and over 120× fewer GPU hours.
Adding simple RL to LogT-SFT further surpassed complex prior RL methods by 9.59 points, with improved tool-use accuracy, efficiency, and reasoning consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 3 A detailed overview of LogT SFT data synthesis engine. Part 1 (top; Section 3.1) synthesizes visual search QA pairs using the full image (I0) along with rich visual contexts (IC and IF , top left) related to randomly selected target objects. After generating candidate QAs, we apply a simple heuristic filter and use a VLM-as-a-Judge to ensure quality. Part 2 (bottom; Section 3.2) generates reasoning traces for the selected QA. For easy questions, we directly generate traces without tool calls (omitted here). For other questions, we first create logic chains (LM and LE) based on two human-like strategies. A logic chain selector then chooses the more appropriate one, which is subsequently used to guide the synthesis of multi-turn reasoning traces with tool use.
Figure 7 System prompt for the QA generator. The remaining rules and in-context examples are omitted for brevity.

Figure 8 System prompt for the reasoning trace generator. Each logic-chain entry of the form ⟨short noun phrase⟩(k) specifies a target object or region and its source image Ik. Here, I0 is the original image, and Ik for k ≥ 1 is the crop returned by the k-th Zoom-in call. The reasoning trace generator locates the specified target in Ik, predicts its bounding box, and invokes Zoom-in on that image using the predicted box. For example, “Backpack (2)” corresponds to “Backpack (I2)” in Figure 3 and instructs the generator to zoom in on the backpack within the person crop returned by the second tool call. The remaining rules and in-context examples are omitted for brevity.

Figure 6 Tool call efficiency. We report the average number of tool calls per question across the seven test sets. Despite achieving better performance compared to prior SOTA, LogT-SFT model uses 2.7× fewer tool calls, and LogT-RL uses 2.3× fewer.

Figure 9 An example of an exhaustive search logic chain and its corresponding tool-use reasoning trace. To locate the pink sign held by a person in the crowd, the logic chain begins by instructing the trace generator (see Section 3.2) to identify the crowd, then systematically search it from left to right. Since the trace generator successfully detects the target sign and the person in the crop returned by the third Zoom-in call, it stops scanning the rest of the crowd and instead zooms in on the identified region to extract the final answer.

Figure 2 Result highlights. By applying SFT to a Qwen2.5VL-7B model using 5.4k to 7.1k of our synthesized data, LogT-SFT surpasses the best-performing Mini-o3-RL on average across seven test sets, while using up to 3.1× less data and >120× fewer GPU hours. With a simple RL setup without any tool-specific design, LogT-RL further outperforms baselines by 9.59.

Figure 1 Main idea. We generate reasoning traces based on human-like strategies including (i) direct answering for simple questions, (ii) multi-hop reasoning by focusing on different regions, and (iii) exhaustive search for more difficult cases. For easy questions where the base model’s average@8 is 1, we synthesize direct answering traces without Zoom-in. Otherwise, we first generate logic chains that specify key tool-use steps and then use them to guide the VLM in synthesizing tool-use reasoning traces.

Figure 4 Training dynamics after applying our simple RL procedure to the baselines and LogT-SFT. During RL, our model’s validation accuracy steadily improves, whereas other SFT baselines perform on par with, or worse than zero-RL. LogT greatly improves the RL performance ceiling.

Figure 5 Tool call accuracy. We report tool call accuracy on V* for the base model and all post-trained models. The base model is prompted to use Zoom-in in a zeroshot setting. Our LogT-SFT and LogT-RL models achieve the highest Zoom-in accuracy.
Figure 13 Instructions for Human Evaluation.
Figure 12 Qualitative case study of SFT data synthesized by Pixel Reasoner, Chain-of-Focus, Mini-o3 and LogT.

Figure 15 Qualitative case study comparingmodel responses to a V* question between baseline models and LogT-RL. We show the generated reasoning traces, including Zoom-in calls, for both baseline models and LogT-RL. While Qwen2.5-VL7B-RL, Pixel Reasoner-RL, and Chain-of-Focus-RL produce the correct final answer, their responses contain hallucinations or self-contradictions. The remaining baselines make erroneous Zoom-in calls and ultimately produce incorrect answers. In contrast, LogT-RL follows a coherent and consistent reasoning chain: it first identifies the front cabin of the truck, then locates the tissue box, and finally answers the question correctly without hallucinations.
Figure 10 Normalized distribution of Zoom-in call counts in theSFTdatasetgeneratedbyLogT. The number of tool calls per trace in the dataset ranges from 0 (direct answering without tool use) to 6.

Figure 11 Ratio of easy questions. We compute the ratio of questions in existing and our SFT datasets for which Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves an average@8 = 1 without needing tools (easy questions). Our dataset synthesized by LogT contains only 24%, significantly lower than existing datasets.
Figure 14 Per-annotator breakdown of human evaluation. All three annotators preferred responses generated by LogT-RL over those from Mini-o3-RL.

Table 6 Ablation on models used for data synthesis. We replace the models used by LogT in Section 3 with much smaller variants and re-synthesize 4k SFT samples. After SFT, the average performance across V*, VisualProbe, and HR-Bench remains nearly unchanged, indicating that our method is robust to the choice of synthesis models.

Table 8 Performance on V*-Rotated. We construct V*-Rotated by rotating images in V* by angles randomly sampled from 30◦ to 330◦. LogT-RL uses a rotation tool at inference time that was not seen during training, improving over the base model by 21.99 points.
Table 7 Error rates across different stages. We randomly sampled 100 samples from each stage and manually evaluated their error rates.
Table 4 Ablation on question difficulty. Training the VLM on the harder half of our SFT dataset leads to significantly improved performance on challenging tasks like those in VisualProbe-Hard.

Table 5 Ablation on logic chain-driven reasoning trace synthesis. Incorporating logical chains into the data generation process of LogT improves overall SFT performance and yields substantial additional gains after subsequent RL.

papers.abstract: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.
authors: Nikhil Kumar Jha, Amitoj Cheema
bullets: Judge choice changes scores by up to 7.2 points, and answer-prompt choice by up to 9.3 points.

A blind human check suggests judges are reliable when they agree; disputed- answer errors by the primary judge favored the baseline over Becos.
Becos was configured using LoCoMo itself, so the evaluation has no held-out set; answers, verdicts, and scoring code are released.

papers.abstract: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.
authors: Jae Hun Hwang, Yechan Seo, Hong-In Won
bullets: Targets deployment failures caused by changes in grippers, base frames, cameras, and appearance.

A two-step task chain succeeds in 54/60 changed-cell chains, while the four evaluated VLAs complete none.
Results and ablations support the combined self-calibration, lens-estimation, and measured-depth components.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/
authors: Chen Liu, Nikolaus Correll
bullets: Addresses the cost and impracticality of collecting teleoperated robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs scenes and predicts object contact regions from egocentric RGB-D and head-motion recordings.
Adapts human actions to a humanoid using grasp planning, stance optimization, whole-body motion generation, and physics-based RL correction.
Produces synchronized robot-view observations, proprioception, and verified action labels for policy training.
A GR00T N1.7 policy trained exclusively on the converted data autonomously performed loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture of E2S2H, illustrated on a bottle-lift recording. From egocentric video and tracked hand landmarks, agentic real-to-sim masks objects and builds a textured visual scene with simplified collision geometry. Each object pairs a visual mesh with a collision model marked by target contact regions. Along the human (orange) and adapted robot (green) camera paths, the robot poses trace adaptation and correction. During the approach with hands out of view (cyan), the whole-body motion generator drives locomotion and unseen arm motion, then begins blending arm targets prior to visibility. Once hands enter the camera view (blue), tracked human landmarks take over arm guidance. Placing the robot directly on the projected human head path (red) does not guarantee a collision-free stance. Stance adaptation is therefore required to keep clear of the table while holding targets within reach in a comfortable posture. Directly copying the human palm onto the robot hand likewise fails, causing finger penetration or missed contact in the grasp comparison above. The final pose (grey) combines bilevel stance adjustment with contact-band Dex3 grasp planning. Kinematic optimization and reinforcement learning in physics simulation refine this plan into a dynamically feasible rollout. E2S2H then renders the robot camera view from the reconstructed scene along the rollout path to produce synchronized training data.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.
authors: Srikar Babu Gadipudi, Somayeh Sojoudi, Claire J. Tomlin
bullets: CBF safety filters make training safer but scale poorly because team constraints grow quadratically with team size.
The method learns only from executed safe actions using implicit Q-learning and distills filter behavior at synthetic near-collision states.
Theory bounds policy constraint violations—and, with sufficient state coverage, per-step collision probability—through distillation loss.
Filter-free policies had no collisions in 1,800 multi-agent test episodes and transferred from three-agent training to teams of up to twenty with constant per-agent computation.
The approach was also tested on Crazyflie quadrotors, with up to five flying simultaneously.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Shankar Gangisetty, Muskan Singh, C V Jawahar
bullets: Tests VLM reliance on visual evidence versus language priors and dataset regularities.
Covers adverse weather, junctions/intersections, and nuScenes-based spatial reasoning.
Uses four protocols: image removal, counterfactual weather changes, paraphrase/negation robustness, and spatial reasoning.
Finds affirmation bias, poor counterfactual sensitivity, near-chance negation performance, and confident answers without images.
Concludes that current open-source VLMs are not sufficiently grounded for autonomous driving decisions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed diagnostic driving evaluation framework.

Together, these diagnostics expose failure modes that are hidden by aggregate benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.
authors: Tao An, Weihang Liang, Tianqi Wang, Chuqing Cao, Wenming Tan, Kai Zhang, Haibo Lei, Tao Xie, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li
bullets: Addresses the high online cost of repeatedly evaluating candidate action sequences in JEPA-based world models.
Generates an action proposal, predicts future scenes and proprioceptive states, then iteratively refines the same plan using the task goal.
Combines goal-discrepancy residual feedback with future-scene context feedback for chunk-wise action refinement.
Learns the action generation and predictive feedback process from offline demonstrations.
Evaluated on short-horizon reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution, achieving competitive performance with a compact model and low online computation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.
authors: Kevin Nguyen, Ceyhun Efe Kayan, Feng Liu, Li Zhang
bullets: BW-PO is a controlled Blocksworld benchmark designed to expose failures in VLM planning under occlusion and depth ambiguity.
The proposed VLM-as-perceiver paradigm limits VLMs to local visual extraction rather than end-to-end planning.
External solvers handle cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation.
Plan success rises from near zero to 84–97% across the evaluated model-specific challenging subsets.
The approach separates failures in depth-ambiguity reconciliation from incomplete visual extraction in dense scenes.
