papers.abstract: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.
authors: Jaeseung Ryu, Jae-Hun Jung
bullets: Evaluates cross-dataset fall detection across nine datasets, holding out each target in turn.
Compares three vision-language models and three visual baselines under zero-target transfer and local target-site personalization.
Source training improves frozen-model mean AUROC for Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL from 0.821→0.912, 0.883→0.947, and 0.939→0.962, respectively.
With five labeled examples per class, source initialization benefits Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN over Target-only training.
Benefits are model- and label-budget-dependent; VLMs also show threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections.

papers.abstract: We study relationship-specific continual reply prediction for one-to-many private communication: a system predicts an author's reply to a recurring contact and updates its personalization state when the actual reply becomes available. We propose TRACE (Temporal Relationship-Aware Communication Evolution), which uses author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model, with a feedback-driven policy controlling revision. On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG. Component ablations show mixed effects and do not establish statistically reliable improvements in Reply Style MSE after multiple-comparison correction. More accurate state forecasts and larger revision budgets do not consistently improve reply-level metrics. These exploratory findings expose the challenge of turning evolving relationship-specific expression estimates into useful generation guidance.
authors: Zihan Hong, Xue Li
bullets: Targets one-to-many private communication where reply style varies by relationship and evolves over time.
Uses author-level language habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model.
A feedback-driven policy revises personalization state when the true reply becomes available.
Across 216 test emails from eight Enron users, four TRACE configurations improved average BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore while lowering Reply Style MSE versus Base LLM and Base RAG.
Ablations found mixed effects; corrected analyses did not establish reliable Reply Style MSE improvements, and better state forecasts or larger revision budgets were inconsistent.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.
authors: Jieyuan Pei, Xin Yan, Mingwei Xu, Haiyi Zhang, Siyu Zou, Zhangyi Hu, Zhuoxuan Li, Yuguang Yang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Cheng Chi, Hui Xiong, Yan Wang
bullets: Uses the VLM’s pre-decoding hidden state to drive and answer scene questions without autoregressive generation.
A linear head scores 5,273 fixed candidate trajectories, enabling offline reward weighting and exact expected-reward reinforcement learning.
Maintains visual capabilities with multiple-choice training and limits drift with KL regularization.
Plans in 84 ms—six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0—while matching or exceeding it on reported driving benchmarks.
Performance remains comparable under delays up to 300 ms but degrades beyond that; at 1.2 s, it falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its native latency.

papers.selection_reason: Uses VLM hidden state as a fast one-pass driving policy; relevant to VLA and inference efficiency.
papers.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
papers.tldr: SuperGlance converts a decoder-only vision-language model into a fast, one-pass driving policy while preserving its visual question-answering ability.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.
authors: Fatih Temiz, Melike Erol-Kantarci
bullets: Targets efficient real-time VLA inference for physically embodied AI with limited onboard resources.
Jointly adapts where inference runs and when latent reasoning should stop based on wireless conditions and task needs.
Models the decision process as a constrained Markov decision process and solves it with TRPO-Lag.
Evaluated on LIBERO manipulation tasks using profiled VLA costs and ray-traced wireless channels.
Achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success than benchmark constrained deep-RL methods.

Fig. 3: Training Performance and Normalized Constraint Costs

Fig. 6: TRPO-Lag action distribution by task suite the offline characteristics in Fig. 2. TRPO-Lag predominantly selects τ = 10−3 for Goal and Object, preserving high task success while requiring fewer recurrent iterations than stricter thresholds. For LIBERO-10, which comprises longer-horizon tasks, it selects τ = 5 × 10−4 in approximately 82% of requests, consistent with the substantial success degradation observed at larger thresholds. Location selection complements these decisions: Spatial and LIBERO-10 are offloaded in 63.0% and 67.9% of requests, whereas Goal and Object are primarily executed locally. These results indicate that TRPOLag also learns suite-dependent operating points that preserve task success while reducing inference latency and managing shared edge resources.

papers.title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
papers.tldr: WEALR uses adaptive wireless edge offloading and latent-reasoning control to improve VLA robot inference under task, latency, energy, and communication constraints.

papers.abstract: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On \nGroups{} four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.
authors: Diana Romero, Salma Elmalaki
bullets: Models teams as a ball settling in an energy bowl whose resting point reflects recent behavior, team history, and other teams.
Uses 52 psychologically motivated parameters, designed for learning from few teams and supporting safe, interpretable prompting.
On held-out four-person teams, it predicted recovery from behavioral drift and retained 30% of the deviation after 32 seconds, versus about 24% observed.
Matched a roughly 40,000-parameter black-box baseline and detected conversation collapse with AUROC 0.85.
In simulation with assumed prompt effects, it removed 2.2× more breakdown time per prompt than periodic prompting.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ANCHOR, a Port-Hamiltonian model for forecasting human team dynamics in mixed reality loops, directly relevant to embodied AI agents and world models for environment prediction.
papers.title: ANCHOR: A Port-Hamiltonian Model for Forecasting Team Dynamics in Human-in-the-Loop Systems
papers.tldr: ANCHOR is an interpretable, compact port-Hamiltonian model that forecasts and helps prevent breakdowns in human team dynamics.

papers.abstract: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.
authors: Spencer H. Bryngelson
bullets: The standard consumer roofline fails to predict ANE performance in practice.
The ANE has separate slow activation and fast weight-stream bandwidths, producing two roofline ridges; its weight-stream ridge is below the GPU’s.
Compute performance declines rather than plateaus at higher single-operand workloads.
FP16 weight streaming is byte-bound, while int8 is limited by dequantizer element rate; int4 improves throughput and efficiency but costs 2.55 ImageNet top-1 points.
The model reproduces behavior across four ANE generations and identifies lower-energy execution paths.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.
authors: Seunghwan Jang, Wei Xiao
bullets: Targets the cost of re-solving HJ reachability whenever obstacles change and the false-safe errors of a single conditioned network.
Caps the obstacle margin to make the value function provably local, enabling body-frame window inputs, small-scene training, and scene-size transfer.
Uses an output structure that enforces conservative value bounds and counterexample mining to expand the learned safe set under the HJ inequality.
Reports recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach with near-zero rollout collisions across tested obstacle settings.
Extends to a 10D quadrotor, achieving markedly lower collision rates than baselines.

papers.abstract: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.
authors: Ran Qi, Yixin Xiao, Dawei Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Jinbang Huang, Xuan Zhao, Yintao Ma, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited gains from improving robot agents and models independently.
Uses code-as-policy so agents create reusable programs for failure detection and recovery.
Converts corrective experiences into end-to-end policy updates for vision-language-action models.
Uses the updated model’s changing failure distribution to guide further agent-program refinement.
Experiments across BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin show sustained performance gains over successive rounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RoboCoEvo. The co-evolution framework of agent and policy improving each other over successive rounds. (a) Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: the agent locates failures in the policy’s failed rollouts and groups recurring failures into failure modes (FMs), shown at the top for each round. For each FM, it writes a detector that identifies the failure state in a rollout (red) and a recovery program that completes the failed subtask from this state in simulation (green). As the policy improves, its rollouts expose FMs that did not occur in earlier rounds. In each subsequent round, the agent writes detectors and recovery programs for the newly identified FMs and refines those of persisting FMs to improve detection accuracy and recovery success. (b) Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: the policy is fine-tuned on the corrective experience together with the original demonstrations, which enables the policy itself to avoid or recover from the targeted failures. The rollouts of the updated policy initiate the next round, and its task success increases over successive rounds. The scores compare the base policy with the policy after RoboCoEvo.

Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy πi. Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K sampled failures and writes a detector dm for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all failed rollouts, from which the agent writes a recovery program ρm for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (left): failure-conditioned augmentation perturbs each localized state s into J states s̃j of the same FM, and ρm completes the failed subtask from both the original and the perturbed states, which yields the corrective experience Ri. The policy is then post-trained on D0 and the accumulated corrective experience to obtain πi+1, whose rollouts start the next round. Steps marked with circular arrows are updated in every round.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of the base policy and RoboCoEvo on targeted failure modes. Each row shows one failure mode on one benchmark. Left: the base policy π0 enters the failure mode and fails to recover. Right: after RoboCoEvo, π1 enters the same failure mode and recovers without the agent. Frames are aligned by stage.

Figure 3: Failure-conditioned augmentation on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. From an observed failure state s (left), the agent edits the robot and object states in the simulator to obtain perturbed states s̃1, s̃2, . . . (right) that preserve the same FM. Each perturbed state serves as an additional initial state for the recovery program, so a single observed failure yields multiple recovery runs.

Figure 5: Per-FM failure rates on RoboTwin, first round. Base vs. first-round policy, first-round detectors. Each spoke is a targeted FM, and shaded sectors group the FMs by task. Bars give the fraction of the task’s test episodes that fail with the FM never recovered from, before (yellow) and after (blue) the round; gray marks their overlap.
Figure 6: Per-FM failure rates on RoboTwin, second round. First-round vs. second-round policy, detectors after the second round of co-evolution. Same format as Figure 5.
Figure 7: Per-FM failure rates on RoboCasa (XR-1). Same format as Figure 5. Round 1 uses the first-round detectors and Round 2 the detectors after the second round.
Figure 8: Per-FM failure rates on BEHAVIOR-1K, tasks 0 to 5. Same format as Figure 5. Round 1 uses the first-round detectors and Round 2 the detectors after the second round.

papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.
authors: Kaihui Wu, Guoming Li, Liang Guo, Yifeng Zhou, Yuehong Hu, Junwei Pan, Zhixiang Feng, Chengguo Yin, Wenqi Fan, Haijie Gu, Jie Jiang
bullets: Addresses the resolution–complexity trade-off between detailed long-history modeling and strict serving budgets.
Uses group-wise tokens, hierarchical merging, NS Fusion, Global Sync, and Full-Resolution Readout to combine local detail with global context.
Ranks highly on the TAAC 2026 benchmark using 5.1× fewer FLOPs than leading baselines, with strong performance on long histories and imbalanced domains.
Outperforms industrial baselines in billion-parameter WeChat Channels evaluations by up to +0.07 percentage points in AUC.
In online A/B testing against the production model, increases GMV by 2.33%.

papers.abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.
authors: Austin H. Cheng, Marcel M\"uller, Andreas Burger, Yeonghun Kang, Tsz Wai Ko, Marta Skreta, Luka Mucko, Ella Miray Rajaonson, Cher Tian Ser, J\'er\^ome F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
bullets: Addresses the gap between language models’ controllability and specialist models’ ability to handle 3D molecular coordinates.
Uses causal-transformer next-token diffusion to autoregressively denoise continuous coordinate tokens without enlarging context.
Trained end-to-end across twelve 3D chemistry tasks, spanning microsolvation, conformer search, and metal-surface adsorption.
A single model performs all tasks and surpasses specialized baselines for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
Demonstrates the feasibility of generalist multimodal models for language-and-chemistry generation.

Figure 2 Next-token diffusion with Nahual. (left) Next-token diffusion provides both the clean current sequence and the noisy next sequence as input. Each token is noised at an independent timestep. (right) The first stack is an LLM-initialized Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) [34]. It encodes the parallel discrete and continuous stream into hidden states hi+1 and predicts the next discrete token’s logits yi+1. A conditioning stem combines hi+1, the embedding of the predicted next discrete token ai+1, and a Fourier embedding of ti+1 into per-token conditioning vectors zi+1. The second stack is a causal diffusion denoiser modulated by per-token adaptive layer normalization.

Our proposed next-token diffusion grounds the transformer in the clean previous sequence and denoises only the next sequence.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.
authors: Angelo Moroncelli, Loris Roveda
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints not present in demonstrations without retraining the policy.
Samples several action chunks, certifies them with a barrier condition, then selects the highest-valued certified chunk.
Certification guarantees safety independently of the critic and bounds deviation from the policy conditioned on feasibility.
CAST-V estimates policy-conditioned viability to preserve future safe control authority; CAST-VL learns it from controller logs.
Across manipulation, quadrotor, humanoid, and unicycle tasks, CAST generally improves joint task-and-constraint success over output filtering.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Edit or select. A keep-out zone, unseen in training, blocks one of the two routes of a frozen unicycle policy. (b) Viability v of the policy’s certified chunks, by simulation: the probability that it keeps sampling certified chunks over the next 8 decisions. Certified chunks exist in the red region too, but lead to a dead end; of the N = 8 drawn at one decision four head into it, and CAST-V executes a viable one. (c) The same map from a network trained on the controller’s logs, without model rollouts (CAST-VL): its boundary v = 0.5 (black) follows the simulated one (white) where the rollouts pass. (d) Joint success on 500 unseen zones per policy; CAST, CAST-V and CASTVL use the task critic, MPPI the model, map and goal.

Figure 10: Two diagnostics. (a) Viability or success as the learning target? Both networks are trained on the same logged episodes of the critic-free controller, with the same features, architecture and recipe; only the label differs (viability of the executed chunk, or the episode’s joint success). Unicycle, unseen zones, three policies × 500 scored scenarios; bands: 95 % intervals, and at 100 episodes the range of three disjoint subsets, in each of which viability is ahead. papers.selection_reason: Runtime safety certification and viability-aware action selection for frozen diffusion robot policies; directly relevant to embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
papers.tldr: CAST safely steers frozen diffusion policies at runtime by certifying sampled action chunks, ranking viable options, and avoiding future dead ends.

papers.abstract: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.
authors: Jianhao Huang, Allan Zhang, Ali Payani, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Reasoning traces expose multi-step structure but may omit facts available through atomic supervision.
The study measures generalization to transitions seen atomically but absent from training traces.
Analysis shows the optimal weight on atomic signals grows with reasoning-chain length and falls as reasoning-trace coverage increases.
These patterns persist in a full transformer layer and are validated in controlled multi-hop and mathematical pretraining settings.

papers.abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.
authors: Alba Maria Tellez Fernandez
bullets: Studies deployment-time compute allocation for a frozen chunked robot policy: more denoising per call versus more frequent replanning.
Evaluates both nominal compute rate and total compute per completed attempt, using discovery and held-out task comparisons.

In synchronous LIBERO simulation with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint and chunk length K=50, d=2 with h=2 achieved 139/160 successes versus 122/160 for d=5, while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step.
Increasing replanning from h=2 to h=5 at d=2 used 60.7% less arithmetic per attempt but produced nearly identical successes; equivalence was not established.
Findings are a scoped case study, not a universal deployment recommendation; arithmetic and latency characterize costs differently.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev return probabilities over caller-defined options and are increasingly used for classification. Large label spaces challenge both accuracy and scalability: larger menus can impair decisions, increase input costs, and exceed option limits. Hierarchical classification reduces menu size but introduces serial calls and error propagation. We propose AdaMenu, which builds a compact candidate menu from retrieved labeled examples and makes a single decision-model request. Its candidate labels adapt to the query, and its default setting also adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores. We evaluate AdaMenu with open and closed decision models on four label sets containing up to 1,016 labels. It outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 model and label-set pairs where both methods run, improving accuracy by 16.6-34.3 percentage points. Relative to the full menu on the three smaller label sets, accuracy differences range from -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points, while input token usage falls by factors of 3.2-22.9. AdaMenu also runs when option limits exclude the full menu, including settings where the hierarchical baseline is unavailable.
authors: Jiangze Yan, Yi Shen, Jieyun Huang, Wenjing Zhang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Ning Wang, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Large label spaces can reduce accuracy, increase input costs, and exceed decision-model option limits.
AdaMenu builds a compact, query-specific menu from retrieved labeled examples and can adapt its size using retrieval scores.
It avoids the serial calls and error propagation of hierarchical classification by using a single decision-model request.
Across four label sets with up to 1,016 labels, AdaMenu outperformed TypeSafe’s beam-search baseline in every comparable setting.
Compared with full menus on smaller label sets, it reduced input tokens by 3.2–22.9× while changing accuracy by −0.5 to +7.2 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.
authors: Joshua Ryo Cheng, Thomas L. Griffiths, Jake C. Snell
bullets: Targets social biases such as name–nationality, occupation–gender, and racial stereotypes.
Uses prompt–response observations from bias benchmarks to infer a low-dimensional latent distribution.
Develops a mathematical formulation and practical reconstruction algorithm for this Bayesian inverse problem.
Demonstrates the approach on the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) in ambiguous social contexts.

papers.abstract: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.
authors: Novanto Yudistira, One Octadion
bullets: Introduces a bounded, gradient-free controller for PEFT-adapted projections whose state depends on observed context but not candidate continuations.
Controls for architecture, initialization, batches, and updates when comparing current-prefix controls with learned-global controls for IA3, LoRA, and DoRA.
Current-prefix control improves accuracy over frozen adapters, but paired comparisons with learned-global control do not reliably show an input-conditioning benefit.
Replacing input-varying corrections with training-prefix means changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; variation contributes only 1.8–2.8% of correction RMS.
Results vary by model family, task, and scoring method; static compilation is evaluated as a deployment simplification, not assumed to be statistically equivalent.

papers.abstract: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.
authors: Yanbin Xu, Ming bo Cai
bullets: Conventional VOE benchmarks aggregate prediction errors across space and time, obscuring where and when violations are detected.
The proposed framework compares errors for possible versus impossible events within violation-relevant spatial regions and temporal intervals.
Experiments compare global, temporal, and spatiotemporal evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric or large-scale natural videos.
Global and localized judgments can diverge: aggregation may hide valid localized discrimination or suggest discrimination without localized evidence.
During continued developmental-video pretraining, localized confidence rises despite only modest accuracy gains, with global-local agreement changing non-monotonically.

(a–c) Two example pairs from the Physical Concepts dataset illustrate judgment disagreement. The scatter plot compares global (x-axis) and localized (y-axis) surprise scores, defined as prediction error for the impossible video minus that for the possible video. Positive scores indicate correct discrimination. The four quadrants distinguish pairs classified correctly by both evaluations, either evaluation alone, or neither. Heatmaps show the surprise score, with red indicating greater error for the impossible video and blue indicating the opposite. Magenta outlines mark annotated violation regions. In Scenario 1, spatial averaging obscures the localized violation signal, yielding correct localized but incorrect global discrimination. In Scenario 2, elevated background error produces a positive global margin despite a negative localized margin. (d) Global and localized accuracy across four V-JEPA models and five physical principles in Physical Concepts. (e) Global, spatiotemporallocal, and spatial-local accuracy across the same models and three physical principles in IntPhys 1. Dashed lines indicate chance performance (50%).

Red indicates greater prediction error for the impossible video. Because two consecutive frames are grouped into a single tubelet, each heatmap corresponds to a pair of consecutive frames. These two examples, one from each dataset, are illustrative and should not be interpreted as evidence that IntPhys 1 is generally more challenging than the Physical Concepts dataset.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces localized violation-of-expectation evaluation for video world models, directly targeting intuitive-physics assessment in predictive video models.
papers.title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
papers.tldr: Localized violation-of-expectation evaluation reveals whether video world models detect physical violations at the correct places and times, which global error metrics can miss or misrepresent.

papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
bullets: Addresses forceful multi-finger manipulation under uncertain contact and interaction dynamics, beyond geometry-based interaction.
Uses tactile-observable interaction representations with cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contacts.
Adapts motor behavior from tactile history while coordinating an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained locomotion controller.
Trained entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands.
Substantially outperforms standard RMA and reactive tactile-policy baselines across four real-world commercial round doorknobs.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation. (a) The upper-body manipulation policy commands the right arm and hand, while a pretrained locomotion controller commands the leg and waist joints to maintain whole-body balance under interaction-induced disturbances. The two policies share whole-body proprioceptive feedback, coupling manipulation and balance within an integrated control system. (b) Each fingertip contact force is parameterized in cone coordinates by the normal load n, force cone angle α , and circularly encoded shear direction (sinφ ,cosφ). This formulation separates the uncertainty source while preserving the contact mechanics. (c) The policy learning proceeds in two stages. First, the privileged encoder and tactile-centric policy are optimized jointly end-to-end under the task objective, forming an oracle policy and yielding a task-relevant interaction latent. Both modules are then frozen, and the adaptation encoder is trained through latent regression to estimate the interaction latent from a 2s history of deployable observations. (d) During real-world deployment, the adaptation encoder updates the interaction latent online from tactile interaction history and conditions the frozen tactile-centric policy to generate manipulation motor commands.

Fig. 4. Qualitative real-world rollouts of TMA. Each row presents a commercial knob in front and top views, followed by a successful rollout from left to right: reaching, multi-finger grasping, knob rotation, and door opening. papers.abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.
authors: Kazi Ashik Islam, Guojing Cong
bullets: Full attention recalls well but has quadratic training/prefill cost and a linearly growing inference cache.
The method complements the existing recent-context hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence start, enabling finer access to both early and recent tokens while remaining causal.
Recurrent and chunkwise-parallel formulations retain log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage.
Mean associative-recall accuracy improves from 76.37% to 96.12%; selected RULER retrieval scores improve from 26.97% to 50.03% at 6,144-token context.
It outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

papers.abstract: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.
authors: Jai Jain, Chihyo Ahn, Yong Liu, Charles Chen, Duc N. M Hoang, Ajay Kumar Jaiswal, Fatih Ilhan, Han-Byul Kim, Lauren Hannah, Richa Dixit, Minsik Cho, Yingyan Celine Lin, Hyesoon Kim
bullets: Problem: Synchronous edge-cloud decoding waits for a full round trip before each verification request, reducing throughput as RTT increases.
Method: An asynchronous pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight and discards stale requests before cloud-model execution.
Method: An RTT-aware router selects among direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, full local reasoning, and cloud speculative decoding.
Results: Asynchronous verification improves throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline.
Results: With 250 ms added RTT, the full system achieves 1.95× and 1.55× baseline throughput on SPROUT and OlympiadBench while sending 47% and 39% of queries to the cloud.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
bullets: MoE training costs can grow with total stored parameters because of memory, communication, and kernel-launch overhead, even when active compute remains similar.
The stack replaces FSDP with DDP and adds expert, pipeline, and optimizer parallelism plus activation recomputation.
NVSHMEM-based rowwise expert parallelism and GPU-managed routing avoid dispatch/combine permutations and synchronization overhead.
Integrated MXFP8 reduces compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, while topology-agnostic checkpoints allow parallel layouts to change between runs.
On NVL8 B300 nodes, it scales from 12.9B to 1.2T parameters across up to 512 GPUs; the authors also report Token Gerrymandering and cases where communication overlap hurts kernel speed.

The old, dense-oriented FSDP path loses throughput as total expert parameter size grows, whereas the new DDP+EP path keeps MoE throughput within a modest margin of its dense baseline. Figure 74 Captured timelines show the two submission regimes. Both Nsight Systems profiles run the same eight-layer development model (128 routed experts, top-8, one shared expert, EP8, BF16, two sequences per rank microbatch) on eight B300 GPUs; only the expert-parallel path differs. In the synchronized trace (a), the per-block host wait appears as cudaEventSynchronize in the CUDA API lane, the CPU and GPU ranges of each forward block stay in lock step, and the GPU kernel rows show recurring gaps. In the rowwise trace (b), no host wait interrupts submission: the CPU finishes submitting the microbatch while the GPU is still executing earlier work, and the GPU-side forward blocks run back to back. Each panel is one captured instance of one rank; the two traces are separate runs, so this figure illustrates the submission mechanism rather than a controlled throughput comparison.

Figure 6 A four-GPU DDP example with no model-parallel sharding. With DP = 4, every GPU holds a static replica of the same attention layers and complete routed-expert pool, experts 0–15, while processing different input data. Figure 36 A host loop executes exact-size expert GEMMs. It avoids padded arithmetic, but GPU-produced row counts must become host-visible before the runtime can submit the per-expert operations. The separate streams in this conceptual drawing are not required by the method; the legacy Olmo fallback submits its GEMMs on the current stream.

Figure 65 Under a pipeline schedule, static per-layer replay needs one saved-context slot per in-flight microbatch. (a) Without a pipeline the backward of each microbatch consumes the layer’s saved context before the next forward overwrites it, so one graph per layer serves every microbatch. (b) With three microbatches in flight, a shared slot is overwritten by F1 and F2 before B0 reads it; three slots, each with its own graph and static buffers, are recycled as each microbatch’s backward for the layer completes. Conceptual illustration after the design described for Megatron-Core (Yan et al., 2026); no measured quantities.

Figure 56 Round-ceiling MXFP8 follows the BF16 training trajectory. The top plot reports cross-entropy loss; the bottom reports total gradient norm. The model has 8.36B active and 166.72B total parameters across 31 layers, with top-4 routing over 128 routed experts and one shared expert. Step 7179 corresponds to approximately 67B tokens, so the plotted continuation spans approximately 11B tokens. Figure 38 Grouped GEMM and capacity-padded BMM across routed-row counts. Grouped GEMM is faster throughout the shaded mid-to-large-model range. The experiment isolates one BF16 square expert projection on one B300 with Nlocal = 16 and d = h = 4096. The horizontal axis is total routed rows across the 16 local experts; routed rows count expert rows, not unique input tokens, since each token contributes one row to each of its top-K experts, and balanced routing gives M/16 valid rows per expert. The green band marks the representative 16K–96K rank-local operating range. Its endpoints summarize variation in microbatch and routing choices rather than one fixed microbatch size, sequence length, top-K, or local-expert count; Appendix Table 42 gives concrete configurations. BMM reserves exactly 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Left: useful throughput counts only valid-row FLOPs. Right: values above one indicate that grouped GEMM is faster. Each point is the mean of 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups; all timed operations are submitted behind one device-side gate and released only after the host has queued the complete batch, so small shapes are not dominated by Python launch gaps.

Figure 8 Global-batch and model-size sweeps expose different limits. Preliminary single-node measurements use eight B300 GPUs, an eight-layer BF16 MoE model, top-4 random routing, no PP, and approximately 3.2B active parameters. Left: with EP disabled and 48 routed experts (19B total parameters), DDP useful-model FLOPs utilization (MFU) rises from 25.2% to 41.4% between 128-Ki and 4-Mi-token global batches (1 Ki = 210 and 1 Mi = 220 tokens), while FSDP rises from 26.4% to 29.8%. Right: total parameters grow from 4.6B to 47B; no-EP DDP runs out of memory at 64 and 128 experts, no-EP FSDP continues to fit but loses useful-model MFU, and DDP+EP8 remains nearly flat. Each point is one run, so the curves show preliminary scaling behavior rather than run-to-run variance. They do not decompose peak memory or attribute the trend to a specific communication phase.

Figure 71 Grouped GEMM also wins across the small-model training range. This one-B300 experiment fixes 16 local experts and a square BF16 projection with d = h = 2048. The green band marks the 96K–192K routed-row range represented by the small configurations in Table 42; their exact widths and local expert counts vary, so the band is an operating-range guide rather than an exact reconstruction of every model. BMM reserves 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Each point averages 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups.

Figure 54 Conversion and layout costs in MXFP8 execution. MXFP8 is faster only when its GEMM savings exceed these costs. This is a schematic cost model, not measured timing. The displayed O(MK + KN) conversion term assumes both operands are quantized on the critical path. In Olmo training, the K × N weight conversion is normally paid during cache refresh and reused across microbatches, leaving activation conversion as the principal per-invocation cost. For small GEMMs, that remaining overhead can still turn the expected speedup into a slowdown.

Figure 9 The distributed optimizer and EP reduce different parts of DDP’s persistent parameter-sized training state. Under the illustrated BF16-execution, FP32-gradient, and two-moment FP32 optimizer policy, naive DDP uses 18 bytes per parameter. Sharding the FP32 main weights and optimizer states evenly over D replica ranks reduces this to 6+12/D bytes while compute weights and gradient buffers remain replicated. Sharding routed-expert compute weights and gradients over the expert-parallel model-sharding degree ME (EP-MP; defined in Section 5) further reduces their per-rank memory contribution to 6/ME + 12/D bytes when D = MEDE . Dense and shared parameters follow their separate replica groups. Figure 30 Submission headroom is the queued, not-yet-executed device work. Both curves are computed exactly from the drawn boxes: headroom jumps up by a kernel’s device duration when the CPU completes that kernel’s submission and drains at unit rate while the GPU executes, so the GPU is idle exactly where the curve sits at zero. (a) Cheap submissions of large kernels (k1–k3) build the lead; a host-heavy stretch of small kernels (k4–k7) spends it faster than it is replaced, and after the lead reaches zero the GPU waits for k7’s submission. (b) Within one microbatch, each Python-driven forward submission costs the CPU more time than its kernel costs the GPU, so the lead carried in from the previous backward drains layer by layer and grazes zero just as the last forward submission arrives. The autograd-driven backward inverts the imbalance, and while the GPU executes it, the CPU is already submitting the next microbatch’s forward: the rebuilt surplus is the lead that forward will spend. Each CPU box’s width is the full host cost of its submission, including Python and dispatcher time. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 31 A per-block synchronization point stops the CPU from running ahead. papers.selection_reason: Efficient and scalable MoE training stack for large language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture/training and AI efficiency.
papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.tldr: A redesigned Olmo-core stack makes large-scale MoE training more efficient and scalable by combining specialized parallelism, communication-free routing, MXFP8, and flexible checkpointing.

papers.abstract: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.
authors: Yupei Wang, Neil Mallinar, Mikhail Belkin, Alex Warstadt
bullets: Introduces Concept Energy, measuring alignment between a concept’s representation subspace and directions emphasized by the loss’s average gradient outer product.
Analyzes 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B.
The first Concept Energy peak generally occurs at or before the steepest rise in probe decodability.
Concept Energy may show sustained or repeated peaks, suggesting continual reinforcement or multi-stage concept learning.
Shows that probe performance alone can miss important variation in how the loss supports concept acquisition.

papers.abstract: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.
authors: Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Karthik Rengarajan, Bharath Narasimhan, Chris von Csefalvay
bullets: Targets objects and grasps that an RL policy repeatedly fails to lift, without requiring object models or category labels.
Humans demonstrate only where to grasp in VR; the robot independently selects its approach.

Adding 58 demonstrations raises success on persistent hard cases from 24% to 45%.
The method also recovers performance on similar undemonstrated cases without reducing unseen-object success.

papers.abstract: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.
authors: Dingyang Chen, Jinfeng Xiao, Zhenyu Zhang, William Hu, Ziyu Wang, Yang Liu, Shirley Zhang, Yuan Ling, Xinyang Shen, Qi Zhang, Peijie Qiu
bullets: Addresses the failure of voting-based self-distillation when model attempts disagree on difficult problems.
Generates easier related “stepping-stone” problems and retains those the model solves consistently.
Provides the student with worked solutions to these problems while hiding final answers; the original problem remains the target.
Achieves the highest average accuracy across five math benchmarks for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode.
Without thinking mode, gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, outperforming the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions by 2.5× and 2.7×.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.
authors: Mohamed Salim Aissi, Olivier Sigaud, Laure Soulier, Nicolas Thome
bullets: VLA fine-tuning on robot demonstrations can cause catastrophic forgetting of the original VLM’s language and visual grounding.
The method decomposes the VLA–VLM task vector with SVD and learns per-component mixing coefficients.
Coefficients are optimized to balance action prediction with vision-language capabilities.
Experiments show strong performance on both capabilities and consistent gains over established merging baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our VLM–VLA merging method. (a) The task vector ∆(l) is extracted by subtracting the VLM weights from the VLA weights for each layer l. (b) ∆(l) is decomposed via Singular Value Decomposition, revealing the orthogonal directions of adaptation introduced during VLA fine-tuning. (c) A scalar mixing coefficient α (l) k is assigned to each singular component, controlling how much of each direction is retained in the merged model. The coefficients α are optimised by minimising a composite objective that jointly penalises degradation of language generation quality and action prediction accuracy with respect to both source models.

Figure 1: (Left) Given the same visual scene, a VLM responds accurately to descriptive language prompts but produces no action output. Fine-tuning into a VLA enables action prediction from a task goal, but at the cost of language grounding — the VLA generates incoherent text when prompted with the same descriptive query. Our merged model recovers both capabilities, producing coherent language responses while retaining the ability to predict actions. (Right) The VLM achieves strong language performance but cannot act, while VLAs excel at manipulation but lose language capability. Our merged models are the only ones that achieve the best of both worlds, reaching the upper-right region of the trade-off space.

Figure 6: Per-layer similarity to source models. (Top) Oursπ0Fast . (Bottom) Oursπ0.5 . For each of the 602 weight matrices, we compute the cosine similarity between the VLM and VLA weights (blue), between the merged model and the VLM (orange), and between the merged model and the VLA (green). In both cases, the merged model is consistently closer to the VLA than to the VLM across all layers, while remaining well above the VLM–VLA baseline throughout.

Figure 8: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 5: Effect of SVD rank. (Left) Training losses for varying rank r ∈ {4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, full}: Ltext is largely insensitive to rank, while Lact improves markedly with higher rank, indicating that the VLA adaptation is diffuse across many singular components. (Right) Downstream evaluation confirms this asymmetry: ROUGE-L saturates from r = 16, while LIBERO success rate requires r ≥ 1024 to exceed 90% — language recovery needs far fewer singular directions than action preservation.

Figure 7: Mean α vs. rank index. (Top) Oursπ0.5 . (Bottom) Oursπ0Fast . For each rank index k, we average α (l) k across all 602 layers. Both VLA variants show the same overall pattern: mean α is near 0 for the most dominant directions and rises monotonically toward the tail of the spectrum, confirming that this asymmetry is not specific to a single action decoding strategy.

Figure 3: Qualitative captioning examples. Given the same visual observation, the VLM produces coherent scene descriptions, the VLA (π0.5) generates fragmented or incomplete text due to catastrophic forgetting, and Oursπ0.5 merged model recovers meaningful captions while retaining action capabilities.

Figure 4: Granularity of mixing coefficients. We compare two levels of granularity for α — per-layer and per-component (ours) — and report the evolution of Ltext, Lact, DKL(πα∥πVLM) and DKL(πα∥πVLA) over training. Per-component α converges to substantially lower values on every metric, confirming that fine-grained SVD-based control is essential to simultaneously preserve language and action capabilities.

Table 1: Vision-language, embodied reasoning, and robot manipulation performance of all methods. The pure VLM cannot act, and both VLAs lose language and reasoning ability despite strong action performance. Existing merging baselines largely collapse on manipulation, while our merged models recover strong performance on all three axes simultaneously, without retraining either source model.
Table 4: Task success rate (%) on three RoboCasa kitchen tasks. All fixed-coefficient merging baselines collapse to zero, while our merged models retain meaningful performance on both VLA variants.
Table 3: Hyperparameters used to optimise α for each VLA variant. λ1, λ2 weight Ltext and Lact respectively; λ3, λ4 weight the KL regularisation terms toward the VLM and VLA respectively.

Table 2: Contribution of each loss component. We ablate each term of the training objective and evaluate using ROUGE-L for language quality and Success Rate SR for action predictions. Best results in bold.
