papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhu990424/RAVEN-Bench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/TerraSenseAnalytics/RAVEN-Bench.
authors: Yu Hu, Jianyang Gu, Yue Cao, Hao Liu, Kangnan Wang, Jozsef Hamari, Zheng Liu, Mohsen Zardadi
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for challenging low-altitude aerial video QA, where targets are small, transient, viewpoint-dependent, and modality-specific.
Contains 100 aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 audited four-way multiple-choice questions.
Supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation under hierarchical capabilities and structured question groups.
Diagnoses paired-input gains, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence.
Evaluations show aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported cross-spectral reasoning; code and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.
authors: Yifan Wang, Hao Ouyang, Qiuyu Wang, Yihao Meng, Wen Wang, Zeyue Tian, Yichong Lu, Hanlin Wang, Qingyan Bai, Zichen Liu, Yujun Shen, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between visual and acoustic timing in cinematic multi-shot storytelling, including J/L-cuts and deliberate silences.
Uses independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks while preserving persistent character identities across shots.
Combines joint audio-video diffusion with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention and a directorial lip-sync mechanism.
On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, controls shot transitions, audio timing, and off-screen dialogue for coherent 15–60-second generations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of DÉCOUPAGE. (a) Dual-track temporal cross-attention guides joint audiovideo generation along independent visual and acoustic schedules, allowing dialogue to continue across shot boundaries. (b) The directorial lip-sync mechanism blends speech and no-speech A2V residuals based on speaker visibility to suppress unintended listener articulation.

Figure 2: Joint audio-video data pipeline. Adjacent shots form audiovisual sequences. FasterWhisper establishes a fixed speech timeline and filters out empty or non-English transcripts. Gemini 3.0 Pro then produces visual and audio captions with persistent character identities. Finally, adjacent speech events assigned to the same character are grouped into character-level audio intervals.

papers.tldr: DECOUPAGE enables screenplay-driven, long-form audio-video generation with independent control over visual cuts, dialogue timing, silences, and visibility-aware lip synchronization.

papers.abstract: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.
authors: Valavan Manohararajah, Vithursan Thangarasa
bullets: Targets the large energy gap between unavoidable token-generation arithmetic and general-purpose GPUs, where memory movement and programmability dominate.
Keeps model weights and all users’ KV caches on-chip, with a datapath specialized to one loadable model architecture.
A pre-silicon design reaches 0.52 mJ per token—1.8× its co-designed arithmetic floor—and supports up to twelve users on-chip.
Compared with a measured NVIDIA B300 serving twelve users, it reports 110× higher per-user decoding speed and 690× lower energy.
Polyglot-DC extends the fixed architecture to distilled drafting, multilingual guarding, agent, and financial-reasoning models, with reported latency and benchmark gains.

figures.caption: Figure 6 | What stands between a model and its arithmetic, and where a token’s data lives. On a GPU, themodel reaches the arithmetic through layers of software andprogrammable hardware, and every token brings the weights and the user’s conversation in from external memory: for Qwen31.7B at a 16K-token context, about 2 GB of weights and 1.9 GB for each user (Section 2.5). On the Exstill design, the architecture is fixed in the silicon, the weights and every conversation are kept on the die beside the arithmetic, and only tokens enter and leave, a few bytes each (Section 3.2). Illustrative, not a floorplan.

Figure 4 | The time between tokens for one user on one NVIDIA B300 with vLLM as shipped, by model size: Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B, Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, each in 16-bit precisionwith 1K tokens of prompt and 1K generated, measured on 14 October 2026. The solid line passes through the smallest and largest models and meets the axis at 1.1 ms; a least-squares line through all seven is nearly the same, 0.17 ms per gigabyte and 1.2 ms. The dashed line is where the models would lie if time followed size, and the shaded region between the two is time that making the model smaller does not recover.

Figure 5 | Where the time between tokens goes on one NVIDIA B300 serving Qwen3-1.7B in FP8 at a 16K-token context. The line is themeasured time between a user’s tokens (Table 1), which grows by 0.28 ms for each user added. The two lower bands are calculated, not measured: the bytes each step reads, from the model’s public configuration, at the B300’s published memory bandwidth of 8 TB/s. The upper band is the remainder. Labels on the right give each part at sixteen users.

Figure 7 | A receipt for every word. Each card is one token the co-designed model wrote on the pre-silicon data-center design at the 5 nm class, with the clock cycles and the energy the token took, split into the arithmetic the model requires and everything else, leakage included. The word ‘pilot’ comes early in a short exchange and ‘machine’ 16,000 tokens into a long one, and the difference between them is what the context behind the second costs. The lower bar is a token of Qwen31.7B on one NVIDIA B300 serving twelve users in FP8, measured on our bench, with its arithmetic measured on our flow, a quarter of one percent of the token.

Figure 3 | The batching dial. Energy per token against the time between a user’s tokens on one NVIDIA B300 serving Qwen3-1.7B in FP8 at a 16K-token context, one to sixteen users (measured, Table 1). Both scales are logarithmic, so a line of constant energy-delay is a straight diagonal; the shaded band lies between the least energy-delay of the sweep, at four users, and the greatest, at sixteen. Batching trades the user’s time for the operator’s energy and leaves their product within a factor of 1.6.

Figure 2 | Energy per token on one NVIDIA B300 serving Qwen3-1.7B in FP8 at a 16K-token context, decoding only, as one to sixteen users share it (measured, Table 1), against the floor, the energy of the same token’s arithmetic alone (measured on our gate-level flow, Section 2.1). The shaded region between them is energy spent on something other than the token’s arithmetic. The energy scale is logarithmic.

Figure 1 | A token’s energy against the floor of its model, at a 16K-token context, on a logarithmic scale. Each bar runs from the floor, the energy of the arithmetic the model requires, measured on our gate-level flow (Section 2.1), to the energy the hardware spends, so its length is the hardware’s multiple. The B300 serves Qwen3-1.7B and is measured (Table 1), from sixteen users, its most efficient setting, to one. The Exstill designs are pre-silicon at the 5 nm class, both within 125 W and 575 mm2, and the co-designed model is held to Qwen3-1.7B’s quality (Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

Figure 12 | The four roles of Polyglot-DC. One request of each kind, the chip holding the role’s weights, and the output that comes back: a chain of tokens proposed for a larger target model, a safety verdict, a tool call, a reasoned answer. The requests and the guard’s, agent’s and finance model’s outputs are the models’ own; the draft’s tokens are in the target model’s vocabulary and are drawn as a chain.

Figure 15 | Speculative decoding across two machines, in the draft-then-verify flow of Xia et al. (2024), the steps numbered in the order of one round. Each machine reads the prompt for itself and keeps its own cache, so no cache ever crosses the link between them. The Exstill card drafts six tokens one after another at about 50 µs each, every token conditioned on the ones before it, and the six token identifiers cross to the target, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro or Muse Spark Open, on whatever system serves it. One forward pass of the target writes its own token for every position. The drafts are kept while they match: four do, the fifth differs, so the target’s own token takes its place and the sixth is discarded. What returns to the card is the count of drafts accepted and that one token; both machines append the same five tokens to their caches, and the next round drafts from there. Had all six matched, the target’s seventh token would have come back as a bonus and the round would have yielded seven.

Figure 10 | What the co-designed model adds, like for like: the two Exstill points of Figure 8, on Exstill silicon at a 16K-token context within the same envelope of 125 W and 575 mm2. The first is the design with the lowest energy-delay for Qwen3-1.7B unchanged, which serves one user; the second is the data-center design with its co-designedmodel, which serves twelve. Energy-delay per token is energy per token divided by the chip’s total tokens per second, so its 79x is the product of the 5.8x and the 13.7x above it. The bars of each group share a linear scale from zero. Both designs are pre-silicon at the 5 nm class.

Figure 11 | The data-center design on the plane of Figure 3: energy per token against the time between a user’s tokens, both on logarithmic scales. The B300 points are the measured sweep of Table 1, one to sixteen users, and the shaded band is the band of Figure 3, the range of energy-delay that batching moves the B300 within. The Exstill point is pre-silicon at the 5 nm class, serving twelve users with its model held to Qwen3-1.7B’s quality. The ratios are against the B300 serving the same twelve users.

Figure 13 | One round of speculative decoding as it is usually run, on one GPU, with a chain of 𝐾 = 6 drafted tokens, the steps numbered in order. The draft model writes six tokens one after another, a small pass each. One forward pass of the target then scores all six positions at once, accepts the three that match what it would have written, replaces the first that does not with its own token, and discards the rest. The pass yields four tokens where the target alone would have written one, an accepted length of 4, and the next round drafts from there. On a GPU the draft and the target take turns on the same device, so the draft’s passes are added to every round. The words are illustrative.

Figure 8 | How close each design comes to the limit. Energy per token at a 16K-token context on a logarithmic scale, against the floor ofQwen3-1.7B as released and the floor of the co-designedmodel, both the arithmetic alone measured on our gate-level flow. Each bar runs from a design’s own floor to its token, so its length is the multiple beside it. The B300 is measured (Table 1); the Exstill points are pre-silicon at the 5 nm class. Both Exstill points lie within the same envelope of 125 W and 575 mm2; the model-unchanged point is the design with the lowest energy-delay for Qwen3-1.7B as released that fits it, and it serves one user (Section 3.6).

Figure 16 | Off the shelf or co-designed, benchmark by benchmark, for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3BThinking. Left, accepted length per verification pass at a chain of 𝐾 = 6 (Table 10, measured), on a scale that runs from 1, the target’s own token alone, to 7, all six proposals accepted. Right, endto-end speedup over the target alone at each draft’s best chain length (Table 11, simulated). The benchmarks are grouped as in the tables, and the printed gains are those of the pooled row and of MBPP, the largest.

Figure 14 | What drafting costs against the pass it serves, on one linear time scale. The target’s pass is one decode step of gpt-oss-120b for one user, as measured by InferenceX (SemiAnalysis, 2026), which verifying a short chain barely lengthens (Section 5.1); the dashed line carries it down for comparison. Six tokens drafted on a B300 is our measurement of Qwen2.5-0.5B under vLLM (Section 5.2), a model less than a third the size of Polyglot-DC1-Draft. Six tokens drafted on the Exstill data-center design is pre-silicon, at 50 µs per token.

Table 2 | The forms of generality of Section 2, what each costs a token on a conventional chip, and how the Exstill design answers it. The first three are the layers, the next two data movement and storage, and the last the generality of the model itself.
Table 7 | The four Polyglot-DC roles. Each is a separate set of weights for the same architecture. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

Table 13 | End-to-end speedup over each target alone for one user, simulated on the pre-silicon Exstill data-center design, with Polyglot-DC1-Draft at the chain length that gives the highest speedup and the next round pre-drafted during verification. For gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-Next the GPU’s verification cost is taken from our B300 measurement; for the three targets no single B300 can hold it is modeled from their published expert counts and sizes. A request is a 2,000- token prompt and a 512-token answer. Accepted lengths are measured as in Table 12; the speedups are simulated. Target names are abbreviated as in Table 12.

papers.selection_reason: Chip co-design for near-floor LLM token generation with on-die KV cache; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
papers.tldr: Exstill co-designs a fixed-function 5 nm chip and language models to approach the arithmetic energy floor, achieving dramatically faster and more energy-efficient token generation while supporting multiple specialized workloads.

papers.abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).
authors: Xin Yu, Fei Xia, Jiaqi Pan, Youbao Tang, Chengzhi Liu, Adams Yu, Sicong Jiang, Yanfei Chen, Lingzhou Xue, Ting Yu
bullets: Addresses Continual Recursive Self-Improvement when benchmarks or policy models change.
Stores recurring harness problems, edit rationales, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context.
Extends this history with new optimization attempts rather than relying only on the current harness.
Across four domains, SIM outperformed harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in reported comparisons.
In coding continuations, SIM improved final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation across ten source runs.

papers.selection_reason: Continual self-improvement with memory for optimizer, fits continual learning.
papers.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: Self-Improvement Memory helps harness optimizers continue improving across changing benchmarks and policy models by retaining the rationale and outcomes of past edits.

papers.abstract: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning--based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms---Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit---to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.
authors: Marya Sabouri Dodaran, Ali Taheri Garakani, Mandana Shabanzadeh Nasrollah-Abadi, Yousef Ashrafi, Mohammad Mahdi Azimi, Erfan Nekouei Ghahfarokhi, Amirhossein Kheiri Holighi, Seyyed Sobhan Hosseini Hajibakandeh, Matin Jamshidi, Amirhossein Gholizadeh Behbahani, Mohammad Hossein Moaiyeri
bullets: Integrates a custom chassis, ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX.
Uses deep-learning perception for lane, traffic-sign, and traffic-light detection.
Employs ROS, modular firmware, and UART communication between embedded and high-level systems.
Supports Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit controllers for trajectory control and navigation.
Demonstrates robust and reliable operation in urban-like, structured driving scenarios.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.

bullets: Targets exaggerated lip motion, unstable lip coloration, error accumulation, and unnatural facial or full-body movements.
Uses reinforcement learning, refined classifier-free guidance for DMD few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation.

Arena evaluations report improvements over LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models.

papers.abstract: World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fr\'echet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.
authors: Jerome Francisco, Kyle Deng, George Flint, Kevin Zhu
bullets: Tests dynamical consistency and causal faithfulness in world-model representations.
Introduces Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), using discrete Fréchet distance to compare latent dynamics with ground truth up to affine gauge.
Evaluates decoder-free TD-MPC2 on a pendulum task across horizons k = 5, 10, and 25, including PCA-subspace interventions.
ARC was most consistently sufficient at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction.
Despite this consistency, substantial relative error remained between the simulator and causal latent; decoder-based models remain future scope.

papers.abstract: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.
authors: Felipe A. Louza, Giovanni Manzini, Guilherme P. Telles
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in repeated matrix-vector products by reducing stored and transferred data.
Partitions CSRV matrix data between RePair grammar compression and ans-fold entropy coding.
Further improves compression through row sorting, delta encoding, and contiguous alphabet remapping.
Experiments on word embeddings and transformer hidden states show greater compactness and lower peak multiplication memory than mm-RePair, with competitive multiplication times.
Combining the method with column reordering improves compactness on sparse matrices but substantially increases compression time; thread scaling remains comparable to mm-RePair.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the partitioning scheme. The integer sequence Sint is partitioned into two components: SA is compressed with RePair as in mm-RePair, and SB is encoded with ans-fold, while V is stored unchanged.

Figure 5: Compression pipeline of hybrid mm-RePair. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), and S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2). When criterion (1) holds, the identifiers of Sint are replaced by their ranks and the reverse mapping wcode is produced (step 3). The remapping is computed once on the whole sequence, so a single wcode serves both components, and it does not affect the partition, which depends only on digram frequencies. The sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), and SA is compressed with RePair into RA and CA (step 5). The rows of CA and of SB are sorted and delta encoded (ole) and entropy coded with ans-fold, as is wcode, while RA is stored as a packed array (step 6). The five blocks on the right form the compressed representation (RA, CA, SB, V ), plus wcode.

Figure 3: Compression pipeline of mm-RePair in its re-ans variant. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), the sequence S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2), Sint is compressed with RePair, modified so that no rule contains the delimiter 0, into the rule set R and the final sequence C (step 3), and R is stored as a packed array while C is entropy coded with ans-fold (step 4). The compressed representation is the triple (R, C, V ), with V stored uncompressed.

The CSRV sequence is encoded as Sint (steps 1–2). Criterion (1) holds, since |Sint| = 36, |Σ| = 12 and b = 4 give 36 · 28 > 32 · 12, producing wcode (step 3). The remapped sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), SA is compressed with RePair (step 5), and the rows of SB are sorted and delta encoded (step 6).

papers.abstract: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.
authors: Joshua Foster, Fredrik Odegaard
bullets: Addresses reserve pricing for highly differentiated products whose demand information is embedded in unstructured listing text.
Fine-tunes a pretrained text-embedding model with the structural likelihood of auction bids to learn valuation-relevant representations.
Uses consecutive upper bids to identify the valuation-tail information needed for optimal reserves without modeling the number of bidders.

The calibrated counterfactual suggests a 14.6% increase over the incumbent reserve policy; recommendations do not require a bid history for the item being priced.

papers.abstract: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at https://github.com/guxiang2002/AerialOcc

papers.abstract: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at https://github.com/brian030128/flipquant.

papers.abstract: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.

bullets: Evaluated decoders, losses, geometric projections, and coordinate frames on simulated and human PushT tasks.

Decoder-head choice had no measurable regret effect; the preregistered claim that frame effects exceed decoder differences was not supported.

papers.abstract: Surgical workflow assistance is inherently anticipatory: systems must reason about how procedures evolve, not just recognize the current frame. However, many prior approaches perform prediction in pixel space by synthesizing future frames, which primarily focuses on appearance fidelity rather than the semantic representations required for downstream reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose a feature-space semantic forecasting framework that models temporal dynamics directly within the representations of a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Specifically, we build a hierarchical target representation from multi-layer VFM features, replace future-frame feature tokens with learnable \texttt{[MASK]} tokens, and train a masked transformer to forecast the corresponding future latent features from observed context, thereby formulating procedural evolution as masked future feature prediction. Experiments on public laparoscopic benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based forecasting baselines, while enabling a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream heads.
authors: Songtao Hu, Hang Su
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pixel-space prediction, which emphasizes visual fidelity over task-relevant semantic reasoning.

Uses a masked transformer to forecast future latent features from observed procedural context.
On public laparoscopic benchmarks, improves phase anticipation, tool-presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based baselines.
Provides a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream prediction heads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.
authors: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of screenshot-and-action learning, which discards tutorials’ audio-visual information.
Uses a watch–act–rewatch paradigm to combine external demonstrations with reflection on agent behavior.
Introduces video-SALMONN-VEX, an audio-visual computer-use agent, and AGGO to optimize video-derived guidance for action prediction.
Augments AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with more than 24K real-world tutorial videos.
Reports a 22% relative OSWorld success increase over the Qwen3.5 backbone; generated guidance also improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively.

papers.abstract: Long-video reasoning requires a system to localize sparse evidence over extended temporal sequences, preserve temporal structure, and generate answers despite substantial multimodal distractors. Existing video retrieval-augmented generation methods typically build indexes from uniformly sampled video segments. In long-video settings, this design readily introduces irrelevant context and is unreliable for questions with explicit temporal constraints. We propose VTG-RAG, a framework for long-video question answering that combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with temporal graph retrieval. First, a two-stage sampling strategy selects core segments with high mean query relevance or high intra-segment relevance variance. The framework then integrates subtitles, speech transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations from these segments into a temporally ordered multimodal graph. Finally, it performs temporally filtered, two-pass retrieval and reasoning across frame, text, and graph evidence spaces. A lot of experiments have proven the effectiveness of the VTG-RAG. Specifically, we evaluate the framework on Video-MME and LongVideoBench. On LongVideoBench, the reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results improve from 48.16% to 50.56% and from 52.13% to 53.32%, respectively, with 24 answer-input frames. These correspond to gains of 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points. The ablation experiments of VTG-RAG further support that the contributions of each component are very important.
authors: Yao Lu, Yunhao Wang, Yaxin Gao, Feifei Teng, Chenxiao Liu, Zhe Tang, Jiaheng Wei, Zhaowei Zhu, Shanqing Yu, Qi Xuan
bullets: Addresses irrelevant context and weak handling of temporal constraints in uniformly sampled video retrieval.
Uses query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling based on segment relevance and intra-segment relevance variation.
Builds a temporally ordered graph combining subtitles, transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations.
Performs temporally filtered, two-pass reasoning over frame, text, and graph evidence.
On LongVideoBench, improves reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results by 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points, respectively, using 24 answer-input frames.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overall architecture of VTG-RAG for long-video question answering. The framework comprises three modules. Query-Adaptive Coarse-to-Fine sampling combines variance-aware coarse scoring with candidate refinement to identify a compact set of core segments. Temporal graph construction integrates visual descriptions, transcripts, entities, relations, and temporal links into a multimodal graph. Time-constrained retrieval and reasoning combines query rewriting, reasoning planning, multispace retrieval, and working memory to retrieve supporting evidence and generate the final answer

Fig. 1 Motivation for VTG-RAG. Uniform segmentation treats all temporal intervals equally, introducing irrelevant or temporally invalid evidence into long-video question answering. In contrast, VTG-RAG combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with temporal graph retrieval to construct a compact and ordered evidence context, applying timestamp-based filtering when a query time is available

papers.abstract: Recognizing individual events does not guarantee correct execution of compositional instructions in streaming video. For example, given the request "Notify me when the pot boils after someone turns on the stove and leaves the kitchen", existing models may recognize the individual events yet notify too early or miss the intended moment, failing to track how their temporal conditions are satisfied over time. To evaluate this gap, we introduce CoTriggerBench, which composes annotated video events into temporally constrained instructions and verifies notification timing and silence through executable event plans and source-event replay. To address this challenge, we propose a real-time VLM agent, TEMPI. TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, and uses Scenario Memory to continuously maintain task progress as event evidence arrives, allowing earlier observations to support subsequent decisions beyond the detector's visual window. Even when no notification is required, relevant events continue to update the scenario state. On CoTriggerBench, TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, outperforming the strongest closed-source and fine-tuned open-source VLM baselines by 15.6 (Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash-Realtime) and 18.1 (MOSS-VL-Realtime) percentage points, respectively. To support efficient on-device streaming inference, we further optimize the streaming inference pipeline by overlapping partial visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill with frame arrival. On an 8 GB RTX 5060, our optimized detector implementation achieves a 4.90$\times$ speedup.
authors: Yehua Huang, Penglei Sun, Xiang Li, Jinhao Zhou, Jiawen Wen, Qingqing Xiao, Zihan Yang, Wenqi Wang, Haolan Chen, Yu Xu, Xiaowen Chu
bullets: CoTriggerBench evaluates instruction-level success, notification timing, and required silence using executable event plans and source-event replay.
TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, then tracks progress with persistent Scenario Memory.
Scenario Memory preserves earlier evidence beyond the detector’s visual window and updates state even when no notification should be issued.
TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, exceeding the reported baselines by 15.6 and 18.1 percentage points.
An optimized streaming pipeline overlaps visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill, yielding a reported 4.90× detector speedup on an 8 GB RTX 5060.

External backends can supply the same event interface.

papers.title: Recognizing Events Is Not Enough: Why Streaming VLMs Struggle in Compositional Instruction Triggering

papers.abstract: A satellite forecast of a typhoon should give a low-error picture of the next two days, together with an ensemble whose members are coherent fields and whose spread responds to the storm at hand. A small direct regression network already gives the lowest squared error on held-out storms, so a generative model has to earn its cost through the part of the future that the regression smooths away. We present TyphoonWorld, a discrete-token world model that generates only that part. Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, the latest frames and the best-track state at forecast time, it samples residual fields lead by lead, and members add these residuals to the regression center. We compare it under one protocol with per-pixel Gaussian networks, a diffusion model of the same residuals, residuals from other storms and an unconditional token world model, on 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out storms of Digital Typhoon. TyphoonWorld matches the squared error of the regression, lowers the CRPS of the area colder than 220 K, a direct measure of deep convection, by 14 to 39% against every other ensemble, and ties its spread to forecast error as closely as the Gaussian network, with a correlation of 0.78 across windows. It uses 56% of the parameters of the unconditional world model.
authors: Xiaoyu Chen, Tianyi Li, Xuanyi Zhang
bullets: Targets the fine-scale future details smoothed out by low-error direct regression forecasts.
A discrete-token world model samples residual fields lead by lead, conditioned on the regression forecast, recent imagery, and best-track state.
Evaluated on 276 windows from 46 held-out Digital Typhoon storms against Gaussian, diffusion, cross-storm residual, and unconditional-token ensembles.
Matches regression squared error and reduces CRPS for deep-convection area by 14–39% versus all comparison ensembles.
Its spread–error correlation is 0.78, while using 56% of the unconditional world model’s parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TyphoonWorld. A direct U-Net estimates the mean at every lead (a). A residual world model reads tokens of the center, two recent frames and the initial state, and samples residual codes lead by lead, which a residual decoder turns into fields (b). Members add zero-sum residuals to the center (c). All tiles come from one held-out window at a 24-hour lead; residual tiles show departures warmer than the center in red and colder in blue.

Figure 3: Case study on a held-out storm. Rows are lead times. Spread and error refer to the twelve TyphoonWorld members and share one color scale. The window has the median CRPS difference between TyphoonWorld and the residual ensemble among windows after genesis.

Figure 2: Skill by lead time on all test windows. TyphoonWorld holds the error of the regression center in (a), stays level with the best energy scores in (b), has the lowest CRPS of the area colder than 220 K at nearly every lead in (c), and keeps spread tied to forecast error in (d), where residuals from other storms average 0.21.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision-language reasoning requires a control decision that conventional grounding methods leave implicit: which input is entitled to determine the answer? Auxiliary text may be a defeasible claim about an image, a binding task instruction, or compatible context. Correcting every image-text conflict toward the image therefore repairs false claims but overwrites valid task rules. We formalize this setting as mixed-authority vision-language reasoning and introduce AITHER, an Authority-Informed Text-Image Hierarchy for Evidence Routing. Its final policy, the Semantic-Frame Router, is a training-free black-box control layer that (i) compiles explicit task directives, (ii) recovers standardized spatial frames from metadata-scrubbed pixels, (iii) resolves the semantic polarity of remaining notes, and (iv) routes among frozen observable candidates with fail-closed semantics. This ordered decomposition converts authority arbitration from an unconstrained prompt preference into a reproducible inference program. Across 1,620 MATRIX predictions, AITHER reaches 95.1% accuracy, exceeding the strongest task-and-frame baseline by 9.1 points with a 95% record-cluster interval of 6.8-11.5 points and no harmed records. It further reaches 100.0% on 1,800 controlled FRAME predictions and 93.3% on GQA-MATRIX. The results show that explicit authority routing can simultaneously improve false-claim correction, preserve task-defined answers, and eliminate clean-context overcorrection.
authors: Xinjin Li, Haoyue Zhang, Xinyi Gou, Yuruo Gong, Yuanjian He, Muzi Li, Yujian Long, Yu Ma, Yiliu Xu, Tianxin Zhou
bullets: Addresses mixed-authority conflicts where image evidence, task directives, and textual claims may have different rights to determine the answer.
Uses an ordered Semantic-Frame Router to compile instructions, recover spatial frames, interpret notes, and route among frozen candidate answers.
Applies fail-closed semantics to make authority arbitration reproducible rather than relying on unconstrained prompt preferences.
Reports 95.1% accuracy on 1,620 MATRIX predictions, 100.0% on 1,800 controlled FRAME predictions, and 93.3% on GQA-MATRIX.
Scope: the approach is training-free, black-box, and evaluated specifically on authority-conflict reasoning settings.

papers.title: AITHER: Authority-Informed Evidence Routing for Mixed-Authority Vision-Language Reasoning

papers.abstract: A robot that returns to a space must tell which objects were added, removed or moved since its last visit, while its trajectory, viewpoints and lighting differ between the two visits. We find that multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) fail at this task mainly because they cannot find the place where an object was. A VLM recognises what each frame shows but cannot check whether an object is still at its place in the other capture. It therefore reports objects that only one capture shows and misses most removed and moved objects. We propose STILL, which reformulates change detection as object verification at a registered place. 3D geometry registers the place of each change hypothesis in the other capture, and one VLM answers, from a scene view and a local place view, whether the object is still at that place, trained with supervision of the same form. Under the official SceneDiff protocol, STILL raises the main metric obj/sc AP from 24.0 to 37.8, and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without any kitchen training data. It improves F1 by more than 21 points over a VLM fine-tuned on the same annotations and adds only about 11% to the runtime.
authors: Jinjie Xie, Baihua Li, Qinggang Meng
bullets: Problem: VLMs struggle to determine whether objects were added, removed, or moved when viewpoints and lighting differ between visits.
Method: Use 3D geometry to register each change hypothesis’s location across captures, then have a VLM verify the object using scene and local-place views.
Training uses supervision matching the place-verification task.
Under the official SceneDiff protocol, obj/sc AP improves from 24.0 to 37.8, and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without kitchen training data.
STILL improves F1 by over 21 points versus a similarly fine-tuned VLM, with roughly 11% runtime overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of STILL. (1) A high-recall proposer, SceneDiff by default, gives change hypotheses hi, each with a frame, a box and a geometric cost ci. (2) π3 reconstructs both captures jointly. Each hypothesis is lifted to 3D and projected into the other capture, and a depth occlusion test selects the frame in which its place is best visible, which gives the registered place pi. This step relies only on the static scene, so it stays correct where the object is gone. (3) One fine-tuned VLM answers two questions. The scene view (5+5 frames) asks whether the object is still at its place in the other capture, and the place view (object crop next to place crop) asks whether it is still at this place. The fused score si is thresholded at the operating point chosen on dev. The verifier is trained on per-object questions of the same form, built from real captures with same-capture hard controls and from synthetic two-view pairs.

Figure 5. The registration paradox. Places found (same frame as the π3 place, IoU≥0.5) for unchanged (open) and changed (filled) objects by the box left in place, SIFT matching and successive versions of learned VLM localisation. Appearance-based registration finds unchanged places about twice as often as changed ones, where the answer is decided. Right: system AP change against π3 places.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on three SD-V scenes and one SD-K scene. Each row shows two of the 5+5 frames of an item, and the counts are over all frames. Gray boxes: ground-truth changed objects. Green: correct detections. Red: false alarms. Over the four items, SceneDiff finds 6 of 17 changes with 4 false alarms, the fine-tuned VLM finds 2 with 2 false alarms, and STILL finds 15 with none.

Figure 1. Change is a question of place. (a) Two captures of a room in which four objects were moved, under a new viewpoint and new lighting. A multi-image VLM fine-tuned on the same data reports objects that only one capture shows and finds none of the four. (b) STILL registers each change hypothesis in a joint 3D reconstruction of both captures, which links the object to the place where it was. (c) At that place, one VLM answers whether the object is still there. A moved chair leaves its place empty, while a plant seen from a new side is still in place. (d) obj/sc AP under the official SceneDiff protocol for the VLM baseline of [1] (Qwen2.5-VL + SAM3), reproduced SceneDiff and STILL.

Figure 2. VLMs see what is present and miss what is gone (SD-V test split, all VLMs are Qwen3.5-9B). (a) Recall by change type at precision ≥0.34. The fine-tuned holistic VLM misses removed and moved objects, which the untrained VLM asked at the registered place (dashed) recovers. (b) Share of no-change controls, cut from one video into interleaved frames or into two halves, with a reported change.

Table 4. Generality across proposers, verifiers and benchmarks. The verifier works with change-agnostic proposals and gains from change-aware ones, registered verification helps even an untrained VLM, and a second VLM family behaves alike. papers.selection_reason: Proposes place-registered verification for scene change detection using VLMs and 3D geometry, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Is It Still There? Place-Registered Verification Makes VLMs Reliable Scene-Change Detectors
papers.tldr: STILL makes VLM-based scene-change detection more reliable by verifying whether each object remains at its registered 3D location.

papers.abstract: Occupancy estimation for automated vehicles is a crucial task that builds a 3D map using vehicle sensors. This map allows the vehicle to identify drivable areas and various obstacle classes. The task involves complex subtasks such as depth estimation, object classification, and segmentation to align semantic information with the 3D grid. Moreover, producing these estimations from multiple sensors demands significant computational power and memory, as high-dimensional data fusion requires complex feature extraction and processing. Consequently, most existing methods rely on large and computationally intensive architectures that are not suitable for real-time or real-world applications. We present a real-time, lightweight architecture that leverages camera and radar sensors through a residual multi-stage head. Unlike prior methods that rely on heavy camera-only blocks, our architecture employs camera-radar fusion and lightweight components. Additionally, we introduce a task-specific data augmentation strategy that enhances data diversity and improves generalisation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, attaining 45.7 mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on Occ3D and 41.9 Ray-level Intersection over Union (RayIoU) (41.9) on OpenOcc datasets, running at 17.2 frames per second (FPS) and using only 5.3 GB of memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.
authors: Ruan Bispo, Tim Brophy, Reenu Mohandas, Anthony Scanlan, Ciaran Eising
bullets: Targets the high cost and complexity of multi-sensor 3D occupancy estimation for automated vehicles.
Uses a residual multi-stage head with lightweight camera–radar fusion instead of heavy camera-only blocks.
Introduces task-specific data augmentation to improve data diversity and generalisation.
Reports 45.7 mIoU on Occ3D and 41.9 RayIoU on OpenOcc.
Runs at 17.2 FPS with 5.3 GB memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed dual-supervised Occupancy Head. The BEV features are expanded and enriched via Z-embedding, which are processed by a ResNet3D backbone and an FPN3D neck. An auxiliary head and a final 3D U-Net decoder perform hierarchical decoding with independent supervision. The final occupancy prediction is obtained by residual fusion of both predictions.

Fig. 1. Our proposed architecture using camera and radar data. Firstly, the camera and radar features are extracted using the respective feature extractors. Secondly, we lift and fuse these features into a BEV using a BEV Transformation and fusion module. Finally, the proposed occupancy head (highlighted in blue) processes the BEV features to produce the 3D occupancy estimation.

Fig. 6. Comparison on the Occ3D [45]. LiNO accurately reconstructs occupancy maps even under GT errors (see camera views). Despite slightly lower RayIoU, LiNO produces visually denser and more consistent voxel predictions than the baseline, which may result from GT sparsity and the sensitivity of the RayIoU to mislabels (red boxes).

Fig. 5. Per-class RayIoU results for the Occ3D [45] (Fig. 5a) and OpenOcc [3] (Fig. 5b) datasets. Each class is evaluated under three distance tolerances: RayIoU@1, RayIoU@2, and RayIoU@4 (1 m, 2 m, and 4 m). Black numbers above each marker denote the mean RayIoU per class across the three thresholds. As the distance tolerance increases, the metric becomes more permissive, leading to higher RayIoU values as larger spatial errors are still counted as correct matches.

Fig. 3. Visualisation of top-view feature maps across different stages of the proposed head. The BEV, FPN, and Occ features correspond to the inputs of the three main blocks illustrated in Fig. 2, while the U-Net output represents the final stage before prediction. Fig. 4. Proposed data augmentation based on morphological closing to fill empty regions.

papers.selection_reason: Real-time lightweight camera-radar 3D occupancy estimation is relevant to 3D perception and efficient inference.
papers.title: LiNO: Lightweight Network for Occupancy Estimation
papers.tldr: LiNO is a lightweight camera–radar occupancy-estimation network designed for real-time 3D mapping with lower computational and memory demands.

papers.abstract: A query-based multi-view 3D detector can transfer well to a new calibrated camera network and still produce badly fragmented tracks: on the AI City Challenge 2026 Track 1 validation set, the frozen Sparse4D detector behind the official challenge winner splits each Person identity into a median of eight fragments, and half of the gaps between fragments exceed the horizon of a causal tracker. We show that most of the remaining headroom of such a system lies after detection. Keeping the public detector frozen, we add (i) class-wise source selection between two input scales, which recovers small and distant people from a 0.75x pass while leaving large objects at the scale the detector was trained for; (ii) a geometry-to-appearance bridge that projects every 3D box into all calibrated views, matches it to 2D person detections, and aggregates robust track-level re-identification descriptors; and (iii) constraint-aware consolidation, which combines a causal short-gap stitch with offline centroid-linkage clustering under two hard constraints, temporal exclusion and metric 3D reachability, plus class-aware long-gap stitching for rigid objects. Every association stage changes object identities only. On the challenge evaluation server the system scores 62.3947 3D HOTA (DetA 57.4501, AssA 56.8131, LocA 80.1272), first on the general leaderboard snapshot of 30 October 2026 (second at the time of writing, after a competitor's detector update) and 5.63 points above our reproduction of the official winner; the constrained association stage alone contributes +3.73 HOTA through a +5.49 AssA gain at unchanged DetA. Controlled fixed-box validation studies, a constraint ablation, sensitivity curves, and a catalogue of negative results support the design.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong capabilities as generalist agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive environments. Yet real-time environments such as video games demand both deliberate control for exploration and split-second reactions to fast-moving hazards. Existing agents struggle to handle both: relying solely on direct VLM actions is too slow for sudden events, whereas delegating execution to fixed scripts leaves the agent blind at the moment of action, leading to frequent misfires whenever the scene shifts. Humans overcome this by pairing normal conscious control with conditioned reflexes-while the mind handles deliberate actions and shapes reflex rules, the reflex itself still relies on live vision to make the final instant decision. Emulating this mechanism, we propose ViCoR (Visual Conditioned Reflex). Alongside normal gameplay actions, the main VLM defines and updates lightweight situational guidance for recurring events, while a fast visual reflex branch (invoking the VLM in no-thinking mode) inspects live local views with motion cues to make the final sub-second action decisions. By offloading 67.8% of high-frequency reactions to the reflex branch (680 ms per check), ViCoR reduces average per-action decision latency by 2.6x (from 14.0 s to 5.4 s) and cuts token consumption by 36.9%. Across 17 diverse 2D and 3D games in the GameWorld benchmark, ViCoR achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving task success rate by +11.8% (from 52.9% to 64.7%) and average normalized progress by +13.9% (from 66.5% to 80.4%) over the strongest deliberative VLM and script baselines. In fast-paced real-time games, ViCoR refines its reflexes across episodes to boost progress by 1.67x, and even with a low-effort main planner, surpasses high-effort deliberative baselines by +8.1% at one-third of the token cost.
authors: Qiancheng Zhou, Wenhua Zhang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between slow deliberative VLM actions and brittle fixed scripts in fast-changing environments.

Across 17 GameWorld games, improves task success from 52.9% to 64.7% and normalized progress from 66.5% to 80.4%.

papers.abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.

papers.title: Editable Video Context: Mid-Context KV-Cache Reuse for Context-Managing Video LLMs

papers.abstract: Training generalist GUI agents requires large volumes of interaction trajectories comprising screenshot sequences paired with grounded UI actions, yet collecting such data through human demonstration is expensive and difficult to scale. Although public software tutorial videos contain rich operational demonstrations, their continuous pixel streams lack discrete action boundaries, semantic intents, and precise spatial coordinates, making them difficult to use directly for model training. To address this, we present T2T (Tutorial-to-Trajectory), a fully automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI agent trajectories at scale. T2T spans desktop, web, and mobile platforms to convert unannotated video tutorials into structured, executable interaction trajectories. To guarantee trajectory quality, T2T combines active segment filtering, keyframe identification via localized UI change, shortcut-free observation frame selection, presence-aware grounding, and two-stage action-space normalization. These refined trajectories are then converted into multi-task training views spanning navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B on a subset of the more than one million human-annotation-free training samples generated by this pipeline. Evaluations show that the model achieves consistent gains across multiple benchmarks covering desktop, web, and mobile environments, including OSWorld-G, ScreenSpot-Pro, AndroidControl, and AgentNetBench, indicating improved core capabilities in grounding, step-level instruction execution, and trajectory-level decision-making. Notably, all gains are achieved without any in-distribution training data from target domains. Learning exclusively from trajectories extracted from public videos via the T2T pipeline, the model exhibits cross-application and cross-task generalization capabilities.
authors: Qingsong Xie, Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Jiacheng Tang, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das

Produces multi-task training views for navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding.
Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on over one million generated samples yields gains across multiple desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks.
Reports cross-application and cross-task generalization without in-distribution training data from the target domains.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated its effectiveness for photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, extracting clean, watertight, explicit surface meshes from 3DGS remains a critical challenge. Previous methods approximate geometry via discrete Marching Tetrahedra, where each grid vertex is assigned a single scalar signed distance value. At complex geometric boundaries and thin structures, this suboptimal parameterization forces severe compromises across shared vertices, causing gradient collisions and geometric frustration. Furthermore, existing optimization objectives neglect element shape conditioning, producing degenerate triangles. We introduce TopSDF, a framework that models the signed distance state as a multivariate Gaussian random field. By learning latent topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices, our formulation expands local degrees of freedom for SDF estimates, allowing the candidate mesh vertices to be placed flexibly along the bipolar edges in the tetrahedra as driven by such topological correlation. Concurrently, we directly integrate variational meshing energies into the joint optimization, coupled with an energy-driven Gaussian densification strategy to improve triangle mesh quality. Our experiments across Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++ show that TopSDF achieves state-of-the-art mesh-based novel view rendering (+0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360) and triangle-mesh quality (from 0.37 to 0.49 aspect ratio).
authors: Khoi Do, Yu-kun Lai, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Addresses geometric compromises at complex boundaries and thin structures caused by assigning one SDF value per grid vertex.
Represents SDFs as a multivariate Gaussian random field with learned topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices.
Jointly optimizes variational meshing energies and uses energy-driven Gaussian densification to reduce degenerate triangles.
Evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++; reports +0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and aspect-ratio improvement from 0.37 to 0.49.
Scope: focuses on extracting explicit triangle meshes from 3DGS while retaining high-quality novel-view rendering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Framework overview and training loop (formalized in Algorithm 1). We revisit the suboptimality in triangle mesh extraction from 3DGS caused by the gradient frustration in a single SDF tetrahedral grid. We propose to assign learnable topological features based on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space at each grid vertex, allowing us to expand the SDF degrees of freedom in localized space. During training, we dynamically adjust candidate vertices by obtaining per-edge relation feature 𝑓𝜙 (v)𝑇 𝑓𝜙 (v) , and then calculate the topological SDF ℎ∗ using Eq. (6) at each grid vertex. The training procedure is as follows: Starting with normal-oriented Gaussians, we sample a set of pivots, assign learnable normals u and SDF y, and obtain the topological SDF ℎ∗. We then perform Marching Tetrahedra on the Delaunay grid formed by pivots; the extracted mesh is regularized via normal-depth alignment loss, while the Tetrahedral grid is regularized by meshing energies, which is used for Gaussian densification.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.
authors: Jinquan Zhang, Run Yang, Dongfu Yin, Qiang Lai, Yufeng Yan, Pengshuai Yin, F. Richard Yu
bullets: A single source-task defense update already improves robustness on held-out target tasks.
SN-TRV combines source defense updates by preserving their mean direction while calibrating update magnitude from source norms.
The transferred update modifies only the target visual encoder and requires no target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or inference modules.
Across three VLA backbones and fixed/adaptive attacks, SN-TRV outperforms naive averaging, though attack coverage remains a limitation.
Physical PiPER trials raise average success against printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.
authors: Ranjith Chodavarapu
bullets: CompHall is not purely visual: some part-whole questions can be answered from text alone, and compositional accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe.
The original loss mostly scored image-placeholder tokens and harmed both LLaVA models; a corrected loss improved CV-Bench spatial accuracy across all three model families.
Control experiments indicate that gains require spatial training questions, while some LLaVA-NeXT improvement transfers to relation words seen only as incorrect options.
On CompHall, improvement was significant only for LLaVA-NeXT; gains were small on true/false statements and did not generalize consistently.
Fine-tuning also increased LLaVA-1.5’s tendency to answer “true” and raised its yes-bias on POPE.

papers.abstract: Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths.On OpenFly's Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Xiangyu Dong, Yang Lu, Xiaoguang Ma
bullets: Targets lower storage, computation, latency, and memory costs in instruction-conditioned aerial VLN.
Uses shared-parameter recursive computation with token-type-aware routing: text and action tokens run to full depth, while visual tokens exit adaptively.
Retains early-exited visual representations and compacts active tokens to shorten later processing.
Introduces a learning strategy that distributes visual tokens across multiple exit depths and avoids routing collapse.
On OpenFly Test-Seen and Test-Unseen, reports the best navigation error, success rate, and success weighted by path length among compared methods, while also reducing inference costs.
