papers.abstract: Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.
authors: Wuyang Zhang, Shichao Pei
bullets: Targets “Agentic Sleeper” attacks that appear legitimate initially, accumulate across sessions and agents, then activate across memory, logic, and infrastructure.
Frames defense as partially observed inference, combining an early-warning inference filter with backward trace-back for entry attribution.
Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, sleeper drift is 2.7–8.9× faster than natural baselines and often evades existing defenses.
Warns at least three sessions before visible degradation and achieves 0.69 top-1 trace-back accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 across 24 variants.
Live LangGraph and AutoGen evaluations show posterior-guided defense reduces propagation below the self-sustaining regime; removing only visibly compromised agents does not.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for image super-resolution can recover scene content while producing distracting artifacts or unbalanced colors. We study whether a large language model (LLM) can improve perceptual quality by editing a small subset of existing U-Net weights without a clean reference image. The proposed framework provides the editor with architecture code, selected weights, activation summaries, and sampling previews. It permits up to 1,020 candidate trials while limiting accepted changes to three layers and fewer than 0.1\% of model parameters. The evaluation protocol uses ResShift, SinSR, and SUPIR and compares GPT-6 Astra with a specified Qwen3-VL model under matched access. Feedback metrics guide editing, while separate quality metrics and blinded human comparisons evaluate the final weights. We also report an executed color calibration experiment using real photographs and two small residual networks. This experiment demonstrates correction of a fixed color shift and reveals that an improving feedback score can accompany worse performance on unseen scenes. A separate lightweight super-resolution experiment isolates modest changes in luminance detail while preserving color. The findings motivate restricted updates and independent evaluation of perceptual weight editing.
authors: Chenzhi Zheng, Zhuoran Zheng
bullets: Targets distracting artifacts and color imbalance without requiring clean reference images.
The editor uses architecture code, selected weights, activation summaries, and sampling previews to propose up to 1,020 trials.
Accepted updates affect only three layers and fewer than 0.1% of model parameters.
Evaluation covers ResShift, SinSR, and SUPIR, with separate feedback, quality, and blinded human assessments.
Auxiliary experiments show fixed color-shift correction and modest luminance-detail changes, while exposing limitations in feedback-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) extend large language models to heterogeneous modalities, demonstrating strong potential across a wide range of open-ended tasks. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been widely adopted to improve reasoning performance in LMRMs; however, existing approaches overlook the critical role of visual perception uncertainty in guiding reasoning processes. We term this limitation Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where the misalignment between visual perception uncertainty and reasoning depth leads to over-allocation of deep reasoning under uncertain visual grounding, resulting in unnecessarily long reasoning trajectories and degraded performance. To address this issue, we propose ThinkWise, a perception-aware RLVR framework that jointly models task difficulty and visual perception state to regulate reasoning depth. Specifically, we introduce an instance-adaptive visual perception modeling mechanism that enables context-aware calibration of perception uncertainty, leading to more accurate perception estimation. We further design a structured reward formulation that jointly considers perception, correctness, and task difficulty. In particular, an answer reward provides supervision for correctness, a perception- and difficulty-conditioned length reward adaptively regulates reasoning depth, and a perception reward encourages trajectories with stronger visual grounding. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkWise consistently improves the trade-off between accuracy and reasoning efficiency across both 3B and 7B models. These results highlight the importance of perception-aware reasoning and establish a principled framework for advancing LMRMs.
authors: Wenkang Zhou, Chen Yang, Jiaheng Peng, Xitong Li, Hongzhi Yin, Yunke Zhang, Lu Yu, Peng-Fei Zhang, Xuhui Ren, Shijie Zhang
bullets: Addresses Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where uncertain visual grounding can trigger unnecessarily deep reasoning and hurt performance.
Uses instance-adaptive visual perception modeling to calibrate perception uncertainty in context.
Combines correctness, perception, and difficulty in a structured RLVR reward, including adaptive length regulation and visual-grounding supervision.
Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and 3B/7B models show improved accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.
Scope: focuses on perception-aware control of reasoning depth in large multimodal reasoning models.

papers.abstract: A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight. A law of softmax attention predicts that a growing crowd of bounded scores dilutes the attention on any patch or register whose score stays fixed. The same law gives a remedy that needs no training: multiply every score, the sink's included, by the ratio of the logarithms of the test and training token counts. Given sufficient margins at the training resolution, this keeps the attention on a match when one is present, and on a sink such as a register when none is, though trained models need not meet those margins. We test these predictions in public vision transformers and in controlled models read far above their training token count. Attention spreads as predicted. Registers lose their share, though production models compensate in part, and the rescaling holds the share of DINOv2's registers nearly level. Applied at test time without training, the rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy in nearly every model, with absolute or rotary positions and with registers, and on images with native detail. The calibrated multiplier rises with the logarithmic ratio on average and varies across models. Its rise is steeper than the square-root rule used in image generators; in controlled models the log ratio is also more accurate, while in the public models the two rules' accuracy difference remains unresolved. The rescaling does not restore the attention a model learned, and why it helps, beyond countering the dilution, remains open.
authors: Neil D. B. Bruce
bullets: Problem: Increasing resolution creates more tokens while each attention row still sums to one, reducing attention to fixed-score patches or register tokens.
Method: Apply a training-free multiplier to all attention scores, including sink/register scores, based on the logarithmic ratio of test and training token counts.
Finding: Attention dilution and register-share loss appear as predicted; the rescaling keeps DINOv2 register attention nearly stable.
Result: Test-time rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy across nearly every tested model, including models with absolute or rotary positional encodings and native-detail images.
Scope: The method does not fully restore learned attention, and the mechanism beyond counteracting dilution remains unresolved; its advantage over square-root scaling varies by model.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention dilution in Vision Transformers at high resolution and proposes a training-free rescaling method to recover accuracy.
papers.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
papers.tldr: Higher-resolution inputs dilute vision-transformer attention across more patches, but scaling attention scores by the log ratio of test-to-training token counts can recover some lost accuracy without retraining.

papers.abstract: Depth-aware augmented reality on phones needs dense geometry of the surrounding room. iPhones and iPads without LiDAR expose only sparse feature points and detected planes, and ARKit often takes tens of seconds to report the first wall. We describe a scan-free pipeline for these devices. A point-map network (MoGe-2) predicts metric geometry from each camera frame, the remaining depth shift is recovered from the camera intrinsics, and each frame's scale is aligned to views already in the map. A persistent voxel map with visibility-based expiry answers occlusion and collision queries. Co-located devices share one coordinate frame by solving yaw and floor-plane translation from sightings of each other. We evaluate the deployed system on 309 device-sessions from 19 device models without LiDAR, with 179 device-sessions from LiDAR phones in the same deployment as a reference population. A first dense depth map was recorded within 10 s in 80% of sessions, while ARKit had reported a wall plane by then in 25%. The median session scale was 0.98 against ARKit's wall planes and 1.00 against its camera translation. Scale changed by a median of 9% between nearby frames, against 0.4% with LiDAR, and depth points spread three times as widely around walls. In multi-device sessions, 69% of devices without LiDAR reached a converged shared frame, against 84% of LiDAR phones. The main remaining error is scale that changes from frame to frame.
authors: Mohammad Rashid
bullets: Addresses slow and sparse room geometry reconstruction on non-LiDAR iPhones and iPads.
Uses MoGe-2 to predict metric geometry, recovers depth shift from camera intrinsics, and aligns frame scales to an existing map.
Maintains a persistent voxel map for occlusion and collision queries, while co-locating devices via shared sightings, yaw, and floor-plane translation.
Across 309 non-LiDAR device-sessions, dense depth appeared within 10 seconds in 80% of sessions, versus wall-plane detection by ARKit in 25%.
Shared-frame convergence reached 69% for non-LiDAR devices, compared with 84% for LiDAR phones; scale variability and wall-spread depth errors remained higher.

papers.abstract: As text-to-image diffusion models see widespread deployment, removing unsafe or undesirable concepts without retraining has become a pressing need. Spectral methods are attractive because they are training-free and reversible, yet current variants apply the same output-value (OV) circuit intervention at every denoising step, assuming concept information is temporally uniform. This wastes intervention where concept energy is low while degrading image quality, an inefficiency that compounds across concept types. Through timestep-resolved spectral analysis, concept-specific energy is found to follow a consistent temporal hierarchy: content concepts decay fastest, object concepts are intermediate, and style concepts persist longest. This paper proposes Timestep-Adaptive Spectral Nullification (TASN), which adapts suppression strength and spectral components to the concept energy profile. Cross-attention at each timestep is decomposed into concept-aligned and concept-orthogonal components, and it is proved that when the orthogonal component is approximately stable, the collateral-minimizing schedule sets suppression proportional to concept energy. TASN implements this with a timestep-adaptive spectral subset tracking only active concept directions, strictly generalizing uniform Spectral Nullification (SN). On five red-teaming benchmarks, TASN lowers attack success rate below uniform SN while recovering the majority of its quality loss; ablations confirm gains arise from temporal targeting rather than reduced suppression, generalizing across concept categories and architectures.
authors: Chanaka Thushitha Bandara, Lakmali Nadeesha Kumari, Sen-Ching Samson Cheung
bullets: Uniform spectral interventions waste suppression when concept information is weak, harming image quality.
Timestep-resolved analysis finds content concepts fade fastest, objects are intermediate, and styles persist longest.
TASN tracks active concept directions and adjusts suppression strength and spectral components throughout denoising.
Across five red-teaming benchmarks, it reduces attack success below uniform Spectral Nullification while recovering most of its quality loss.
Ablations attribute the gains to temporal targeting, with generalization across concept categories and architectures.

papers.abstract: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at https://github.com/anwaarua/life4d.
authors: Anwaar Ulhaq
bullets: Addresses the lack of validity estimates for geometry that has not been recently observed.
Models persistence, modification, growth, removal, and replacement using continuous-time, class-specific transition priors.
Combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence; functional anchors support prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies.
Reduces combined error and calibration error in controlled experiments and achieves 9.8% combined error with 0.016 ECE on Urb3DCD-v2, outperforming reported baselines.
Re-survey prioritisation provides only modest gains over random selection with two observations; code and an evaluation protocol are released.

papers.abstract: Computer vision methods for video understanding, such as object detection and tracking, inherit the way videos are captured and displayed: as successive frames processed sequentially. However, a video is an inhomogeneous 2D+time volume of pixels, named voxels, and frames are only one family of cuts through it. In this frame-based representation, static backgrounds introduce computational redundancy, and motion can only be understood across several frames. In this position paper, we study another family of cuts: spacetime images (STIs), obtained by sampling any set of pixels other than frames, for instance a line of pixels followed over time. Such images are familiar in narrow forms, from line-scan inspection and kymographs to spatiotemporal slices for motion analysis, but have received little attention as a general input representation for computer vision and are often limited to (x,t) or (y,t) cuts. We define new cuts leading to STIs in their general form, explain how to read their content, and show that a family of cuts tiles the video so that existing dense annotations transfer at no cost. We also detail how motion appears in an STI, spatially and in the frequency domain, and discuss applications such as walking pedestrians, deposited objects, and dynamic scenes. Two pilot experiments illustrate the representation. The first trains a segmentation network entirely in the spacetime domain, on transferred annotations, and performs background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods, without explicit temporal modeling. The second recovers the pan speed of a camera as a moving cut, identified by a simple criterion on the frequency spectrum of the resulting image, turning a temporal estimation problem into the choice of a cut. Our position is not that STIs should replace frames, but that slicing the video volume is a design variable worth studying in its own right.
authors: Jade Lambert, S\'ebastien Pi\'erard, Anthony Cioppa, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
bullets: Problem: Frame-by-frame processing is redundant for static backgrounds and requires multiple frames to understand motion.
Method: Sample arbitrary sets of pixels over time to create STIs, including cuts beyond conventional (x,t) or (y,t) slices.
Contribution: Define general STI cuts, explain their spatial and frequency-domain content, and show that a family of cuts can tile videos while transferring dense annotations at no cost.
Results: Pilot studies perform background subtraction with a spacetime-trained segmentation network and estimate camera pan speed from STI frequency spectra.
Scope: STIs are proposed as a complementary design choice, not a replacement for conventional frames.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering systems can produce confident responses that are weakly supported by their input images. Contrastive decoding can reduce this dependence on language priors, but a fixed correction may also overturn a correct answer, while selective answering can conceal errors by reducing coverage. We develop evidence-calibrated selective decoding, a framework that separates three decisions: whether local visual evidence supports a candidate, how strongly to correct the original distribution, and whether the resulting answer should be released under a verification budget. Evidence Verification across Crops (EVC) measures visual support and disagreement; Adaptive Contrast Correction (ACC) applies a bounded modification within the backbone's plausible candidate set; Budgeted Selective Answering (BSA) calibrates an answer-admission threshold on held-out images. We provide a complete mathematical specification, bounded-perturbation analysis, and an evaluation protocol that distinguishes forced answering from selective risk. Our quantitative analysis re-examines published baselines on POPE instantiated over MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, together with four MME subtasks. These public measurements reveal variation across backbones, tasks, and correction settings that motivates adaptive control. The proposed framework has not yet undergone model-level evaluation; its effectiveness remains a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established empirical result.
authors: Shiyu Gu, Luis Miguel Santana, Rafael Enrique Cruz
bullets: Targets confident VQA answers that are weakly supported by the image.
Uses Evidence Verification across Crops to measure visual support and disagreement.
Applies bounded, adaptive contrast correction within plausible candidate answers.
Uses a held-out-image verification budget to set answer-admission thresholds.
Analyzes published measurements across POPE/MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA, and MME, while explicitly leaving model-level validation for future work.

papers.abstract: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic Artificial Intelligence remains limited by low interpretability and a lack of finely annotated multimodal data. Most existing datasets provide only coarse disease labels without the granular pathological findings required for differential diagnosis. We present LogicEye$^{Agent}$, a dual-pool inference and verification agent that emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria. Using LogicEye$^{Agent}$, we curate LogicEye$^{Data}$, a large-scale multimodal dataset of 804,461 fundus and OCT images paired with structured pathological reports spanning 38 diseases and 29 subtypes, with quality assured through joint verification by multimodal large language models and clinical experts. Building on this dataset, we further develop LogicEye$^{Bench}$, which incorporates a category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation. Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings effectively curtails diagnostic hallucinations and establishes a solid foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology. The code is available at:https://github.com/Eden35/LogicEye-Agent-Driven-Multimodal-Dataset-for-Interpretable-Ophthalmic-Diagnosis.

Builds a benchmark with category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation.
Grounding disease labels in verified visual findings is intended to reduce diagnostic hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.
authors: Yucheng Zhou, Yunjia Xi, Di Yin, Jianbing Shen
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between conventional generative targets and the representations used for visual understanding.
Predicts a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of continuous visual representations, with pixel rendering added separately afterward.
Controlled comparisons attribute most understanding gains to the representation-prediction objective rather than data differences.
Achieves a 51.71 visual mean across 16 benchmarks versus 46.36 for an understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, with text performance also improving.
Probes and interventions indicate richer object/spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific evidence; results focus on transfer to understanding.

papers.abstract: Video generation models have become increasingly capable of synthesizing realistic human motion, yet they often lose track of the very structure that makes the motion plausible. As generated human motion becomes more complex, videos can suffer from progressive body deformation and appearance drift across frames. Existing motion-controlled methods use explicit representations to stabilize generation, but typically rely on pre-defined motion sequences as references. This raises a fundamental question: if the base generator already produces a usable coarse motion, why replace it with an external one? ReMoVe answers this question by treating the coarse output as a motion hypothesis rather than a final result. ReMoVe recovers and refines the underlying motion, then renders the refined motion as 3D mesh and transfers facial appearance onto it, thereby improving motion accuracy and identity consistency. We further derive depth from the same 3D scene and camera trajectory to impose scene-level spatial consistency beyond the mesh. By jointly conditioning video generation models on mesh and depth, ReMoVe synthesizes high-quality motion videos with controllable camera trajectories and enhanced spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity, while retaining the base generator's motion prior and offering accurate camera control.
authors: Jie Li, Muxin Pu, Hongyi Cai, Mingkang Dong, Jianyuan Guo, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses progressive body deformation, appearance drift, and weak scene-level consistency in complex human video generation.

Renders refined motion as a 3D mesh, transfers facial appearance, and derives depth from the same scene and camera trajectory.
Jointly conditions video generation on mesh and depth to improve structural stability, temporal coherence, appearance consistency, and motion-following fidelity.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.
authors: Lei Zhou, Youwen zhu, Rongke Liu
bullets: Output-level verifiers may infer unlearning from provider-controlled predictions without confirming removal of training-data influence.

Across tested settings, ODR deception was highly effective, while RUV achieved high verification accuracy and rejected most deceptive submissions.

papers.abstract: World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.
authors: Huijun Qiao, Ziqiang Zhang, Jinnong Liao
bullets: Addresses the limited treatment of replaceable exogenous environmental drivers in unified world-model state evolution.

Shows that forecast accuracy and intervention fidelity are distinct evaluation objectives; scope is limited to the tested renewable-energy settings and interventions.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.
authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi

papers.abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.
authors: Yibo Liu
bullets: Studies knowledge transfer in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules.
Compares one agent retaining eight lives of history with eight one-life agents linked by 300-character notes.
After eight generations, the agent chain learns only about as much as the single agent after four lives.
Handoff loss mainly comes from repeated compression; changing agents contributes none, and one-time compression contributes less.
Writing each note from the full prior record recovers 70–82% of the loss, while evidence prompts, note revision, and structured ledgers do not help.

papers.abstract: 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4) is an important approach for efficient large language model (LLM) inference. Recent hierarchical formats such as HiFloat4 (HIF4) improve the representational range of 4-bit quantization through multi-level scaling. However, the same local mantissa representation in HIF4 may not be equally suitable for weights and activations, which exhibit distinct distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose HiMX, a mixed-mantissa framework built upon the hierarchical scaling structure of HIF4. Our key observation is that the two HIF4-compatible mantissa representations, S1P2 and E2M1, exhibit complementary quantization behavior: the denser S1P2 format provides higher resolution for concentrated weight distributions, while the wider-spaced E2M1 format provides complementary quantization characteristics for activation tensors. HiMX enables operand-tailored mantissa representations while converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands with operand-specific widths, allowing different operand formats to share a unified integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Yanzhao Li, Hui Dong, Sifan Cheng, Jingwei Zhang
bullets: W4A4 quantization is efficient but weights and activations have different distribution characteristics.
HiMX combines HIF4-S1P2 for weights, which offers denser resolution, with HIF4-E2M1 for activations, which provides wider spacing.
Operand-specific widths convert the heterogeneous mantissas into integer operands compatible with one unified MAC array.
On Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, the mixed format reduces average end-to-end accuracy loss compared with homogeneous HIF4 configurations.
The approach is evaluated for W4A4 LLM inference; the abstract does not establish broader hardware or model generality.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed HIF4 3-level microscaling[7] quantization architecture for (a) S1P2 and (b) E2M1 variants. A 64-element block shares an E6M2 global scale factor (SF), augmented by eight 1-bit mid-level scale extensions (E18) and sixteen 1-bit fine-level scale extensions (E14) to capture local magnitude variations prior to element quantization.

Figure 5: Comparison of the 64-element dot-product architecture between (a) the original HIF4-S1P2 configuration and (b) the proposed HiMX S1P2×E2M1 configuration. Both datapaths preserve the three-level HIF4 hierarchical scaling and hierarchical accumulation structure, while HiMX introduces a wider integer representation for the E2M1 activation operand and the corresponding multiplication datapath.
Figure 4: GEMM Output MSE under different HIF4 mantissa pairings (W ×A). The heterogeneous S1P2W × E2M1A pair (HiMX) achieves the lowest matrix multiplication error.

papers.abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.
authors: Zichen Zhu, Dingye Liu, Nan Jiang, Danyang Zhang, Hang Zheng, Shijie Zheng, Situo Zhang, Kunyao Lan, Yingzi Ma, Sheng Jiang, Lu Chen, Kai Yu

Across 2,560 test tasks and seven models, the best Pass@1 result is 68.2%; key challenges include answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination.

papers.abstract: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.
authors: Ha Pham Thien Dinh, Ming Liu, Jiesi Guo, Matteo Vergani, Kewen Liao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that pretrained LoRA adapters usually require the same model backbone.
Retrieves a relevant adapter from a modality-aware library and transfers it using a learned linear bridge between feature spaces.
Transfers Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL across ten text tasks and reuses Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs on five multimodal tasks.
Outperforms randomly initialized LoRA on most evaluated tasks.
Scope: evaluated on selected text and multimodal continual-learning tasks and backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: GRAFT pipeline. A task retrieves one LoRA from its modality’s library. The text library separates pretrained Qwen2.5 LoRAs (purple, bridge required) from Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs learned on earlier tasks (green, used directly). The latter group is initially empty and can be used from task 2 onward, if selected; no reported run selected from it. Multimodal LoRAs already work with Qwen2.5-VL. After training, metadata is updated and the LoRA is added to the appropriate library. Solid arrows show task processing; dashed arrows show library additions. The bridge is detailed in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Activation-space bridge. Paired activations from the frozen backbones define T once offline. During target-task adaptation, T stays fixed while the LoRA A and B matrices train. Folding T into the trained A matrix produces a Qwen2.5-VL LoRA with no separate bridge at inference. Only offline calibration needs the source model.

Table 1: Warm-start results across text and multimodal tasks. Text tasks use GRAFT: the top-ranked retrieved Qwen2.5-7B adapter is re-expressed for Qwen2.5-VL-7B through the bridge. Multimodal tasks use the top-ranked retrieved Qwen2.5-VL-7B adapter directly. No adapters are merged. Both arms are trained for eight epochs and scored at their own best-validation epoch on 500 test items per task. Accuracy is reported as a percentage; ∆Acc and ∆F1 are absolute differences in accuracy and macro-F1, in points, and are computed from the unrounded scores. Every numeric result is the mean over four task orders, with text and multimodal means computed separately; per-order values are given in Table 4. Class counts and training-set sizes are given in the appendix.

Table 4: Change in accuracy, in points, under the four task orders listed in Appendix D. Each order includes the same ten text and five multimodal tasks. The Mean column averages A–D and matches ∆Acc in Table 1. Differences between orders include training and checkpoint-selection variation and do not isolate an effect of library contents.

papers.abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.
authors: Ningxin Pan, Guochen Yan, Jialong Wu, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Tool access improves aggregate VQA accuracy but can cause correct no-tool answers to become incorrect.
Tool-enabled reasoning trajectories are substantially shorter, indicating greater reliance on external outputs and less intrinsic visual reasoning.
ReVision adds optional, tool-free intrinsic reconsideration alongside search and code execution.
The model decides when to reconsider, avoiding fixed reflection stages and paired rollouts.
It improves over standard tool use across all six benchmarks by 1.28–7.51% and uses a comparable number of reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.
authors: Pascal Janetzky, Michael Klar, Manuel Wenzel, Tobias Schlagenhauf, Stefan Feuerriegel
bullets: Addresses domain-incremental learning as manufacturing product configurations change over time.
Uses five years of real-world Bosch maintenance data spanning 25 configurations.

papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.
authors: Jian Hu, Yifan Zhang, Hao Zhang, Binfeng Xu, Shaokun Zhang, Hongqing Peng, Zhiding Yu, Pavlo Molchanov, Jan Kautz, Yi Dong
bullets: Addresses group-based RL’s repeated rollouts, synchronization barriers, and instability on stale, variable-length trajectories.
Combines One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization to control policy drift and length-amplified negative updates.
Trained stably for 6,000 updates with policy lag around four on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, and at lag eight on Qwen3-30B-A3B tool-use experiments.
Reached 38.0 mean accuracy across five math benchmarks on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, exceeding the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 points with half the rollouts.
Preserved tool use on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, achieving 98.3% seen and 96.5% unseen ALFWorld success.

Figure 1: FlashREINFORCE at a glance. Each fresh batch supplies its baseline, receives one update, and is discarded. Sequence trust screens complete trajectories; sample mean limits length-amplified negative updates.

papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled more natural interaction with visual and spoken information, creating new opportunities for intelligent audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection systems. AVQA extends traditional visual question answering by requiring models to jointly understand an input image and a spoken question to generate accurate, context-aware responses. Despite recent advances, AVQA and hallucination detection tasks remain challenging for modern standard Arabic (MSA) due to the limited availability of multimodal datasets and the need to reason across Arabic speech and text modalities alongside visual inputs. In this paper, we present an MLLM-based framework for AVQA that takes an image and a spoken question as input and generates answers. In addition, we utilized this framework to detect hallucination in text-image pairs. The proposed approach is evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Task (Ayn-VQA) benchmark, which focuses on culturally grounded Arabic AVQA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively understands spoken queries, grounds their responses in the visual content, and produces accurate answers. The results underscore the capacity and limitations of different LLM architectures for both English and MSA and under various conditions.
authors: Nouar AlDahoul, Yasir Zaki
bullets: Targets AVQA by jointly interpreting an image and a spoken question to generate context-aware answers.
Extends the framework to detect hallucinations in text–image pairs.
Evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Ayn-VQA benchmark for culturally grounded Arabic AVQA.
Reports effective spoken-query understanding and visual grounding, while highlighting capacity and limitations across LLM architectures, languages, and conditions.

papers.abstract: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.
authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva-Vazquez, Alexis Matheu Perez, Florentin Smarandache
bullets: Projects intermediate-layer readouts onto support, refutation, and hedging lexicons to estimate truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) profiles.
Initial signatures—refutation under conflict, indeterminacy under false belief, and verdict collapse—largely disappear under matched prompt controls.
The balance B = log10(F) − log10(T) remains sensitive to evidence polarity across tested layers and also distinguishes false from true first-person beliefs.
The two-battery design shows why template controls are essential and provides a reusable protocol for auditing lens-based measurements of model internals.

figures.caption: Figure 1. papers.abstract: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.
authors: Maryam Shoaeinaeini, Brent Harrison
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed feedback and the limitations of transition-level return decomposition.
A vision-language model identifies the active subgoal at each timestep.
A two-stage LLM prompting process generates a matching latent reward formulation.
Subgoal-conditioned rewards reduce temporal variance and improve sample efficiency.
On MiniGrid and BabyAI tasks, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse rewards, RUDDER, and LaRe.

Skill-LR achieves the lowest loss distribution among all methods, followed by LaRe, while Global Skill LR and RUDDER exhibit substantially larger losses. This suggests that subgoal-conditioned latent reward decomposition yields a more stable and learnable return-modeling objective in more challenging hierarchical tasks.

papers.abstract: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.
authors: Thamme Gowda
bullets: Metric disagreement can obscure quality loss, so MetricX24-XXL is paired with CometKiwi-XXL for evaluation.
Removing unused vision components and non-task vocabulary, plus int8 weights or fp8 activations, causes no resolved loss; int4 leaves a small residual.
QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain rather than reliably recovering quality.
A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at T=0.3 improves both 8-bit and 4-bit systems.
On post-submission WMT26 evaluation, both compressed systems remain competitive with bf16; differences between reranked variants are treated as noise.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can improve long- horizon interactive decision-making through test-time evolu- tion, yet existing methods face three information bottlenecks: memory retrieval overemphasizes textual similarity, candi- date harnesses are often behaviorally redundant, and whole- harness rewriting may overwrite useful evidence or introduce cross-component inconsistency. We introduce Trident, which improves experience utilization, behavioral exploration, and harness evolution through boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion- based updating, respectively. We evaluate Trident on five benchmarks spanning text games, web interaction, and cod- ing tasks. Across qwen-32B, mistral-small-3.2-24B, and gpt- oss-20B, Trident achieves the best average performance and consistently outperforms non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and automated prompt optimization base- lines. Compared with the strongest baseline, APEX, Trident yields relative average gains of 30.7%, 30.8%, and 38.3% on the three backbones, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity stud- ies further show that the three designs provide complementary gains and remain robust to parameter variations.
authors: Kaijie Chen, Liang Yan, Yilan Wei, Jiachen Luo, Zhihao Dou, Jiashu Qu, Haoran Liu, Junli Wang
bullets: Addresses three bottlenecks: similarity-biased memory retrieval, redundant candidate harnesses, and risky whole-harness rewriting.
Uses boundary-aware memory reading, diversity-aware candidate routing, and order-aware insertion-based updates.
Evaluated across five text-game, web-interaction, and coding benchmarks with three LLM backbones.
Achieves the best average performance and outperforms several non-learning, memory-based, reflection-based, and prompt-optimization baselines.
Ablations show the components provide complementary gains and are robust to parameter variations.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is wasteful and lossy when a multimodal model must re-encode the same video for every query: context limits force sparse sampling or truncation, and no reusable representation remains for later questions. We present VidEngram, an agentic video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers later questions from that memory. VidEngram captions video and audio jointly with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with specialized retrieval tools to produce grounded answers. The web interface makes this process inspectable: users can watch memory formation, inspect retrieval traces, verify cited evidence in the video player, and explore entity relationships. On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner outperforms a strong single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (37.0% vs. 32.3%), with gains concentrated on longer videos where single-pass coverage becomes sparse. Because perception is paid once, subsequent queries use low-cost text-only planning.
authors: Zinuo Cheng, Yueqian Lin, Zhongxi Wang, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Addresses repeated video re-encoding, context limits, and information loss in long-video question answering.
Jointly captions video and audio, then organizes memories into segment, episode, and entity layers.
Uses specialized retrieval tools and a text-only planner to generate grounded answers with inspectable evidence traces.
On OmniVideoBench, achieves 37.0% versus 32.3% for a single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline, with larger gains on longer videos.
Subsequent queries avoid repeated perception, reducing them to low-cost text-only planning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: VidEngram architecture. Offline (build once): each video is segmented, captioned by Qwen2.5-Omni into eleven structured fields, and consolidated into a three-layer memory (segment → episode → entity) in the memory manager. Online (answer many): a ReAct agent answers each question from memory through specialized retrieval tools and timestamp citations, so users can inspect how an answer was produced without re-encoding the full video.

Figure 1: Memory formation view. The user watches the source video while the eleven-field structured-caption feed is populated in real time, making the stored memory inspectable before later questions are asked.
Figure 3: ReAct retrieval workflow. The planner selects among six tools; the memory manager returns evidence, and the agent iterates until it has enough support to answer with a timestamp citation.

papers.selection_reason: Targets long-video understanding with persistent hierarchical memory and agentic retrieval.
papers.title: VidEngram: Agentic Long-Term Video Understanding via Structured Hierarchical Memory
papers.tldr: VidEngram enables efficient long-video QA by building a persistent hierarchical memory once and using an agentic text-only planner for later grounded queries.

papers.abstract: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.
authors: Fei Ding, Yongkang Zhang, Yuhao Liao, Zijian Zeng, Huiming Yang
bullets: LLM reasoning errors can propagate because existing verification typically occurs only after generation finishes.
A vocabulary marker triggers analysis, error localization, truncation, and rewriting at any point in the reasoning stream.
The token carries no reasoning content and introduces approximately 13% overhead, analogous to ECC parity bits.
Speculative forking reduces false-positive latency, while segmented rewards make trigger timing learnable end to end.
On HMMT25 with Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next, it improves performance by 10.8 percentage points at 1.13× overhead and is reported as 88× more token-efficient than Best-of-8.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Stage 1: Vocabulary extension adds check token c; SFT finetunes on constructed data (auxiliary trigger loss guarantees pmin > 0), providing the model with triggering and localization capability. Stage 2: RLOO with segmented reward finetunes trigger precision; the optimal threshold q∗ has a closed-form solution. Inference: upon outputting c, speculative forking creates a main branch (speculative continuation) and a check branch (correction analysis); true positives trigger truncation-rewriting, false positives directly use the main branch (zero latency).

Figure 3: Check token workflow (true-positive path). After the error segment s4–s6 (orange), outputting c (red) triggers self-checking. After precise localization, s1–s3 (green) are retained, and truncation-rewriting (blue) proceeds. On false positives, the check branch is discarded, and the main branch’s speculative continuation directly becomes the final sequence (zero latency cost).

Table 1: Functional comparison with existing methods. “Precise Loc.”: text-level localization finer than reasoning-step granularity; “Learned”: trigger mechanism learned through endto-end training; “General Reas.”: systematically evaluated on multi-step reasoning tasks. Detailed analysis of each method is in Appendix C.

Table 3: Main results (Qwen3-32B, Acc avg@32 %, mean ± 95% bootstrap CI over 5 random seeds). †PRM uses base model weights (Appendix J). All three predictions are validated: (H1) HMMT25 +10.8 > AIME25 +9.2 > LiveCodeBench +7.2 pp; (H2) token efficiency 10.8/0.13 ≈ 83 pp/×, Best-of-8 efficiency 6.6/7.0 ≈ 0.94 pp/×, ratio ≈ 88×; (H3) precise truncation advantage: HMMT25 +7.0 > AIME25 +5.7 > LiveCodeBench +4.0 pp, monotonically increasing.

Table 4: Ablation study (Qwen3-32B, AIME25 Acc avg@32). Key findings: (1) optimal r− = −0.2 matches closed-form prediction; (2) Ca=100 is saturated; (3) precise truncation yields +2.8 pp over step-level truncation; (4) auxiliary trigger loss contributes +1.7 pp and reduces FP rate by 5.5 pp; (5) RL contributes an additional +5.0 pp on top of auxiliary loss. Full ablation in Appendix L.
Table 5: Full notation table. r+avg = βr+ + (1− β)r+small.
Table 6: Parameter sensitivity. Larger |r−| raises q∗ (more conservative); higher a lowers q∗ (more aggressive); larger r+avg lowers q∗.
Table 2: Key notation. Full notation table in Appendix B.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a check-token mechanism for built-in self-verification and truncation in LLM reasoning chains, a novel architectural/methodological advance for LLMs.
papers.title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Check Token adds an ECC-like trigger to LLM reasoning that enables real-time self-verification and precise error truncation with low overhead.

papers.abstract: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.
authors: Furkan Horoz
Ozgur Kara
Kaan Oktay
Adil Kaan Akan
Atakan Kara
Anand Bhattad
James Matthew Rehg
bullets: Distillation reduces sampling latency but causes severe variation collapse across random seeds.
Student models retain overall activation variance, but concentrate it in fewer directions than their teachers.

papers.abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized. In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints. We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.

papers.abstract: Parallel mechanisms pose distinctive challenges to large language models (LLMs), as valid reasoning depends jointly on mechanism topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types, and modeling assumptions. Yet existing LLM benchmarks provide little systematic coverage of such domain-specific knowledge, constraint-sensitive analysis, and constructive design. To fill this gap, we introduce MECHBENCH, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs in parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design. MECHBENCH contains standard and challenge tiers spanning six capability categories and nine executable analysis and design tasks. It is constructed through MECHFORGE, a domain-grounded framework that combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review, and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric-based evaluation, and program verification. We further develop MECHGPT as a diagnostic domain-adapted model. Experiments show that strong knowledge performance does not directly translate into executable mechanism reasoning: leading closed-service models achieve over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier, while domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design. These results establish MECHBENCH as a systematic testbed for measuring domain-specific LLM capabilities in mechanism science.

papers.abstract: Plan-conditioned driving world models are used to compare candidate plans, so their forecast should change with the plan as the real scene would, yet widely used control metrics check only whether the camera follows the command. Recorded drives already contain real outcomes of plans that were never driven: retiming a log gives pose-matched images and LiDAR for other speeds, and a stereo rig records a laterally shifted view. Against these references, released world models move their camera but barely move the scene: their scene response, the share of the real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, reaches at most about a third of real video's, and the trajectory score cannot tell an executed speed command from an ignored one. Interventions inside the generator trace the failure to the plan's channel. The forecast geometry follows the context frames; once they carry the planned geometry, plan tokens add little. ReTime-Compose therefore delivers the plan as geometry, without training. It transports the frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras, and the frozen model completes only what no frame covers. Frozen generators then follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and to speed-up plans in two.
authors: Yuqiao Feng
Xiaoyu Ao
bullets: Existing control metrics can miss whether a forecast reflects the planned scene dynamics.

ReTime-Compose transports logged frames to the planned camera geometry and lets a frozen model generate only uncovered content.
It closely matches real responses to a 0.54 m lateral shift across KITTI, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2, and improves speed-plan responses across multiple generators.

papers.abstract: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

Tianren Ma

papers.abstract: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.
authors: Minh-Nam Tran
Abulhair Saparov
bullets: Addresses limitations of prior NIAH benchmarks, including synthetic data, reused datasets, manual annotation, and overly simple reasoning paths.
Automatically builds verifiable long-context QA examples from citation subgraphs of papers published after evaluated models’ knowledge cutoffs.
Evaluates eight LLMs across the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families.
Accuracy declines as reasoning depth and subgraph size increase; at depths 16 and 32, some models perform no better than random guessing on YES/NO questions.
Results suggest models often stop searching citation relationships before reaching answers, despite all required facts being present in context.
